title: The Seated Woman of Çatalhöyük Flanked by Felines
medium: Fired terracotta with traces of burnishing
collection: Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, Ankara, Turkey
description: Woman enthroned between two big cats: their heads form the ends of the arm-rests, and her hands come down to rest on them like a queen patting her hounds. The cats are the seat itself, one at each side, while her heavy breasts, folded belly and thick thighs fill the middle. The group is baked clay, modelled by hand, only about 12 cm high, yet it weighs roughly a kilogram. Treat her head and one of the cat heads with suspicion: they were missing when the figure came out of the ground, and what you see today is modern replacement work.
context: Ian Hodder, later head of the Çatalhöyük excavations and author of 'Çatalhöyük: The Leopard's Tale', describes how James Mellaart read the figure: a powerful naked woman on a seat of felines, the classic tamer of nature, so he named her a Mother Goddess. Mellaart unearthed her in 1961, and she now sits in the Museum of Anatolian Civilizations in Ankara, usually dated to around 6000 BCE. Cultural anthropologists have since backed away from such sweeping labels, and the cats are not settled either: leopard is the usual reading, though some accounts say lionesses.
feline_symbolism: The paired cats are often read as an early 'Mistress of Animals' motif, a woman who commands wild beasts.
title_eng: The Seated Woman of Çatalhöyük Flanked by Felines
location: Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, Ankara, Turkey
image_credit: Dosseman · Own work

title: Dagger with Wild Cats Hunting Ducks (the "Nilotic" Dagger)
title_original: Χάλκινο εγχειρίδιο με διάκοσμο παραποτάμιου τοπίου
title_eng: Bronze Dagger with Riverside Landscape: Wild Cats Hunting Ducks
medium: Bronze, inlaid with gold and silver
description: Along a dark bronze blade only 16 cm long runs a river. Papyrus heads bloom in gold, fish jump clear of the water, and ducks scatter in panic. The spotted wild cat, left of centre, is worked in gold and silver and has already sunk its claws into one of the ducks, body stretched flat in mid-pounce. Further along towards the tip, more birds flee. The colours come from different metals laid into the bronze, yellow gold and pale silver against the dark ground, so the scene glitters like a painting done in jewellery.
context: Same burial group as the famous 'Agamemnon mask': that is how the National Archaeological Museum places this dagger, found in Tomb V of Grave Circle A at Mycenae (inv. P 765). Scenes like this are conventionally called 'Nilotic landscapes' because papyrus, ducks and hunting cats look Egyptian, but the museum makes a cheekier point. They pre-date the corresponding Egyptian pictures, and they copy the wall paintings of Thera and Minoan Crete, where recent plant studies point to streams hidden in reeds, with waterfowl and fish. Wild cats seem to have been brought to Thera and Crete very early, possibly to control rodents. So this riverbank may be much closer to home than the Nile.
feline_symbolism: Put on a weapon, the cat seizing its prey is a hunter's emblem: speed, stealth and a quick kill, the qualities a warrior would want his dagger to carry.
image_credit: Gary Todd · Greek Prehistory Gallery, National Archaeological Museum, Athens, 20 July 2016 (CC0)

title: Enthroned Woman Holding a Leopard Cub, from Hacılar
title_original: Hacılar, Leopar Yavrusu Tutan Tahtta Oturan Kadın Heykelciği
title_eng: Enthroned Woman Holding a Leopard Cub, from Hacılar
collection: Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, Ankara, Turkey
location: Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, Ankara, Turkey
description: Barely the height of a coffee cup, a seated woman clasps a young leopard to her chest. She is all curves: heavy thighs folded under her, a broad back, a small head with a pointed chin and pressed-on pellets of clay for eyes. The cub is a modest lump against her chest, under her folded arms, and in the photo it is easy to miss, so you have to know it is there. Once you do, the pose reads clearly: this is a body built for holding something precious and slightly dangerous.
context: Mellaart's Hacılar dig ran from 1957 to 1960, a few years before his far more famous campaign at Çatalhöyük, and the finds from it are on display at the Museum of Anatolian Civilizations in Ankara. That timing gives a small chain of leopards: this clay woman with her cub came out of the ground first, and in 1961 the Çatalhöyük woman enthroned between two big cats followed, not far away in the same museum. Mellaart argued that the female figurines of this period represented a female deity, the reading later scholars treat with more caution.
feline_symbolism: A woman nursing or holding a wild cat cub suggests a power over nature that is protective rather than violent: the predator raised, not killed.
image_credit: Dosseman (Dick Osseman) · Own work, 3 July 2019

title: Leopard Reliefs from Çatalhöyük
collection: Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, Ankara, Turkey
location: Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, Ankara, Turkey
description: Clay plaster modelled straight onto a house wall, later cut out for display: two pairs of leopards, one pair above the other. In the upper pair the animals face each other with a gap between them, and their bodies are covered in little black rosettes and crosses, a Neolithic painter's shorthand for spots, done with more enthusiasm than zoology. The lower pair is fatter and smoother, two cats nose to nose around a pair of round bosses where the heads once were, tails curling up at either end, with only patches of the painted spots still showing.
context: Level VII, Shrine 44, was the building Mellaart found decorated with leopards in relief, plastered and painted, according to the later Çatalhöyük project's own reports. The Ankara display makes the telling point: so many coats of plaster and paint cover the leopard heads that the reliefs must have stayed on the walls for years, refreshed again and again by the people living with them. Leopard skins turn up across the site too, for example on the figures swarming around the bull in a famous mural, and Ian Hodder, who later directed the excavation, titled his popular account 'Çatalhöyük: The Leopard's Tale'.
feline_symbolism: The leopard seems to have been the dominant wild animal of Çatalhöyük's imagery, tied to hunting, danger and perhaps the authority of whoever wore its skin.
image_credit: Dosseman (Dick Osseman) · Own work, 3 July 2019

title: Cuff Bracelets Decorated with Cats
artist: Unknown royal goldsmith of Thutmose III
date_display: Reign of Thutmose III, c. 1479–1425 BCE
description: On the gold spacer at the centre of this cuff lie three cats in a row, two in gold and one between them in red carnelian, each with ears pricked and forepaws stretched out. The spacer, just over 5 cm across, keeps the rows of tiny barrel beads in order, so the animals do a structural job as well as a decorative one. On either side the beads, each under a centimetre, run in bands of gold, carnelian, lapis lazuli and turquoise-coloured glass. The cuff is about 16.8 cm long and 5 cm wide, and the colours would have shifted as the wrist moved.
context: Local Qurnawi men found the tomb in 1916, and its jewellery was sold on the antiquities market, with most of it eventually bought by the Metropolitan Museum between 1918 and 1988. The credit line of this cuff records the habit: the Fletcher Fund of 1919 to 1922, the Rogers Fund of 1922 and a Lila Acheson Wallace gift of 1988. The tomb belonged to three minor wives of Thutmose III, Menhet, Menwi and Merti, in Wadi D of the Wadi Gabbanat el-Qurud near Luxor. Their names fit Canaanite forms, and Herbert Winlock suggested they were daughters of Syrian rulers. Water seeping in over the millennia had dissolved mummies and wood, but the metal and stone survived.
title_eng: Cuff Bracelets Decorated with Cats (Tomb of the Three Princesses)
medium: Gold, carnelian, lapis lazuli, turquoise glass
dimensions: L. 16.8 cm; W. 5.1 cm; Th. 2.2 cm; cat spacer 5.2 × 2.9 cm
collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, United States
feline_symbolism: The Met links the cats to Bastet, the gentler counterpart of the lioness Sakhmet.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Cat Eating Fish beneath the Lady's Chair (Tomb of Nakht, TT52)
title_original: Scene from the Tomb of Nakht (TT52)
medium: Tempera on mud plaster over limestone bedrock
collection: Tomb of Nakht (TT52), Sheikh Abd el-Qurna, Thebes, Egypt
description: Look under the chair rather than at it. While the banquet goes on above, a striped tabby crouches beneath the lady's seat, back humped into an almost perfect dome, head ducked low over a pale fish on the floor at lower left. Its tail runs flat along the ground line behind it, and a chair leg curls down on the right. It wears no collar and no lead, and nobody in the scene pays it any attention. The painters gave it the same crisp outline and flat colour as the people above, on plaster laid over the rock of the tomb, so the cat reads as part of the household inventory: chair, wife, fish, cat.
context: Nakht was a 'scribe and astronomer of Amun', and his tomb TT52 at Sheikh Abd el-Qurna, on the west bank at Thebes, is dated probably to the reign of Thutmose IV (about 1401 to 1391 BCE). Norman de Garis Davies published it in 1917, in a volume for the Metropolitan Museum's Robb de Peyster Tytus Memorial Series. The banquet scene hides a joke about manners: Immortal Egypt notes that in Egyptian tombs almost nobody is shown actually eating, while animals are shown eating far more often than people, so the fish-munching cat under the chair is doing what the diners cannot.
title_eng: Cat Eating Fish beneath the Lady's Chair (Tomb of Nakht)
dimensions: Detail approx. 45 × 50 cm; wall mural approx. 1.8 × 2.2 m
image_credit: Unknown author Unknown author · Matthias Seidel, Abdel Ghaffar Shedid: Das Grab des Nacht. Kunst und Geschichte eines Beamtengrabes der 18. Dynastie in Theben-West, von Zabern, Mainz 1991 ISBN 3805313322

title: Cat Amulet
description: Carved from lapis lazuli and only 1.3 cm long, roughly the size of a fingernail, this cat sits upright on a small rectangular plinth, head lifted and ears pricked. At this scale the carver could give only the essentials: a rounded haunch, straight forelegs, a blunt muzzle. A tiny hole drilled through a loop behind the head shows it was strung and worn rather than looked at from across a room. Bend close and the deep blue turns out to be shot through with grey-white streaks and glints of golden pyrite, most of them pooled around the base.
context: Mary Anna Palmer Draper's bequest brought this amulet to the Met in 1915, and it is listed in Gallery 117. The record dates it to Dynasty 18 of the New Kingdom, about 1550 to 1300 BCE, which makes it far older than the Late Period bronze cats that fill most cases. In the Met's Egyptian holdings it sits at the small end of a long range of cat objects that runs up to Ptolemaic bronze cats made to hold a mummified animal, such as 56.16.1, which is more than twenty times its length. The museum's catalogue title is about as plain as Egyptology gets: 'Amulet, cat'.
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, United States
image_credit: This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the Metropolitan Museum of Art . See the Image and Data Resources Open Access Policy

title: Royal Limestone Sarcophagus of Prince Thutmose's Cat, Ta-Miu
title_original: Sarcophage de la chatte Ta-Miu du prince Thoutmôsis
description: Seated upright with ears tall and pointed and a neat band at its neck, a cat takes up the middle of this relief, beside an offering table at the left heaped with bread, a jug, plucked geese and a joint of beef, one goose laid flat across the top. This is a small limestone sarcophagus made for a cat, built like a human coffin box with a lid, and the carving is shallow and crisp. A standing figure begins at the right edge of the photograph. Hieroglyphs run along the top edge and over the lid, just as they would on a coffin for a person of rank.
context: Her name was Tamiut, 'Lady Cat', and her owner was Prince Thutmose, whose titles are carved on the sarcophagus: Crown Prince, overseer of the priests of Upper and Lower Egypt, high priest of Ptah at Memphis and sem-priest. The limestone box comes from Mit Rahina, ancient Memphis, and is now in the Egyptian Museum, Cairo (CG 5003). The blog Tales from the Two Lands enjoys the thought that so grand a prince 'still loved his cat enough to ensure it was well fed in the afterlife'. One caution: the same source reports a 2014 paper by Heimo Hohneck that casts doubt on the sarcophagus, so treat it as probably, not certainly, ancient.
feline_symbolism: The cat receives exactly the offering-table cult a dead human would, and the inscription places it under the protection of Isis and Nephthys.
title_eng: Royal Limestone Sarcophagus of Prince Thutmose's Cat, Ta-Miu
submovement: Memphite relief sculpture, reign of Amenhotep III
image_credit: Larazoni · https://www.flickr.com/photos/laraz/2063179834/

title: Nebamun Hunting Fowl in the Marshes (Tomb-Chapel of Nebamun)
artist: Unknown Master of the Nebamun Tomb-Chapel
medium: Plaster fragment with tempera painting and gilded cat eye
dimensions: Overall: 81 × 98 cm; cat detail approx. 28 × 35 cm
description: Left of centre, a tawny, striped cat steals the scene. It scrambles up a papyrus stem, one bird clamped in its jaws and more caught in its paws, while Nebamun strides across his small boat with a throw-stick raised. His wife stands behind him, a cone on her wig, and their young daughter kneels between his feet holding a lotus. Lean close and you will find the cat's eye is gilded with gold leaf, a detail you only catch from a few centimetres away. Around it the marsh is full of lotus flowers, fish and butterflies, painted with quick, loose strokes.
context: Gold leaf on a cat's eye is the only gilding of its kind known on Theban tomb-chapel paintings, the British Museum notes, and its label adds a reason: a cat could also stand for the Sun-god hunting the enemies of light and order. Nebamun was a middle-ranking scribe and grain counter at Thebes around 1350 BCE. His tomb was found around 1820 by Giovanni d'Athanasi, working for the British consul-general Henry Salt, who sold the paintings to the British Museum in 1821 (EA 37977). The tomb itself was then lost, and d'Athanasi died in poverty without revealing where it was, though scientific analysis in 2008 to 2009 points to the area of Dra' Abu el-Naga'. Eleven restored fragments went on show in a new gallery in 2009.
feline_symbolism: Cats were household pets, but here the cat may also stand for the sun god hunting the enemies of light and order; the gilded eye points to that religious reading.
title_eng: Nebamun Hunting Fowl in the Marshes (British Museum EA37977)
image_credit: anonymous · The Open University

title: Wall painting of a cat killing a serpent (facsimile of the Tomb of Sennedjem, TT 1)
title_original: Mural from the Burial Chamber of Sennedjem (TT1)
artist: Charles K. Wilkinson, copying a Deir el-Medina tomb painter
artist_dates: Reigns of Seti I and Ramesses II (c. 1290–1270 BCE)
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, United States
description: A big tabby cat sits back on its haunches beside a leafy tree and cuts off the head of a serpent with a long blade, calm as a cook at a chopping board. One forepaw drives the knife down, and red drops spatter where the severed head lies at lower centre. The serpent is the chaos snake of the Book of the Dead, its body looping in blue with black dots up the right side, and the ground behind everything is a flat yellow. This is a copy, not the wall itself: Charles K. Wilkinson painted it at full size in tempera on paper in 1920 to 1921, copying the burial chamber of Sennedjem in Deir el-Medina.
context: Salam Abu Duhi and three other local men found Sennedjem's undisturbed burial chamber (TT1) in January 1886. It held 165 objects and over 20 burials from his family, and Eduardo Toda y Güell and Jan Herman Insinger cleared it quickly for Gaston Maspero, head of the Antiquities Service. The finds went to the Boulaq Museum in Cairo, and some were then sold to museums and private collections to fund further excavation, the most important to the Met and Berlin. Sennedjem was a 'servant in the Place of Truth', one of the craftsmen who cut the royal tombs. The Met's copy came through the Rogers Fund in 1930 and links the scene to Chapter 17 of the Book of the Dead.
title_eng: Wall painting of a cat killing a serpent (facsimile of the Tomb of Sennedjem, TT 1)
feline_symbolism: The Great Cat killing Apep shows the sun's nightly victory over chaos, and the Met ties the image to Chapter 17 of the Book of the Dead.
image_credit: Charles Wilkinson · This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the Metropolitan Museum of Art . See the Image and Data Resources Open Access Policy

title: Papyrus of Hunefer: The Great Cat of Heliopolis Slaying Apep
title_original: rw nw prt m hrw, Spell 17
medium: Ink and opaque watercolour on papyrus
description: Knife in paw, a spotted cat with tall ears sits at the right of this small vignette and saws into the neck of a serpent, pinning the head down with its forepaws. The snake of darkness loops twice behind it in black-spotted white, and at the left a tree stands in painted green. The image is ink and colour on papyrus, set in a red-bordered frame above a line of hieroglyphs, and tiny compared with the long roll it belongs to. The cat keeps its calm, level gaze on its work, which makes slicing up a snake look like routine administration.
context: Before the scene of the cat cutting off Apep's head, E. A. Wallis Budge noted in Hunefer's papyrus, the deceased kneels in adoration before five ram-headed gods, named as Ra, Shu, Tefnut, Seb and Ba-neb-Tattu. Hunefer was a scribe of divine offerings, overseer of royal cattle and steward of Seti I in the Nineteenth Dynasty, and his Book of the Dead is in the British Museum (EA 9901). It is best known for a different scene, the judgement in which Anubis leads Hunefer in, his heart is weighed while the monster Ammit waits and Thoth records the result. The cat vignette is easy to miss beside that set piece.
title_eng: Papyrus of Hunefer: The Great Cat of Heliopolis Slaying Apep
submovement: Ramesside Illustrated Funerary Papyri (Book of the Dead)
location: British Museum, London (Department of Egypt and Sudan)
feline_symbolism: The cat is the sun god, who in one account defeats the serpent Apophis (Apep) in feline form, a nightly victory of order over chaos.
image_credit: Hunefer · Jon Bodsworth (photographer)

title: Ostracon of a Cat Minding Geese
medium: Ink and pigment on limestone flake (ostracon)
description: Walking upright like a herdsman, a spotted cat holds a long crook out in front of it with both paws, a small net bag of provisions dangling from the end, its pointed ears and sharp muzzle turned to its flock. In front of it, in two rows of three, go six geese or ducks, and above them sits a nest full of eggs. It is drawn and painted on a flake of limestone, the scrap paper of ancient Egypt, in black outline with touches of red on the birds' legs and bills. The joke is the reversal: the predator has become the shepherd, and the birds look entirely unworried.
context: Limestone flakes served as notebooks for private letters, laundry lists, reminders and purchases and copies of literary texts, and some, like this one, as sketch pads where the picture is the point. This flake comes from Deir el-Medina, the village of the royal tomb-builders at Thebes, and is in the Egyptian Museum, Cairo (JE 63801). Scenes of animals behaving like people are well known, but their meaning is uncertain: scholars have read them as parodies of a hierarchical society, as illustrations of lost fables, or as something an artist drew for fun in his spare time. The date is debated too, with the source cited here giving the 18th Dynasty, around 1550 to 1292 BCE.
title_eng: Ostracon of a Cat Minding Geese
feline_symbolism: Several scholars read such scenes as parody of the social hierarchy, an upside-down world where the cat tends what it would normally eat.
image_credit: Egyptian Museum, Cairo, Egypt · Public Domain

title: Ring with Cat and Kittens
title_original: Ring with Cat and Kittens in the Papyrus Marshes
culture: Ancient Egyptian (New Kingdom, Ramesside Period – Third Intermediate Period)
dimensions: Bezel 1.6 × 1.3 × 1.7 cm; inner diam. 1.9 cm; shank (papyrus) L. 6.3 cm
collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, United States
description: On top of this faience ring sits a mother cat, bolt upright, while a cluster of kittens crowds around her feet like an audience waiting for a speech. The whole bezel group is less than 2 cm in any direction. The shank is not a plain hoop: it is modelled as papyrus, some 6 cm of it, bound stalks opening into openwork umbels, so the cat family seems to sit in a marsh thicket that wraps around the finger. Faience is a glazed quartz paste rather than true pottery, and its turquoise glaze let workshops turn out small, bright, cheap things like this in quantity.
context: Patricia A. Cotti and the Friends of Egyptian Art helped the Met buy this ring in 2017 (2017.34), and the museum dates it broadly to about 1300 to 664 BCE, from the Ramesside Period into the Third Intermediate Period. It is shown in Gallery 125. Kittens point to Bastet: as the Cleveland Museum of Art notes of a faience basket amulet, statuettes of the goddess frequently show her carrying basketfuls of kittens. The odd detail is that papyrus shank: at 6.3 cm it is longer than the bezel is wide, so the ring is mostly marsh and only a little bit cat.
feline_symbolism: Cat-and-kitten groups are tied to Bastet, whose statuettes often carry baskets of kittens; a wish for fertility is the usual, if unstated, reading.
submovement: Ramesside to Third Intermediate Period faience rings
location: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (Gallery 125)
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Cat and Mouse (Ostracon of a Cat Serving an Enthroned Mouse Lady)
title_original: Ostracon of a Cat Serving a Mouse Lady (Ramesside Period, c. 1200 BCE)
description: Standing upright on its hind legs like a servant, a tabby cat with pricked ears and a tail hanging straight to the ground holds a half-round feather fan on a pole in one paw and, in the other, a plucked bird. Facing it, a female mouse in a long skirt sits on a folding stool with crossed legs and holds up a dish. The mouse has drooping breasts and a flower on her forehead, details that make her look like a lady of rank at a banquet. The whole thing is drawn in ink on a limestone flake, and the scene fills it neatly from edge to edge.
context: Scholars' best guess is that the cat serving the mouse comes from a fable that was popular in the 19th or 20th Dynasty, or perhaps it is a humorous satire, as the Brooklyn Museum puts it. The draughtsman borrowed the layout of a real banquet scene, where servants fan and feed a seated lady, and then swapped the cast. Brooklyn's description adds a nice detail: the mouse holds a cloth of the kind often held by pharaohs, and the cat holds a similar one. The comedy rests on the reversal, since the cat, the mouse's natural enemy, is waiting on her with a fan and a plucked goose.
title_eng: Ostracon of a Cat Serving an Enthroned Mouse Lady (Brooklyn 37.51E)
culture: Ancient Egyptian (New Kingdom, Ramesside Period, 19th–20th Dynasty)
collection: Brooklyn Museum, New York, United States
feline_symbolism: The reversal of predator and prey is usually read as parody of a hierarchical society, a world turned upside down.
image_credit: Brooklyn Museum, New York, United States · Public Domain

title: Tomb of Inherkha: Great Cat of Heliopolis Slaying Apophis
title_original: Mural from the Tomb of Inherkha (TT359)
medium: Tempera on mud plaster and smoothed limestone wall
dimensions: Detail: 70 × 92 cm; burial chamber frieze approx. 1.9 × 3.4 m
collection: Tomb of Inherkha (TT359), Deir el-Medina, Thebes, Egypt
description: Book of the Dead scenes cover Inherkha's tomb, and in one of them a cat attacks the serpent Apophis: one forepaw pins the snake's head to the ground while the other drives a red-bladed knife into its neck. The cat is the sun god Ra in the form of the Great Cat, oddly long-eared, almost hare-like, tongue out, sitting at the left of a bright yellow field. At the right a persea tree spreads blue-grey branches dotted with red fruit, and the spotted snake winds round its trunk. The confident outline belongs to painters who decorated tombs for a living, in a village where tomb owners and neighbours did exactly that.
context: Inherkhau, called Inherkha here, was 'Foreman of the Lord of the Two Lands in the Place of Truth' under Ramesses III and Ramesses IV in the Twentieth Dynasty. His tomb TT359 at Deir el-Medina is not his only one: he also owned TT299. He was the son of the similarly titled foreman Huy, and his wife was named Wab. The outer chamber has offering scenes with Inherkhau, his wife and their son Kenna, and the decoration includes the Book of Gates, the Book of the Dead and two rows of kings, queens and princes. The cat scene belongs to the painted burial chamber and remains in the tomb.
title_eng: Tomb of Inherkha: Great Cat of Heliopolis Slaying Apophis (TT359)
feline_symbolism: The sun god, in the form of a cat, slays the serpent Apophis, the nightly victory of order over chaos.
image_credit: Ismoon ( talk ) 17:37, 5 May 2020 (UTC) · own work, scan from ISBN 978-2-85-088235-7

title: Amulet of Bastet
collection: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland, United States
description: Daylight shows between the front legs of this 4.4 cm cat, which sits bolt upright on a low base with its neck long, muzzle lifted and ears up. The legs are carved free in openwork, a bold thing to attempt in hematite, an iron ore that polishes to a dark metallic shine. Here the polish is so high that the studio lights slide down the neck and forelegs like water. The base is shaped from hieroglyphs, the tail curls round the left side, and a suspension loop on the back shows the little cat was worn.
context: The amulet dates to Egypt's Third Intermediate Period, about 1069–715 BCE. Cleveland explains that the base combines the hieroglyph for 'ointment jar', which is also used to write the name of Bastet, with the sign for 'protection', so the stand spells out what the cat is for. The provenance is the fun part. The amulet belonged to Howard Carter, the excavator of Tutankhamun's tomb, until his death in 1939, after which it passed to his niece Phyllis Walker. She sold it to an English private collector; it later went through the Sussex Armoury and was bought by the Cleveland Museum of Art in 1973.
feline_symbolism: The cat is Bastet's sacred animal, and the hieroglyphs of the base turn it into a written wish for her protection.
submovement: Third Intermediate Period Hardstone Amuletic Carving
image_credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Amulet of Bastet as a Seated Cat
dimensions: H. 2.93 cm; W. 1.1 cm; D. 2 cm
description: Less than 3 cm high, this seated cat is cast in copper alloy and striped in gold like a tabby: bands ring its neck and forelegs, and rows of short gold dashes run down its chest and flanks. Even the eyes are rimmed in gold, which gives it a wide-awake stare. It wears a collar, and a scarab sits on its forehead, the same two marks of divinity found on much larger Bastet bronzes, here shrunk to the size of a fingertip. There is a loop on the back for a cord. The metal has darkened almost to black, which makes the gold stand out.
context: Sale number 416 of the Hoffmann collection is still attached to this tiny cat, beside the Louvre's E 10661 and a second inventory number, AF 2237. Jean Henri Hoffmann's Egyptian antiquities were auctioned in Paris on 13 to 17 May 1895, and the purchase was approved on 30 May. Dated by style to the Late Period, 664 to 332 BCE, the amulet is displayed in Room 334 of the Sully wing among objects chosen to show Egyptian materials and techniques, which suits it: the point of the piece is how much casting and inlay can be fitted onto something the size of a thumbnail.
feline_symbolism: The collar and frontal scarab mark the cat as Bastet herself rather than an ordinary pet.
title_eng: Amulet of Bastet as a Seated Cat
image_credit: Rama · Own work

title: The Gayer-Anderson Cat
title_original: Bronze Statuette of the Goddess Bastet (EA 64391)
culture: Ancient Egyptian (Late Period, 26th Dynasty to Ptolemaic Period)
submovement: Saite & Late Period Monumental Votive Bronzes
description: A gold ring through the nose and another in the ear: this 42 cm bronze cat wears its jewellery like a temple official. It sits upright on long, straight front legs, chin raised, with a scarab on the head, a winged scarab engraved on the chest and a protective wedjat amulet on a plaque hanging from a finely incised collar. The eyes are empty now and probably once held stone or glass, which gives the face a sleepy, inward look. The patina has gone a mottled sea green.
context: Cracks run almost all the way round this cat's body, and X-rays show that only an internal strengthening system keeps the head on. The repairs were done by Major Robert Grenville Gayer-Anderson, a keen restorer of antiquities, who also chipped away a heavy coating of crystalline verdigris and red patina himself. He gave the statue to the British Museum together with Mary Stout Shaw, and a copy stays in the Gayer-Anderson Museum in Cairo. Cast in the Late Period, around 664 to 332 BCE, and said to come from Saqqara, it is about 85% copper and 13% tin, and the stripes on its tail are metal of a different composition.
feline_symbolism: The cat represents the goddess Bastet, and the wedjat amulet on its chest adds a charm of protection.
image_credit: Peter D. Tillman from USA · Gayer-Anderson Cat, British Museum

title: Seated Cat
collection: Brooklyn Museum, New York, United States
description: Sitting bolt upright on long, straight forelegs, this bronze cat stares straight ahead, its ears two tall, narrow triangles. The pose is the formal, upright one used for images of Bastet. Time has darkened the metal to a deep chocolate brown, and the paws grip a small rough base. A faint line runs across the chest. The museum's label notes that many of the finer bronze cats of this kind carry a scarab on the head and a wadjet-eye on the chest, but in this photograph those marks are hard to make out, so the figure reads as pure silhouette: a long neck, a small head, a calm stare.
context: Pierced ears, probably meant for loops of gold: that is the Brooklyn label's guess for many of the finer bronze cats of this type. The label adds that feline images of Bastet began in Dynasty XXII, around 945 to 718 BCE, and became extremely numerous in the Late Period. This one is dated 664 to 343 BCE and came as a gift of Mrs. Nasli Heeramaneck (78.243). Its picture is a small piece of internet history: a visitor photographed it in February 2009 for 'Wikipedia Loves Art', a project in which museum visitors shared photographs of collection objects under a free licence.
feline_symbolism: As an image of Bastet's animal, the cat stood in for the goddess and carried the donor's request to her.
image_credit: Photographed February 2009 by Wikipedia Loves Art participant " one_click_beyond " Uploaded from the Wikipedia Loves Art photo pool on Flickr. Wikipedia Loves Art at the Brooklyn Museum This photo of item # 78.243 at the Brooklyn Museum was

title: Bronze Statuette of Bastet as a Seated Cat
medium: Solid-cast copper alloy with traces of gilding
description: Perched on top of a tall, narrow pillar capped with a projecting cornice, a small cat sits like a statue set on a miniature shrine. Around its neck hangs a collar with a wedjat eye, and a scarab sits on its forehead. It is solid-cast in copper alloy, only 18.2 cm high including the pillar, and once had gilding: traces of gold survive on the right eye only, so one eye still catches the light and the other has gone dull. The lean neck and long front legs give it the alert outline of Late Period cat bronzes.
context: A stack of numbers records this cat's journey: E 672 today, N 3915 in an older Louvre series, and 'Clot bey C 16 n°23' from the collection of Antoine Barthélémy Clot, known as Clot Bey, the seller. It entered the museum's inventory in 1852 by purchase. The record dates it by style to the Late Period, 664 to 332 BCE, and identifies it, cautiously, as Bastet: the label carries a question mark. It is displayed on the first floor of the Sully wing, Room 643. The Louvre's own name for it is just 'figurine'.
feline_symbolism: The wedjat collar and frontal scarab suggest the cat is Bastet, as the Louvre tentatively proposes.
title_eng: Bronze Statuette of Bastet as a Seated Cat
image_credit: Musée du Louvre, Paris, France · CC BY-SA 3.0

title: Bastet as a Cat Nursing Two Kittens
description: Stretched out on a flat slab, a mother cat lies with two kittens standing pressed against her belly to nurse. The whole group is only 5 cm high and about 10 cm long, cast in copper alloy, and the low, horizontal composition is unusual next to the upright, formal cats that fill most Egyptian bronze cases. The kittens are reduced to small, rounded shapes. Her front legs reach forward, her head lifts and turns straight out at you, ears up, as if keeping an eye on the room while the kittens get on with it.
context: Room 332 of the Louvre's Sully wing has a case about livestock, hunting and fishing, and a goddess lives in it, among the farm animals. The record calls the group Bastet as a cat, lying down and suckling two kittens, dated by style to the Late Period, 664 to 332 BCE. The museum bought it from a Mme Perimony, with the purchase approved on 31 October 1912 (inventory E 11295). It is not alone in its case: the Louvre keeps the cat with the kitten under her chin, and a block of four seated cats, in the same showcase.
feline_symbolism: The nursing mother presents Bastet as a protector of motherhood and young.
title_eng: Bastet as a Cat Nursing Two Kittens
image_credit: Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China · Ancient Egypt Bronze Nursing Cat

title: Bronze Statuette of a Cat Playing with her Kitten (Chatte couchée, jouant avec son petit)
description: Sprawled along a half-round base, a mother cat has her kitten tucked against her chest, and the pair are cast together in copper alloy, about 10 cm across. The Louvre's older French title says she is playing with her young one, and the group has that relaxed quality: hind legs stretched out behind, a row of teats along the belly, head lifted and turned towards us, the kitten pressed under her chin at the right. A hieroglyphic dedication belongs to the piece according to the museum's record, though it does not show in this photograph.
context: Tadimout, a woman titled 'mistress of the house' (the Louvre queries the reading of her name), is named in the dedication together with Bastet, so this was a gift paid for by a private person. The group belonged to Henry Salt, the British consul-general and collector, and entered the Louvre inventory in 1826. It still carries Salt's number 270 and the catalogue number 'Champollion B. 313', tying it to Jean-François Champollion, the decipherer of hieroglyphs, whose descriptive catalogue of the museum's Egyptian monuments lists it. It lives in Room 332, Case 3, with the farm animals.
title_eng: Bronze Statuette of a Cat Playing with her Kitten (Louvre N 3930)
submovement: Late Period votive bronzes (dedications to Bastet)
feline_symbolism: A cat with kitten links Bastet to motherhood, and the dedication shows a woman asking the goddess for her favour.
title_original: Chatte couchée, jouant avec son petit
image_credit: Rama · Own work

title: Carved Statuette of Four Seated Cats (Quatre chats assis)
description: One block of acacia wood carries four seated cats, a little group only 14 cm high and 27 cm long. They were carved in the round and then painted black, and where the paint has flaked a paler layer shows through in patches, so the surface looks dusted with gold. Look at how the repetition works: four sets of ears, four upright chests, four pairs of front legs, with the slight unevenness that tells you a hand, and not a mould, made each one. The second cat from the left is noticeably smaller, and the third pricks its ears highest.
context: Laboratory analysis by the CTFT in 1971 identified the wood as acacia, so nobody has to guess the timber. The Louvre dates the group to the Late Period (664 to 332 BCE) on stylistic grounds. It came from Antoine-Barthélemy Clot, the French doctor known in Egypt as Clot Bey, who ran the Kasr al-Aini medical school for Muhammad Ali; his old collection number (C 9 no. 15) still travels with it, and it entered the Louvre's inventory by purchase in 1852. Its main number is E 615, with N 3910 as a secondary one. In 1994 the cats left Paris for a garden-themed exhibition in Dijon, 'Nil était une fois'.
title_eng: Carved Statuette of Four Seated Cats (Louvre N 3910)
image_credit: Rama · Own work

title: Statuette of cat
dimensions: H. 11 cm; W. 3 cm; L. 6 cm; H. with tang 12 cm
collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, United States
description: A small cast cat in copper alloy, just 11 cm tall, sits bolt upright, its long forelegs pressed together and its ears two firm triangles. A short tang under it once slotted it into a separate base, which pushes the full height to about 12 cm; today the tang disappears into a plain white mount. At this size every feature has to be stated simply: the body is a single smooth volume, a thin incised line marks the collar at the neck, and the face is a small blunt wedge. Green corrosion crusts the base, and the surface has darkened to a deep brown-black.
context: Two tags at the Met read 'Cats' and 'Goddess': the museum files this statuette under both an animal and a deity, which is exactly the ambiguity of these bronzes. It is dated broadly to 664 to 30 BCE, the long stretch from the Late Period into Ptolemaic rule, and came from Egypt. It entered the collection in 1904 as a gift of Darius Ogden Mills, and it is shown in Gallery 130. The measurements in the Met's record are small: 11 cm tall, 3 cm wide and 6 cm long, or 12 cm with the tang, a size that would sit in a cupped hand.
feline_symbolism: Cat bronzes of this period are generally read as offerings to Bastet; the Met tags this one with 'Goddess'.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Square Bowl with Pampas Cats
description: Pampas cats stare out from the walls of this squared-off bowl, each reduced to geometry: a frontal face of blocky eyes and a stepped mouth, a body spotted with round dots, a banded tail curving up beside it like a striped horn. On one side two cats sit shoulder to shoulder. The form is unusual for a vessel, a soft square about 18 cm across and only 9 cm deep, so the cats get four flat-ish walls. The ochre, red, grey-green and cream sit on top of the fired clay as post-fire paint, while the inside stays plain dark brown and the base is solid red.
context: Cleveland bought the bowl in 2021 with the J. H. Wade Fund, after it had passed from Margrith Brenner of Zurich to a New York private collector. Before the sale it was on loan to the Princeton University Art Museum, from 2015 to late 2020. Fun fact: Cleveland is specific about the species. Its label names the animal as the pampas cat, a small, reclusive wild feline that lives on the margins of farmland, and suggests that Paracas potters decorated their ceramics with it because it preyed on the rodents and other pests of farmers, linking it to fertility and prosperity.
feline_symbolism: Cleveland suggests the pampas cat, a hunter of crop pests, was linked with the fertility of nature and, by extension, human prosperity and continuity.
image_credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Double-Spout Bridge Vessel with Incised Feline
culture: Peru, South Coast, Paracas (Cavernas) style (700 BCE–1 CE)
medium: Earthenware with incised decoration and post-fire resin-based paint
description: An abstracted feline wraps around this round vessel, which rises to two spouts joined by an arched bridge. Its face sits front and centre under the bridge, a black mask with heavy-lidded eyes and a red mouth, while its body arches away to the left as a red, spotted hump on stepped legs, and a banded crescent curves beneath like a grin. The smoky black firing now shows only on the spouts, bridge and base; the colours came afterwards, as resin-based paint pressed into the incised fields. It is about 14 cm across and 11 cm high. Look at the foot of one spout: a tiny modelled head peers out.
context: Dated broadly to 700 BCE-1 CE by Cleveland, this vessel was made on Peru's south coast by Paracas potters in the Cavernas style. The museum received it as a gift of John Wise. Cleveland is candid that 'little is known' about what these abstracted felines meant, and the double-spout-and-bridge form, common on fine south-coast ceramics, probably carried meaning that is now lost. Oddity: in 1966 this clay pot appeared in a Cleveland exhibition called 'Treasures of Peruvian Gold', a hint that curators have long hung Paracas pottery beside the metalwork. The museum's identification of the cat is the pampas cat, a small wild hunter of field pests.
title_eng: Double-Spout Bridge Vessel with Incised Feline
image_credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Small Globular Bottle with Feline
culture: Peru, South Coast, Paracas (Cavernas) style (700 BCE–1 CE)
medium: Earthenware with incised decoration and resin-based paint
description: Barely 10 cm high and 7.5 cm across, this little bottle carries an abstracted feline incised into its surface, and it seems to have two faces. One side stares with huge ringed eyes under prong-like ears and pokes out a red tongue; the other is a broader mask with arched, heavy-lidded eyes, a red dot of a nose and a mouth full of blocky teeth. The clay was fired in a smoky kiln that turned it black, still visible on the neck and base, and only then were the incised areas filled with resin-based paint, so the colour sits in the grooves like inlay.
context: Made by Paracas potters on Peru's south coast in the Cavernas style, which Cleveland dates to 700 BCE-1 CE, the bottle was a gift to the museum from John Wise, the same donor behind a larger double-spout vessel with a similar cat (1948.477). Fun fact: like its sibling, it was shown in Cleveland's 1966 exhibition 'Treasures of Peruvian Gold', despite being made of clay. Cleveland's record says little is known about what these abstracted felines meant, and notes that their colour was applied as resin-based paint after firing in a smoky atmosphere. Other Cleveland records identify such felines as pampas cats.
image_credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Cat
culture: Egypt, Late Period, Dynasty 26 or later
dimensions: 9.2 x 2.3 x 5.5 cm; without tang 7.5 cm
collection: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland, United States
description: Long-necked and narrow-chested in the classic votive pose, this seated bronze cat wears jewellery: an embossed pendant at its chest and a gold hoop, almost as big as the ear itself, through one ear. The figure is tiny, 9.2 cm with its tang and 7.5 cm without, so the gold is a bright point against the dark metal. The long forelegs are held straight with daylight between them, and the tang under the base means it was made to stand in a socket or plinth. The earring is what turns a generic cat into somebody's well-dressed one.
context: Blanchard's 'Egyptian Museum' in Cairo was in fact an antiquities shop, run by R. H. Blanchard, and it is where John L. Severance bought this cat. It came to Cleveland with his bequest and was shown in the museum's Exhibition of the John L. Severance Collection in November 1942, the year Silvia Wunderlich wrote about it in the museum's Bulletin. Cleveland places it in Egypt's Late Period, Dynasty 26 or later, with a date range of 664 to 30 BCE, and says such figures were made as votive offerings, deposited with the deceased. Cats were the sacred animal of Bastet, goddess of fire, cats and protector of the home.
feline_symbolism: Cleveland identifies cats as the sacred animal of Bastet, protector of the home, and reads this figure as a votive offering.
image_credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Box for a cat mummy inscribed for Bastet
collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, United States
description: Crouched on the lid of a long, low metal box, a cat braces its front legs, tucks its hindquarters and stretches its neck forward as if it has just spotted something at the far end of the room. The whole thing runs 34.7 cm from end to end but only 8 cm wide and 17.6 cm high including the figure. The box below is the business end: it was made to hold a mummified animal, and the cat on top announces what was inside. Look at the cat's body: its whole coat is combed with fine incised lines, a texture the plain box never gets.
context: Purchased in Egypt from Mohammed Mohassib in 1912, through the Rogers Fund, this box is dated 664 to 30 BCE and is displayed in Gallery 134. Such boxes were deposited in catacombs together with linen-wrapped cat mummies, as at the extensive catacombs at Bubastis and Saqqara, and this one is open at the back, where the mummy was inserted. An inscription on the front gives the name of the donor, so the offering was personal. It has relatives at the Met in the same metal: boxes topped by a falcon, by two ichneumons and by a coiled, rearing snake.
title_eng: Box for a cat mummy inscribed for Bastet
feline_symbolism: The box is inscribed for Bastet, so the cat on the lid signals both the animal inside and the goddess receiving it.
image_credit: This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the Metropolitan Museum of Art . See the Image and Data Resources Open Access Policy

title: Cat Statuette Intended to Contain a Mummified Cat
title_eng: Cat Statuette Intended to Contain a Mummified Cat (Met 56.16.1, Profile View)
dimensions: H. 27.4 x W. 11.9 x D. 23.3 cm; 2.5 kg; H. with tangs 32 cm
collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, United States
description: Hollow on purpose, this seated cat is cast in leaded bronze and stands 27.4 cm high (32 cm with the tangs that fixed it to a base). It was made as a container for a mummified cat, a sculpture and a coffin in one. It sits tall on long, straight forelegs, its tail swept round the base until the tip rests against the front paws. Look at the chest: an incised necklace hangs round the neck with a wedjat-eye pendant, and the pierced right ear once held a gold ring, now lost. It weighs about 2.5 kg, and the tangs underneath show it stood on a separate support.
context: Mummified cats were buried within the precincts of Bastet's temples, and the most important cemeteries lay at Bubastis and Saqqara; this statuette, dated 332 to 30 BCE, was the container for one such mummy. It came from Egypt, was bought through the Harris Brisbane Dick Fund in 1956 and is shown in Gallery 134. Cleveland owns a close cousin (1917.998), a 51 cm hollow bronze cat with an open base, which suggests these cases were a recognised product rather than one-offs. Fun fact: the Met records its weight twice, 2.5 kg for the cat and 3.7 kg with its modern mount.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Cat Coffin
collection: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland, United States
description: Fifty-one centimetres of hollow bronze make up this seated cat, its tail curled around its right side, which Cleveland notes is the usual arrangement, the tip running round the base to meet the front paws. Its forelegs are startlingly long and straight, and the small, wide-eyed face looks straight out. It is open at the bottom because it is a coffin: the body of a sacred cat was meant to go inside. Look at the chest. Faint scratches there trace a necklace that seems to have been incised into the bronze after casting, a small finishing touch that only shows when light rakes across the metal.
context: Although the cat feels like the most Egyptian of animals, Cleveland points out that it became an object of worship only late in Egyptian history. The museum dates this coffin to the Ptolemaic dynasty (305 to 30 BCE) and stresses that it is unusually large. The dealer Dikran G. Kelekian of New York sold it to the museum, and it came in 1917 as a gift of the John Huntington Art and Polytechnic Trust. It has appeared in Cleveland exhibitions from the 1941 Silver Jubilee show to 'A Cleveland Bestiary' (1981). Fun fact: the necklace is so faint that the museum files it under 'did you know'.
feline_symbolism: Cleveland describes it as made to hold the mummified remains of a sacred cat, tied to the late flourishing of cat worship.
location: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland, United States
image_credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Papyrus Column with Two Cats
title_eng: Papyrus Column with Two Cats (Louvre E 11204)
culture: Ancient Egyptian (Late Period to Ptolemaic Period)
collection: Freer Gallery of Art, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, D.C.
location: Freer Gallery of Art, Smithsonian Institution
description: Hardly wider than the capital they sit on, two cats perch side by side on top of a papyrus column in this faience amulet, only 4.4 cm tall and about a centimetre wide, their heads pressed together. The column is the papyrus-stalk form Egyptians used for amulets: a faceted shaft on a small square foot, rising to a flared head incised with pointed leaves. At this scale the modelling is summary, two compact bodies and two pairs of ears, and a dark streak in the bright turquoise glaze runs down between the cats like a shared shadow.
context: Charles Lang Freer signed the deed of gift for his collection in 1906, but the Freer Gallery received it only in 1920, when the building was finally complete. This amulet had joined his collection in 1908, bought in Cairo from the dealer Ali Arabi Jr. The Smithsonian places it in the Ptolemaic dynasty (305 to 30 BCE) and notes that amulets like it were often provided with loops so they could be strung and worn as a necklace. It has been shown in 'Charles Lang Freer and Egypt' (1998 to 2011) and again in 'A Collector's Eye: Freer in Egypt', which opened in 2023.
feline_symbolism: Comparable amulets are described by the British Museum as the cats of Bastet on a papyrus column, so the pair probably invokes the goddess's protection.
image_credit: Freer Gallery of Art, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, D.C. · Public Domain

title: Etruscan Bronze Incense Burner with Clambering Cat (Thymiaterion)
collection: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland, United States
description: Halfway up the shaft of this 61 cm bronze incense burner, a small spotted cat or panther clings on with its forepaws and climbs. Above it a crested bird, perhaps a rooster, perches higher on the shaft, so the hunt is frozen mid-climb. At the base a youthful nude male, perhaps the wine god Dionysos, shoulders the shaft with one hand on his hip, standing on a tripod with cloven-hoofed feet. At the top a flat plate with a shallow dip held the incense; holes in each corner of the square upper plate likely held more animals or ornaments that are now missing.
context: Count de Sarzana once owned this Etruscan thymiaterion, made in the 100s BCE, before it was bought by the Cleveland Museum of Art through the John L. Severance Fund. Cleveland describes the type as at least three parts, tripod stand, shaft and incense bowl, often with a figural support like this one. John Cooney published it in the museum's Bulletin in 1971, and Laura Ambrosini included it in her 2002 study of Etruscan bronze thymiateria. Oddity: in 1962 this pre-Roman burner was shown in a Cleveland exhibition titled 'Art and Humanism in the Renaissance', an unusual career move for an incense stand.
title_eng: Etruscan Bronze Incense Burner with Clambering Cat (Thymiaterion)
location: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland, United States
image_credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Parrots Drinking at a Porphyry Basin, with a Lurking Cat
title_original: Mosaico con gatto e pappagalli alla fontana
medium: Opus vermiculatum stone and glass paste polychrome tesserae
collection: Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Napoli (MANN), Naples, Italy
description: Lower right, beside the red pedestal, a striped and spotted tabby crouches with one forepaw raised and its ears pricked toward the basin above. On the rim, two green parrots with long tails and red collars flank a paler, speckled bird bent down to drink (a dove, by some descriptions). That ambush is the whole joke. A split pomegranate lies on the ground at left. The panel is made in opus vermiculatum, tesserae so small they let the mosaicist shade feathers and fur almost like paint.
context: The mosaic was found in 1855 at Santa Maria Capua Vetere, ancient Capua, where it served as the central emblem of a floor, and it is now in the mosaic section of the Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Napoli (inv. 9992). Sources date it to the early 1st century BCE; one picture library gives 80-60 BCE. Fun fact: it is a remix. Birds drinking at a bowl was a well-known Hellenistic motif, and the Capua designer swapped in parrots and added a lurking cat, turning a peaceful scene into one with suspense. The emblem was cut from its floor, which is why it now hangs on a museum wall.
title_eng: Parrots Drinking at a Porphyry Basin, with a Lurking Cat
submovement: Campanian Late Republican Floor Mosaics (Opus Vermiculatum)
location: Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Napoli (MANN), Naples, Italy
image_credit: Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China · Roman Mosaic: Parrots drinking at the fountain, from Capua Vetere

title: Cat Pouncing on a Partridge (House of the Faun, Pompeii)
title_original: Mosaico con gatto che azzanna una pernice
submovement: Pompeian Hellenistic Mosaic Emblema (House of the Faun)
medium: Opus vermiculatum polychrome limestone, marble, and glass tesserae
collection: Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Napoli (MANN), Naples, Italy
description: In the top register a spotted tabby has its teeth in a bird, a quail in most descriptions, a partridge in others, pinning it with a forepaw while the victim's wings fly up in a brown-and-white fan. The cat stares straight out of the picture, whiskers splayed, as if daring you to object. Below, the mosaic calms down into a still life of things Romans liked on the table: two ducks (one with lotus buds in its beak), four small birds tied by the feet, shellfish (a mussel, a date mussel, a cockle, a murex) and seven little fish. Fine opus vermiculatum shades fur and plumage tessera by tessera.
context: The panel comes from the House of the Faun in Pompeii (VI.12.2), a grand house built in the 2nd century BCE that also gave Naples the Alexander Mosaic. Like most of the house's floors, it was lifted and moved to the Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Napoli, where it is inventory 9993. The date usually given is around 100 BCE. Fun fact: the bird is still contested. Italian sources say quail, English captions often say partridge, so pick your bird and defend it.
title_eng: Cat Pouncing on a Partridge (House of the Faun, Pompeii)
dimensions: Upper register: 45 × 45 cm; full emblema: 85 × 52 cm
location: Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Napoli (MANN), Naples, Italy
image_credit: Carole Raddato from FRANKFURT, Germany · Mosaic depicting a cat with a partridge (above) and ducks, fish & shellfish (below), from the House of the Faun, Pompeii, Naples Archaeological Museum

title: Floor Mosaic Emblema with a Cat Attacking a Bird and Two Ducks
medium: Opus vermiculatum polychrome marble and hardstone tesserae
collection: Museo Nazionale Romano, Palazzo Massimo alle Terme, Rome, Italy
description: Up top, a striped tabby crouches low with its teeth in a bird's neck, the prey's brown wings flung up behind its head, while the cat turns wide eyes straight out at us. Below, two ducks rest together, one holding a lotus flower in its beak. The ducks are not the cat's prey, despite the old title; they are a separate, quieter scene. Both bands are worked in opus vermiculatum, tiny tesserae that let the maker shade the cat's coat. The little square sits in the middle of a pale floor, so it reads like a framed picture laid on the ground.
context: The mosaic paved the dining room (triclinium) of a Roman villa on the Via Ardeatina, in the Cecchignola estate, then well outside the city and now part of Rome. It dates to the first quarter of the 1st century BCE and is in the Museo Nazionale Romano, Palazzo Massimo alle Terme (inv. 124137). The emblem was once shown on its own at the Museo delle Terme and was remounted and moved to Palazzo Massimo in 1995. Fun fact: not everyone is a fan. One guide to the museum's highlights calls it 'actually of mediocre quality', then admits that anyone who owns a cat will recognise the scene instantly.
title_eng: Floor Mosaic Emblema with a Cat Attacking a Bird and Two Ducks
submovement: Roman Late Republican Polychrome Floor Mosaics
image_credit: Marie-Lan Nguyen (2009)

title: Rhyton Terminating in the Forepart of a Wild Cat
title_original: Rhyton terminating in the forepart of a wild cat
collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, United States
description: Out of the lower end of this silver drinking horn bursts a wild cat, mouth wide open in a snarl, ears up, forelegs flung forward with the toes spread, as if it were leaping from the vessel. Mercury gilding picks out its collar and eyes, a band of leaves around the rim, and a panel of vine leaves and grape clusters across its chest, which fits a vessel for wine. The rest is bare silver, so gold and silver alternate across the surface. The whole thing is about 28 cm high and 30 cm deep, and it is made in two parts (a and b).
context: Made in Parthian Iran around the 1st century BCE, this rhyton is a horn-shaped drinking vessel of a kind long made in Iran, finished with an animal forepart. The Met acquired it in 1979. Fun fact: the credit line is a small crowd. The purchase combined the Rogers Fund, gifts from Enid A. Haupt, Mrs. Donald M. Oenslager, Mrs. Muriel Palitz and Geert C. E. Prins, the Pauline V. Fullerton Bequest, and several older bequests (Mary Cushing Fosburgh, Edward C. Moore, Stephen Whitney Phoenix) sold off 'by exchange'. In other words, the Met traded parts of its own past to buy this cat.
title_eng: Rhyton Terminating in the Forepart of a Wild Cat (Met 1979.447a, b)
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Shell with Inlaid Feline
medium: Spondylus shell with shell, stone, and gold inlay
description: A pampas cat in inlaid shell and stone stands stiff-legged across this ornament, its dark purple face turned straight at us with round orange eyes and a turquoise mouth. Its pale body carries bean-shaped and crescent spots, its tail is banded dark and light, and just below its front paws sits a gold gourd or fruit. The background is a Spondylus shell whose outer surface was carved away to expose a layer of bright orange, so the cat sits on a glowing ground. The piece is about 7.5 cm square. The beans are the clever bit: the cat's spots are also crops.
context: Sometime between 100 BCE and 700 CE, Nasca lapidaries on Peru's south coast made this ornament. The piece came to Cleveland as a gift from Helen Humphreys in memory of her parents, Mr. and Mrs. Henry Humphreys. Fun fact: Cleveland notes that in both Paracas and Nasca art the small, non-domesticated pampas cat is strongly associated with beans and other crops, and suggests it may have been thought to guard the fields from rodents and other pests.
feline_symbolism: Cleveland links the pampas cat in Nasca and Paracas art with beans and other crops, possibly as a protector of fields against rodents.
image_credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Veii Floor Mosaic: Cat, Rooster, and Two Ducks (Gatto, gallo, due anatre e mele)
medium: Polychrome marble, limestone, and glass paste tesserae (opus vermiculatum)
collection: Musei Vaticani, Museo Pio Clementino, Sala degli Animali, Vatican City
description: Mid-pounce, a long grey tabby stretches on a diagonal from raised hindquarters down to the forepaw pinning a red-combed rooster, whose dark tail feathers curl up in two hooks behind the cat's head. Its wide violet eyes stare straight at us. Below, two ducks rest on a strip of green ground beside a sprig of apples, and an olive branch floats in between: a farmyard and a fruit bowl in one frame. It is the kind of mixed still life, live animals beside food, that Roman house-owners liked underfoot, worked in small polychrome tesserae so fur and feathers are built from graded stone colours.
context: Labelled Antonine (mid to late 2nd century CE) and as coming from excavations at Veii in 1811-13, this panel is shown in the Sala degli Animali of the Museo Pio-Clementino in the Vatican, inventory 420. The Sala itself is an 18th-century creation: Pope Pius VI set up the two rooms between 1775 and 1799 as a 'stone zoo' of ancient animal sculpture, much of it restored and sometimes reworked. Fun fact: a popular Rome guide claims a near-identical cat-and-chicken mosaic comes from Hadrian's Villa at Tivoli, so the panel's findspot depends on whom you ask; the museum label's Veii provenance is the one to trust.
title_eng: Veii Floor Mosaic: Cat, Rooster, and Two Ducks (Gatto, gallo, due anatre e mele)
location: Musei Vaticani, Museo Pio Clementino, Sala degli Animali, Vatican City
image_credit: Fabrizio Garrisi · Own work

title: Stirrup Spout Bottle with Cat
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: Its legs tucked under a compact, loaf-shaped body, the cat crouches, and from its back rises the hollow arched handle and single spout that make the Moche stirrup-spout bottle instantly recognisable. The head juts forward, rounded ears pricked, heavy-lidded eyes half shut, as if it has noticed something worth getting up for but not quite yet. The bottle is 21.3 cm tall and only 9.5 cm wide, and its slip finish here is a dark, almost black sheen with brown patches where it has worn. The stirrup doubles as a handle, so the bottle could be lifted and poured without touching the sculpted cat.
context: Made in the 4th to 7th century CE, this bottle came from Moche potters on Peru's north coast. Stirrup-spout bottles, with a hollow arched handle ending in one spout, were among the Moche's signature vessel forms, and sculpted animals were a favourite subject. The Met received it in 1965 as a gift of Nathan Cummings. Fun fact: the Met's title and tags say simply 'cat', without guessing at ocelot or another wild species, a caution that is worth copying.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Lindisfarne Gospels: Incipit Page of Luke with a Cat (Cotton MS Nero D IV, fol. 139r)
title_original: Lindisfarne Gospels, Luke incipit page (Cotton MS Nero D IV, f. 139r)
medium: Egg tempera, orpiment, red lead, and organic pigments on vellum
description: At the bottom right corner of the frame on the opening page of Luke's Gospel, a cat's head pokes out: pointed ears, a pale muzzle, a round eye with a dark pupil, while its long, scale-patterned body runs straight up the right-hand border. Everything else on the page is spirals, interlace, red dotting and a giant initial Q, so the cat is a joke hidden in plain sight. Once you see the head you cannot unsee it.
context: The Lindisfarne Gospels were made on Holy Island around 715-720, almost certainly by one hand, Eadfrith, Bishop of Lindisfarne (d. 721), in honour of St Cuthbert. They are now British Library Cotton MS Nero D IV, and the cat is on folio 139r, the incipit of Luke. The vellum came from roughly 150 calf skins, and Eadfrith mixed his palette from a handful of local minerals and plant extracts. Fun fact: about 250 years later a priest called Aldred squeezed an Old English translation between the Latin lines, and in his colophon he credits Eadfrith, the binder Ethelwald and the metalworker Billfrith, so we know who made this cat.
title_eng: Lindisfarne Gospels: Incipit Page of Luke with a Cat (Cotton MS Nero D IV, fol. 139r)
image_credit: Eadfrith · Lindisfarne evangeliarium

title: Book of Kells: Cat Chasing a Rat with the Host (MS 58, fol. 48r)
medium: Iron gall ink and mineral pigments on vellum
description: Between two lines of text sits a plump little cat, striped blue and yellow, head turned to watch a long, pale rat stretched out in full flight to the right, a round piece of what looks like Eucharistic bread clamped in its jaws. Both are outlined in brown and ringed with red dots; a tiny blue-and-yellow rosette waits at the end of the line. It is a small drama painted in the same pigments as the grand initials. The rat's prize is the sort of detail that gets argued about: a joke, a riddle, or a warning about crumbs in the sacristy.
context: The Book of Kells, a Gospel book now Trinity College Dublin MS 58, was made around 800, probably in a Columban monastery (Iona, Kells, or both; the question is still debated). Its earliest firm mention is in the Annals of Ulster for 1007, when it was stolen from the sacristy at Kells for the sake of its jewelled shrine and later recovered. Trinity's own teaching material illustrates fol. 48r as 'the cat catching the rat', and notes that the cats in the book prowl, hunt and sit among the lines without obvious religious symbolism. Fun fact: the cats are numerous enough that a Trinity MPhil thesis was written on them alone (Henry Byrne, 'Cats in the Book of Kells', 2011).
title_eng: Book of Kells: Cat Chasing a Rat with the Host (MS 58, fol. 48r)
image_credit: Unknown author Unknown author · Book of Kells folio 48 recto

title: Book of Kells: Cats and Mice Contending for the Eucharistic Host (MS 58, fol. 34r Chi-Rho Detail)
title_original: Book of Kells, Chi-Rho page (MS 58, fol. 34r)
culture: Hiberno-Saxon / Celtic Christian (Iona, Scotland or Kells, Ireland)
medium: Tempera, orpiment, kermes, and indigo pigments on vellum parchment
description: Near the foot of the giant Greek letters of the Chi-Rho page, the most crowded page in the Book of Kells, two cats sit on a dark red ground, and between them two mice tug at a round Eucharistic wafer. More mice perch on the cats' backs, so the much-repeated reading of cats carrying mice is right there to see. Both cats look oddly unbothered, ears up, watching the theft happen under their whiskers. You have to get close: the animals are a few centimetres tall on a page that is otherwise spirals, knotwork and gold-coloured pigment. They are the domestic punchline at the bottom of the sacred monogram.
context: Folio 34r opens Matthew 1:18, the 'second beginning' of Matthew where Christ's life story starts, and the Chi-Rho monogram swells to fill the whole page. Wikipedia, following the specialist literature, calls it the largest and most lavish surviving Chi-Rho in any Insular Gospel book. The manuscript, made around 800 in a Columban monastery and now Trinity College Dublin MS 58, was stolen from Kells in 1007 and recovered. Fun fact: scholars attribute the Chi-Rho to the so-called 'Goldsmith', an artist who used colour to imitate metal, so the cats live inside an imitation of jewellery.
title_eng: Book of Kells: Cats and Mice Contending for the Eucharistic Host (MS 58, fol. 34r Chi-Rho Detail)
image_credit: Unknown author Unknown author · Book of Kells folio 34 recto

title: Monkey and Cats (猴貓圖)
description: Patched in dark grey on white, the cat on the left has got away: it scampers off with its tail up and twists its head back toward the thief. On the right a tethered monkey sits hunched in a ball of soft brown fur, clutching a second kitten to its chest and gazing upward, looking very pleased with itself. The captive kitten peers out from under the monkey's chin, calm but wary. There is no landscape, just the stake and its looped rope against bare silk, so all the drama is in the bodies. The fur is built from fine hair strokes under ink washes.
context: A garden and pond built at home just to watch animals up close: that, the National Palace Museum says, was how Yi Yuanji (c. 1000-c. 1064) of Changsha worked, after he began as a bird-and-flower painter and then spent years in the mountains of Hunan and Hubei watching monkeys. The handscroll (31.9 x 57.2 cm, ink and colour on silk) is in the National Palace Museum, Taipei. It carries a brief title by Emperor Huizong and, on the paper behind, colophons by Zhao Mengfu, Zhang Xi and Bi Long (dated 1790). Fun fact: Zhao Mengfu's colophon reads the scene exactly as a cat owner would, one kitten held, the other frightened, and orders the owner to treasure it.
submovement: Northern Song bird-and-flower and animal painting
medium: Handscroll; ink and color on silk
image_credit: Yi Yuanji · "Grand View: Painting and Calligraphy from the Northern Sung Dynasty", Taipei, National Palace Museum, 2006-12, ISBN 957-562-504-8 Transferred from zh.wikipedia ; transferred to Commons by Acsakw using CommonsHelper

title: Diquís Gold Pendant of a Double-Headed Feline
title_original: Diquís Delta Cast-Gold Feline Pendant (Costa Rica, c. 700–1500 CE)
description: A gold feline struts on stubby legs, its big square head turned toward us with bulging button eyes, rounded ears and a grin full of pointed fangs. The twist is at the other end: the raised tail ends in the head of a second feline, so the animal has a face at each end. The body is cast, with legs and head reduced to compact, rounded forms that would survive being worn on a cord. Look for the second head first, then follow the curve of the tail back to the main animal. Most visitors spot one cat; the pendant has two.
context: The pendant is displayed in the Museo del Oro Precolombino in San José, run by the Banco Central de Costa Rica, and is attributed to the Diquís (South Pacific) region of Costa Rica, 700-1550 CE. Fun fact: the museum's caption is matter-of-fact, 'a gold pendant in the form of a feline whose tail ends in the head of another feline', and leaves the species open; the jaguar identification comes from outside cataloguers.
title_eng: Diquís Gold Pendant of a Double-Headed Feline
submovement: Diquís cast goldwork (South Pacific Costa Rica)
medium: Cast tumbaga (gold-copper alloy) with depletion gilding
collection: Museo del Oro Precolombino, San José, Costa Rica
location: Museo del Oro Precolombino, San José, Costa Rica
image_credit: Mariordo (Mario Roberto Durán Ortiz) · Own work

title: Cats at Play (宋人戲貓圖 軸)
artist: Anonymous late Ming court painter (traditionally attributed to a Song artist)
submovement: Late Ming court painting (traditionally attributed to Song)
medium: Hanging scroll; ink and color on silk
description: A big white long-hair grooms a grey kitten on a bench at left, another kitten hides underneath, a white cat balances on top of a green drum-shaped stool while a spotted one sniffs at its base, and a white cat with a dark patch noses about by the bamboo fence at bottom right. The museum counts eight in all, among lake rocks, bamboo, a tree and peonies. The garden is furnished: brocade screens with tassels, a clothes rack with dragon and phoenix finials, and a lacquered table holding vases of coral and lacquer boxes. Check the eyes: thin slit pupils, the museum says, put the hour around midday.
context: Slit-thin pupils date the scene: the museum's note says a cat's pupils are round at dawn and dusk and shrink to a line in strong daylight, so the painter was marking midday. The catalogue calls the scroll 'transmitted as' a Song painting, and the long-standing title, 'Song people's cats at play', is only that tradition. Seals show it passed through the household of Prince Guo (Hongzhan) before entering the Qing palace collection, where it was listed in the third series of the Shiqu baoji catalogue. Fun fact: the museum counts eight cats, among lake rocks, bamboo, a peach tree and peonies.
title_eng: Cats at Play (宋人戲貓圖 軸)
image_credit: Unknown author Unknown author · https://www.shuge.org/meet/topic/91208/

title: Kitten (Song Dynasty Album Leaf, Li-tai Hua-fu-Chi)
title_original: 歷代畫幅集 冊 幼貓
medium: Album leaf; ink and fine mineral color on silk (gongbi)
description: The kitten stands on bare silk and turns its head to look straight at us, white on the chest, muzzle and legs, with grey-brown tabby markings over its back and a striped tail held up behind. The painter laid light grey washes on the head, ears, face, back, tail and hind legs, flicked white specks onto the face and limbs, and used darker ink for the body markings. The pupils were done in three tones of ink so they seem to catch shifting light. Do not skip the paws: soft and round like plum blossoms, they are the most kitten-like thing in the picture.
context: Fourth leaf of an album of paintings from various dynasties (Li-tai hua-fu chi) in the National Palace Museum, Taipei, catalogued as anonymous, Song dynasty (960-1279). The description praises the brushwork for making each kind of fur distinct, which is the whole point of a picture this small. Fun fact: the museum's note compares this dappled cat to a pet of Princess Qionghua of the Later Tang, who called her own spotted cat a 'bridle cicada cat'; later poets borrowed 'bridle cicada' as a nickname for cats.
location: National Palace Museum (Li-tai Hua-fu-Chi Album, Leaf 4)
image_credit: Unknown author Unknown author · https://culture.teldap.tw/culture/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=222

title: The Aberdeen Bestiary: The Cat (Musio / Cattus) (Univ Lib MS 24, fol. 23v)
medium: Egg tempera, burnished gold leaf, and iron gall ink on vellum
collection: University of Aberdeen Special Collections, Aberdeen, Scotland
description: On burnished gold, a blue cat stalks along a wavy blue hill, a second rears up on a red mound, and between them an orange cat curls into a tight ball. The interesting part is missing: the mice. The text says the cat is called musio because it is the enemy of mice, yet the Aberdeen painter left the mice out, and the text goes on to praise the cat's piercing sight, which overcomes the dark of night with the gleam of its eyes.
context: The Aberdeen Bestiary (Aberdeen University Library, Univ. Lib. MS 24) was written and illuminated in England around 1200. Its recorded history starts in 1542, when it appears as no. 518, 'Liber de bestiarum natura', in the inventory of Henry VIII's Old Royal Library at Westminster, a collection built partly from monastic books dispersed at the Dissolution. It probably moved to Marischal College in Aberdeen around the time James VI became king of England. Fun fact: the book was never finished, so its pages keep sketches and notes that show how it was planned, and scholars compare it constantly with its near-twin, the Ashmole Bestiary in Oxford.
title_eng: The Aberdeen Bestiary: The Cat (Musio / Cattus) (Univ Lib MS 24, fol. 23v)
feline_symbolism: The bestiary text explains the name musio as 'mouse-catcher' and praises the cat's eyesight, which can pierce the dark.
location: University of Aberdeen Special Collections, Aberdeen, Scotland
image_credit: Я вырезал это изображение из полностраничного изображения страницы Абердинского бестиария, взятого с сайта Абердинского университета: http://www.abdn.ac.uk/bestiary/ · Изображение с описанием http://art.biblioclub.ru/picture_119356_koshki_m

title: The Rochester Bestiary: The Cat Chasing Mice (Royal MS 12 F XIII, fol. 43r)
title_original: The Rochester Bestiary Cat Miniature (England, c. 1230, Royal MS 12 F XIII)
description: Flat out over a green hillock runs a long ochre cat, speckled with dots, ears pricked, tail streaming, after two black mice that bolt to the right as silhouettes. As elsewhere in the Rochester Bestiary, the miniature comes at the end of the passage it illustrates, and you can see the handover: the line just below already starts the next animal, 'est pusillum animal ex humore terre natum', the mouse. That passage is the standard entry: cats are the enemies of mice, and their eyesight cuts through the dark.
context: The Rochester Bestiary (British Library, Royal MS 12 F XIII) was made around 1230-40, probably at St Andrew's Priory, Rochester Cathedral. It has 55 finished miniatures; after the vulture (f. 52v) the pictures stop and the spaces stay empty. The painter seems to have worked a decade or more after the scribe, and by adding a fourth lion where three were planned he pushed every later picture after its text. Fun fact: the book was once stolen from the priory. A 14th-century note records its return by 'brother John Malling', and a John Malling was excommunicated in 1387 as an apostate and thief. It reached the royal library by 1542 and the British Museum in 1757.
title_eng: The Rochester Bestiary: The Cat Chasing Mice (Royal MS 12 F XIII, fol. 43r)
medium: Tempera, burnished gold leaf, and ink on vellum
feline_symbolism: The bestiary text presents the cat as the enemy of mice, with eyes that see through the night.
image_credit: Master of the Rochester Bestiary · British Library, London · Public Domain

title: The Harley Bestiary: The Cat (Musio) and Mice (Harley MS 4751, fol. 30v)
medium: Tempera and ink on vellum (no gold)
description: Squeezed together in a roundel, three cats sit side by side, two grey and one ginger with darker stripes, and only the ginger one is working: it reaches out and holds a grey mouse up in its forepaws while its companions gaze off. The painter of this book used no gold at all, and Payne describes its colours as sometimes sombre; here a starry blue ground and a dark red disc do the work.
context: Harley MS 4751 is a Latin bestiary of the so-called second family, made in England around 1230–1240, possibly at Salisbury. It runs to 74 vellum leaves (about 30.8 × 23.2 cm) with 106 coloured miniatures in square and round frames, each tagged with a red label, and it is a close sibling of Bodleian MS Bodley 764. It came to the British Library with the Harley manuscripts. Fun fact: little notes to the painter still survive in the margins, such as "hic est Ceru" beside the stag, telling him which beast went where. The British Library's bloggers, less solemn, dubbed the fiddling cat on this page an ancestor of Keyboard Cat.
title_eng: The Harley Bestiary: The Cat (Musio) and Mice (Harley MS 4751, fol. 30v)
feline_symbolism: The bestiary text calls the cat musio, the enemy of mice, and credits it with eyes sharp enough to pierce the darkness of night.
image_credit: Master of the Harley Bestiary · British Library, London · CC BY-SA 4.0

title: Luttrell Psalter: Tabby Cat Holding Mouse in Margin (Add MS 42130, fol. 190r)
culture: English (Lincolnshire, commissioned by Sir Geoffrey Luttrell)
submovement: East Anglian High Gothic Manuscript Illumination
medium: Tempera and shell gold on vellum
description: Upright in the margin of folio 190r, a grey tabby with wavy stripes sits with ears up and a long ringed tail swept out behind, pinning a small brown mouse under one outstretched forepaw and eyeing it sideways.
