Around it the Luttrell Psalter's crowd of grotesques, farm workers and hybrids carries on, and because the cat sits outside the text block, the psalm above continues as if nothing were happening. The farmyard scenes the book is famous for share their margins with household animals doing ordinary, slightly cruel, things.
context: The psalter was made for Sir Geoffrey Luttrell (1276–1345), lord of the manor of Irnham in Lincolnshire, by one scribe and at least five artists. Its date is argued over: Eric Millar suggested 1335–40, Lucy Sandler 1325–30 and Michelle Brown 1330–45. The book measures about 35 × 24.5 cm and has some 309 vellum leaves. It stayed for generations with the Weld family of Lulworth. Fun fact: when Herbert Weld Blundell sent it to Sotheby's in 1929, British Museum lawyers showed it actually belonged to Mary Angela Noyes, and the museum bought it from her with a loan from J. P. Morgan Jr. It is now British Library Add MS 42130.
title_eng: Luttrell Psalter: Tabby Cat Holding Mouse in Margin (Add MS 42130, fol. 190r)
image_credit: Ioreth · Zuffi, Stephano. Cats in Art. New York: Harry N. Abrams, Inc., 2007.

title: Cats and Flying Butterflies (明宣宗戲貓圖卷)
title_original: 明宣宗耄耋圖真蹟 卷
artist: Emperor Xuanzong of Ming (Xuande Emperor, 朱瞻基)
medium: Handscroll; ink and light color on paper
description: Cats lounge, curl and play along this long handscroll, each little group set alone on bare buff ground with columns of inscription in between, and butterflies flit in the air above them: the sort of picture that is really a pun you can unroll. The Chinese title, maodie tu, plays on sound: mao for cat, die for butterfly, together echoing the words for great old age. Read from right to left, the scroll sets the cats at leisure below with the butterflies overhead, a birthday wish dressed up as a garden afternoon. The image on file is stitched together from photographs of separate sections, so expect the odd seam.
context: A donated-paintings number, 贈畫000722, tells how this handscroll reached the National Palace Museum in Taipei: by gift rather than from the old Qing imperial collection. The museum's title calls it Xuanzong's Maodie tu, 'authentic trace' (明宣宗耄耋圖真蹟 卷), but that phrase belongs to an old title, a past owner's claim rather than a verdict. The Xuande Emperor, Zhu Zhanji (1399–1435), was a serious amateur painter, often compared with the Song emperor Huizong. Fun fact: the museum's note on another of his cat paintings, the peony picture, explains that the word for cat sounds like the word for old age, which is the pun this scroll's title relies on.
feline_symbolism: Cat (mao) puns on mao 耄, advanced age, so the cat works as a wish for long life; the NPM spells out the same pun for the emperor's Peonies in a Vase.
image_credit: Xuande Emperor · The National Palace Museum Collection

title: Kittens Playing Beneath Flowers (明宣宗畫花下貍奴圖 軸)
title_original: 明宣宗畫花下貍奴圖 軸
artist: Emperor Xuanzong of Ming (Xuande Emperor, 朱瞻基)
description: Beneath a pitted Taihu garden rock and wild chrysanthemums, a grey tabby crouches with its striped tail wrapped round, and in front of it a white cat with dark patches lies curled in a soft crescent, peering out at us over its own flank. The painter laid in their bodies with soft washes first and only then drew the fur and stripes on top, so the animals read as warm, solid bodies with markings floating on them. The rock gets the opposite treatment: hard outlines, then scratchy dry-brush texture. The picture is small, about 41.5 × 39.3 cm, with a big calligraphy panel mounted above it.
context: An inscription dates the painting to the bingwu year, 1426, the first year of the Xuande reign, when Zhu Zhanji (1399–1435) had just taken the throne. The National Palace Museum in Taipei holds it among the former Qing imperial paintings (故畫000421) and records it in the Qing imperial catalogue Shiqu baoji. Fun fact: the museum's note says the cats closely follow the manner of Li Di, a painter of the Song court academy, and compares the emperor himself with the painter-emperor Huizong.
medium: Hanging scroll; ink and color on silk
image_credit: Xuande Emperor · The National Palace Museum Collection

title: Cat with Peonies in a Bronze Pot (壺中富貴圖)
artist: Emperor Xuanzong of Ming (Xuande Emperor, 朱瞻基)
medium: Hanging scroll; ink and light color on paper
description: Head tipped back to stare up at the bronze vase hanging from a blue cord at the top of the sheet, a long-furred cat sits at the very bottom of the picture, white with ginger patches and a ringed tail, its coat drawn hair by hair. The vase is stuffed with white peonies: only three blossoms, but the leaves pile up in layers. Off to the right stands a low three-legged basin of the type made at the early Ming imperial kilns, a bit of product placement for the emperor's own porcelain. Above, a long inscription by Grand Secretary Yang Shiqi fills the sky.
context: Dated by its inscription to the fourth year of the Xuande reign (1429), this scroll is by Zhu Zhanji (1399–1435), the fifth Ming emperor, who wrote poems and painted well enough to be compared with the Song emperor Huizong. It carries the seal 'Xuande mige tushu zhi bao' and an inscription by the grand secretary Yang Shiqi (1365–1444), and is listed in the Shiqu baoji sanbian catalogue. The museum's own English title says only 'attributed to' the emperor. Fun fact: the museum explains that the word for cat sounds like the word for old age and the peony stands for wealth and rank, so the cat is a working part of the rebus, not a pet that wandered in.
title_eng: Cat with Peonies in a Bronze Pot (Wealth and Prosperity in a Pot)
feline_symbolism: The museum explains that the cat's name sounds like mao 耄, old age, so cat plus peony reads as a wish for long life and riches.
image_credit: Xuande Emperor · The National Palace Museum Collection

title: Great Malvern Priory Misericord: The Mice Hanging the Cat
title_original: Misericord: The Mice Hanging the Cat
medium: Carved English oak choir stall misericord bracket
description: Hanging from a gallows beam at the centre, a cat holds its forepaws up to the wood, its round face staring straight out with an air of mild surprise. On the left three rodents (rats or mice, depending on whom you ask) haul it aloft. The world turned upside down, carved in oak under a choir seat. An owl perches on each side as a supporter, ear tufts up. The casting is the joke: owls hunt mice too, so the executioners go about their work with the next predators already watching. The carving sits on the underside of a hinged seat and was only on show when the seat was tipped up.
context: Great Malvern Priory's choir keeps a set of medieval misericords, small ledges that let monks half-sit through long services. Wikipedia counts 22 fifteenth-century misericords plus 12 Victorian additions. Older accounts describe two medieval sets, twelve Labours of the Months and twelve miscellaneous subjects, and date the miscellaneous group to the late fourteenth century, about a century before the calendar carvings, so the date of this one is open to argument. The stalls were shuffled after the priory was dissolved in 1539, and their original order is lost. Fun fact: the geograph photograph is captioned 'Turning the Tables', and the owls on each side really are waiting to pounce on the rodents.
title_eng: Great Malvern Priory Misericord: The Mice Hanging the Cat
image_credit: Geograph: Julian P Guffogg · This image was taken from the Geograph project collection. See this photograph's page on the Geograph website for the photographer's contact details. The copyright on this image is owned by Julian P Guffogg and

title: Great Malvern Priory Misericord: Cat Gripping Mouse
title_original: Great Malvern Priory Misericord: Cat and Mouse
medium: Carved English oak wooden seat bracket
description: Crouched low on its ledge, a cat clamps a mouse under its forepaws and jaws, round eyes turned out toward us and its tail curled into a loop behind. It is carved in oak on the bracket beneath a tip-up choir seat, with a leaf-shaped support curling down at each side. The photographer who recorded it calls it 'a modern carving to replace an old or lost misericord', and the scene is the plain one: no hanging cat, no avenging mice, just the cat winning. Medieval stalls elsewhere in the choir tell the story the other way round.
context: Twenty-two of the priory's misericords are fifteenth-century and twelve are nineteenth-century, according to Wikipedia, which also records major restoration here under Sir George Gilbert Scott in 1860. The Geograph photographer's caption puts this cat and mouse among the modern pieces: 'a modern carving to replace an old or lost misericord'. Popular accounts describe a genuinely medieval misericord in the same choir where rodents hang a cat from a beam, so the stalls now show the story both ways round.
title_eng: Great Malvern Priory Misericord: Cat Gripping Mouse
image_credit: Bob Embleton · Geograph Britain and Ireland

title: The Virgin and Child with a Cat (Recto and Verso Studies)
title_original: Studio per la Madonna del gatto
medium: Pen and brown ink over stylus underdrawing; the other side pen and brown ink with brown wash
description: Cat-handling goes badly in this pen sketch. The Christ Child sits on the Virgin's knee and hugs a cat to his chest, and the cat, head up at the right, leans hard the other way, plainly planning its exit. Mary looks down at the pair, her hair in loose curls, the whole group packed into a thin arched frame ruled round it. The lines are quick and doubled, and the cat's body is reduced to one dark scribbled mass at the lower right. The sheet is double-sided: the museum records a second pen version of the same subject on the back.
context: Two sides, one idea: the British Museum describes pen and brown ink over stylus underdrawing on the front, with the same subject on the back, and dates the sheet to about 1478–81. That puts it in Leonardo's first Florentine years, when he kept returning to a Madonna with a playing or struggling cat. Fun fact: the Museum holds other Leonardo cat sheets too, among them a separate study of cats under accession number 1857,0110.1.
title_eng: The Virgin and Child with a Cat (Recto and Verso Studies)
image_credit: Photograph © The Trustees of the British Museum (public-domain artwork), via Wikimedia Commons

title: The Last Supper
description: On the chequered floor in front of the table, at the lower right, a grey tabby crouches with its tail curled, squaring up to a dog that snarls back at it. Off to the left a little white dog stands begging on its hind legs beside a man in red. Rosselli seats Christ and the apostles round a horseshoe table in a coffered room, and the white cloth is almost bare: one chalice in front of Christ. Judas sits alone on the near side with his back to us. Gilded and silvered kitchenware stands in the foreground as a little still life, and three windows behind the diners open onto Gethsemane, the Arrest and the Crucifixion.
context: The fresco, about 349 × 570 cm, was painted around 1481–82 on a wall of the Sistine Chapel, where Florentine painters had been sent to Rome as part of a reconciliation between Lorenzo de' Medici and Pope Sixtus IV. Rosselli brought many assistants, among them his son-in-law Piero di Cosimo, and Biagio d'Antonio is credited alongside him. Its frieze reads REPLICATIO LEGIS EVANGELICAE A CHRISTO, pairing it with the Moses scenes opposite. Fun fact: Vasari ranked Rosselli among the weaker painters in the chapel, yet his bright colours reportedly pleased the pope more than his colleagues' work.
submovement: Florentine Quattrocento Wall Painting & Sistine Chapel Fresco Cycle
feline_symbolism: The quarrelling cat and dog next to Judas are usually read as underlining his treachery and the discord he brings to the table.
image_credit: Cosimo Rosselli · Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"r/rosselli/cosimo/lastsup"

title: Hortus Sanitatis (Garden of Health): The Cat (Cattus)
title_original: Hortus sanitatis, Tractatus de animalibus, cap. xxv: Cattus
description: On a riverbank beside a stone fountain whose spouts pour into a basin and run off as a stream, a big striped cat sits upright at the left, mouth open as if it has something to say, while a smaller, paler one sits on the far bank. The woodcut is plain black line, all hatching and no colour, cut so that it could be read at a glance. It sits at the foot of a page of dense gothic type, just under the closing lines of the dog entries. An early owner has written Koth under the picture in brown ink, which looks like the Polish word for cat, kot, in an old spelling.
context: Five sections of the natural world and an appendix on urine: Jacob Meydenbach printed the Hortus sanitatis in Mainz on 23 June 1491. It followed Peter Schöffer's Mainz herbals of 1484 and 1485, which covered plants, and added animals (164 chapters), birds, fish and stones, with a woodcut at the head of chapters throughout. The leaf shown comes from a copy in the National Library of Poland, digitised on Polona. Fun fact: the same animal book that gives the cat its chapter also has the unicorn, and the dragon among its mythical beasts, so the cat sits in some very odd company.
medium: Woodcut and letterpress on paper (printed book, folio)
submovement: German Incunabula & Early Natural History Printmaking
image_credit: Jacob Meydenbach (printer), Mainz, 1491 · National Library of Poland (SD Inc.F.1074) / Polona

title: Cat, from Album of Sketches from Life (寫生冊 貓)
description: A single cat curled into a ball, done almost entirely in ink wash on paper. Its eyes are wide open and slide diagonally upward, so the animal looks sleepy and alert at the same moment, which anyone who has lived with a cat will recognise. Shen Zhou keeps the outline loose but lets the paws peek out from under the bottom edge of the round body, a small observed detail that makes the shape read as a real animal rather than a fur cushion. There is no setting at all, only paper.
context: Sketches from Life (寫生冊) holds sixteen paintings of plants and animals plus a leaf of the artist's own calligraphy, painted in 1494 when Shen Zhou (1427–1509) was about 67, the founding figure of the Wu school of Suzhou. A colophon by Gao Shiqi records that the album first belonged to Li Zhaoheng of Jiaxing before passing to Gao; it later entered the Qing imperial collection and is now in the National Palace Museum, Taipei, which had it certified a National Treasure in 2014. Fun fact: the museum's spotlight page says Shen wrote poems about the animals and plants in this album at different points in his life, so the cat has a poem as a companion piece.
title_eng: Cat, from Album of Sketches from Life
image_credit: 國立故宮博物院 · https://digitalarchive.npm.gov.tw/Collection/Detail/3870?dep=P

title: Adam and Eve
collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: Between the two nudes, almost underfoot, a cat lies curled with eyes narrowed, its long tail snaking out towards Eve's heel. Just to the left, beside Adam's foot, a mouse sits with its tail trailing, and nobody pounces. Dürer engraves the forest behind them line by line until it nearly turns black, and the animals keep turning up: an elk's antlered head by the tree trunk, an ox and a rabbit in the undergrowth, a parrot on Adam's branch, a goat on the far crag. A tablet hangs from that branch reading ALBERTVS DVRER NORICVS FACIEBAT 1504.
context: Four humours, four animals: museums reading this print link the rabbit to the sanguine temperament, the ox to the phlegmatic, the elk to the melancholic and the cat to the choleric, and the cat and mouse hint at the quarrels that follow the Fall. Dürer cut the plate in Nuremberg in 1504, and Adam's pose is derived from the Apollo Belvedere. The signature tablet announces him as a man of Nuremberg. The Met's impression (19.73.1) came through the Fletcher Fund in 1919. Fun fact: the British Museum records five states of this plate, an unusually high number for Dürer, so the engraver kept reworking it.
feline_symbolism: The four animals are usually read as the four temperaments, the cat standing for the choleric; held in balance before the Fall, the cat leaves the mouse alone, a truce that will end with the bite of the apple.
image_credit: Albrecht Dürer · This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the Metropolitan Museum of Art . See the Image and Data Resources Open Access Policy

title: Penelope with the Suitors
description: Low on the chequered floor, tucked under the beam of Penelope's loom, sits a grey cat with a dark-ringed tail and pale yellow eyes, one front paw resting on a stray roll of yarn. It looks straight out at us, a domestic extra squeezed between a sandalled foot at the left and a blue-stockinged leg at the right. Above it the suitors crowd in, one showing off a falcon, and a man with a staff, probably Odysseus in disguise, steps through the door in the same red and blue as the bow and arrows hanging over Penelope's head. Through the window the Odyssey carries on: Odysseus's ship flying the Petrucci arms, the Sirens and Circe's pigs.
context: Eight frescoes, one wedding: Pandolfo Petrucci, ruler of Siena, commissioned the set for his palace to celebrate his son's marriage to a niece of Pope Pius III, and three survive in the National Gallery. Pintoricchio painted this one about 1509. A tale of a wife who stayed faithful for twenty years was a pointed choice for a bride, and perhaps a personal one for Petrucci, who had been banished from Siena in the late 1490s. Transferred to canvas (125.5 × 152 cm), it was bought at the Alexander Barker sale on 6 June 1874 (NG911). Fun fact: Circe's pigs are painted as Cinta Senese, the belted local breed, so the sorceress's victims look distinctly Sienese.
image_credit: Sailko · Own work

title: Studies of Cat Movements and Positions
description: About twenty animals tumble over one sheet: cats playing, fighting, cringing, hunting, washing themselves, curled asleep and standing stock still, all in pen and brown ink with brushed wash over chalk. One at the left arches its back with its fur puffed out like a bottle brush, and in the middle rows pairs roll over each other in scraps. Some bodies twist so far they stop looking like cats and start looking like springs, and a few of the sleeker sprawlers are lionesses. Just below the middle a small dragon curls among them, drawn with exactly the same supple spine. Mirror-writing in Leonardo's hand fills the lower right and runs along the bottom edge.
context: Cats, lions and a dragon is the Royal Collection's own title, a fair warning that the sheet is not all house pets: the catalogue counts seven drawings of a prowling lioness among the domestic cats, plus one coiling dragon. It dates the page to about 1517–18, and the mirror-writing hints at Leonardo's long-planned studies of movement. Fun fact: the sheet reached the Royal Collection by a famous route, bequeathed to Leonardo's heir Francesco Melzi, bought by the sculptor Pompeo Leoni around 1582–90, then owned by the Earl of Arundel by 1630 and probably acquired by Charles II (RCIN 912363).
title_eng: Studies of Cat Movements and Positions
medium: Black chalk, pen and ink, wash on paper
image_credit: Royal Collection Trust (rct.uk), public-domain scans via Wikimedia Commons

title: The Annunciation
collection: Museo Civico Villa Colloredo Mels, Recanati
description: Mid-floor between the Virgin and the angel, a striped tabby bolts away with its tail up, the only creature in the room acting the way a real one would. The angel has dropped to one knee at the loggia's threshold, lily in hand, one arm flung up, while God the Father leans out of a cloud above the pergola outside. Mary kneels at a lectern at the left, both palms raised, and looks out at us as if we were the intruders. Lotto fills her room with clutter worth checking: a curtained bed in the dark, a shelf with a book and a candlestick, a towel on a peg and an hourglass on a stool.
context: Scared cat, startled Virgin: the critic Giulio Carlo Argan contrasted Titian's Virgin, a praying queen who nobly turns to receive her messenger, with Lotto's, 'a good girl' caught by surprise while praying. Lotto painted the canvas (166 × 114 cm) about 1534, possibly for the Recanati brotherhood of traders, who moved to a new seat in 1533; a minority view puts it as early as about 1527, when he was still in Venice. It is first mentioned in 1601 and now hangs in the Museo Civico at Villa Colloredo Mels, Recanati. Fun fact: Argan found Lotto's Virgin so human, and the cat so lively, that the picture reads like a household accident rather than a throne-room audience.
feline_symbolism: Italian Wikipedia's account reads the fleeing cat as a sign of evil put to flight by the Incarnation, and also as a gentle touch of irony.
image_credit: Lorenzo Lotto · The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

title: The Supper at Emmaus
description: Two animals ignore the miracle. A small white dog with ginger patches sits on the tiled floor at lower left, a few steps from the innkeeper, and a grey-and-white cat peeks out from under the stool at the far right edge, almost cut off by the frame. Between them Christ raises a hand over the bread, one disciple throws up both palms in recognition, and a servant in a plumed red hat brings in another dish. Bassano paints the cherries on the cloth, the glass of red wine, the carpet under the tablecloth and the flask on the floor with the same attention he gives the saints.
context: Dogs and cats are nowhere in the Gospel of Luke, which Bassano knew perfectly well. The Kimbell Art Foundation bought this canvas in 1989 through Acquavella Galleries in New York (APx 1989.03); it is dated about 1538, oil on canvas, 100.6 × 128.6 cm, and a much larger altarpiece of the same subject, 235 × 250 cm, is in Cittadella. Art historians read the food, the wary dog and the menacing cat as signs of his habit of drawing from life. Fun fact: when Veronese crowded his Wedding at Cana with portraits of Venetian painters, he cast Jacopo Bassano among the musicians.
image_credit: Photograph by FA2010 (Wikimedia Commons), released into the public domain

title: Netherlandish Proverbs (To Bell the Cat)
description: Leaning over a striped tabby that lies flat against the bricks of a low wall at the left of the village, a man in full armour ties a bell round its neck: to bell the cat, the plan every mouse agrees with and none will carry out. Armour, it turns out, is what it takes. Around him a whole Flemish village has gone mad, acting out roughly 126 proverbs at once. People bang their heads against walls, fill in the well after the calf has drowned, and a woman in red drapes a blue cloak over her husband. Bruegel paints it all briskly and matter-of-factly, so the cat's predicament gets no more fuss than anyone else's foolishness.
context: Around 126 proverbs and idioms have been identified in this panel, and more keep being proposed. Bruegel painted it in Antwerp in 1559 on oak, 117 x 163 cm, and it hangs in the Gemäldegalerie, Berlin. Its older title, The Blue Cloak or The Folly of the World, comes from the centre, where a wife hangs a blue cloak on her husband, which means she is cuckolding him. The Berlin museum lists the picture as Netherlandish Proverbs, oil on oak, and the proverb count is still not settled.
feline_symbolism: To bell the cat means attempting a dangerous or impractical plan, from the fable of the mice who decide the cat should wear a bell but find no volunteer.
image_credit: Google Arts & Culture, Gemäldegalerie, Staatliche Museen zu Berlin (public-domain artwork), via Wikimedia Commons

title: The Wedding at Cana
submovement: Venetian High Renaissance Monumental Decorative Painting
description: Down at the lower right, a small grey cat is curled up at the foot of a big pale wine amphora while a servant bends beside it, pouring from another jar. Some 130 figures pack the lower half of this canvas, the most expansive painting in the Louvre, and while the miracle of water into wine plays out at the table, the cat has parked itself beside the jar that holds the evidence. Two white dogs sit at bottom centre, a dwarf holds a bright green parrot, and in the middle a band of musicians, Veronese himself among them, plays on regardless.
context: The Benedictines of San Giorgio Maggiore in Venice signed the contract on 6 June 1562 for the end wall of their refectory and paid Veronese 324 ducats; he delivered in September 1563. On 11 September 1797 French soldiers cut the canvas horizontally, rolled it up and carried it to Paris, and in 1815 Vivant Denon claimed it was too fragile to send back, so Canova took another picture home instead. Fun fact: tradition identifies the musicians as Veronese and Tintoretto on viola, Jacopo Bassano on cornetto and Titian in red on the violone, so two of the painters in the band also painted cats of their own.
image_credit: Paolo Veronese · https://artsandculture.google.com

title: Madonna of the Cat (Madonna del Gatto)
description: Rearing up on its haunches at the lower left edge, a ginger-and-white cat stretches its forepaws towards the goldfinch that young John the Baptist dangles above it. A rosy, domestic Holy Family fills the rest of the canvas: Mary nurses the infant Christ, Joseph leans in from the right with a hand on a yellow-draped table, and John's reed cross leans against the wall behind. A wicker basket and cushions sit on the floor. The figures climb on a diagonal up to the right, a restless arrangement that already points towards the Baroque.
context: A goldfinch, a cat and a coat of arms make up the plot. The National Gallery says the goldfinch foretells Christ's Passion and that the cat poised to pounce on it is an unusual motif in Holy Family pictures. Barocci painted the canvas (112.7 × 92.7 cm) about 1575 for Antonio Brancaleoni, Count of Piobbico, and it passed down the female line to the countess's daughter Isabella. Cornelis Cort's engraving of 1577 spread the composition, and about 35 preparatory drawings survive. The Gallery received it with the Revd William Holwell Carr's bequest in 1831 (NG29). Fun fact: the Brancaleoni arms show a lion rampant beneath a cross, so the cat and John's reed cross may be a family pun.
title_eng: Madonna of the Cat (Madonna del Gatto)
feline_symbolism: The goldfinch foretells Christ's Passion, so the cat stalking it brings the threat of that future into a cosy family scene.
image_credit: Sailko · Own work (Wikimedia Commons), CC BY 3.0

title: Montaigne and his Cat
title_original: Quand je me joue à ma chatte
description: Left of the table, a cat sits bolt upright, facing Montaigne across it like an equal in conversation. The philosopher, in ruff and fur-trimmed gown, leans over the tabletop with his hands out, coaxing. Strang worked in a deliberately old-fashioned, linear manner, so the scene looks almost like a sixteenth-century print come back to life, all firm contour and crisp hatching: a carved cabinet behind the cat, a dark archway behind the man, plates on the chimneypiece. His initials W.S. sit in the plate at lower left, and a pencilled '1st state' is visible below. The joke underneath is Montaigne's own: who is entertaining whom.
context: 'Quand je me joue à ma chatte, qui sait si elle passe son temps de moi plus que je ne fais d'elle': Montaigne's famous line from the Apology for Raymond Sebond (Essays, Book II, chapter 12) is the whole subject of this plate. The British Museum record describes Montaigne seated, leaning towards a cat on a table at left, plates and jars on a fireplace under an arch behind, and dates the etching to 1902, first state. Fun fact: the cat is Montaigne's star witness against human vanity, and a Scottish etcher took the hint three centuries later.
feline_symbolism: For Montaigne the cat is a test case for human arrogance: if she may be amusing herself with him, humans cannot claim to be the only minds in the room.
image_credit: William Strang · https://www.nationalgalleries.org/art-and-artists/32723

title: The Annunciation
description: Curled in a tight ball in the lower left corner, nose tucked in, a small cat sleeps through the most important announcement in Christian history. Gabriel kneels in gold and rose with a lily, one hand held out, and Mary, standing at her prie-dieu, answers with one palm raised and the other open, a quiet gesture in soft light. A red curtain swags across the top of the room. Through the window behind them Barocci gives a view of the Palazzo Ducale in Urbino, so the miracle happens with a local landmark in the background.
context: A chapel at Loreto was the destination: Barocci painted the altarpiece in 1582–84 for the chapel of Francesco Maria II della Rovere, Duke of Urbino, in the basilica there. It is oil on canvas, 248 × 170 cm, and the Vatican Museums record it as Cat. 40376. Fun fact: it was carried off to Paris in 1797, returned to Italy in 1815 and then placed in the Vatican Pinacoteca, so the sleeping cat spent eighteen years as a prisoner of war.
feline_symbolism: The NGV's essay reads the sleeping cat, with the view of Urbino, as a naturalistic detail that balances the miraculous encounter.
image_credit: Sailko · Own work (Wikimedia Commons), CC BY-SA 3.0

title: Two Children Teasing a Cat
collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: On the right edge of the table, a ginger-and-white tabby crouches with its head lowered and eyes narrowed to slits, while a boy dangles a crayfish just above its ear and keeps his other hand on its back. The girl leans in, laughing. A second crayfish lies loose on the tabletop, and nobody has noticed it. Annibale stops the clock one second before trouble, which is the whole joke. The faces are broad and unidealised, the brushwork loose, the background plain brown, so all attention goes to three heads and one claw.
context: Boy Bitten by a Crayfish is the lost Sofonisba Anguissola picture, known from a drawing, that this canvas borrows its theme from. Annibale painted it (66 x 88.9 cm) around 1587 to 1588 in Bologna; with no documents, the date rests on its Venetian-looking brushwork, which fits his known trip to Venice in those years. Once given to his brother Agostino, it was assigned to Annibale by Roberto Longhi, and the Metropolitan Museum acquired it in 1994. Fun fact: Sofonisba and Caravaggio showed the bite; Annibale shows the moment before, and Bolognese painters liked the idea enough to make several derivatives, including Crespi's Girl Playing with a Cat and a Mouse.
title_eng: Two Children Teasing a Cat with a Crayfish
image_credit: Annibale Carracci · Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"c/carracci/annibale/1/children"

title: Sight (One of the Five Senses)
description: The felid is easy to miss: a small lynx peers out from the lower right corner, just under the hand mirror, ears up and eyes wide, the animal that stood for keen eyesight. Above it Sight is played by a fashionable young woman who holds up the mirror but turns her eyes to us, while a man in a floppy hat, wearing a decidedly mischievous look, gets a hand on her breast. The pen-and-brown-ink drawing is worked up with wash and white highlights, and her face alone is touched with red chalk, so it glows warmer than everything around it. Goltzius signed with his HG monogram on the mirror frame.
context: Indented lines give this sheet away as a working drawing: Goltzius pressed through the paper to transfer the design for one plate of a Five Senses series, made in Haarlem around 1595 to 1596 and engraved by his close collaborator Jan Saenredam. Boijmans points out that Goltzius swapped the usual stiff personifications for contemporary flirting couples, closer to genre than allegory, and that the senses' traditional animals (the lynx here, a deer in Hearing) shrink to small corner details. The drawing belonged to F.J.O. Boijmans in Utrecht and came to Rotterdam with his 1847 bequest, so it has been in the museum since it opened in 1849.
medium: Pen and brown ink, brown wash, white heightening, red chalk, indented for transfer
feline_symbolism: The lynx was the classic emblem of sharp sight, which is why it turns up as Sight's attribute, even if Goltzius makes it a footnote to the flirtation.
image_credit: Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen, Rotterdam (public-domain artwork), via Wikimedia Commons

title: Tibert the Cat Summons Reynard the Fox
title_original: Tibert de kat dagvaardt Reinaert de vos
description: Tibert the cat stands at the left with tail raised high, head lowered towards the foxes as if reading out the king's summons. Four foxes gather in front of a rocky den, two sitting up, one lying at ease and one peering out from behind, Reynard among them. It is a small etching, under ten centimetres high, that plays like a scene from a courtroom drama. Everdingen was a landscape man first, so the animals act out their story in a proper outdoor setting, with overhanging rock, scrubby trees and a wicker basket on its side at lower right, and they look like real animals rather than people in costume.
context: Fifty-seven plates make up Everdingen's Reynard the fox series, which Stedelijk Museum Alkmaar dates to around 1670; the Rijksmuseum gives this sheet 1665 to 1675. Everdingen (1621–1675), from Alkmaar, etched them as a landscape specialist, which is why the animals sit in proper rocky country. In the medieval story the king sends Tibert to fetch Reynard to court, and the fox repays him by luring him into a trap. The plates had a long afterlife. They illustrated Gottsched's 1752 German Reineke edition, and in 1843 Henry Cole, writing as 'Felix Summerly', published forty of them in London after acquiring the original coppers.
title_eng: Tibert the Cat Summons Reynard the Fox
submovement: Dutch Golden Age etching (Everdingen's Reynard the Fox series)
image_credit: Rijksmuseum · http://hdl.handle.net/10934/RM0001.collect.70690

title: Still Life of Fish and Cat
title_original: Stilleven met vis, kaars, artisjokken, krab en kat
collection: National Museum of Women in the Arts, Washington, DC
description: Paws clamped on a small fish with another beside it, a tabby crouches at the left edge of the table, ears up and eyes fixed on us, as if daring anyone to take them back. Behind it a big carp lies across a perforated ceramic colander, scales glinting, with a smaller fish tucked underneath. In front, a tangle of red crayfish crawls towards the edge, and at right a heap of oysters and shells ends in one opened oyster, wet and pearly. Peeters lines up the textures like a sampler: fur, slime, glazed clay, crayfish armour, rough shell. The cat is the only thing on the table still breathing.
context: A 1594 baptism record may be hers, but some scholars push Peeters's birth back into the 1580s, since otherwise her accomplished 1607 pictures would be the work of a 12- or 13-year-old. Active in Antwerp from about 1607, she was one of the earliest painters to specialise in still life and the only Flemish woman known to do so that early. The National Museum of Women in the Arts in Washington dates this panel to after 1620; it came as a gift of the museum's founders, Wallace and Wilhelmina Holladay. NMWA reads it as plain household abundance, without the moral subtext still lifes often carry.
title_eng: Still Life of Fish and Cat
image_credit: Clara Peeters · Bridgeman Art Library : Object 51954

title: The Cardinal's Leisure
description: Cats have taken over the floor: a big ginger-and-white cat lies on the unrolled map like a paperweight, kittens tumble across it, and one white kitten is flipped onto its back near the hem of the Cardinal's red robe. Richelieu leans sideways out of his chair, quill still in hand, to look down at them, while a bearded man behind the desk goes on reading his papers. Delort paints what academic history pictures did best, heavy red silk, a carved high-backed chair, ship models, an embroidered wall hanging, and sets against it the soft disorder of cats. France's most feared man is upstaged by animals playing with his paperwork.
context: Lot 87 in George I. Seney's collection sale, held in New York from 31 March to 2 April 1885, was this canvas, signed 'C. DeLort' at lower right. It entered the Detroit Institute of Arts (F72.241) as a gift of Mrs. Helen L. DeRoy in 1972 and is catalogued there as The Cardinal's Leisure, oil on canvas, 78.7 by 61 cm. The picture leans on a popular story that Richelieu kept fourteen cats in a cattery at his Palais-Cardinal, but the evidence is thin: the anecdote that he endowed Marie de Gournay's cat and its kittens turns up only in popular sources.
feline_symbolism: The cats are companions and comic relief, a 19th-century way of giving a feared statesman a private soft spot.
image_credit: Charles Édouard Delort · https://www.dia.org/art/collection/object/cardinals-leisure-42360

title: A Boy and a Girl with a Cat and an Eel
title_original: Twee kinderen met een kat en een aal
description: A boy in a fashionable hat clamps a cat against his chest and dangles an eel just out of its reach, grinning at someone we cannot see. The cat is not enjoying the game: it stares out at us, ears up and wary, hind legs braced against his arm. His little sister looks straight at us with a warning finger raised, which would be more convincing if her other hand were not gripping the cat's tail, ready to pull. Leyster sets the two clean faces and crisp white collars against a dark ground, so the trouble reads instantly. The ebony frame is a 17th-century Dutch one, fitted in 2011.
context: A proverb sits behind the grin: 'he who plays with cats gets scratched', which the National Gallery links to this panel, painted in Haarlem around 1635, a couple of years after Leyster joined the painters' guild and set up a workshop with apprentices of her own. Unusually, the culprits are well-off middle-class children, when naughty children in Dutch pictures were more often poor. It came to the gallery in 1943 with the bequest of C.F. Leach. Leyster's own reputation had a rough ride: her works were long credited to Frans Hals or to her husband Jan Miense Molenaer, until her monogram turned up under a false Hals signature in 1893.
title_eng: A Boy and a Girl with a Cat and an Eel
feline_symbolism: The cat is the trouble waiting to happen: under the proverb, whoever torments it is about to get scratched.
image_credit: Judith Leyster · National Gallery, London (official image, via Wikimedia Commons)

title: Young Man with a Cat
collection: Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister, Museumslandschaft Hessen Kassel
description: Clamped against the young man's chest at the bottom edge of the panel, a tabby has its ears back and its mouth open in a pink protest while his hand presses down on its head. He hardly seems to notice. Under a broad black hat with a white plume, he turns a flushed, half-smiling face to us. This is a half-length genre head of the Haarlem type, on an oak panel very nearly square, about 45 by 43 centimetres, where the point is the sitter's mood and the quick handling. The Kassel cataloguer singles out that face: its modelling is restless, more agitated than in Leyster's secure pictures.
context: Kassel bought this panel in 1962 from the Basel dealer H. F. Fankhauser and catalogues it as Judith Leyster, attributed. Frima Fox Hofrichter, author of the Leyster catalogue raisonné, dates it 1635, the year before Leyster married Jan Miense Molenaer. Not everyone is convinced. Bernhard Schnackenburg's 1996 Kassel catalogue notes how the restless face departs from her secure work, yet finds no grounds to hand it to anyone else, such as one of Frans Hals's sons. Fittingly for Leyster, whose pictures spent two centuries passing as Hals's, the argument still runs in both directions.
image_credit: Judith Leyster · http://altemeister.museum-kassel.de/32783/

title: Nemuri-neko (Sleeping Cat Architectural Relief Carving)
title_original: 日光東照宮 眠り猫
artist: Attributed to Hidari Jingorō (左甚五郎)
description: Curled among gilded peonies, a soft grey cat sleeps with its eyes shut and its head lowered onto its forepaws. It sits in a kaerumata, the frog-leg bracket over a beam of the shrine's eastern corridor near the Sakashita Gate, framed by gold-leaf blossoms, green leaves and a turquoise cloud band. The carving is small, so most visitors find it by spotting the crowd standing under it. Round the back, sparrows play among bamboo, and that is the usual key to the joke: a cat this relaxed is no threat to the birds.
context: The carving belongs to the lavish rebuilding of Nikkō Tōshō-gū, the shrine to Tokugawa Ieyasu, enlarged under the third shōgun Iemitsu and completed in 1636. It sits on the route up to the Okusha, Ieyasu's tomb. Tradition credits Hidari Jingorō, a carver so legendary that some scholars doubt he existed; the real hand is unknown. The east and west corridors became a National Treasure in 1951, and the shrine is part of the UNESCO site Shrines and Temples of Nikkō (1999). Readings pile up. The sleeping cat plus carefree sparrows means peace; peony plus cat is a Chinese pun for wealth and long life; or the cat is a guard against mice on the path to the tomb.
medium: Carved wood painted with mineral pigments
submovement: Early Edo shrine carving (Tōshō-gū, Kan'ei rebuilding)
feline_symbolism: A cat asleep while sparrows play on the other side is read as an image of peace under Tokugawa rule; the peony-and-cat pairing also puns on wealth and longevity.
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons

title: Peasant Family in an Interior
title_original: Famille de paysans dans un intérieur
description: Look beside the copper cooking pot on the floor: a small white cat with grey patches peeps out, anxiously keeping an eye on the viewer. Its opposite number is a little pop-eyed dog at lower left that seems lost in its own thoughts. Above them three generations of a peasant family sit by the hearth, staring out at us more than at each other. A barefoot boy plays a recorder, the grandmother holds a glass of wine, and bread, wine and salt sit on the table. At 113 by 159 cm, this is the largest and most ambitious of the brothers' peasant interiors.
context: Three brothers worked together in Paris and rarely signed individually, so the question of which one held the brush never quite goes away. For this canvas the Louvre gives the work to Louis Le Nain (c. 1593–1648), with his brother Antoine as a possible partner, and dates it about 1642. It came from the dukes of Marmier at Ray-sur-Saône, was sold in Paris in 1914, passed through George Demotte and was bought for the Louvre in 1915 with Arthur Pernolet's bequest. Scholars including Cuzin and Dickerson have read the bread and wine as a hint at the Eucharist and an act of charity; the Louvre's notice calls that reading 'very fragile' and sees studio props, the animals included.
image_credit: Attributed to Louis Le Nain / Antoine Le Nain · https://www.panoramadelart.com/Le-nain-famille-paysans-interieur

title: Head of a Cat (small size)
description: Nothing but a head: a striped tabby seen dead on, round eyes with bright catchlights fixed on us, ears pricked, whiskers fanning out past the jaw in single hair-thin lines. It is etched on a plate about 7 centimetres square, small enough to cover with a palm, and signed W Hollar fec 1646 at lower left. No body, no setting, no story, just the specimen-like attention Hollar paid to shells, insects and fur muffs. The catalogue title adds (small size), which tells you a larger plate of the same subject exists. At this scale the print works like a page from a naturalist's notebook.
context: Prague-born and London-based, Hollar (1607–1677) spent the Civil War years in Antwerp and etched almost anything put in front of him: cities, costume, maps, animals. The University of Toronto's Thomas Fisher Rare Book Library holds an impression in its Hollar collection, classed under natural history and filed as plate P2108, catalogued as Head of a cat (small size). His best-known cat is a different and odder print entirely: Le vray portrait du chat du grand duc de Moscovie, attributed to him and dated 1663, an impression of which is in the Bibliothèque nationale de France.
image_credit: Wenceslaus Hollar · Artwork from University of Toronto Wenceslaus Hollar Digital Collection Scanned by University of Toronto High-resolution version extracted using custom tool by User:Dcoetzee

title: Peasant Court with an Old Woman and a Cat
description: On the old woman's lap at lower left, a ginger-and-white cat is held steady while she parts the fur on its head with her fingers. The panel is modest, 49 by 64 centimetres, and painted on oak, which suits Teniers's quick, silvery handling: a few strokes for a wheelbarrow, a smear of light for a copper basin, a white cloth dropped by a tub. Thatched houses, a tall plank fence and a well with a copper jug fill the yard under a grey sky. The woman and the cat are the only living company here, and the cat turns farmyard clutter into a household.
context: Hungary got this panel in 1953, when the holdings of the Budapest Municipal Gallery were transferred to the Museum of Fine Arts. Teniers (1610–1690) of Antwerp, court painter to Archduke Leopold Wilhelm in Brussels, made his fortune with small scenes of Flemish peasants, sold to collectors who never set foot in such yards. The museum's title, Peasant Court with an Old Woman and a Cat, does most of the iconographic work; Teniers turned out these yard scenes in quantity, and most of his figures are types, not portraits.
title_eng: Peasant Court with an Old Woman and a Cat
title_original: Boereninterieur met oude vrouw en kat
image_credit: David Teniers the Younger · Own work , Yelkrokoyade , 20 July 2011

title: The Virgin and Child with the Cat and Snake
description: At lower left, a cat crouches on a cushion by the step, one paw out to play with the hem of Mary's skirt, and from under that same skirt, near the bottom centre, a small snake slides out, trodden under her foot. The Holy Family has moved into a Dutch living room. Mary sits low by the fireplace cradling the Child, cheek to cheek, with a chair behind her, while Joseph peers in through the window from outside. The leaded panes behind her head line up into a makeshift halo. The signed plate is small, under 15 centimetres wide.
context: A copper plate outlived its prints: it passed from the dealer Clement de Jonge (1679) through Basan and later owners, was last printed in 1906, and was bought by the V&A in 1993 with Art Fund support, then varnished so no one could print from it again. Rembrandt etched it in Amsterdam in 1654 and signed it 'Rembrandt f. 1654'. The V&A notes that he based the group partly on an engraving of the Virgin and Child by Andrea Mantegna, then dressed it in contemporary clothes. The National Gallery of Art in Washington owns an impression given by Philip Hofer in 1941.
title_eng: The Virgin and Child with the Cat and Snake
feline_symbolism: The snake under Mary's foot casts her as the new Eve defeating sin; the cat, toying at her hem, keeps the scene firmly domestic.
image_credit: Rembrandt van Rijn · This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the National Gallery of Art . Please see the Gallery's Open Access Policy .

title: Barbershop with Monkeys and Cats (Barbierstube mit Affen und Katzen)
description: Cats take the barber's chairs while monkeys do the shaving: this is the singerie, the genre in which animals act out human trades. In the middle chair a ginger tabby sits wrapped in a white cloth while a monkey scrapes at its chin. At left another cat has a bowl held under its chin, and at right two cats wait on a table, one in a pink bib. A lute lies on the red-tiled floor at lower right, and a small monkey sits at lower left. It is painted on copper, a support that lets the brush lay down crisp, enamel-smooth detail, ideal for fur, whiskers and the gleam of a razor.
context: Younger brother of David Teniers the Younger, Abraham Teniers (1629–1670) worked in Antwerp and helped his brother develop the monkey-and-cat satires that collectors loved in the mid-1600s. The Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna dates this copper to the second third of the 17th century (inv. GG 1786). It has a long imperial pedigree: it is recorded in the Habsburg Schatzkammer in 1747/48 and in the picture gallery by 1781. The theme travelled widely in print. A Coryn Boel engraving after David Teniers, The Monkeys' Barber Shop, is in Washington, and the Rijksmuseum has a print simply titled Een aap scheert een kat, 'a monkey shaves a cat'.
feline_symbolism: In singeries cats and monkeys parody human vanity and pretension; the cat as unwilling customer sharpens the satire.
image_credit: Coryn Boel after David Teniers the Younger · This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the National Gallery of Art . Please see the Gallery's Open Access Policy .

title: Interior with a Sleeping Maid and her Mistress (The Idle Servant)
description: Up on the cupboard above the sleeping maid, a grey tabby helps itself to the raw goose, flattened over the dish with its jaws in the bird. The National Gallery notes, unkindly, that Maes seems to have had only a vague idea of what a cat's teeth look like. Below, the maid has dropped off on a stool, head propped in her hand, sleeves rolled after cooking. Her mistress, in a crisp white apron, turns to us with an open palm, smiling. Pots and pans litter the floor, and up a few stairs a proper family dinner goes on in the room beyond.
context: A Dutch saying holds that a kitchen maid should keep one eye on the pan and the other on the cat; this one manages neither, and the picture may play on it. Maes, a former pupil of Rembrandt, painted this signed and dated panel in 1655, soon after going home to Dordrecht. The maid's slump borrows the traditional pose of Acedia, Sloth, though the mistress looks amused rather than outraged. Its view through to a second room is among the first of its kind, a device Maes kept using. Richard Simmons bequeathed it to the National Gallery in 1847, and it hangs today in a 17th-century Italian frame.
title_eng: Interior with a Sleeping Maid and her Mistress (The Idle Servant)
feline_symbolism: The thieving cat is the cost of idleness, the proverb's warning made literal.
image_credit: Nicolaes Maes · http://www.nationalgallery.org.uk/paintings/nicolaes-maes-the-idle-servant

title: Old Woman Saying Grace, Known as 'The Prayer without End'
title_original: Oude vrouw in gebed, bekend als 'Het gebed zonder end'
description: Out of patience, the cat rears up on its hind legs in the lower right corner and hooks its claws into the tablecloth, while the old woman bows over her folded hands with her eyes shut. She is saying grace, and she is taking her time. Bread, a salmon steak on a pewter plate and a stoneware jug sit one good tug from the floor. On the shelf behind her stand an hourglass and a funnel, keys hang below, the props of a careful household and of time running out. Maes paints her nearly life-size on a big canvas, 134 by 113 centimetres.
context: Het gebed zonder end, 'the prayer without end', is the Dutch nickname, and it takes the cat's point of view. Maes painted the canvas in Dordrecht around 1656 and signed it with a monogram. The Rijksmuseum puts the virtue in her self-control and sense of duty to God: the begging cat does not distract her. The picture went from A. Lacoste in Dordrecht to the Amsterdam society Felix Meritis, which gave it to the city of Amsterdam in June 1889. The city lent it to the Rijksmuseum that November, and it has stayed on loan ever since.
title_eng: Old Woman Saying Grace, Known as 'The Prayer without End'
feline_symbolism: The cat stands for worldly appetite and distraction, set against the old woman's patient devotion.
image_credit: Nicolaes Maes · Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"m/maes/old_pray"

title: The Large Cat (De grote kat)
description: Crouched at rest, a tabby fills almost the whole plate, eyes narrowed to sleepy slits, forepaws tucked, nose towards a few leafy plants at lower right. Visscher engraves every stiff whisker and builds the striped fur from fine, soft lines until you can almost feel the nap. Behind the cat, at far left, a mouse has squeezed through the bars of an arched window and peers out. The cat does not care. That is the joke, and maybe the sermon: a guard animal dozing while the thief walks in. Even the signature joins the scene, written on a scrap of paper lying on the ground at lower left.
context: A stone at lower left is inscribed 'Corn. Visscher fecit'. Visscher (1629–1658) of Haarlem, praised by Houbraken for his drawing from life, engraved the plate in 1657, a year before he died young, and his relative Claes Jansz. Visscher published it. Two states are known, and impressions are in the British Museum, Rijksmuseum, National Gallery of Art and elsewhere. It was popular enough to be copied: the Rijksmuseum's RP-P-1904-722 is an anonymous copy after it. The Leiden Collection compares it with Gerrit Dou's cat on a ledge, painted the same year, though it thinks a direct link unlikely. The preparatory drawing sold in 1883 and is now lost.
feline_symbolism: The sleeping cat ignoring the mouse may allude to Proverbs 19:15, where sloth leads to hunger.
image_credit: Rijksmuseum · http://hdl.handle.net/10934/RM0001.COLLECT.191123

title: Las Hilanderas (The Spinners / The Fable of Arachne)
description: The workshop cat is easy to miss: a grey shape curled on the floor at bottom centre, among tufts of fleece and a ball of yarn, right by the old spinner's bare foot. Around it the weaving workshop is in full swing: an older woman at the spinning wheel on the left, a young one in a white blouse winding yarn on the right, helpers bending over the wool. Up a step at the back, in a bright alcove, elegant ladies stand before a finished woven hanging copied from Titian's Rape of Europa. Velázquez paints with startling economy; the spinning wheel's spokes dissolve into a blur.
context: Pedro de Arce, a royal huntsman, owned this canvas, whose 1664 inventory calls it a 'Fábula de Aracne'. Velázquez painted it around 1657. For centuries it was read as a view of Madrid's Santa Isabel weaving works, until Diego Angulo showed in 1948 that it stages Ovid's story of Arachne, who out-wove Athena and was turned into a spider; the old woman is the goddess in disguise. It passed to the Medinaceli family and the royal Alcázar, probably survived the palace fire of 1734, and reached the Prado in 1819. Somewhere along the way strips were added, about 50 cm on top and 37 cm at the sides, now hidden behind a double wall.
title_eng: Las Hilanderas (The Spinners / The Fable of Arachne)
image_credit: Diego Velázquez · Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"v/velazque/09/0901vela"

title: Old Woman Eating Porridge
title_original: Oude vrouw die pap eet met een kat
collection: Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (Eijk and Rose-Marie van Otterloo Collection)
description: Lower right on the floorboards, a grey-brown tabby lies curled and looks straight out at us instead of up at the spoon, while an old woman in a white cap and blue apron eats her porridge. Metsu paints it small, on a panel only 35.5 by 28 centimetres, the size of a page, so the figure, bowl and cat are close and intimate. A tipped-over copper pot, a stray slipper and a wedge of cheese on the white cloth fill the corners. Pictures like this belong to the early Metsu, before his glossier Amsterdam interiors: plain people, plain food, and a domestic animal to make the scene feel lived in.
context: Secretan sale, Paris, 1889: that is where this panel's documented history begins. Metsu, born in Leiden in 1629, moved to Amsterdam around 1657, and the RKD dates the panel to about 1654 to 1657. It now belongs to the Eijk and Rose-Marie van Otterloo collection, which the couple have pledged to the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, where it is registered under a loan number. It is not the Dresden picture the old record claimed.
image_credit: Gabriel Metsu · https://rkd.nl/explore/images/246721

title: Cat Musicians
artist: Anonymous, style of David Teniers the Younger
description: Six cats, two of them kittens, crowd a pink-draped round table around an open songbook, and a grimacing tabby at the back is plainly going for the high note. An owl perches on the book like a conductor, a monkey in a red-and-yellow coat blows a shawm at lower left with a second monkey in a feathered hat behind him, and one more cat peers in through a slot in the wall at top right. The table stands on carved fish, a snack the singers cannot reach. It is a small panel, about 25 by 31 centimetres, catalogued as in the style of Teniers.
context: 'Style of David Teniers II' is how the National Trust catalogues this small panel (25.4 × 31.1 cm) at Erddig, near Wrexham, giving it to an anonymous painter around 1750, long after Teniers died in 1690. Erddig stayed with the Yorke family from 1733 until Philip Scott Yorke gave it to the National Trust in 1973. Fun fact: the Yorkes were unusual for commemorating their servants in portraits and poems, so a family that painted its staff also kept a picture of cats giving a concert.
feline_symbolism: Singing cats were a stock image of cacophony and folly, mocking human music-making.
image_credit: anonymous · Art UK

title: Merry Company in a Pergola (The 'Cat Family')
description: At the left, not the centre, a young woman leans over the table where a striped mother cat sprawls with her kittens, two small faces peering up beside her. That cluster is why the Budapest picture is nicknamed 'The Cat Family'. Around it a merry company crowds under the pergola: a man hoists a glass high, a youth plays the flute, a little boy saws at a fiddle, a spotted dog yaps and a crow struts past the barrel. Steen paints it big, about 150 by 148 centimetres, so the party fills the canvas at almost life size, with the feline family mirroring the human one.
context: Hofstede de Groot listed this canvas as no. 525 in his 1908 Steen catalogue. Steen (1625/26–1679) painted it around 1660, and the Museum of Fine Arts in Budapest, inv. 337, titles it Merry Company in a Pergola (The 'Cat Family'). Fun fact: it spent June 1945 to December 1946 at the Munich Central Collecting Point, the Allied depot where looted and displaced art was sorted after the Second World War, before going back to Hungary.
title_eng: Merry Company in a Pergola (The 'Cat Family')
image_credit: Jan Steen · Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"/s/steen/page2/m_party"

title: Woman Eating, Known as 'The Cat's Breakfast'
title_original: Het ontbijt van de kat (Vrouw die een kat voert)
description: Forepaws against the woman's skirt, a grey tabby rears up at lower left, reaching for the scrap she lowers from her plate. Her breakfast is herring and bread, and she is sharing it. A water pump stands at the left, a dead hen lies over a barrel in the foreground, and a vase of tulips and white blooms sits on a little table at right. The stems and leaves now look blue because the yellow in the original green has faded. The picture is officially titled Woman Eating, which gives the cat a starring role it has no right to.
context: Herring with bread, washed down with beer, was an everyday 17th-century breakfast, which the Rijksmuseum notes is exactly what the woman is eating. Metsu painted this panel in Amsterdam around 1661 to 1664 and signed it 'G. Metsu' at the top. The painting belongs to the city of Amsterdam, which lent it to the Rijksmuseum in March 1892; it has since travelled to Leiden (1966), Tokyo (2007) and the Metsu retrospective in Dublin and Washington (2010-11). Its nickname, Le Déjeuner du chat, has made the cat the star of a picture officially titled Woman Eating.
title_eng: Woman Eating, Known as 'The Cat's Breakfast'
image_credit: Gabriel Metsu · www.rijksmuseum.nl : Home : Info : Pic

title: Children Teaching a Cat to Dance, Known as 'The Dancing Lesson'
title_original: De dansles (Kinderen leren een kat dansen)
submovement: Dutch Golden Age Comedic Genre & Moral Didacticism
description: The household cat, mostly white, dangles by its forepaws from the hands of a grinning boy in a red hat, made to step to the tune. A gang of children has decided it should learn to dance. A girl in a blue skirt plays the shawm, the loud, reedy ancestor of the oboe, and a spotted dog leaps up at the cat. A man looks down on the whole business from a small window above, and a lute hangs on the wall at right. Steen keeps the scale domestic, on a panel 68.5 by 59 centimetres, and the cat, unwilling dancer, is the only one not laughing.
context: A mischievous prank: that is how the Rijksmuseum sums up the scene, which is fair. Steen (1625/26–1679), the great comic narrator of Dutch genre, painted this panel sometime between 1660 and 1679 and signed it 'JSteen'. The picture came to the museum in 1880 with the bequest of Jonkheer J.S.H. van de Poll of Amsterdam. Fun detail: the museum's own Dutch and English texts do not quite agree, since the Dutch description also has a dog barking at the scene, while the English says nothing about it.
title_eng: Children Teaching a Cat to Dance, Known as 'The Dancing Lesson'
feline_symbolism: Teaching a cat to dance was a byword for useless effort and childish folly, the kind of misbehaviour Steen loved to stage.
image_credit: Jane023 · Own work

title: A Cat Overturning a Vase of Flowers
title_original: Le Chat renversant un vase de fleurs
description: A strangely human face, eyes wide and mouth open in a yowl, pops up at lower left, with one paw on a wooden mousetrap. The cat went for a mouse, and the bouquet it was meant to ignore is on the brink: a honeysuckle sprig and an ear of wheat have already slipped over the stone ledge, and water splashes at the foot of the vase. Striped tulips and roses burst out of the dark above. Everything is painted with Mignon's hard, petal-by-petal clarity, so the accident lands on a picture built to look perfectly still. The canvas is about 89 x 70 cm.
context: Lyon has turned this alarmed, human-nosed cat into its online mascot. Mignon (1640–1679) came from Frankfurt and worked in Utrecht, where he followed his master Jan Davidsz. de Heem but gave his flowers firmer form and colour. The Rijksmuseum owns a close variant, The Overturned Bouquet (SK-A-267), signed 'A. Mignon: fe.', with the same cat, trap and toppled vase. The Lyon museum also points out that the cat-and-mousetrap motif has been compared to an emblem in the Emblemata amatoria, where the mouse stands for a man who can live neither with love nor without it.
title_eng: A Cat Overturning a Vase of Flowers (The Mousetrap)
submovement: Dutch Golden Age flower still life (circle of Jan Davidsz. de Heem)
feline_symbolism: Lyon reads the spilled water and falling blooms as a last vanitas allegory, with the cat as the bringer of the disorder that ends all earthly beauty.
image_credit: Abraham Mignon · Œuvre appartenant au Musée des Beaux-Arts de Lyon

title: Children Teaching a Cat to Read
description: A grey-and-white cat is being taught to read, which goes about as well as you would expect: a boy in a feathered cap pins it in his arms while a girl on a low seat holds the open book up to its face and lifts her other hand like a schoolmistress. Another boy grins from behind the table at right, and an older girl looks on, smiling. Steen stages the lesson on a small panel, about 45 × 35.5 cm, and the joke works because the cat stays entirely a cat while the children treat it as a pupil. Children playing at school are, at that moment, skipping the real thing.
context: A Sotheby's note on a painting by a follower of Steen proposes that its composition was conceived as a pendant to this Basel cat-reading picture, which shows how quickly the subject was copied. Steen (1625/26–1679), the Leiden painter of noisy households, painted this oil on panel around 1665 to 1668. It is in the Kunstmuseum Basel (inv. G 1958.39), not the Rijksmuseum. He returned to the idea of children drilling a cat more than once: the Rijksmuseum's Children Teaching a Cat to Dance (SK-A-718) has a girl playing a shawm while the cat screeches, a dog barks and an old man scolds from a window.
title_eng: Children Teaching a Cat to Read
image_credit: Jan Steen · http://sammlungonline.kunstmuseumbasel.ch

title: Cat and Rock (猫石图卷)
artist: Bada Shanren (Zhu Da, 八大山人 / 朱耷)
description: The plump, sleepy cat is tiny in this view of the whole scroll: a soft ink shape curled on top of a rock left of centre, while the rest of the paper fills with broad dark leaves, flowers and grasses, punctuated by red seals. The scroll is 34 cm high and about 2.18 m long, made to be unrolled an arm's length at a time from right to left, so the cat arrives as a surprise somewhere along the way. Bada Shanren builds fur and stone from washes of different density, pale under dark, so the animal and its perch share the same soft weight.
context: A descendant of the Ming imperial house who became a monk after the dynasty fell, Bada Shanren (Zhu Da, 1626–1705) turned into one of the great individualist painters of the early Qing. This handscroll is in the Palace Museum, Beijing (新00077585). In 2026 the Palace Museum lent a group of his late works, including a Cat, Rock and Flowers handscroll, to Nanchang for the 400th anniversary of his birth. Fun fact: a China Daily reading of the cat calls it 'chubby and sleepy' and sees in it both a leisurely life and a painter looking for inner peace after years of anger and worry.
image_credit: Bada Shanren · https://minghuaji.dpm.org.cn/paint/detail?id=fe46cad67fd84873bff14d6bbf16e207

title: Cat (One of a Pair)
description: Curled into neat ovals, two black cats poke out small pale tongues at each other; this entry is one of the pair, photographed here side by side. Each is a porcelain cat about 12.4 cm tall, coated in black enamel so that it reads as a sleek black animal, and the two were made as matching ornaments. The round, goggling eyes are not original: the museum records them as a modern plastic repair, so the stare is a twentieth-century replacement. Tails wrap round the flanks, and one cat has an opening in its back.
context: Producing this cat in the eighteenth century under the Qing dynasty was Jingdezhen, the great porcelain centre of Jiangxi province. It came to the Metropolitan Museum in 1931 with the Friedsam Collection, the bequest of Michael Friedsam. The Met's own title is simply 'Cat (one of a pair)', and its medium line records 'modern plastic repair of eyes'. Fun fact: that repair means the wide-eyed stare that gives these cats their comic charm is a twentieth-century addition, and the original gaze is unknown.
medium: Porcelain with black enamel (Jingdezhen ware), modern plastic repair of eyes
collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
submovement: Qing dynasty Jingdezhen black-enamelled porcelain figure
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Still Life with Cat and Fish
title_original: Nature morte au chat et aux poissons
description: Calico, white with ginger and black patches, the cat crouches on a stone ledge at left with one paw pinning a cut fish on a dish, and looks straight at us as if caught. Above, two fish hang from a single hook against the wall. Chardin lets those hanging fish cut down through the horizontal shelf, so the eye drops from scales to fur. A brass mortar and pestle, an onion and a spring onion sit at right. The paint is laid on thickly in warm colour; Thyssen notes that later painters admired how he handled the fish scales and the cat's coat. The canvas is 79.5 × 63 cm, signed and dated 1728.
context: Rémond, a former royal maître d'hôtel, is the first known owner of this pair of 1728 canvases: they were auctioned after his death in 1778 and later passed through the Beurnonville and Rothschild collections, until the Thyssen-Bornemisza collection bought them in 1986. The companion is Still-Life with Cat and Rayfish, and variants of the pair are in the Nelson-Atkins Museum in Kansas and the Burrell Collection in Glasgow. Fun fact: literature before 1979 misread the date as 1758, which would have made it a late work; Pierre Rosenberg corrected it to 1728 for that year's Chardin exhibition.
title_eng: Still Life with Cat and Fish
image_credit: Jean-Baptiste-Siméon Chardin · https://www.museothyssen.org/en/collection/artists/chardin-jean-baptiste-simeon/still-life-cat-and-fish

title: The Ray (La Raie)
description: To the left, a white-and-tabby cat with arched back and tail straight up picks its way over a heap of opened oysters, ears back, half thief and half alarmed by the sight above it. The ray hangs gutted from a hook in the middle of the wall, and its pale underside reads like a face with a grin. On the white cloth to the right sit a copper pan, a dark stoneware jug, a bottle and a knife balanced over the edge. The canvas is large, 114 × 146 cm, and the cat is small, which makes its nerves all the funnier.
context: On 3 June 1728, a few hours of open-air exhibition at the corner of Place Dauphine and the Pont Neuf, the Exposition de la Jeunesse, gave The Ray its first public outing. On 25 September that year the Académie royale chose it, with The Buffet, as Chardin's reception pieces and admitted him the same day. It stayed with the Académie until the Revolution and then entered the Louvre (INV 3197). Fun fact: it has collected strong opinions ever since: Diderot found it disgusting, Matisse admired it, and Proust compared the opened skate to the nave of a polychromatic cathedral.
image_credit: Sailko · Own work

title: The Cat and the Two Sparrows
title_original: Le Chat et les deux moineaux
submovement: French Rococo book illustration (Oudry's La Fontaine Fables)
description: On the tiled floor a cat crouches with a sparrow clamped in its jaws, tail hooked up behind, while a second bird lies at lower left. Above it the birdcage on the console table stands empty, its little door open. This is the engraved plate for La Fontaine's fable of the cat who grew up beside a sparrow, ate a stranger sparrow, and then his old friend. A tablet at the bottom names it 'LE CHAT ET LES DEUX MOINEAUX. Fable CCXV.', and the lines below credit 'J. B. Oudry inv.' at left and 'J. Duret sculp.' at right. Burin over etching turns Oudry's wash drawing into crisp lines and cross-hatching.
context: Fable CCXV in the Desaint & Saillant edition of La Fontaine's Fables choisies (Paris, 1755–1759) is Book XII, fable 2, and the plate is signed 'J. B. Oudry inv.' and 'J. Duret sculp.': Oudry drew it, Pierre-Jacques Duret cut it in copper. The BnF's digitised copy on Gallica is the source of the image shown here. Fun fact: La Fontaine gives the cat in this fable the name Raton, the same name he uses for the cat in The Monkey and the Cat.
title_eng: The Cat and the Two Sparrows (Fables de La Fontaine)
feline_symbolism: In La Fontaine's fable the cat stands for appetite dressed up as loyalty: it avenges its friend and then eats him too.
image_credit: Pierre-Jacques Duret / After Jean-Baptiste Oudry · This file comes from Gallica Digital Library and is available under the digital ID bpt6k1049446f/f147

title: La Toilette (Woman Fastening Her Garter)
description: At the young woman's feet, a small ginger cat sprawls on its side and looks straight out at us, one paw near a ball of wool or twine stolen from the blue sewing bag hanging on the fire screen, the thread trailing across the floor. Above, the young woman ties her garter while her maid, seen from behind, offers her a cap. The room is a pile-up of yellow silk walls, a gold Chinese screen with birds, a fan, bellows, a brush and loose fabric, with a fire going in the grate. The cat is the only figure making more mess than the sitter.
context: Count Carl Gustaf Tessin, Swedish ambassador in Paris, bought La Toilette directly from Boucher for 648 livres, and it reached Stockholm in June 1742. After his death it was auctioned in 1771, then passed through Swedish and Viennese Rothschild collections and appeared on the New York market in 1967, from where it entered the Thyssen-Bornemisza collection. Fun fact: the woman was once thought to be Boucher's wife, Marie-Jeanne Buzot, but the Thyssen notes that her portraits, such as the one in the Frick, look nothing like this figure and that showing a wife so undressed would have been indecorous.
image_credit: François Boucher · Musée du Louvre

title: The Graham Children
description: Behind the chair at right, a grey tabby hauls itself up over the back, claws hooked on the top rail, and fixes its eyes on the goldfinch in the gilded cage above. The bird flinches. Below, the four Graham children perform for us: Richard Robert turns a little bird organ painted with Orpheus and grins up at the cage, Anna Maria lifts her flowered silk skirts to dance, and Henrietta dangles a bunch of cherries toward baby Thomas in his little carriage. A clock topped by a cherub with scythe and hourglass reads about 1.45. Life-size, 160.5 x 181 cm.
context: Apothecary to George I and George II, Daniel Graham had his children painted by Hogarth at their home at 11 Pall Mall; the canvas is signed and dated 1742 and is one of the largest pictures Hogarth made. The National Gallery suggests the portrait was commissioned because the baby, Thomas, had already died; Hogarth based his face on a chalk study made after death, now in the British Museum. The picture passed through the Graham and Watson Taylor families and the Earls of Normanton before Lord Duveen gave it to the Gallery in 1934.
feline_symbolism: The National Gallery reads the cat stalking the caged goldfinch as a hint of how suddenly death took one of the Graham children from their prosperous home.
image_credit: William Hogarth · The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

title: A Girl with a Kitten
medium: Pastel on blue paper, mounted on canvas
description: A grey-and-white kitten with round amber eyes peeps up from the girl's hands at lower left, and both of them have plainly been told to sit still. The girl turns her head to the left in near profile, a striped blue bow at her throat. The sheet is pastel on blue paper, later laid down on canvas, 59.1 × 49.8 cm. The face is blended with the stump instead of drawn with the point of the crayon, and it has none of the white highlights you would expect from Perronneau, which gives the girl a soft, slightly unfocused look. The kitten is the most alert creature in the picture.
context: 'Probably by' is the National Gallery's hedge on this pastel: it catalogues it as probably by Jean-Baptiste Perronneau (1715/16–1783) and dates it 1743, although it bears a signature and the date 1745. The Nevill family owned it until Sir Joseph Duveen bought it and presented it to the Gallery in 1921. The Gallery reads the unidentified sitter as an idealised portrait, not a genre scene. Fun fact: the doubts are technical. The face is blended with the stump instead of drawn with the point, the anatomy is weak for an artist who won the Académie's first prize for drawing after the model in 1734, and if genuine it would be his earliest dated pastel; yet the materials are certainly eighteenth-century and nothing suggests later reworking.
feline_symbolism: The National Gallery notes that cats in children's portraits sometimes stand for the wildness of nature pressing in on childhood innocence.
image_credit: After Jean-Baptiste Perronneau · Copy of a painting of Jean-Baptiste Perronneau .

title: Knife Handle (Kozuka)
medium: Copper-silver alloy (shibuichi), iron, gold, silver, copper
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: A plump cat lies curled on this narrow strip of metal, under 10 cm long and 1.4 cm wide, front paws tucked forward and eyes on a small gold butterfly hovering out of reach at left. Beside it blooms a silvery-blue peony with gold and copper leaves. The ground is shibuichi, the grey copper-silver alloy Japanese metalworkers prized for its soft, matte tone, split by a diagonal into a pale upper field and a dark russet lower one; the picture is built up in iron, gold, silver and copper, each metal chosen for its colour. At this scale the cat is a few millimetres of inlay. It weighs 28 grams.
context: A kozuka is the handle of the small utility knife that slides into a pocket on the side of a sword scabbard, and owners swapped and collected them as miniature pictures. This one is unsigned and dated by the Met only to the Edo period, ca. 1615–1868. It came to the museum in 1929 with the bequest of Mrs. H. O. Havemeyer, part of a large group of Japanese sword fittings now in the Arms and Armor department. Fun fact: the Met catalogues a sword fitting like this as arms and armour, so a cat with a butterfly lives in the same department as plate armour.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Cat
description: A small seated cat, 12.7 cm high, lifts its plain cream head to one side with two dark dot eyes and big upright ears, while its body is swirled with chocolate-brown stripes like a marbled tabby. That marbling is agateware, the trick of wedging clays of different colours together so the pattern runs right through the body, and the Met's catalogue links this cat with it. It is salt-glazed stoneware from around 1745: salt thrown into the kiln at full heat vaporises and fuses with the clay, leaving a thin, faintly pitted skin of glaze. It weighs about half a kilo, so it sits firmly wherever it is put.
context: English potters of the 1740s made little salt-glazed animals alongside their teapots and jugs, and most of these figures were never marked. The Met owns three cats of this kind, all dated about 1745 (34.165.18, .19 and .20), given in 1934 by Carleton Macy; this is the middle one in size. Fun fact: the three are 11.4, 12.7 and 15.4 cm tall, yet the museum records each as weighing about one pound, so the smallest cat is, proportionally, the most solid of the set.
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Magdaleine Pinceloup de la Grange, née de Parseval
title_original: Magdaleine Pinceloup de la Grange, née de Parseval
collection: The J. Paul Getty Museum, Los Angeles
description: Madame Pinceloup sits bolt upright, back parallel to her chair without touching it, and cradles a large grey-blue cat in the crook of her arm. The cat looks straight at us with mild bemusement, round yellow eyes and all, which is more than its owner manages; she gazes off to the left. Her dress is trimmed with flowers and blue ribbons, and the little gold bells on the cat's collar answer the pearls at her throat. The Getty identifies the cat as a Chartreux from its size and colour. Perronneau's signature and date sit at right, level with her ribbon. Oil on canvas, 65.1 × 52.4 cm.
context: A signature and '1747' fill the right margin of this oil, which has a companion portrait of the sitter's husband, Charles-François Pinceloup de la Grange, in which he looks more at ease than she does. The Getty acquired the picture in 1984 (84.PA.665) and identifies the cat as a Chartreux by its size and colour.
