Fun fact: Perronneau put cats into several portraits of women and girls, among them Marie-Anne Huquier with a kitten at the Louvre and the girl in the National Gallery pastel, and the Getty argues the cats underline the sitters' elegance; here the cat's bells answer the pearls at her throat.
title_eng: Magdaleine Pinceloup de la Grange, née de Parseval
feline_symbolism: The Getty reads the Chartreux, one of the oldest French breeds, as a mark of refinement, its collar bells rhyming with the sitter's pearls so that both appear as elegant objects for looking at.
image_credit: Jean-Baptiste Perronneau · http://www.getty.edu/art/collection/objects/747/

title: The Trapped Cat and the Frightened Mouse (Rat ?), Folio from a Kalila wa Dimna
title_original: صورة السنور في الشبكة والجرذ يخاطبه
culture: India, Gujarat (probably after an Egyptian original)
submovement: Illustrated Arabic Kalila wa Dimna manuscript painting, second quarter 16th century
medium: Folio from an illustrated manuscript; ink and opaque watercolor on paper
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: Caught in the hunter's net, drawn as a neat brown grid, stands a pale cat with dark spots, an orange collar and a curled tail. Just outside the mesh a dark, long-eared creature in a matching collar faces it, a blue animal slinks under the tree, and a big-eyed owl perches at top right. The Met hedges the rodent as mouse or rat with a question mark. The painting shares the page with Arabic text, a line of it in red; the leaf is 31.8 × 22.6 cm, with a text block of about 21.9 × 12.4 cm. The style is flat, all clear outlines and solid colour.
context: An illustrated Arabic Kalila wa Dimna, the book of animal fables descended from the Indian Panchatantra, supplied this folio, which the Met dates to the second quarter of the sixteenth century. It entered the Met in 1981 with the Alice and Nasli Heeramaneck Collection, a gift of Alice Heeramaneck. Fun fact: the Met's own title keeps the zoological doubt on record, 'the Frightened Mouse (Rat ?)'.
title_eng: The Trapped Cat and the Frightened Mouse (Rat ?), Folio from a Kalila wa Dimna
image_credit: This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the Metropolitan Museum of Art . See the Image and Data Resources Open Access Policy

title: Myojakdo (Cats and Sparrows)
medium: Hanging scroll; ink and light color on silk
description: A tree full of sparrows, and two cats working out how to reach them: a grey tabby with white paws clings halfway up the trunk, claws splayed on the bark, and turns its face out toward us with round yellow eyes, tail swinging free, while a black-and-white cat sits in the grass below, head tipped straight up. The sparrows, six of them according to the museum, perch in the branches above the cropped view shown here. Byeon paints it in ink and light colour on silk, 93.7 × 42.9 cm, a tall, narrow format that lets the climb run from the bottom of the scroll to the top. The fur is built from fine, close brushstrokes.
context: Cat (myo) and sparrow (jak) sound like Sino-Korean words for 'old age' (mo, a person of 80 or 90) and 'magpie' (jak, an auspicious bird), so the pairing was a Joseon wish for long life. The National Museum of Korea, which bought the scroll in 1908, catalogues it as Deoksu 1003, attributed to Byeon Sang-byeok and dated to the 18th century. Fun fact: Byeon was a court portraitist who helped paint King Yeongjo, yet his cats and chickens earned him the nicknames 'Byeon Cat' and 'Byeon Rooster'.
image_credit: 국립중앙박물관 · https://www.emuseum.go.kr/detail?cateClass=&cateListFlag=&keyword=%EB%B3%80%EC%83%81%EB%B2%BD&pageNum=8&rows=9&reltRows=10&sort=&highQualityYn=&isImgExistOp=&mckoglsvOp=&isIntrstMuseumOp=&filedOp=&detailFlag=&dq=&ps01Lv1=&ps01Lv2=

title: The Four Stages of Cruelty: First Stage of Cruelty
title_original: The Four Stages of Cruelty: First Stage of Cruelty (Plate 1)
collection: Yale Center for British Art, New Haven
description: Cats get the worst of this street. Over the wall at left, two cats hung by their tails from a lamp bracket claw at each other while a crowd of boys jeers. In the bottom left corner a dog is set on a cat whose entrails spill onto the cobbles. High up at the back, another cat, tied to a pair of bladders, is flung from a garret window. In the centre Tom Nero forces an arrow into a dog while a better-dressed boy offers his tart to make him stop, and the verses below spell out the moral. The line work is deliberately coarse.
context: Cheap prints for cheap seats: Hogarth wanted The Four Stages of Cruelty within reach of 'men of the lowest rank', so he kept the engraving deliberately rough and sold ordinary impressions at a shilling each. Published on 21 February 1751 with verses by the Rev. James Townley, the set was meant to shame the casual torture of animals on London streets; he had first commissioned woodcuts, which proved too costly. Yale's impression is the one shown here. Fun fact: the soft-hearted boy offering his tart is traditionally said to be the twelve-year-old Prince George, later George III.
title_eng: The Four Stages of Cruelty: First Stage of Cruelty
image_credit: William Hogarth · ewEJT9oTA1U1_A at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

title: Cat and Mouse (toy)
description: A grey-striped white cat sits up on its haunches and clutches a mauve mouse to its chest with both forepaws, green eyes rolled skyward as if butter would not melt. The whole animal is a cabinet trinket only 7.6 cm tall, with a gilt mount at the neck whose enamel band is lettered MIGNONE, French for dainty or darling. The stripes are brushed on in dark hatching over glassy white porcelain, with coral pink on nose and ear linings. The oval base, ringed by a scalloped gold rim, carries a brown and purple mound and a spray of painted flowers. Small enough to close a hand around, it is built to be turned over and admired.
context: Charles Gouyn was a jeweller in St James's, London, and the V&A says his porcelain factory was the first in England to make scent bottles, bodkin cases and similar trinkets, which people at the time called 'toys'. The Met catalogues this cat as a two-part object (the 'a, b' in its accession number) made around 1755, with an enamel mount inscribed MIGNONE; it came from R. W. M. Walker to the collector Irwin Untermyer, who gave it in 1964. Fun fact: Gouyn had helped Nicholas Sprimont set up the Chelsea porcelain factory around 1745 before starting his own, so these St James's cats are close cousins of the Chelsea ones.
submovement: London soft-paste porcelain 'toys' (Saint James's Factory, Charles Gouyn)
medium: Soft-paste porcelain with enamel and metal mount
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
feline_symbolism: On a sister bottle the motto 'Cruelle et belle' turns the cat with its prey into a flirtatious emblem of a beautiful, heartless lover.
image_credit: Saint James's Factory · The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of Irwin Untermyer, 1964 (CC0, Open Access); via Wikimedia Commons

title: The Painter's Daughters with a Cat
title_original: The Painter's Daughters with a Cat
description: Barely there, the cat is a ghostly ochre head with two dark eyes floating against the elder girl's yellow sleeve, a few strokes never taken further. Margaret, in front, cradles it while her older sister Mary wraps her arms around her, partly to help hold the squirming animal and, it seems, to pull its tail. The girls' faces are finished, Margaret's lips pursed as she eyes us sideways; almost everything else is not. Feathery gold, blue and grey strokes around them suggest storm clouds, sun and trees. Loose drawn lines still show in the unfinished hands and dress. Oil on canvas, 75.6 × 62.9 cm.
context: Bath, a year or so after the family moved there in late 1759, is where the National Gallery places this double portrait of Mary and Margaret Gainsborough, probably painted about 1760–1. It stayed in the family, passing from the sisters to the heirs of their aunt Susannah Gardiner, until Christie's sold it on 11 May 1923 and Knoedler bought it for 3,045 guineas and sold it on to the Gallery that year. Fun fact: the sketched cat was partly painted out in a yellow that does not match Mary's dress; when Richard Lane issued a lithograph around 1827 as The Orphans, he left the cat out entirely.
title_eng: The Painter's Daughters with a Cat
image_credit: Thomas Gainsborough · Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"/g/gainsbor/03daught"

title: Gukjeong chumyo: Autumn Cat in a Garden with Chrysanthemums
medium: Ink and light color on paper
description: A spotted cat crouches in an autumn garden beside a spray of chrysanthemums, ears up, gazing hard at something off to the left that we cannot see. Its coat is grey tabby stripes broken by big black patches, every hair laid in with a fine brush, and its yellow eyes are the brightest note on the sheet. Tucked and coiled, it could be wary or a second from pouncing. The painting is small, 29.5 × 23.4 cm, in ink with light colour on paper, and the rusty-pink flowers and grasses stay loose and airy so the attention goes to the solid little animal beneath them.
context: Nicknamed 'Byeon Cat' and 'Byeon Rooster', the Joseon court painter Byeon Sang-byeok was so associated with animals that the names stuck. Gukjeong chumyo, 'Autumn cat in a garden with chrysanthemums', is in the Kansong Art Museum, Seoul, the collection built by Jeon Hyeong-pil to keep Korean art in Korea. Fun fact: Byeon was also a sought-after portraitist who helped paint King Yeongjo twice, in 1763 and 1773, yet his surviving reputation rests mostly on cats like this one.
title_eng: Autumn Cat in a Garden with Chrysanthemums
image_credit: Byeon Sang-byeok or Hwajae (Byeon's pen name) · [1] Image scanned from a pamphlet published from Gansong Art Museum.

title: Beautiful Woman Playing with a Cat
medium: Hanging scroll; ink and color on silk
collection: Museum of Far Eastern Antiquities (Östasiatiska museet), Stockholm
description: Tiny and busy, a white kitten with a red ribbon rolls on the veranda boards at lower left, clawing at a flowered ball. A young woman in a long-sleeved furisode kimono, red over a pale robe sprinkled with blue irises, steps from a doorway holding the red string tied to it. That is the whole drama, painted at the scale of a person: the scroll is about 179 cm tall, in ink and bright colours on silk. Beyond the veranda sit low stones and bamboo, painted in the manner of the Kano school, a polite nod to the official style framing a very unofficial game.
context: Hand-painted scrolls, not prints, were the medium of Tsukioka Settei (1710–1786), a leading painter of beautiful women in Osaka. The Stockholm museum catalogues this one as a vertical scroll of the 1770s (OM-1984-0020), and it was shown in its 2011 exhibition Japan: Objects and Images Tell Stories, which traced the lives of samurai, merchants and craftspeople through more than 300 Edo-period objects. Fun fact: the museum's own description spells out the game, with the kitten playing with a flowered ball that the woman holds on a red string while the garden outside is painted in the formal Kano style.
title_eng: Beautiful Woman Playing with a Cat
submovement: Edo Period Kamigata School Bijin Painting
image_credit: Tsukioka Masanobu Settei (1710 - 1786) Details on Google Art Project · xgHA8xy1UPu5vQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

title: Figure of a Girl with Cat
artist: Nymphenburg Porcelain Factory, model probably by Dominicus Auliczek
collection: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland
description: Up on a rococo scroll arch, the cat has the high ground, one paw raised, peering across at a girl in a broad-brimmed hat who stands by a column and gazes straight up at it. The group, 24.5 cm high, was made at the Nymphenburg factory outside Munich around 1770 and left in plain white glaze, so everything reads through light and shadow. It is modelled in the round, the cat still legible from behind, meant to stand on a table or mantel where people would pick it up and turn it.
context: Dr. Kurt Rossacher of Salzburg owned this figure before Severance and Greta Millikin of Cleveland acquired it in 1962; it reached the Cleveland Museum of Art with Mrs. Millikin's bequest in 1989 (1989.185). The museum credits the model, probably, to Dominicus Auliczek (1734–1804), and gives the factory as Nymphenburg, founded in 1747. Fun fact: it went on view in 'The Severance and Greta Millikin Collection', a Cleveland exhibition that ran from 5 July to 2 September 1990.
title_eng: Figure of a Girl with Cat
image_credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Nekomata: The Fork-Tailed Monster Cat (Gazu Hyakki Yagyō)
title_original: 画図百鬼夜行: 猫股 (ねこまた)
description: Laid out on one page, three cats read like a before-and-after. At lower left an ordinary cat pokes its face out by the lattice of a shōji screen. On the right a cat with a hand towel over its head rests its front paws on the veranda, not quite able to stand. In the middle a striped third cat, also toweled, rears fully upright on two legs, forepaws up as if mid-dance. Above them hangs a round ornament sprouting a spray of leaves. Black ink only, cut into a woodblock and printed, so the drama comes from line and from the bare white paper.
context: Three volumes, Yin, Yang and Wind, make up Gazu Hyakki Yagyō ('The Illustrated Night Parade of a Hundred Demons'), published by Toriyama Sekien in 1776. The nekomata, the old cat that grows a forked tail and supernatural powers, appears in Yin. Sekien drew heavily on Sawaki Sūshi's 1737 painted scroll Hyakkai Zukan, but his innovation was to put the monsters into a cheap, reprintable book. Fun fact: the first written nekomata, in Fujiwara no Teika's diary Meigetsuki in 1233, was a mountain beast with cat's eyes and a dog-sized body, a long way from this towel-wearing dancer.
title_eng: Nekomata: The Fork-Tailed Monster Cat (Gazu Hyakki Yagyō)
medium: Woodblock-printed book illustration; ink on paper
collection: Smithsonian Libraries (digitised copy on Internet Archive)
feline_symbolism: The nekomata stands for the fear that a cat kept too long will grow uncanny; folk belief linked such cats with stealing corpses.
location: Tokyo National Museum / National Diet Library
image_credit: Toriyama Sekien · http://www.linet.gr.jp/

title: Kasha (from Gazu Hyakki Yagyō)
title_original: 今昔画図続百鬼: 火車
description: The kasha comes out of a storm cloud to steal a corpse, and in Sekien's hands it is a shaggy cat-demon, wild-maned and wide-eyed, rearing on clawed hind feet. Sekien draws it in black ink for a woodblock-printed book, so everything depends on contrast: the dark, boiling cloud built from stippled dots, ribbons of flame trailing off to the right, and the white of the paper around it. A bushy tail swings down between its legs. It is a single page from a cheap illustrated encyclopedia of monsters, and it shows how a fear about funerals could be fixed into one memorable image.
context: 'Fire cart' is the literal meaning of kasha, a yōkai said to steal corpses. It began as a blazing vehicle, then a demon-like warden carrying sinners to Buddhist hell, and by the late seventeenth century it had merged with legends of the corpse-stealing nekomata and taken on a cat's shape. Toriyama Sekien illustrated it as a cat in his 1776 Gazu Hyakki Yagyō, and that picture helped fix the look. Fun fact: in the folktale type neko danka ('cat patron'), the kasha is a cat only play-acting, to win its temple abbot a rich funeral.
medium: Woodblock-printed book illustration; ink on paper
collection: Smithsonian Libraries (digitised copy on Internet Archive)
feline_symbolism: The cat-kasha draws on the belief that cats were drawn to corpses, making the cat the thief that robs the dead of a proper funeral.
image_credit: Toriyama Sekien · scanned from ISBN 4-0440-5101-1 .

title: Woman with a Cat
title_original: بانویی با گربه (Zand Dynasty Woman with a Cat)
collection: Shangri La Museum of Islamic Art, Culture & Design (Doris Duke Foundation for Islamic Art), Honolulu, Hawaii
description: At the woman's feet, in the lower right corner, a pale, round-faced cat sits with huge eyes fixed on us and a thin tail curling over the carpet. A full-length figure fills a canvas more than one and a half metres tall and not even ninety centimetres wide, a proportion that makes sense once you know Zand painters cut canvases to slot into palace wall niches; the pointed arch at the top still traces one. She raises a wine glass beside a bowl of red fruit and a glass flask. Shangri La catalogues the picture simply as Woman with a Cat, and the cat earns the billing.
context: Made in Iran in the late eighteenth century, under the Zand rulers (c. 1751–1794), this painting belongs to an age when large oil paintings decorated palace walls. Sotheby's notes on a comparable Zand canvas that paintings were cut to fit wall niches and that this shape was common in Zand royal residences. Doris Duke acquired it for Shangri La, her Honolulu house, now a museum of Islamic art, where it carries accession number 34.8. Fun fact: the picture lives a double life online. The museum's Google Arts & Culture record calls it Woman with a Cat, while Wikimedia Commons titles the same canvas Cupbearer with a Cat, a sign that the androgynous beauties of Persian painting regularly confuse cataloguers.
image_credit: Anonymous Unknown author · https://artsandculture.google.com/asset/woman-with-a-cat-unknown/gwG4RAuhI5R8WA

title: Portrait of Julia Manteuffel née Duhamel with a Cat
description: A fluffy white cat lies cradled in Julia Duhamel's arms, head tipped back to gaze up and away, one pink-padded paw resting on her forearm. She smiles out at us under a blue-ribboned cap. The oval is a compact oil on canvas, about 65 by 52 cm, and the cat made it into the Polish title: Portret Julii z Duhamelów Manteuffel z kotem, 'with a cat'. A pet in a young sitter's arms was a standard trick for loosening up a formal portrait, and a press photo of the picture from the 2018 Warsaw exhibition was simply captioned Julia Duhamel with a Cat.
context: Curator Dorota Juszczak called Marcello Bacciarelli (1731–1818), the Rome-born court painter to Poland's last king, Stanisław August, 'a sort of Matejko of the eighteenth century' when she opened 'Marcello Bacciarelli. Najpiękniejsze portrety' at the Royal Castle in Warsaw in June 2018, marking two hundred years since his death. This portrait travelled there from the Raczyński Foundation collection at the National Museum in Poznań (inv. FR 722). Fun fact: the castle supplied the online image, which is likely why an earlier catalogue entry parked the painting in Warsaw.
title_eng: Portrait of Julia Manteuffel née Duhamel with a Cat
title_original: Portret Julii z Duhamelów Manteuffel z kotem
image_credit: Marcello Bacciarelli · www.zamek-krolewski.pl

title: The Angora Cat
description: A long-haired white Angora is the star, and it is busy: up on its hind legs on a rug-draped table, paws pressed to a glass gazing globe, ready to attack its own reflection. Around it the studio piles on textures for contrast: the young woman's pale yellow satin rendered fold by fold and a brightly coloured, long-fringed Turkish rug spilling off the table edge. She rests one hand on the globe and holds a fan in the other. Check the shadows: a man peers round the door, and a little spaniel scampers in at lower left. The canvas is a modest 65 by 53.5 cm.
context: Acquired in 2011 as a gift from the city of Cologne for the museum's 150th anniversary (WRM 3652), the picture is dated c. 1783–85 and labelled by the Wallraf-Richartz-Museum as Jean-Honoré Fragonard's (1732–1806). Many writers credit it jointly to his sister-in-law and pupil Marguerite Gérard (1761–1837), who went to live with him at fourteen. Fun fact: Gérard and Fragonard made nine etchings together in 1778, and historians now believe she alone made five of them.
feline_symbolism: Angoras, the first long-haired cats known in Europe, were favourites at the French court from Louis XIII to Louis XVI, so the breed itself signals luxury.
image_credit: Jean-Honoré Fragonard / Marguerite Gérard · Rheinisches Bildarchiv Köln/Wallraf-Richartz-Museum&Fondation Corboud/Foto:Britta Schlier

title: Hwangmyo nongjeop: Yellow Cat Frolicking with a Butterfly
description: An orange-and-white cat crouches at the lower right of the sheet, body pulled tight, head twisted round to track a black butterfly fluttering above. At the left a rock is built up with soft, dry strokes, and red pinks (dianthus) grow beside it over pale green grass. The butterfly's wings get the sharpest brushwork in the picture, as if Kim wanted it to be the one thing the cat, and we, cannot stop looking at. The cat's striped tail stretches out stiffly behind it, the one part not yet committed to the chase. A vertical inscription and seals sit at the upper right.
context: Cats stood for the age of seventy and butterflies for eighty in old Korea, so this pairing may well be a birthday wish for a long life. That reading comes from Baik In-san, a senior curator at the Kansong Art Museum, who floated it as a possible gift. Kim Hong-do (1745–1806), known as Danwon, painted for the Joseon court. The leaf was among about 80 flower, bird and animal paintings from the Kansong collection shown at Seoul's Dongdaemun Design Plaza in 2015. Fun fact: until it began showing at the Plaza, Kansong, Korea's first private museum, held just two two-week exhibitions a year, so a public outing like this was rare.
title_eng: Yellow Cat Frolicking with a Butterfly
medium: Album leaf; ink and light color on paper
submovement: Late Joseon court painting (Dohwaseo painter, animal and flower subject)
feline_symbolism: Following Chinese wordplay, the cat stood for age seventy and the butterfly for age eighty, so together they wish the recipient a long life.
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons

title: The Cat's Lunch
description: A big long-haired cat, white with brown and black patches, sits on a red tasselled stool and is already lapping from the plate a young girl holds out. She half kneels at left in grey satin, turned to the right and smiling. The French inventory lists every prop as if taking stock of a kitchen: stool, drapery, ewer, bowl, spoon, and here they all are, green drapery under the cat, pewter ewer and spoon-filled bowl on the floor. A small black-and-white spaniel sits between girl and stool, staring up at the plate, presumably wondering why the cat gets served first. Fur and pewter get equal patience.
context: Léon Chiris is the name the French national inventory gives as the painting's former owner: the canvas (61 × 50 cm, signed 'M. Gérard' at lower left) ended up in Grasse, Gérard's home town, and is now town property in the Musée Fragonard (inv. 2010.0.369). The inventory records it as a gift to the town. Fun fact: the database dates it only loosely, to somewhere between the last quarter of the eighteenth century and the first quarter of the nineteenth, so the 'c. 1785' label is a guess; it also gives the picture a second title, 'Young girl giving her cat a drink'.
image_credit: Marguerite Gérard · https://www.flickr.com/photos/repolco/7167210055/sizes/l/in/photostream/

title: Cat Fight (Riña de gatos)
description: No people, just two arched backs and a lot of sky: that is the whole picture, two cats squaring off on top of a brick wall. On the left a black cat bristles, tail low; on the right a grey tabby bares its teeth, one forepaw lifted. Ivy trails over the bricks, and a little weed sprouts between them. The canvas is about 56 cm high and nearly two metres long, a strip shaped to hang above a door. Goya studies the animals closely rather than prettily. The paint surface is softer than in his other cartoons, which writers put down to long years in damp basement storage.
context: Between May 1786 and the end of 1787 Goya painted this as a full-size design, or cartoon, to be woven for the royal palace of El Pardo; sources disagree on the room, the Fundación Goya naming the king's conversation room and Wikipedia the Prince and Princess of Asturias's dining room. Vicente López listed it in his 1834 inventory, it reached the Prado by 1870 and then sat in the basement until 1986 (P006323). Fun fact: scholars still argue over it. Janis Tomlinson flatly rejects Goya's authorship, calling the composition mediocre, while Arnaiz finds it entirely in keeping with his style.
submovement: Tapestry cartoons for the Royal Tapestry Factory of Santa Bárbara
image_credit: Francisco Goya · http://www.museodelprado.es/es/pagina-principal/coleccion/galeria-on-line/galeria-on-line/zoom/1/obra/rina-de-gatos/oimg/0/

title: Felina with a Kitten
description: A white kitten is hugged up against a girl's shoulder, narrowed eyes and pink nose peering out of the crook of her arm, and the title does the joking: 'Felina' turns the child into a cat-girl before the kitten gets a look in. She grins at us from under russet curls in a pale gold dress, dark trees behind. The Detroit Institute of Arts records it as an oil on canvas of 1788. Holding a small animal kept a young sitter busy and gave the painter a second face to work with. Watch where fur meets skin: in late Reynolds those soft edges are where the paint loosens up.
context: Number 378 in the Royal Academy's twentieth exhibition catalogue, in 1788, was a girl with a kitten called Felina, and Reynolds had been the Academy's President since its founding in 1768. The Detroit Institute of Arts lists that catalogue entry in the painting's exhibition history and holds the canvas as a bequest of Mrs. Horace E. Dodge, in memory of her husband (F71.68). Fun fact: the title does the joking, since 'Felina' is simply 'cat-like' with a girl's name on it.
image_credit: Joshua Reynolds · https://www.dia.org/art/collection/object/felina-kitten-58340

title: Manuel Osorio Manrique de Zuñiga (1784–1792)
title_original: Don Manuel Osorio Manrique de Zúñiga
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: Behind the magpie on its string, three cats lurk at the edge of the dark: a calico, white with black and ginger patches, crouching with wide amber eyes; a grey tabby beside it, staring straight out; and a black cat further back, nearly lost in the shadow except for two round eyes. The magpie holds Goya's visiting card in its beak, and the boy's white satin shoe peeks in at the right edge. The image shown is a detail: on the full 127 × 101.6 cm canvas a small boy in red holds the string beside a cage of finches. Nobody in the picture has noticed the cats except us.
context: The sitter is Manuel Osorio Manrique de Zúñiga (1784–1792), son of the Count of Altamira, who commissioned the portrait; Goya painted it in 1787–88, and the boy died aged eight. The picture sold in Paris in 1878, belonged to the playwright Henri Bernstein, passed to the dealer Joseph Duveen in 1925 and was bought by Jules Bache in 1926 after his daughter Kathryn Bache Miller fell for it. It came to the Met with the Bache Collection in 1949 (49.7.41), yet hung periodically in Miller's apartment until her death in 1979. Fun fact: Goya slipped his signature into the plot by handing his card to the bird.
feline_symbolism: Commentators often read the caged birds as the innocent soul and the cats as a lurking evil force, a reading sharpened by the boy's early death.
image_credit: Francisco Goya · Livre Goya : un regard libre . Exposition présentée à Lille, Palais des Beaux-Arts, 12 décembre 1998-14 mars 1999 ; Philadelphie, the Philadelphia Museum of Art, 17 avril 1999-11 juillet 1999. Paris : Réunion des Musées Nat

title: A Woman and a Cat
medium: One sheet of a triptych of woodblock prints; ink and color on paper
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: Paws in the air, a white kitten with black patches and a red collar has tangled itself in the hem of a sheer robe, mouthing the fabric at the bottom of the sheet. Above, a woman kneels and lifts the gauzy garment, biting one edge to hold it, eyes lowered toward the culprit. A black lacquer sewing box with a pincushion stands behind her and scissors lie at lower left, so this was meant to be quiet needlework. The sheet, 38.4 by 25.9 cm, was once part of a woodblock triptych, each colour printed from its own carved block in register.
context: Around 1793–94, when pictures of beautiful women by Kitagawa Utamaro (c. 1753–1806) dominated Edo print publishing, this sheet was designed as part of a triptych. The Met holds it as JP1672, from the H. O. Havemeyer Collection, bequest of Mrs. H. O. Havemeyer, 1929. Fun fact: the Met's subject tags for the sheet are just 'Women' and 'Cats', which sums it up, since the woman sews and the kitten does the unpicking.
image_credit: Kitagawa Utamaro · This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the Metropolitan Museum of Art . See the Image and Data Resources Open Access Policy

title: Ode on the Death of a Favourite Cat (Design 9)
title_original: The Poems of Thomas Gray, Design 9
description: Selima is half woman, half cat: she reclines in a pink gown, cat's ears poking up beside her bonnet, while a striped tabby tail curls up behind the printed page in an S. Below, her reflection floats upside down in faint pencil on the water among bellflowers and dusky fish. Blake's design 9 is built around this inlaid letterpress page of Gray's poem, worked in watercolour, pen, ink and graphite. Yale titles it from the lines 'The pensive Selima, Her ears of jet, and emerald eyes, She saw; and purr'd applause'. The sheet is 41.9 by 32.4 cm.
context: Gray's mock-heroic elegy of 1747 mourns a cat of Horace Walpole's drowned in a tub of goldfish, and Blake lets the drowning hang in the air: Selima's tail still curls above the printed page while her reflection floats upside down in pencil below. Blake made his illustrations to Gray's poems in 1797–98, painting around inlaid pages of the printed text, and this sheet is in the Yale Center for British Art, Paul Mellon Collection (B1992.8.11(5)). Fun fact: Walpole owned two cats, Zara and Selima, and the poem borrows the second name.
title_eng: Ode on the Death of a Favourite Cat, Drowned in a Tub of Gold Fishes
medium: Watercolor with pen and black ink and graphite, with inlaid letterpress page
collection: Yale Center for British Art, New Haven
image_credit: William Blake · ngHcMkqjvCtW5Q at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

title: The Sleep of Reason Produces Monsters (Los Caprichos, Plate 43)
title_original: El sueño de la razón produce monstruos
submovement: Los Caprichos satirical etching and aquatint (Goya)
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: A large cat, usually read as a lynx, sits on the floor at lower right with tufted ears and wide eyes, the one creature not fussing over the sleeper. A second, dark cat crouches behind the artist's back, only its glowing eyes picked out. The artist slumps over a desk, head buried in his arms, while owls and bats pour out of the dark; one owl pushes a chalk holder at him. Etching gives the crisp lines of feathers and fur; aquatint lays down the grainy night. The desk front carries the title, 'El sueño de la razon produce monstruos'. The plate measures 21.2 by 15.1 cm.
context: Plate 43 of the 80 aquatints of Los Caprichos, published in 1799, grew out of a drawing of 1797 on which Goya noted that the sleeping artist's 'only purpose is to banish harmful, vulgar beliefs'. The Met's impression (18.64(43)) was a gift of M. Knoedler & Co. in 1918. Fun fact: the art historian Philip Hofer argued, from a preparatory sketch, that Goya first meant this image as the frontispiece of the whole set, then tucked it into the middle as number 43.
title_eng: The Sleep of Reason Produces Monsters
feline_symbolism: Owls are often read as folly and bats as ignorance; one critic has Goya borrowing the lynx's piercing sight to expose such vices, which casts the wakeful cat as the clear-eyed exception.
image_credit: National Library of Medicine - History of Medicine · https://www.flickr.com/photos/nlmhmd/4379551324/

title: Figure of a Cat
description: Small enough to sit in two cupped hands, this cat is 10.2 cm high, 13.3 cm long and 7.6 cm deep, made in hard-paste porcelain at Meissen around 1800. It lies with front paws stretched out and tail curled round its flank, head up, staring straight ahead. Its patches are painted as fine hatched strokes, so the fur looks drawn rather than coloured, and the whisker pads are pricked out in dots. Hard paste is the dense, glassy porcelain fired at very high temperature, so body and glaze fuse into one skin. Figures like this were made for cabinets and mantelpieces, to be turned in the hand.
context: First European hard-paste porcelain was what Saxony's factory made, and the Brooklyn Museum's record lists this cat as hard-paste porcelain from the Meissen factory in Germany, about 1800, unsigned and uninscribed, 10.2 × 13.3 × 7.6 cm (4 × 5¼ × 3 in.), accession 81.53.6. Fun fact: that date puts it well after the factory's famous modelling of the 1740s by Johann Joachim Kändler, whom an older catalogue id wrongly credited; he died in 1775, so this cat is a later, quieter arrival.
image_credit: Brooklyn Museum · Brooklyn Museum

title: Cat and Three Kittens
artist: Ch. Fenderich (drawer and publisher), after Gottfried Mind
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Washington, D.C.
description: A big mother cat, white with grey-brown patches, crouches in a loaf with paws tucked in, eyeing a dish of spilled food and a ball of wool trailing its thread at the left. Three kittens keep to the right, one curled behind her and two huddled nose to nose in front. The print is a lithograph washed with pale colour, so the grain of the crayon shows under the tints. The lettering below names Ch. Fenderich as the man who drew and published it and Childs & Inman's lithographic press in Philadelphia as its printer; the Library of Congress calls it a copy of plate 2 of Mind's Katzengruppen ('cat groups').
context: Philadelphia, 1832: a Swiss artist's cats had crossed the Atlantic. The Library of Congress catalogues this sheet as part of a series titled 'Collection of Cats', a copy of plate 2 of Gottfried Mind's Katzengruppen, drawn and published by Ch. Fenderich from Childs & Inman's lithographic press. The date comes from the series cover page and the title was devised by Library staff, so even the caption is a cataloguer's. Fun fact: Mind (1768–1814), later nicknamed 'the Raphael of Cats', reportedly revealed his gift by telling his master Sigmund Freudenberger of a cat in one of the master's sketches, 'That is no cat!', and was challenged to do better.
image_credit: Popular Graphic Arts · Library of Congress Catalog: http://lccn.loc.gov/2003653668 Image download: https://cdn.loc.gov/service/pnp/cph/3b00000/3b06000/3b06200/3b06251r.jpg Original url: http://hdl.loc.gov/loc.pnp/pga.10607

title: Cat Eating While Kittens Play
artist: After Gottfried Mind (lithograph associated with Joseph Brodtmann)
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Washington, D.C.
description: Mealtime is also playtime: the mother cat is eating, and the kittens have decided this is the perfect moment to start a brawl. She crouches at left, eyes squeezed shut, gnawing a scrap held between her paws, her big patched body ending in a tail that sweeps up in a curl. Behind her hind legs two kittens tussle, one pawing at the other's face. It is a lithograph drawn on stone with greasy crayon, so the soft stippled grain of the fur is the crayon's own. Head-down absorption against tangled young is the everyday cat behaviour Mind made his name on.
context: Vigée Le Brun, passing through Bern in 1807, is usually credited with calling Gottfried Mind 'the Raphael of Cats'. Lithographs after his designs, associated with Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862), carried his compositions to buyers who would never own an original; the Library of Congress dates such sheets between 1820 and 1860, long after Mind's death in 1814. Fun fact: Mind was read through the medicine of each era: George Fairholme, who compiled his work as Mindiana in 1831, called him a 'cretin imbecile', while modern writers often call him an autistic savant.
submovement: Reproductive lithographs after Gottfried Mind (Joseph Brodtmann)
image_credit: Rawpixel · Own work

title: Cat Napping While Three Kittens Play
artist: After Gottfried Mind (lithograph associated with Joseph Brodtmann)
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Washington, D.C.
description: Napping at the centre, a broad patched mother cat lies low with her eyes closed; her three kittens refuse to. One sits alert at far left, one stretches out to bat a crumpled ribbon, and the third clambers up her flank to peer over her back. A saucer sits off to the right, empty. Anyone who has lived with a litter knows the arrangement. The lithographic crayon turns sleeping fur into a soft, even grey, while the kittens' movement is carried by outline and placement. Mind's gift was noticing that rest and play need different drawing.
context: Freudenberger's studio was Mind's school: at about fourteen he was apprenticed to the Bern painter Sigmund Freudenberger, learning drawing and watercolour largely by colouring prints. After Freudenberger died in 1801, the widow kept him on, because she saw the commercial value of his independent work. Lithographs after his designs, linked to Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862), kept them in circulation after Mind's death in 1814. Fun fact: his widow-employer was right about the market; his cat pictures sold well enough that cats became his whole specialty.
title_eng: Cat Napping While Three Kittens Play
submovement: Reproductive lithographs after Gottfried Mind (Joseph Brodtmann)
location: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Washington, D.C.
image_credit: Rawpixel · Own work

title: Domestic Cats
artist: After Gottfried Mind (lithograph associated with Joseph Brodtmann)
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Washington, D.C.
description: Perched on a padded stool edged with studs, the mother cat leans over its rim to touch paws with a kitten below. Three kittens play around the legs: one sits under the seat looking up, one sprawls on its side tugging a string, and a patched one rears against a leg on the right. A shallow dish stands at lower left. Mind liked to set his animals on real objects, which gives the print a floor and a scale; a kitten beside a stool leg reads as small in a way it never would on blank paper.
context: Champfleury, the French critic, put Mind's drawings into his 1869 book Les chats, reviving interest in him among French artists and intellectuals decades after his death in 1814. Lithographs after designs by Gottfried Mind, associated with Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862), had spread them earlier, between about 1820 and 1860. Fun fact: Mind remained mostly illiterate and struggled to write his own name, yet his cats were praised for precision and naturalism.
submovement: Reproductive lithographs after Gottfried Mind (Joseph Brodtmann)
image_credit: Rawpixel · Own work

title: Cat and Puppy
artist: After Gottfried Mind (lithograph associated with Joseph Brodtmann)
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Washington, D.C.
description: Atop a rough stone block, a cat stands with its back arched and fur up, glaring down; a shaggy puppy rears against the side with front paws on the stone and mouth open, barking up at her. Broken chips of stone litter the ground. The block gives the print a ground and a scale, and the cat wins on dignity and on altitude. Interspecies scuffles were a favourite joke of animal printmakers. It is a stone lithograph, so the fur is built from fine crayon grain rather than lines.
context: Bears as well as cats: Mind spent a lot of time at Bern's Bärengraben, the bear pit, drawing the animals and building a rapport with them, and his bear studies were highly regarded too. Prints after his designs, linked to the lithographer Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862), carried this kind of scene well beyond Switzerland after his death in 1814. Fun fact: he had no formal training in animal anatomy, yet his depictions were praised for precision and for capturing movement without turning animals into little people.
submovement: Reproductive lithographs after Gottfried Mind (Joseph Brodtmann)
image_credit: Rawpixel · Own work

title: Cat and Three Playful Kittens
artist: After Gottfried Mind (lithograph associated with Joseph Brodtmann)
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Washington, D.C.
description: Striding off to the right, tail out straight, the mother cat looks back at us with wide, faintly startled eyes, while three kittens tumble behind her at the left. They are fighting over a length of wool: one rolls on its back with the thread in its mouth, one grips a scrap from above, and the ball has rolled away at lower left. A loose cord is a draughtsman's gift: one curving line ties the group together and gives every kitten something to do. In lithograph it reads as a crisp dark line against the soft grey fur.
context: Cats rested on Mind's shoulders and lap while he worked, according to accounts summarised on Wikipedia, which makes the close observation in a scene like this less surprising. He lived and died in Bern, in 1814, and lithographs after his designs, associated with Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862), reached a wide buying public afterwards. Fun fact: his talent for cats was reportedly discovered when, apprenticed to Sigmund Freudenberger, he criticised a cat in a sketch of his master's with the words 'That is no cat!'
submovement: Reproductive lithographs after Gottfried Mind (Joseph Brodtmann)
location: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Washington, D.C.
image_credit: Rawpixel · Own work

title: Cat with Three Newborn Kittens
artist: After Gottfried Mind (lithograph associated with Joseph Brodtmann)
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Washington, D.C.
description: Round as a loaf of fur, the mother cat crouches with paws tucked under, staring off to the left with wide eyes. Beside her lie a dish with food spilling out and a ball of wool trailing thread, and three tiny kittens fill the right: one creeping behind her and two huddled nose to nose. Newborns are hard to draw, little more than blunt heads and folded legs, and the lithograph has to make three near-identical lumps read as three animals. It is the same group as the Philadelphia copy of Mind's Katzengruppen elsewhere in this catalogue, drawn again on a different stone.
context: A Hungarian joiner's son from Worblaufen near Bern, Mind got his first look at prints through his father's employer, the paper manufacturer and art collector Samuel Emanuel Gruner, whose collection included Johann Elias Ridinger's animal engravings. Lithographs after his designs, linked to Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862), later carried his mother-and-litter subjects well beyond Switzerland. Fun fact: Gruner is also the man who sold J. M. W. Turner a blank sketchbook during Turner's 1802 visit to Bern.
submovement: Reproductive lithographs after Gottfried Mind (Joseph Brodtmann)
image_credit: Rawpixel · Own work

title: Sword Guard (Tsuba)
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: With a gold cloth draped over its head and shoulder, a cat rears up on its hind legs at lower left, tongue poking out, front paws raised as if mid-dance. Across the plate a grinning, balding old man in copper leans in, long gold-tipped nails curled over the rim. The guard, the plate between blade and grip, measures only 8.6 by 7.9 cm and 6 mm thick, yet weighs 164 grams of mostly iron. Gold, silver and copper glint against the near-black ground. The Met's own subject tags are just two words: Men, Cats.
context: Peace was good for metalworkers: with few battles to fight in the Edo period, sword fittings turned into small picture surfaces for any subject a client fancied. This guard came to the Metropolitan Museum as part of the bequest of Edward G. Kennedy in 1932 (33.40.43) and is dated only to the 18th century, with no maker or school named. Fun fact: it is filed under Arms and Armor, so a cat dancing with a cloth on its head lives in the same department as plate armour.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Le Chat mort (Study of a Dead Cat)
submovement: French Romantic painting (Géricault late studies from nature)
collection: Musée du Louvre, Paris (Département des Peintures)
description: A dead cat, grey-and-white, sprawled across a plain wooden block with its head hanging over the near edge and one foreleg dangling toward the floor. Géricault paints it in oil on a canvas 50 by 61 cm, close to the size of the animal itself, and gives the corpse the same attention he gave his human studies: no props, no owner, just the body and a hard light raking from the left against a near-black ground. Watch the ears and closed eyes droop downward, and how fast 'a cat' turns into weight, slackness and fur that no longer lies right.
context: Room 941 in the Sully wing is where the Louvre's own record puts this dead cat, in the Department of Paintings, as RF 2003 6, oil on canvas, 50 × 61 cm. The museum dates it only to the nineteenth century (1800–1900); 'c. 1820' comes from Commons, and Géricault died in 1824. Fun fact: the Louvre acquired the picture by purchase only in 2003, so a study of a painter who died at thirty-two (Rouen 1791, Paris 1824) joined the national collection almost two centuries after he made it.
title_eng: The Dead Cat (Study of a Dead Cat)
image_credit: Théodore Géricault · http://cartelen.louvre.fr/cartelen/visite?srv=rs_display_res&critere=G%C9RICAULT&operator=AND&nbToDisplay=20&langue=fr&x=31&y=9

title: Domestic Cat and Kitten Drinking Milk from a Saucer
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Washington, D.C.
description: A stout tabby-and-white cat and her tiny striped kitten bend over a saucer of milk, two heads lowered to the same point and nearly touching. The mother is a broad, rounded mass with dark patches across her back; the kitten, front legs braced, stands on the far side with its tail curled up. The Library of Congress catalogues it as a lithograph, so Mind's watercolour becomes grainy greys and dark accents. A small '3' in the upper right marks it as one plate in a series, and 'CF' sits at lower right, beside the kitten. The sheet is 23 by 31.4 cm.
context: A Library of Congress cataloguer devised the title; the print itself is signed 'CF' at lower right and numbered 3 at upper right. The Library credits Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862) as lithographer and Gottfried Mind (1768–1814) as artist, and dates the sheet between 1820 and 1860, so it postdates Mind's death. It belongs to the Popular Graphic Arts collection of the Prints and Photographs Division (LCCN 2012645540). Fun fact: 'CF' is a tempting match for Ch. Fenderich, who drew and published copies of Mind's cat groups in Philadelphia in 1832, as another sheet in this catalogue shows, though the catalogue record does not say so.
title_eng: Domestic Cat and Kitten Drinking Milk from a Saucer
submovement: Reproductive lithographs after Gottfried Mind (Joseph Brodtmann)
image_credit: Brodtmann, Joseph, 1787-1862, lithographer; Mind, Gottfried, 1768-1814, artist · Library of Congress Catalog: http://lccn.loc.gov/2012645540 Image download: http://cdn.loc.gov/service/pnp/pga/05400/05431v.jpg Original url: https://www.loc.g

title: Domestic Cat Eating While Two Kittens Play
title_original: Katze frisst, während zwei Kätzchen spielen
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division (Popular Graphic Arts collection)
description: A heavy-bodied tabby-and-white cat crouches at left with her head down over her food, a small rectangular scrap on the floor, eyes squeezed shut in concentration and tail curling up behind her. Tucked under her hindquarters, two kittens get on with the more important business of play, one pawing at the other's face. The sheet is black lithographic ink on paper about 23 by 32 cm. Check the corners: a printed 10 sits at upper right, the initials 'CF-' at lower right, and the cataloguers read a partial watermark, 'LHEU...', at bottom right.
context: The design goes back to Gottfried Mind (1768–1814), the Bernese draughtsman who spent his working life in the studio of the painter Sigmund Freudenberger and, after 1801, of Freudenberger's widow, drawing cats, bears and children. The stone was drawn by Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862), a lithographer and publisher born in Überlingen who worked in Zürich and Schaffhausen and died in Basel. The Library dates the sheet loosely to 1820–1860 and keeps it in its Popular Graphic Arts collection. Fun fact: Mind's nickname, “the Raphael of Cats”, is usually credited to Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun, but the Public Domain Review points out that no primary record of her saying it survives; Champfleury seems to be the one who spread the story.
title_eng: Domestic Cat Eating While Two Kittens Play
image_credit: Brodtmann, Joseph, 1787-1862, lithographer; Mind, Gottfried, 1768-1814, artist · Library of Congress Catalog: http://lccn.loc.gov/2012645552 Image download: http://cdn.loc.gov/service/pnp/pga/05400/05443v.jpg Original url: https://www.loc.g

title: Domestic Cat Napping with Three Playful Kittens
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division (Popular Graphic Arts collection)
description: The mother is nearly out for the count, eyes half shut, her bulk settled in the centre of the sheet; her three kittens are not. One sits upright at far left like a sentry, one sprawls in front of her batting a curl of ribbon, and the third clambers onto her back from the right, mouth open. An empty saucer waits at the right edge. The sheet measures 23 × 31.7 cm, carries a printed 6 at upper right and is initialled 'C.F.' at lower right. On the back someone pencilled '1227 U 5 D 57', a code that turns up on several sheets from the same group.
context: “That is no cat!” is what the teenage Gottfried Mind is said to have told his master Sigmund Freudenberger about a cat in one of the master's compositions, before drawing a better one and being allowed to finish the figure. Mind (1768–1814) had been apprenticed at about fourteen, and his first job was colouring Freudenberger's etchings of peasant life; animals took over only later. Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862), a Swiss lithographer best known for natural-history plates such as Schinz's books on birds and fishes, put the drawing on stone. The Library of Congress dates the print between 1820 and 1860. Fun fact: that studio story is repeated in most biographies of Mind, including Wikipedia's.
title_eng: Domestic Cat Napping with Three Playful Kittens
title_original: Schlummernde Katze mit drei spielenden Kätzchen
image_credit: Brodtmann, Joseph, 1787-1862, lithographer; Mind, Gottfried, 1768-1814, artist · Library of Congress Catalog: https://lccn.loc.gov/2012645542 Image download: https://cdn.loc.gov/service/pnp/pga/05400/05433v.jpg Original url: https://www.loc

title: Domestic Cat on a Stool Playing with Three Kittens
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division (Popular Graphic Arts collection)
description: The adult cat has taken the high ground. She crouches on a padded, stud-trimmed stool and hooks one paw down over the edge toward the three kittens below, so the action runs up and down the sheet instead of across the floor. One kitten sits under the stool looking out at us, one lies flat beneath it, and the third stands on its hind legs at right, reaching up. A shallow dish sits at left. It is a lithograph in black on paper of 23 × 31.8 cm, with a 4 printed at upper right and 'C.F.' at lower right. Library of Congress staff supplied the title.
context: A studio in Bern run first by Sigmund Freudenberger and then by his widow, who kept him on after 1801, was where Gottfried Mind (1768–1814) made his cat drawings. Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862), a lithographer and publisher active in Zürich and Schaffhausen, translated a run of them into numbered lithographs; the Library of Congress dates this impression between 1820 and 1860. Fun fact: Mind's English biographer George Fairholme, in his 1831 Mindiana, described the artist at work with a favourite cat sitting “in the hollow formed by his neck & shoulders” while other cats warmed his knees.
title_eng: Domestic Cat on a Stool Playing with Three Kittens
title_original: Katze auf einem Schemel mit drei Kätzchen
image_credit: Brodtmann, Joseph, 1787-1862, lithographer; Mind, Gottfried, 1768-1814, artist · Library of Congress Catalog: http://lccn.loc.gov/2012645541 Image download: http://cdn.loc.gov/service/pnp/pga/05400/05432v.jpg Original url: https://www.loc.g

title: Domestic Cat Sleeping with Three Kittens Resting
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division (Popular Graphic Arts collection)
description: Nobody is playing in this one, or almost nobody. A big tabby-and-white mother sleeps curled at right, eyes shut, with one kitten draped asleep across her neck like a scarf. At left, two more kittens rest in a heap, though one of them is wide awake and stares straight out of the sheet. The sheet is 23 × 27.1 cm, narrower than the numbered plates, and has no plate number. Instead a small round stamp at bottom centre reads 'im Museum zu Basel', which the Library records without explanation.
context: The design is Gottfried Mind's (1768–1814); the lithograph is by Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862), the Überlingen-born printmaker who worked in Zürich and Schaffhausen and died in Basel. The Library of Congress holds the sheet in its Popular Graphic Arts collection and dates it between 1820 and 1860. Fun fact: Mind's reputation came wrapped in the medical language of his day. Engravings published after his death called him “the Swiss cretin”, Fairholme's Mindiana (1831) used “cretin imbecile”, and later psychiatrists cited him as a case of preserved talent; modern writers often reclassify him as an autistic savant, a diagnosis nobody can now confirm.
title_eng: Domestic Cat Sleeping with Three Kittens Resting
title_original: Schlafende Katze mit drei ruhenden Kätzchen
image_credit: Brodtmann, Joseph, 1787-1862, lithographer; Mind, Gottfried, 1768-1814, artist · Library of Congress Catalog: http://lccn.loc.gov/2012645539 Image download: http://cdn.loc.gov/service/pnp/pga/05400/05430v.jpg Original url: https://www.loc.g

title: Domestic Cat Standing on a Block with a Playful Puppy
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division (Popular Graphic Arts collection)
description: On a rough stone block, a cat stands with its back arched high, ears flattened and head lowered, glaring down at a shaggy puppy who has planted both front paws on the block and gazes up hopefully. Broken chips of stone litter the ground beside them. The lithograph is printed in black on a sheet of 23.2 × 32 cm, with the number 7 at upper right and a pencil inscription on the back. Among the Mind cat plates the Library holds, it is the one where a dog gets a look in.
context: Bern's bear pit, the Bärengraben, supplied the models for the bears of Gottfried Mind (1768–1814), who was said to get on unusually well with the animals; he also drew children at play and, above all, cats. Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862) turned a set of his animal drawings into numbered lithographs, and the Library of Congress dates this one between 1820 and 1860. Fun fact: as a boy Mind passed through Pestalozzi's school for poor children, where the famous educator noted him down as “a strange creature, full of artist-caprices”.
title_eng: Domestic Cat Standing on a Block with a Playful Puppy
title_original: Katze auf einem Holzblock mit einem spielenden Welpen
image_credit: Brodtmann, Joseph, 1787-1862, lithographer; Mind, Gottfried, 1768-1814, artist · Library of Congress Catalog: http://lccn.loc.gov/2012645549 Image download: http://cdn.loc.gov/service/pnp/pga/05400/05439v.jpg Original url: https://www.loc.g

title: Domestic Cat with Three Newborn Kittens Beside a Saucer
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division (Popular Graphic Arts collection)
description: A round, hunched mother cat sits in the middle of the sheet with her chin low and eyes wide, as if daring anyone to approach the three newborn kittens behind and beside her. One curls up at her back; two huddle in front at right, still blunt-faced and tiny. To the left lie a saucer of spilled food and a ball of yarn. The print is a lithograph on a sheet of 23.2 × 31.5 cm. A printed 2 at upper right marks one of the earliest plates, the paper is watermarked 'Basel', and the verso carries the code '1227 U 5 D 57'.
context: On stone, this design by Gottfried Mind (1768–1814) became a lithograph by Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862), who also produced natural-history plates for books on birds, reptiles and fishes. Mind drew cats in Bern for most of his adult life, working in the studio of Sigmund Freudenberger's widow after the painter died in 1801, and the Library of Congress dates this impression between 1820 and 1860. Fun fact: the Public Domain Review singles out Brodtmann's lithograph of a mother cat with three kittens as one of the ways Mind's cats reached a public far beyond the Bernese studio where, as one obituary put it, he “spent his whole life on the selfsame stool”.
title_eng: Domestic Cat with Three Newborn Kittens Beside a Saucer
image_credit: Brodtmann, Joseph, 1787-1862, lithographer; Mind, Gottfried, 1768-1814, artist · Library of Congress Catalog: http://lccn.loc.gov/2012645547 Image download: http://cdn.loc.gov/service/pnp/pga/05400/05435v.jpg Original url: https://www.loc.g

title: Domestic Cat with Three Kittens at Play
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division (Popular Graphic Arts collection)
description: A mother cat strides off to the right, tail out straight and face turned to us with a wary look, while her three kittens roll in a knot behind her, tangled in a length of yarn with two little balls spilling loose. One kitten paws at a scrap of ribbon on its sibling's head. The sheet is a lithograph on paper measuring 22.7 × 27.2 cm, narrower than most numbered plates and without a plate number. A small round stamp at bottom centre reads 'im Museum zu Basel', and the credit 'Brodtmann nach Mind' is printed at lower right, keeping draughtsman and lithographer neatly apart.
context: Half a century after Mind's death, the critic Champfleury used one of his drawings as the frontispiece of his 1868 book on cats, the one Édouard Manet advertised with the poster known as “The Cats' Rendezvous”. Gottfried Mind (1768–1814) spent his career in Bern drawing cats, bears and children; Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862) made lithographs after him, and a Brodtmann sheet in the Swiss National Library carries the same “Brodtmann nach Mind” signature. The Library of Congress dates this impression between 1820 and 1860. Fun fact: that Champfleury book is a big reason Mind's name survived into the later nineteenth century.
title_eng: Domestic Cat with Three Kittens at Play
image_credit: Brodtmann, Joseph, 1787-1862, lithographer; Mind, Gottfried, 1768-1814, artist · Library of Congress Catalog: http://lccn.loc.gov/2012645538 Image download: http://cdn.loc.gov/service/pnp/pga/05400/05429v.jpg Original url: https://www.loc.g

title: Domestic Cat with Two Kittens Inspecting the Ground
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division (Popular Graphic Arts collection)
description: Three heads go down together. A broad tabby mother and two kittens nose at something small and dark on the ground, a scrap the Library of Congress cataloguers sensibly declined to name. One kitten creeps in from the left with its tail up; the other is pressed so close to its mother that their faces almost merge. A saucer of milk sits to the right. The lithograph is printed on a sheet of 23.1 × 31.8 cm with the number 8 at upper right. The paper is watermarked 'in Basel', and the verso carries the code '1227 U 5 D 57' shared with companion plates.
context: Admirer though he was, the English collector George Fairholme conceded that Mind “had not studied the anatomy of animals”, yet he praised his accuracy all the same and noted visible corrections in the drawings, a sign that the famous facility was worked for. Gottfried Mind (1768–1814) worked in Bern, first as an apprentice to the painter Sigmund Freudenberger and later in the studio run by Freudenberger's widow. Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862), a Swiss lithographer and publisher, put a numbered run of Mind's cats on stone; the Library of Congress dates this impression between 1820 and 1860. Fun fact: Fairholme collected Mind's drawings and wrote the first English account of him, Mindiana (1831).
title_eng: Domestic Cat with Two Kittens Inspecting the Ground
title_original: Katze mit zwei Kätzchen bei der Untersuchung
image_credit: Brodtmann, Joseph, 1787-1862, lithographer; Mind, Gottfried, 1768-1814, artist · Library of Congress Catalog: http://lccn.loc.gov/2012645550 Image download: http://cdn.loc.gov/service/pnp/pga/05400/05440v.jpg Original url: https://www.loc.g

title: Domestic Cat with Two Kittens Playing with a Ball of String
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division (Popular Graphic Arts collection)
description: Upright in profile, a mother cat looks down at a striped kitten crouched in front of her with a ball of string trapped under its paws, the loose thread snaking off to the right. A second kitten peeks out from behind her back, watching the game with round eyes. The lithograph is printed on paper 23.6 × 32 cm, the largest sheet in this group, with the number 5 at upper right and a watermark reading 'in Basel' at bottom centre. The verso carries the pencilled code '1227 U 5 D 57' found on several sister plates.
context: A dead frog preserved in a jar shares the desk with a cat in Gottfried Mind's self-portrait, a version of which is now in the British Museum, and nobody has explained the frog. Mind (1768–1814) lived in Bern; Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862) made lithographs after his drawings and also produced natural-history plates for Heinrich Rudolf Schinz's books on birds, reptiles and fishes. The Library of Congress dates the impression between 1820 and 1860 and holds it in its Popular Graphic Arts collection. Fun fact: the self-portrait shows him drawing with the cat right beside him, so the sitter, the studio and the frog were all in one picture.
title_eng: Domestic Cat with Two Kittens Playing with a Ball of String
title_original: Katze mit zwei Kätzchen und einem Wollknäuel
image_credit: Brodtmann, Joseph, 1787-1862, lithographer; Mind, Gottfried, 1768-1814, artist · Library of Congress Catalog: http://lccn.loc.gov/2012645548 Image download: http://cdn.loc.gov/service/pnp/pga/05400/05438v.jpg Original url: https://www.loc.g

title: Sleeping Cat
medium: Porcelain with overglaze color enamel and gold (Hizen ware)
description: A porcelain cat sleeps curled up, small enough to sit in two hands at 9.5 × 14.6 cm, chin resting on folded front paws and tail wrapped along its flank. It wears a red collar patterned in white, tied in a bow behind the ears, with a gold bell, the standard accessory for these models. The fur is the clever part. The Cleveland Museum of Art notes that very fine lines were incised into the clay and thin strokes of orange and gold brushed over the glaze, so the orange patches read as soft fur. Look at the closed eyes: two curved orange slits that make the nap look smug.
context: Late in the Edo period, in the early to mid-1800s, potters in Hizen, the porcelain country of north-western Kyushu, made sleeping cats like this one. Cleveland notes that cats with collars and bells were popular decorative objects, and that some doubled as incense burners or hand warmers; this one was purely for display. Its provenance runs from the Cleveland industrialist John L. Severance (1863–1936) to his relatives Severance and Greta Millikin, whose gift brought it to the museum in 1964. Fun fact: in 2001 it travelled to Australia for the exhibition Monet & Japan, shown in Canberra and Perth.
image_credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Koma-neko (guardian cats) of Kijima-sha, Kotohira Shrine
title_original: 金刀比羅神社 狛猫
artist: Unknown stonemason (donated by Tango silk merchants)
description: Only one of the two stone cats makes it into this photo: the open-mouthed one, lichen-mottled grey granite, ears pricked, round eye fixed ahead and whiskers carved as fine grooves on the muzzle. Behind it hang a straw rope and paper streamers, and a wooden signboard names the Kijima shrine (Kijima-sha) inside the precinct of Kotohira Shrine in Mineyama. The pair follow the komainu script: facing the shrine, the left cat opens its mouth on 'a' and holds a kitten against its body; the right cat keeps its mouth shut on 'un'. A Kyotango photo archive reads them as mother and father.
context: Kotohira Shrine was founded in 1811 by the lord of the Mineyama domain on the Tango peninsula, a district that lived by silk and is still known for Tango chirimen crepe. The deity of the Kijima sub-shrine is a god of sericulture, and cats earned their place by keeping rats and mice away from silkworms and cocoons. According to the Kyotango photo archive, the statues were donated in 1832 by silk merchants and wholesalers, among them the Tonomura family and Komuro Rishichi of the Sanyaya house in Iwataki. Fun fact: the local tourism office calls this the only shrine in Japan with koma-neko in place of koma-inu, a claim not independently tested here; since a 2011 local project the grounds have also filled with some 400 ceramic cats.
title_eng: Koma-neko (guardian cats) of Kijima-sha, Kotohira Shrine
collection: Kijima-sha, Kotohira Shrine (金刀比羅神社), Mineyama, Kyōtango, Kyoto Prefecture
submovement: Late Edo Shinto Stone Shrine Sculpture
feline_symbolism: The cats are working guardians: the sub-shrine's deity protects sericulture, and the statues honour the animals that kept rodents away from the silkworms.
image_credit: Asturio Cantabrio · Own work

title: Girl in Red Dress with Cat and Dog
title_original: Girl in Red Dress with Cat and Dog
collection: American Folk Art Museum, New York
description: Stretched across the girl's red lap, a white cat is held in both her hands, tail hanging down in an S-curve against the dress and pink-rimmed eyes turned toward us. After the dress it is the brightest thing here. The girl wears a coral necklace and lace-trimmed sleeves. A brown-and-white dog lies on the floor at lower left, chin on its paws, and the sitter's white pantalettes frill out beneath the hem. Everything sits against a near-black ground, which is why the red reads so loudly. The painting is oil on canvas, about 30 by 25 inches.
context: A million dollars, a first for folk art, is what this canvas fetched in 1985, according to Wikipedia, after the New York Times reported a $682,000 bid; it reached the American Folk Art Museum in 2001 as a gift of the Siegman Trust, Ralph Esmerian, trustee (2001.37.1). Ammi Phillips (1788–1865) is credited with over eight hundred portraits, only eleven of them signed. Fun fact: for decades his 1830s portraits were credited to an anonymous 'Kent Limner', named after a 1924 antiques show in Kent, Connecticut, until Barbara and Larry Holdridge showed in 1958 that Phillips had painted them.
title_eng: Girl in Red Dress with Cat and Dog
image_credit: Ammi Phillips · Collection American Folk Art Museum, New York, Gift of the Siegman Trust, Ralph Esmerian, trustee, 2001.37.1, Photo by John Parnell, New York

title: The Peaceable Kingdom
collection: Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco (de Young museum)
description: Hicks's leopards are why this painting is here, and there are two: one prowls across the lower left with its mouth open, the other lies below it with its chin down and a wide-eyed stare. Following Isaiah 11:6–9, the animals of the prophecy gather in the foreground with children, everyone suspiciously calm, a white-faced ox and a heavy-maned lion at the centre, a lamb and a wolf at lower right. In the distance William Penn makes his 1682 treaty with the Lenape, a ship at anchor behind them. This late version, around 1846, is oil on canvas, 63.5 × 72.4 cm.
context: More than sixty versions of The Peaceable Kingdom came from Hicks's brush, each a prophecy of God's kingdom on earth drawn from Isaiah 11:6–9, and this one, of about 1846, was a gift of Mr. and Mrs. John D. Rockefeller 3rd to the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco (1993.35.14), where it is shown at the de Young. Hicks (1780–1849) was a prominent Pennsylvania Quaker. Fun fact: in the distance he painted William Penn's 1682 purchase treaty with the Delaware or Lenape people, offered as the historical model of a peaceable kingdom on earth.
feline_symbolism: In Isaiah's prophecy the leopard lying down with the kid marks the end of predation in God's kingdom, and Hicks uses the big cats as the hardest test case for that peace.
image_credit: Edward Hicks · tAHzgNBfxNbfkw at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

title: Embroidered Carpet (the Caswell Carpet)
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: Find the blue cat: it sits in a square on the bottom row, just left of centre, deep blue with a white bib on a striped ground. It has company. In the very next square to the left a pair of grey cats lounge on another striped panel, and in the left column near the bottom two puppies cuddle in a third. The Met's subject tags list birds, cats, dogs, flowers and plants, and the blue cat later got a children's book of its own. The whole carpet is wool worked in chain stitch, 396.2 × 373.4 cm, laid out as a grid of separate squares. The initials 'ZHG' and '1835' are stitched along the top edge.
context: Hulda Cole, a librarian in Castleton, Vermont, told the writer Catherine Coblentz in 1946 about a local girl whose embroidered carpet now hung in the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Its blue cat became the hero of Coblentz's novel The Blue Cat of Castle Town (1949), a Newbery Honor book in 1950. The Met credits the carpet to Zeruah H. Guernsey Caswell, dates it 1832–35 and records it as a gift of Katharine Keyes in 1938, in memory of her father, Homer Eaton Keyes. Fun fact: the book's heroine is the carpet's maker, and the story ends with her embroidering the carpet.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Emma Homan
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: A grey tabby climbs the rose bush at lower left, standing on its hind legs on the rim of a terracotta pot, front paws hooked into the branches and yellow eyes turned toward us among the pink roses. Beside it, a small girl in a frilled white bonnet, coral necklace and brown dress picks a rose. Emma Homan was about two when John Bradley painted her, around 1844, and he gave her the full formal portrait anyway, on a canvas of 86.4 × 68.9 cm. Bradley's manner ran to bright colour, light outlines and plenty of detail: look for the fallen white rose on the patterned carpet at lower left.
context: Five portraits of the Totten family carry the inscription 'Drawn by I. Bradley from Great Britton', the best clue to where the painter came from, and the misspelling is part of the charm. City directories list John Bradley as a portrait painter near Houston Street in Manhattan from 1836 to 1847, and nothing is known of him after that. The sitter, Emma Homan (1842–1908), grew up to be the botanical artist Emma Homan Thayer, who wrote on American wildflowers, so the roses in her toddler portrait look like a forecast. The Met received the painting in 1966 from Edgar William and Bernice Chrysler Garbisch.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Kamada Matahachi Slaying the Monster Cat of Mount Suzuka
title_original: 鎌田又八勢州松坂の人無双強力なり同国鈴鹿乃山中にてとしふる大猫を殺す (inscription)
medium: Woodblock print (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
description: Enormous is the point: the cat's white, orange and black-spotted body fills the sheet, claws splayed at the corners, yellow eyes wide and fangs bared, while Kamada Matahachi crouches on top of it and drives his sword down toward its head. His robe is patterned with blue dragons; pink begonias and broad leaves spill up from the bottom. The inscription says Kamada Matahachi of Matsusaka in Seishū (Ise Province) was a man of matchless strength who killed a great cat grown old with years in the Suzuka mountains. The sheet is a vertical oban woodblock print, 36.2 × 25.2 cm.
context: Mid-19th century is as close as the British Museum will date this print, which it holds as 2008,3037.21219 and cross-refers to B. W. Robinson's 1982 supplement to his catalogue of Kuniyoshi prints. Matahachi was a local hero of legend from Matsusaka, and his fight sits within the Edo taste for monster-cat stories on stage and in print. Fun fact: the inscription's toshifuru ōneko, “great cat grown old”, explains the monster in two words. Folk belief across Japan held that aged cats turned into bakeneko, with tales from Ibaraki and Nagano naming twelve years as the tipping point.
title_eng: Kamada Matahachi Slaying the Monster Cat of Mount Suzuka
submovement: Late Edo Ukiyo-e Woodblock Printmaking (Utagawa School)
feline_symbolism: The cat is a bakeneko-type monster: in Edo folklore great age turned a house cat into something supernatural, and the hero's victory restores order.
image_credit: Print artist:Utagawa Kuniyoshi (歌川国芳) · https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/A_2008-3037-21219

title: Ō itai (Ouch! That Hurts!), No. 7 from Sankai medetai zue (Excellences of Mountain and Sea Illustrated)
medium: Woodblock print (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
description: A cream-coloured cat in a red collar squirms upside down against the woman's chest, front paw on her collar and mouth clamped on her fingers, and the title tells you how that is going: Ō itai!, 'Ouch! That hurts!'. She looks down at it with a surprisingly calm face. The British Museum describes the main scene simply as a woman playing with a cat. In the inset above, a fisherman in a small boat wrestles the big octopus of Namerikawa in Etchū Province named in the cartouche. It is a vertical oban woodblock print, 36.9 × 25.2 cm, number 7 of its series.
context: The series is Sankai medetai zue (Excellences of Mountain and Sea Illustrated), published in the 8th month of 1852. Each sheet pairs a half-length woman with an inset of a famous regional product, and according to the British Museum's notes the insets were done by Kuniyoshi's pupils; Commons also lists Utagawa Yoshitori among the hands. Fun fact: the titles riff on the series' medetai (“auspicious”) by ending in -tai, so this sheet is ō itai, no. 19 is hayaku kimetai (“I want to settle it quickly”) and no. 2 is hayaku mitai (“I want to see it soon”).
title_eng: Ō itai (Ouch! That Hurts!), No. 7 from Sankai medetai zue (Excellences of Mountain and Sea Illustrated)
title_original: 山海愛度図会 ヲゝいたい 越中滑川 大蛸 七
submovement: Late Edo Ukiyo-e Woodblock Printmaking (Utagawa School)
image_credit: Utagawa Kuniyoshi · http://visipix.com/search/search.php?userid=1616934267&q=%272aAuthors/K/Kuniyoshi%201797-1861%2C%20Utagawa%2C%20Japan%27&s=19&l=en&u=2&ub=1&k=1

title: Hayaku kimetai (I Want to Settle It Quickly), No. 19 from Sankai medetai zue (Excellences of Mountain and Sea Illustrated)
medium: Woodblock print (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
description: While the woman reads a printed fortune, the cat behind her shoulder has decided the future can wait: a cream cat with black patches on its head and back, curled into a ball with eyes shut and chin tucked down. That is the British Museum's own description of the scene, and the title on the sheet, Hayaku kimetai ('I want to settle it quickly'), supplies her side of the mood. The inset shows fishermen on the shore with baskets, harvesting the octopus of Takasago in Harima Province. It is a vertical oban woodblock print, number 19 in its series.
context: No. 19 of Sankai medetai zue (Excellences of Mountain and Sea Illustrated), published in the 8th month of 1852, pairs a half-length woman with an inset of a regional product drawn by Kuniyoshi's pupils. The British Museum holds this impression (2008,3037.02115). Fun fact: the series title on the sheet writes medetai as 愛度, with the characters for “love” and “degree”, instead of the usual 目出度, a small bit of wordplay that turns “auspicious” into something closer to “degrees of affection”.
title_eng: Hayaku kimetai (I Want to Settle It Quickly), No. 19 from Sankai medetai zue (Excellences of Mountain and Sea Illustrated)
title_original: 山海愛度図会 はやくきめたい 播州高砂 蛸 十九
submovement: Late Edo Ukiyo-e Woodblock Printmaking (Utagawa School)
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons

title: Sheet from Myōdensu jūroku rikan (Sixteen Wonderful Considerations of Profit)
medium: Woodblock print (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
description: Burrowing into the hem of the woman's striped robe, a white cat with orange patches keeps its tail up and its teeth bared on the fabric, while she kneels over a bowl at her toilette. A Buddhist holy man with a halo watches from a hanging scroll at upper right. The British Museum's records show that Kuniyoshi slipped a cat into at least two of the sixteen designs: one beside a woman at her toilette, another crawling into the outer robe of a woman seated at a stove. Here the cat seems to do both jobs at once.
context: The series, Myōdensu jūroku rikan (Sixteen Wonderful Considerations of Profit), was published around 1845 by Enshūya Matabei. Its title is a pun: rikan (利勘), reckoning profit, stands in for rakan (羅漢), the Buddhist arhats, so the Sixteen Arhats become sixteen object lessons. Each woman's sheet carries a mock-arhat name; the National Diet Library copies include Asane sonja, the late riser, and Tanki sonja, the short-tempered one. Fun fact: those names write sonja with 損, the character for “loss”, so the venerable ones become, roughly, the venerable losers.
title_eng: Sheet from Myōdensu jūroku rikan (Sixteen Wonderful Considerations of Profit)
submovement: Late Edo Ukiyo-e Woodblock Printmaking (Utagawa School)
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons

title: Okabe, from Tōkaidō gojūsan tsui (Pairs for the Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō)
medium: Woodblock print (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
description: Filling the whole upper left of the picture, a huge, ghostly grey cat head with pricked ears, glowing yellow eyes and bared teeth rises like smoke behind the old woman. She leans forward, white hair streaming, toward a young girl who flinches away at lower left. The station is Okabe on the Tōkaidō, and the print turns on a belief recorded with it: a girl who reached a temple after dark might be offered lodging by an old woman, who would become a witch, take the shape of a cat and devour her. It is a large vertical oban print published by Ibaya Kyūbei.
context: Tōkaidō gojūsan tsui (Pairs for the Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō), published between 1844 and 1847, pairs each post station on the road from Edo to Kyoto with a story. The Japanese notes on the Commons copy tie this one to a kabuki play by Tsuruya Nanboku IV, Hitori tabi gojūsan-tsugi (独道中五十三駅).
