Fun fact: that stage link suggests the cat arrived by way of the theatre, since the scene those notes cite is the play's “bakeneko of Okazaki”, a different station, rather than from any cat tale tied to Okabe itself.
title_eng: Okabe, from Tōkaidō gojūsan tsui (Pairs for the Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō)
title_original: 東海道五十三對 岡部
submovement: Late Edo Ukiyo-e Woodblock Printmaking (Utagawa School)
feline_symbolism: The cat here is a shapeshifter: Edo folklore credited old cats with turning into bakeneko that could take human form, and the old woman who is really a cat is one of its stock figures.
image_credit: Utagawa Kuniyoshi · http://visipix.com/search/search.php?userid=1616934267&q=%272aAuthors/K/Kuniyoshi%201797-1861%2C%20Utagawa%2C%20Japan%27&s=23&l=en&u=2&ub=1&k=1

title: The Favorite Cat
dimensions: Image: 31 × 22 cm; image and text: 33.7 × 22.1 cm; sheet: 35.3 × 25.6 cm
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: A tabby cat sits for its portrait, square to the viewer, head and broad chest filling the frame, round yellow-green eyes wide open and a pink nose the only other touch of colour. The forehead is splashed with dark leopard-like spots, the whiskers are long fine lines, and the chest fur is built from soft curved bands. The title, The Favorite Cat, does the sentimental work in three words, lettered beneath with Currier's imprint. The Met catalogues it as a hand-coloured lithograph, the picture 31 × 22 cm, the printed area 33.7 cm high with lettering. The colour went on by hand, so no two impressions match exactly.
context: Colouring was an assembly line: a dozen or more women, often immigrants from Germany with an art background, each added one colour and were paid $6 for every 100 prints, and small prints sold for five to twenty cents. The Met credits Nathaniel Currier as publisher and dates the sheet 1838–48, before James Merritt Ives, the firm's bookkeeper, became his partner in 1857 and the name Currier and Ives first appeared. That makes this one of the solo-Currier sheets. It came to the museum with the bequest of Adele S. Colgate in 1962.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Scene at Okazaki: Onoe Kikugorō III as the Spirit of the Cat Stone (Gojūsan-tsugi no uchi Okazaki no ba)
medium: Woodblock print triptych (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
description: A giant cat face fills the smoke behind the centre sheet, all whiskers and saucer eyes. Below it sits Onoe Kikugorō III as the Neko-ishi no kai, the spirit of the cat stone, cat ears poking from grey hair, conjuring the monster against the samurai Shirasuga Jūemon, played by Mimasu Gennosuke I on the right. Ichimura Uzaemon XII, as the young lord Inabanosuke, holds the left sheet beside a lantern that shows a cat's shadow. Two small cats in headscarves dance on their hind legs. It is an actor print first: three tall ōban sheets, the cast of the season's hit play for Edo fans to buy.
context: Edo's Ichimura theatre staged the Tōkaidō travel play usually titled Ume no haru (or Ume no hatsuharu) gojūsan-tsugi in 1835, and its Okazaki scene introduced a cat that turns into a demon. Kuniyoshi designed this triptych for it. The British Museum's impression is catalogued as (2008,3037.19408) 'Gojūsan-tsugi no uchi [Okazaki no ba]', and the Japan Society showed another from the Hiraki Ukiyo-e Collection. Fun fact: the role stuck to Kikugorō for the rest of his career. When he retired in 1847, the cat came back on stage for his farewell run, and Kuniyoshi and Kunisada both made new prints of it.
title_eng: Scene at Okazaki: Onoe Kikugorō III as the Spirit of the Cat Stone (Gojūsan-tsugi no uchi Okazaki no ba)
submovement: Late Edo Ukiyo-e Woodblock Printmaking (Utagawa School)
feline_symbolism: The cat here is a bakeneko, a cat grown old enough to become a shape-shifting demon; in the Okazaki story it disguises itself as an old woman.
image_credit: Utagawa Kuniyoshi · scanned from ISBN 978-4-336-04139-5 .

title: Cats Suggested as the Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō
title_original: 其のまま地口・猫飼好五十三疋
submovement: Late Edo Ukiyo-e Woodblock Printmaking (Utagawa School)
medium: Woodblock print triptych (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
description: Fifty-five cats sprawl across three sheets, each one standing in for a stop on the Tōkaidō road from Edo to Kyoto, plus the two ends. Some catch rats, some eat fish, one squeezes out of a basket. Each cat sits beside a station name in a red cartouche, and the joke is that the pose rhymes with it. Miya, the 41st station, sounds like oya, 'parent', so a mother cat lies with two kittens. Ishibe sounds like mijime, 'miserable', and gets a scrawny, scruffy cat in the bottom left. Look for the lone all-black cat in the middle sheet and the mice scampering along the top edge.
context: Hiroshige's best-selling Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō (1833–34) is the target of this parody, which Kuniyoshi published around 1847–50; dates in the literature range from 1847 to 1850. Landscape turns into puns, and even the title is a joke, swapping Tōkaidō for 'Myōkaikō', roughly 'fondness for keeping cats'. Fun fact: animal parodies like this flourished because the Tenpō reforms of the early 1840s banned prints of actors and courtesans, so Kuniyoshi learned to slip people, and jokes, into cats.
title_eng: Cats Suggested as the Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō
image_credit: 歌川国芳 (Utagawa Kuniyoshi, 1798 - 1861) · http://visipix.com/search/search.php?userid=1616934267&q=%272aAuthors/K/Kuniyoshi%201797-1861%2C%20Utagawa%2C%20Japan%27&s=22&l=en&u=2&ub=1&k=1

title: Inumura Daikaku Stabbing the Monster Cat, from Kyokutei-ō seicho Hakkenshi zui-ichi
medium: Woodblock print (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
description: A giant calico cat, orange and black patches on white, sprawls upside down across the sheet while Inumura Daikaku, one of the eight dog-warriors of the Hakkenden, drives his blade in near its throat. The cat's head lies at bottom left, fangs bared and whiskers flying, and its clawed paws grip the warrior from both sides. The cat is far bigger than the man, which is the point: Kuniyoshi's warriors always fight something oversized. Notice the long scroll looped over Daikaku's shoulders and across the cat's body, a paper-and-ink joke on a print series that advertises itself as 'the best of refined authors'.
context: Eight heroes whose names all contain the character for 'dog' drive Kyokutei Bakin's enormous novel Nansō Satomi Hakkenden, published over 28 years (1814–42) in 106 booklets. This sheet comes from Kuniyoshi's series Kyokutei-ō seicho Hakkenshi zui-ichi (The One and Only Eight Dog History of Old Kyokutei, Best of Refined Authors), which the British Museum dates to about 1835. A dog-hero killing a cat demon is about as on-brand as Edo fiction gets. Fun fact: Bakin went blind before he finished the novel and dictated its last parts to his daughter-in-law, Michi Tokimura.
title_eng: Inumura Daikaku Stabbing the Monster Cat, from Kyokutei-ō seicho Hakkenshi zui-ichi
submovement: Late Edo Ukiyo-e Woodblock Printmaking (Utagawa School)
feline_symbolism: The cat is the villain, a monstrous cat demon that the dog-named hero must destroy.
image_credit: Utagawa Kuniyoshi · http://www.britishmuseum.org/research/search_the_collection_database/search_object_image.aspx

title: The Famous and Unrivalled Hidari Jingorō (Meiyo migi ni teki nashi Hidari Jingorō)
medium: Woodblock print triptych (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division
description: At bottom left, a white cat with black patches sits twisted round to lick its leg, the only figure in the room ignoring the sculptor. The left-handed Hidari Jingorō kneels on a cushion stamped with Kuniyoshi's own kiri (paulownia) seal, chisels and a whetstone tub at his knees. Behind him crowd his creations, so lifelike they wear the faces of kabuki stars: a bearded sage, a veiled lady, a red-robed Daruma, two masks on the floor. Commons metadata identifies the faces as Morita Kan'ya XI, Onoe Kikugorō IV, Ichikawa Danzō VI, Ichimura Uzaemon XII and Matsumoto Kōshirō VI. By legend, Jingorō's best-known work was a cat.
context: Hidari means left and migi means right, and the title, Meiyo migi ni teki nashi Hidari Jingorō (The Famous and Unrivalled Hidari Jingorō), turns on it: he is unmatched 'on the right' though he carves with his left. Ebisuya Shōshichi published the triptych around 1847–50, judging by its censor seals, and the Kuniyoshi Project lists it among the artist's disguised self-portraits, reading the sculptor as Kuniyoshi himself. Fun fact: Jingorō may never have existed. Tradition credits him with the Nemuri-neko, the sleeping cat carved above a gate at Nikkō Tōshō-gū, and with a carved woman who came to life before a mirror.
title_eng: The Famous and Unrivalled Hidari Jingorō (Meiyo migi ni teki nashi Hidari Jingorō)
submovement: Late Edo Ukiyo-e Woodblock Printmaking (Utagawa School)
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons

title: Netsuke of Cat
title_original: 象牙彫 眠り猫根付 (懐玉斎正次)
description: Carved from a single piece of ivory, this cat is small enough to close a fist around: 2.5 cm high, 3.2 cm wide, 2.2 cm deep. It crouches low with its tail wrapped forward along its side, head turned and tipped up as if someone just said its name. Dark staining picks out the ears, brows and the line of the haunch, and the honey-coloured ivory has a glassy shine. That compact shape is practical: a netsuke had to sit snugly against a man's sash without snagging. The Met photographs it from several sides, because on a netsuke the underside, where the cord ran, is part of the design.
context: Netsuke were toggles. Men's kimono had no pockets, so pouches and inrō boxes hung on cords from the obi, and a carved netsuke held the cord in place. Cats were a natural subject for a compact katabori (carved-in-the-round) piece. This one came to the Met in 1910 as a gift from Mrs. Russell Sage. Fun fact: the Met dates it only to the 19th century, a span that straddles the Edo-to-Meiji change, the moment Western dress began putting netsuke out of work and sending so many to Western collectors.
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Cat quilt
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: Cats sit bolt upright all over this red-and-green cotton quilt, small appliqué silhouettes with pricked ears, tilted at angles so they seem to orbit the spoked wheel at the centre. Look first at the top middle, where a pair sits under the big heart. Around them grow tulips, hearts, birds and odd palm-like trees on vines that wind out to the corners. The maker cut the shapes from paper templates and stitched them down, so every cat has the same flat, cookie-cutter outline, a bit like a stencil that learned to purr. It is a big bed quilt, 227.3 by 197.5 cm.
context: Paper templates did the work: the Met says many of the motifs, the cats, hearts, trees, birds and flowers, were cut following paper patterns, a technique common in New York State quilts, and calls two related New York quilts far less fanciful. The maker is unknown, but the Met's text assumes she stitched in some of her favourite things: cats, plants and love. Allison L. Reddington gave the quilt to the museum in 2020 in celebration of its 150th anniversary. Fun fact: bold pictorial quilts like this are rare among mid-nineteenth-century examples, which tended to follow more regimented patterns.
feline_symbolism: The Met reads the cats as favourite things of the maker rather than symbols, noting 'we must assume' this; other New York quilts with cats have been given political or fraternal readings, but nothing is proven.
submovement: New York State pictorial appliqué quilt
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Figure of a Baby in a Cradle Holding a Kitten
title_original: Figure of a Baby in a Cradle Holding a Kitten
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: A kitten curls on the baby's chest, so small and so white that it reads only as a soft lump against the baby's gown. The baby lies in a hooded, basket-weave cradle on stubby feet, curly head on the pillow, eyes closed, all in unglazed white Parian porcelain small enough for a mantel shelf: 11.1 cm high, 16.5 cm long, 7.9 cm deep. Little raised beads stud the rim and the hood. Parian was made to look like carved marble, so baby, kitten and wickerwork share one matte, sugary white. That is the charm and the joke: a mould-cast ornament dressed as sculpture.
context: Marble from the Greek island of Paros lent its name to Parian ware, a bisque porcelain developed around 1845 by Mintons to imitate carved stone. Because it could be prepared as a liquid and cast in a mould, it allowed mass production of busts and figurines. Fun fact: the early history of its invention was confused at the time, with several firms claiming credit, and Copeland's Thomas Battam was the first to claim it, under the name 'Statuary Porcelain'. The Met lists this figure as American, dated broadly 1830–70, maker unrecorded, and received it in 1947 as a gift of Dr. Charles W. Green.
title_eng: Figure of a Baby in a Cradle Holding a Kitten
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: The Awakening Conscience
description: Under the table at left, a tabby cat crouches over a bird it has caught, a tiny scene of predator and prey that most people only spot after the main event. Above, a young woman rises from her lover's lap, eyes lifted, while he lounges back in his chair beside the piano, mouth open mid-song. The room is crammed with new, glossy things: a gilt clock under a glass dome, a tangle of wool on the red carpet. Hunt paints every surface hard and bright in oil, and the sheet music on the piano is Thomas Moore's 'Oft in the Stilly Night', a song about lost happier days.
context: Thomas Fairbairn, a Manchester industrialist and patron of the Pre-Raphaelites, commissioned the picture and paid Hunt 350 guineas for it in 1853–54. Annie Miller, to whom Hunt was engaged until 1859, sat for the woman. Fairbairn found her original expression too painful to live with and persuaded Hunt to soften it; Hunt reworked the face and retouched the canvas again in 1864 and 1886. The painting stayed in the Fairbairn family until an anonymous Christie's sale in January 1946, and Sir Colin and Lady Anderson gave it to the Tate in 1976. Fun fact: Ruskin defended it in The Times in 1854, insisting that not a single object in the room was without meaning, which rather puts pressure on the cat.
feline_symbolism: The cat playing with a bird under the table mirrors the woman's situation as a kept mistress, caught and toyed with.
image_credit: William Holman Hunt · https://www.flickr.com/photos/gandalfsgallery/5626470779

title: The Painter's Studio: A Real Allegory (L'Atelier du peintre)
title_original: L'Atelier du peintre: Allégorie réelle déterminant une phase de sept années de ma vie artistique et morale
description: In a canvas almost six metres wide, the cat is easy to miss. It is a white cat sprawled playfully on the floor at Courbet's feet, right beside the small boy who stands watching him paint a landscape, while a nude model clutches a white sheet to her chest and looks over his shoulder. To the left crowd figures from every corner of French society, behind them a lay figure slumped like a crucified body; to the right stand Courbet's friends and supporters, one of them reading at a table. The cat is the one figure in the middle with no opinion about art.
context: Rejected for the Exposition Universelle of 1855, the huge canvas ended up in a 'Pavilion of Realism' that Courbet built at his own expense beside the fair, as the Musée d'Orsay explains. He had painted it in Ornans and given it the deliberately odd subtitle 'a real allegory' of seven years of his artistic life. The canvas, 361 by 598 cm, is now in the Musée d'Orsay (RF 2257). Fun fact: one of the friends on the right is the critic Champfleury, who in 1869 published Les Chats, a book of essays on cats that collected cat images by contemporary artists.
title_eng: The Painter's Studio: A Real Allegory Summing Up Seven Years of My Artistic and Moral Life
image_credit: Gustave Courbet · Unknown source Unknown source

title: Girl with Cat (Girl with Kitten)
description: Slung against her right side, its head pressed up by her cheek, a grey tabby rides on the girl's shoulder, its fur nearly melting into the dark background. The canvas is large, just over a metre tall (107 × 84.7 cm), a lot of oil paint to give a child and a pet. Hunt painted it in 1856, fresh from two years at Barbizon beside Jean-François Millet: an ordinary subject, plain colour, a sitter doing nothing grand. She looks down, in a pink dress with braided trim, lace cuffs and black bows, hands folded under the cat. The cat is the reason the girl is holding still.
context: Seeing Millet's The Sower at the 1851 Salon turned a Paris-trained Vermonter into a Barbizon convert. William Morris Hunt (1824–1879) had studied with Thomas Couture; he returned to America in 1855, became Boston's leading portraitist, and talked Boston collectors into buying Millet and other French painters, which is a big reason the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (accession 00.504) is so rich in Barbizon pictures. Fun fact: the Great Boston Fire of 1872 destroyed many of Hunt's own paintings, so early canvases like this one are survivors.
image_credit: William Morris Hunt · https://www.mfa.org/collections/object/girl-with-cat-31115

title: Asakusa Ricefields and Torinomachi Festival (One Hundred Famous Views of Edo)
title_original: 名所江戸百景 浅草田甫酉の町詣
description: Back to us, a white cat sits on the sill of a Yoshiwara room, looking out through the lattice across the Asakusa rice fields toward Mount Fuji. Birds cross the evening sky. Out in the fields a line of tiny pilgrims heads to the Tori no machi (rooster festival) at the Ōtori shrine of Chōkoku-ji, carrying good-luck rakes. Nobody human appears in the room, but there are clues: a towel and bowl on the sill, and on the floor a folded paper with bear's-paw hairpins that rhyme with the pilgrims' rakes. The cat is the only one left at the window, which is exactly the point.
context: Print 101 of Hiroshige's One Hundred Famous Views of Edo is dated the eleventh month of 1857, when the festival fell. The series ran from 1856 to 1859, published by Sakanaya Eikichi, and was completed by Hiroshige II after Hiroshige died in 1858. The familiar image of this sheet comes from the Brooklyn Museum's impression. Fun fact: the festival is never shown head-on. Hiroshige hints at it through the hairpins, which echo the rakes the pilgrims carry, and one common reading has the cat standing in for the courtesan, who has just finished her work.
medium: Woodblock print (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
submovement: Late Edo Landscape Ukiyo-e Woodblock Printmaking
feline_symbolism: Scholars commonly read the white cat as a stand-in for the absent courtesan resting after work.
image_credit: Utagawa Hiroshige · Online Collection of Brooklyn Museum

title: Kittens Playing (Spelende katjes)
description: A long-haired grey-and-white mother cat with green eyes keeps watch from the right while four kittens wreck a wicker basket: one hangs over its rim, a ginger one pounces on a white sibling rolling on its back, and a dark tabby peers out from the shadows at far left. One paw has already landed in the saucer of milk. The canvas is modest, 49 by 61 cm, and the Boijmans dates it to about 1890, when she was nearly seventy and at the height of her cat fame. Her trick: chaos caught in the act, on a stage of red drapery.
context: A gift from Mrs. Ch. and Mrs. E. Jossmann in 1939 brought this canvas to Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen, which later lent it to the 2017 exhibition Kattenliefde. Henriëtte Ronner-Knip (1821–1909) learned to paint from her father, Joseph August Knip, and kept the family afloat when he went blind. After marrying in 1850 she moved to Brussels and narrowed her subjects to dogs and then cats; from about 1870 she built an international market for playful long-haired cats in bourgeois interiors. Fun fact: she was the first woman admitted as an active member of the Amsterdam artists' society Arti et Amicitiae.
image_credit: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip · Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen

title: A Cat Curled Up, Sleeping (Un chat endormi)
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: Curled into a sleeping ball, a cat is drawn in graphite on a sheet smaller than a postcard: 11.7 by 10.8 cm. The back is a loose cloud of grey hatching, while the darkest strokes go to the patched head, tucked down on the right with a white blaze and one ear just showing. A few wavy lines underneath suggest a cushion or cloth. This is Manet with nobody watching, no Salon jury and no scandal, just a pencil working out how a coil of fur and a tucked head make one rounded shape. A sleeping cat is the most cooperative model a painter can hope for, until it wakes.
context: Two years before Olympia put a black cat at the centre of a public row, Manet drew this sleeper in 1861. The Met acquired it in 1995 (Bequest of Clifford A. Furst, by exchange), together with a companion sheet from the same year, A Cat Resting on All Fours, Seen from Behind (1995.494), so the two studies now sit side by side in the Drawings and Prints department. Fun fact: cats kept coming back in Manet's graphic work. In 1869 he contributed the etching Cat and Flowers to his friend Champfleury's book Les Chats, a collection of essays and artists' cat images.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Vase
title_original: Vase à pieds léonins et félins
artist: Firm of Ferdinand Barbedienne (made by); Louis-Constant Sévin (designer)
description: Gilt cat legs carry this tall blue vase: three slim limbs that end in neat paws on the floor, each rising to a small stylised cat head at the shoulder, with a long loop handle springing up behind it. Cleveland calls them cat legs, not the lion feet you might expect, and ties them to ancient Egypt. Above them the body is champlevé enamel in turquoise, blue and red, with scrolling foliage, a Greek key band and red cabochons set in a gold collar. The amphora shape is Greek and the scrolls are medieval Islamic, so one 78.7 cm object hosts three civilisations.
context: A Paris firm run by Ferdinand Barbedienne made this vase around 1862, to a design by Louis-Constant Sévin. The model was introduced at the International Exhibition in London that year, and it proved popular enough to spawn several colour and shape variations. Cleveland bought this example in 1996 from the Barbedienne line of descent (Gustave Leblanc-Barbedienne) with the Severance and Greta Millikin Purchase Fund. Fun fact: in 2012–14 it toured the US for Inventing the Modern World: Decorative Arts at the World's Fairs, 1851–1939, which seems fitting for an object that debuted at a world's fair.
submovement: French Second Empire Historicism & Champlevé Enamel
image_credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Olympia (The Black Cat at the Foot of the Bed)
submovement: Second Empire Realism (Manet, Salon scandal of 1865)
description: At the far right end of the bed a black cat stands with its back arched and tail straight up, almost lost against the dark green curtain until you catch its yellow eyes. Manet put it exactly where Titian's Venus of Urbino has a small sleeping dog. Olympia, modelled by Victorine Meurent, lies on white sheets with an orchid in her hair and a black ribbon at her throat, and looks straight out; the maid, modelled by a woman known as Laure, brings a paper-wrapped bouquet from an admirer. The cat is the only figure that reacts to the arrival.
context: Critics at the Salon of 1865 called the painting immoral and vulgar, and according to Antonin Proust the administration had to take precautions to keep the canvas from harm. After Manet's death Claude Monet organised a subscription to buy it for France, with Winnaretta Singer the largest donor, and the state bought it from Suzanne Manet in 1890 for 19,415 francs. It went to the Luxembourg, then to the Louvre in 1907 on Clemenceau's order, and to the Musée d'Orsay in 1986. Fun fact: the model, Victorine Meurent, later became a painter herself and exhibited at the Salon in 1876, 1879, 1885 and 1904.
feline_symbolism: Swapping Titian's dog of fidelity for a black cat with an arched back pointed to night-time promiscuity, helped along by the French slang sense of 'chatte'.
image_credit: Édouard Manet · Google Arts & Culture — ywFEI4rxgCSO1Q

title: Woman with a Cat
description: Paws splayed and head thrown back, a fluffy white cat sprawls across a young woman's arms, filling the lower left of the canvas. Her free hand supports it from below, and she tilts her head down at it with a half smile, a ruffled lace cap on her dark hair and a white wrap sliding off her shoulders. The painting is modest, 78.3 by 57.2 cm, and the dark ground swallows the edges, so flesh, fabric and fur carry all the light. Cat and wrap are painted in nearly the same creamy whites, which makes the animal read as one more fold of the woman's dress.
context: A white cat sits in the central group of Courbet's The Painter's Studio, near the nude model and a young boy, and the critic Champfleury, one of the friends painted into that picture, later wrote a whole book about cats, Les Chats (1869). Courbet had shown the Studio in his own pavilion in 1855. This smaller canvas, La Femme au chat, is dated 1864 and is now in the Worcester Art Museum, Massachusetts (accession 1940.300). Fun fact: the museum's own cat-themed exhibition MEOW (2016) put it on a self-guided tour of the museum's cat art, alongside an Egyptian cat sculpture.
image_credit: Gustave Courbet · Self-photographed , 28 April 2010

title: My Little White Kitties – Into Mischief
title_eng: My Little White Kitties – Into Mischief
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: Two white kittens have tipped over a cup on a green tablecloth and are now lapping up the evidence, pink tongues in the spreading puddle of milk, tails up like exclamation marks. A heavy red drape hangs behind them and the carved wooden table edge runs along the bottom. It is a hand-coloured lithograph sold by the sheet: the image is 20.7 by 31.5 cm on a sheet of 28.4 by 35.7 cm, a size made for framing over a parlour table. The colour was laid on by hand over a black lithographic drawing, so each impression differs slightly, and here the colourist kept the kittens almost bare paper.
context: Sold by a firm that billed itself as 'the Grand Central Depot for Cheap and Popular Prints', this milk-spill scene sat in a catalogue that ran from battle scenes and ship portraits to winter landscapes. The Met dates the sheet 1857–71, the firm's first fourteen years under the name Currier & Ives, and catalogues it as a hand-coloured lithograph. It came to the museum with the 1962 bequest of Adele S. Colgate. Fun fact: that slogan was not modesty, it was a business plan: the firm sold through pushcart vendors, peddlers, bookshops, the mail and a London office.
title_original: My Little White Kitties – Into Mischief
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Cats (recto); Sketch of Two Figures Embracing (verso)
medium: Black ink applied with pen (reed) and brush on medium beige laid paper
description: On a beige laid sheet, 23.5 by 17.1 cm, three cats sit side by side: one on the left fully worked up, facing us with a heavy black shadow behind it, and two to the right left as bare outlines seen from behind, one barely more than a curved back and an ear. A reed pen gives a thick, uneven line that catches and splutters, so fur comes out as quick strokes rather than careful hatching, and the brush adds pools of shadow. Turn the sheet over and the mood changes completely: the verso, in graphite, is a sketch of two figures embracing. Ribot clearly used every inch of paper.
context: A bookkeeper in Rouen and then a foreman in Algeria, Théodule Ribot came to painting late, and made his name at the Salon of 1861 with dark kitchen scenes. His early biographers claimed the inky backgrounds came from painting by lamplight in his evenings, a story Cleveland repeats with a raised eyebrow. He belonged to the circle around François Bonvin and drew a positive response from Courbet. The drawing came from the Shepherd Gallery, New York, in May 1977, and entered the Cleveland Museum of Art in 2010 with the bequest of Muriel Butkin. Fun fact: in 1884 fellow artists including Monet, Rodin and Puvis de Chavannes gave him a medal inscribed 'To Théodule Ribot, the independent painter'.
image_credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Le Chat Botté (Puss in Boots)
title_original: Le Maître Chat ou le Chat botté
description: Puss in Boots strides down a riverbank with both paws flung in the air and mouth wide open in a shout, plumed hat askew, cape flying, a dead rat dangling from his belt beside a drawstring sack. Behind him, half hidden in the reeds, a man's head bobs in the water. Doré drew it for the 1862 edition of Perrault's fairy tales, and one of the professional block-cutters who translated his drawings cut it into wood. The cat gets the swagger Doré gave his knights. Up close the image is built from tiny parallel cuts that turn into fur, leather and shadow once you step back.
context: Hetzel published Doré's illustrated Contes de Perrault in 1862, and a Lausanne library copy credits the wood engraver Pannemaker with cutting this plate, the cat-and-ducking scene. The tale is older than Perrault, whose Le Maître chat ou le Chat botté appeared in 1697. The earliest written version is Straparola's 'Costantino Fortunato' in The Facetious Nights (c. 1550–53), and Giambattista Basile retold it in 1634 as 'Cagliuso'. Fun fact: in Straparola the clever cat is a fairy in disguise, helping a poor boy from Bohemia to dupe a king and win a princess.
feline_symbolism: Puss is the classic trickster helper, a cat whose wit wins his poor young master a fortune and a princess.
image_credit: Gustave Doré · http://www.veranijveld.com/gustave-doreacute-a-multitalented-visual-artist.html

title: The Cats' Rendezvous (Le Rendez-vous des chats)
medium: Lithograph in black on ivory wove paper, laid down on ivory cloth
description: Chimney pots and a fat wooden post frame two cats on a Paris rooftop: a solid black one seen from behind, tail looped up in a big question-mark curl and head turned toward the other, and a white one, drawn mostly as bare paper, glancing back over its shoulder. A big lithograph for its day: the image alone is 43.9 by 33.4 cm. Manet keeps the black cat almost solid and lets the white one exist as blank paper: ink against no ink. The flattened shapes owe a debt to the Japanese prints Paris was collecting in the 1860s.
context: A lithograph stone drawn in 1868 became the advertisement for Champfleury's Les Chats, a book of essays on cats with illustrations by contemporary artists, published in 1869 by J. Rothschild. Manet also contributed an etching, Cat and Flowers, to the book itself. The Art Institute of Chicago's impression (1987.15, John H. Wrenn Fund) is printed in black on ivory wove paper laid down on cloth. Fun fact: the Courtauld's label for a related Manet cat etching points out that the flattened shapes show Japanese influence, and that single cat motifs from Hokusai's sketchbooks ended up in the 1870 edition of the book.
image_credit: Édouard Manet · https://digitalcollections.nypl.org/search/index?filters%5BnamePart_mtxt_s%5D%5B%5D=Manet%2C%20%C3%89douard%2C%201832-1883&keywords=&layout=false#/?scroll=81

title: Champfleury: Les Chats (Poster / Illustrated Edition)
title_original: Champfleury - Les Chats: Histoire, Mœurs, Observations, Anecdotes
submovement: French Realist lithography and early Japonisme
medium: Lithograph with lettering (affichette); printer Lith. du Sénat, Barousse
description: Red capitals frame a rooftop scene: 'Champfleury - Les Chats' across the top, 'Deuxième édition avec 52 dessins' up both sides, and 'Un volume illustré, Prix 5 francs, En vente ici' below. Inside, Manet's black tom stands seen from behind with its tail hoisted in a tall hook and its head in profile, while a white cat stands its ground beside a post, half turned away. A pale moon sits behind the chimney pots. Black shape against bare tan paper keeps both cats almost flat, which suits a poster. The sheet measures about 33 × 43 cm, roughly the size of a shop-window card.
context: Five francs was the price printed on this shop-window card for the second edition of Champfleury's Les Chats, the book of cat history and anecdote by the critic who had championed Courbet and Realism. Manet's rooftop pair had first appeared as a plain lithograph in 1868, and here the printer wraps the same design in red lettering. The Bibliothèque nationale de France owes its impression to the collector Étienne Moreau-Nélaton, whose legacy was registered on 1 August 1927. Fun fact: the Courtauld's label for a Manet cat etching notes that single cat motifs from Hokusai's sketchbooks ended up in the 1870 edition, so a Paris cat book was already looking hard at Japan.
feline_symbolism: The rooftop tryst trades on the Parisian image of the cat as a night-time free spirit, which suited a book that presented the cat as the artist's and writer's animal.
image_credit: Manet, Édouard (1832-1883). Lithographe · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: The Cat and the Flowers (Le Chat et les fleurs)
description: Nose first into a pot of blossoms, a dark cat with a white chest and belly rears up at a wooden ledge, its forelegs hooked over the edge. Behind it is a second pot, an iron lattice railing, and flowers poking through the grid. Manet combines etching and aquatint, yet the cat itself is built from dense, rippling lines that follow the lie of the fur, while the flowers are left lighter and flatter. The plate is small, about 17 × 13 cm, set on a large cream sheet that makes it look even smaller.
context: Sources cannot agree which edition of Champfleury's Les Chats this plate belongs to. The Met's impression is catalogued as the final state of three, 'third edition (Mégnin)', the Courtauld calls the 1870 printing the fourth, and the San Francisco museums list a 'second ed.' of 1870. Manet made the plate in 1869 for the expanded book, published in Paris by J. Rothschild, and it was also sold as a stand-alone print, which is why impressions turn up in so many collections. The accession number 1979.194 belongs to the Baltimore Museum of Art's impression.
medium: Etching and aquatint on laid paper
image_credit: Édouard Manet · https://collection.artbma.org/people/5742/edouard-manet

title: A Flood
description: Hunched on the foot of a drifting wooden cradle at the left, a small black cat peers down at the brown floodwater. The baby lies inside under a flowered quilt, wide awake, hands raised, gazing up at raindrops on a bare branch where a small bird perches. A cream jug bobs at the lower right. Behind them a little bridge is nearly under water, a haystack and a house stand flooded to their lower edges, and men in a boat are pulled along by the current at top right. The canvas is big, about 99 × 145 cm, so the cat is close to life-size.
context: Local newspapers reported in 1864 that a baby in its cradle had been washed out of a house in the Sheffield flood, and Manchester Art Gallery names that as the immediate inspiration for this picture. Millais then turned a disaster into a comedy of mismatched reactions: the baby is oblivious to the danger and mesmerised by the glistening droplets on the branch overhead, while the cat does the worrying. The gallery acquired the canvas in 1891 (accession 1891.7). Fun fact: the painting is signed and dated with Millais's monogram, and visitors still argue over whether it is charming or grim.
image_credit: John Everett Millais · Manchester Art Gallery

title: Woman Churning Butter (La Baratteuse)
description: A peasant woman stands at a tall wooden churn, both hands on the dasher, head bent to the work. At her feet a cat presses against her skirts, angling for a spill or a treat, and she ignores it completely. Behind her, sacks of grain lean in the shadows of the dairy, which is where the cat ought to be on mouse duty. Millet builds the figure with dense hatching on a plate under 18 × 12 cm, so the cat is a small warm smudge of lines against her heavy hem.
context: A pencilled 'St ii/iii' at lower right marks this impression, in the British Museum (1865,1209.798), as the second of three states of Millet's etching of La Baratteuse, made at Barbizon in 1855–56 as part of a small group of prints of rural labour that spread his peasant subjects far beyond the Salon. Impressions are common in museums; the MFA Boston and the National Gallery of Victoria hold others. Fun fact: the third and final state carries the scratched address of the printer Auguste Delâtre, so the plate went on earning after Millet had finished with it.
feline_symbolism: The National Gallery of Victoria reads the cat as a gentle joke about duty: it begs at the churn when its real job is guarding the grain sacks from mice.
image_credit: Jean-François Millet · © The Trustees of the British Museum, shared under the museum's open terms via Wikimedia Commons

title: A Cat with Three Kittens (Een kat met drie jongen)
collection: Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed (RCE), Dutch state art collection
description: Nose to nose, a mother cat in black, brown and white and a fluffy white kitten, standing on its hind legs to reach her, meet at the top of a red cloth draped over a wicker basket. A calico kitten peers over the cloth, and a tabby kitten creeps out underneath, close to a loose thread. The panel is small, about 24 × 19 cm, and signed 'Henriëtte Ronner' at lower left. At that scale her method shows best: fur built up in short strokes that follow the direction of growth, eyes picked out with a single wet highlight, and the kittens' poses giving the eye a route around the family.
context: The prefix NK stands for Nederlands Kunstbezit, the Dutch state collection of works recovered from Germany after the Second World War and still under provenance research, so even a kitten picture has a wartime file. This panel, NK2003, is managed by the Cultural Heritage Agency (RCE) and held in its depot. Henriëtte Ronner-Knip (1821–1909) was born in Amsterdam, settled in Brussels and became best known for her cats, which she sold to buyers across Europe.
image_credit: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip · https://wo2.collectienederland.nl/doc/nk/NK2003

title: Woman with a Cat (Femme au chat)
description: A brown tabby, eyes narrowed to slits, is hugged against a young woman's shoulder, one forepaw draped over her arm like a stole. Renoir paints the pair as one soft mass: fur, piled-up hair and white blouse are built from the same loose, feathered strokes, so it is hard to say where the animal ends and the sleeve begins. She looks down, half smiling, a ring with a green stone catching the light on the hand that holds the cat. The canvas is modest, 56 × 46.4 cm, and the wall behind is a minty green. Nothing happens except closeness, which is the point.
context: Ernest Hoschedé, the department-store owner and early Impressionist collector, is the first known owner. The picture went under the hammer at his sale in Paris on 6 June 1878 (no. 75) and was bought by Count de Rasty. The Countess de Rasty sold it in 1925 or 1926 to Paul Rosenberg; Benjamin E. Levy had it by 1932 and gave it, with his wife, to the National Gallery of Art in 1950 (1950.12.1). Fun fact: Renoir painted it about a year after the first Impressionist exhibition of 1874, and within three years it had changed hands at a sale.
image_credit: Pierre-Auguste Renoir · https://www.nga.gov/collection/art-object-page.37637.html

title: The Cat and the Rat (Le Chat et le Rat)
description: A striped cat lounges on a mossy mound at the foot of a huge hollow tree, paws tucked, looking pleased with itself, while a rat sits up on its haunches at the far left and keeps a sensible distance. In a hollow of the trunk an owl peers out. This is La Fontaine's fable of the uneasy deal: the cat, caught in the hunter's net, needs the rat to gnaw the cords, and the owl is the third animal in the story. The artist skips the trap and shows the wary afterwards. The engraving after his drawing is sized to sit with the text of a family edition.
context: Grippe-fromage, 'cheese-grabber', is the cat's name in La Fontaine's fable, and Ronge-maille, 'mesh-gnawer', the rat's. It is Book VIII, fable XXII, in which a hunter's net catches the cat and the rat has to weigh up how safe a rescue would be. The picture comes from the Hetzel edition of the Fables ('Bibliothèque d'éducation et de récréation'), with animals drawn by Louis-Eugène Lambert (1825–1900); the BnF copy is dated 1870 on Commons. Fun fact: Lambert went to stay with George Sand at Nohant in 1844 for a month and stayed fourteen years.
title_original: Le Chat et le Rat (Fables de La Fontaine)
feline_symbolism: La Fontaine's moral is that a pact with a natural enemy should not be trusted: the rat accepts the cat's thanks from a safe distance.
image_credit: Jean de La Fontaine · This file comes from Gallica Digital Library and is available under the digital ID bpt6k5461375p/f470

title: The Cat and the Fox (Le Chat et le Renard)
description: Up in the fork of a pale, split old tree, a cat peers down, ears up, safe and smug; it has already used its one trick. Below, the fox rears on its hind legs at the trunk, mouth open, while the hounds' heads push out of the undergrowth at left. This is La Fontaine's pair of pious pilgrims: the fox boasts a sackful of tricks, the cat admits to just one, and when the dogs arrive, up the tree is the one that works. Lambert, a specialist in cats and dogs, gets to draw both his favourite animals in one fable, and the cat wins by altitude.
context: A sackful of tricks against a single one: that is the whole joke of the fable, and the picture puts the cat's one trick, climbing, at the top of the frame. The vignette comes from the Hetzel edition of La Fontaine's Fables ('Bibliothèque d'éducation et de récréation'), with animals drawn by Louis-Eugène Lambert (1825–1900); the BnF copy is dated 1870 on Commons. Lambert studied under Eugène Delacroix, who also financed his work, and under Paul Delaroche, and debuted at the Salon in 1847. Fun fact: his Salon nickname 'Lambert des chats' also appears as 'Raphaël des chats', the same title given to Gottfried Mind.
title_original: Le Chat et le Renard (Fables de La Fontaine)
feline_symbolism: The fable makes the cat the patron saint of one good idea, against the fox's cleverness: 'Le trop d'expédients peut gâter une affaire.'
image_credit: Jean de La Fontaine · This file comes from Gallica Digital Library and is available under the digital ID bpt6k5461375p/f512

title: The Cat and the Two Sparrows (Le Chat et les deux moineaux)
description: Tail up and a sparrow already in its jaws, a tabby cat crouches on a kitchen floor, while the second sparrow stands on its outstretched paw, apparently unaware of how this ends. The cat was raised from kittenhood alongside a pet sparrow; a second sparrow turns up, a quarrel starts, and the cat sides with its friend by eating the intruder, then enjoys the taste enough to eat its friend too. Lambert's vignette for one of La Fontaine's darkest fables gives the cat the starring role, beside an empty dish, with a cupboard and a half-open door behind.
context: Fable 2 of Book XII, the last book of La Fontaine's Fables, is the source of this plate from J. Hetzel's illustrated edition for the 'Bibliothèque d'éducation et de récréation', with the animals drawn by Louis-Eugène Lambert (1825–1900). The BnF copy (Gallica bpt6k5461375p, folio 621) is dated 1870 on Commons. Lambert, a Delacroix pupil nicknamed 'Lambert des chats' at the Salon, was the obvious man for the job. Fun fact: a family-education publisher still printed this one, cannibalised best friend and all.
title_eng: The Cat and the Two Sparrows
title_original: Le Chat et les deux moineaux (Fables de La Fontaine)
feline_symbolism: Here the cat is nature that cannot be trained out: friendship lasts exactly as long as appetite allows.
image_credit: Jean de La Fontaine · This file comes from Gallica Digital Library and is available under the digital ID bpt6k5461375p/f621

title: The Cat and an Old Rat (Le Chat et un vieux rat)
description: Rodilardus, the terror of the rats, hangs head-down from a rope among strings of onions, front paws dangling, playing dead. Below, a crowd of mice and rats rears up on a ledge in a little dance of relief, one sniffing at an upturned bowl. His second con, rolling in flour and lying in a meal tub, is still to come; this vignette catches the first. An old rat, tailless from earlier campaigns, keeps his distance and knows a cat is still a cat. Lambert's drawing, cut by the engraver A. Jourdain, turns the beam into a stage and the rodents into an audience.
context: 'Le Chat et un vieux Rat' closes Book III of La Fontaine's Fables, and this plate comes from J. Hetzel's illustrated edition, with the animals drawn by Louis-Eugène Lambert (1825–1900) and the block cut by A. Jourdain, whose signature runs under the lower left corner. The BnF copy (Gallica bpt6k5461375p, folio 202) is dated 1870 on Commons. Lambert was nicknamed 'Lambert des chats' at the Salon. Fun fact: La Fontaine borrowed the cat's name, Rodilardus ('gnaw-bacon'), from Rabelais.
title_eng: The Cat and an Old Rat
title_original: Le Chat et un vieux rat (Fables de La Fontaine)
feline_symbolism: The cat stands for disguised danger; the fable's moral praises the caution that comes with age.
image_credit: Jean de La Fontaine · This file comes from Gallica Digital Library and is available under the digital ID bpt6k5461375p/f202

title: The Cockerel, the Cat and the Young Mouse (Le Cochet, le Chat et le Souriceau)
description: Curled on the straw at right, the cat has its eyes half shut and its paws neatly together, the picture of modesty, while a cockerel stands on the rim of an upturned tub, beak wide open in mid-crow. Between them, tiny at the bottom left, the young mouse looks up at the noisy one. On its first outing the mouse decides the loud, red-crested, flapping bird is terrifying and the soft-furred, gentle-eyed creature lovely; its mother explains it the other way round. Lambert puts the real menace in the role of the charmer, which suited an artist who spent his career painting cats at their most appealing.
context: Two signatures sit at the lower corners of this plate: 'Eug. Lambert' at left and 'Joliet sc.' at right, crediting the draughtsman and the engraver. It comes from the La Fontaine published by J. Hetzel in the 'Bibliothèque d'éducation et de récréation', and the BnF copy (Gallica bpt6k5461375p, folio 309) is dated 1870 on Commons. The fable is in Book VI. Lambert, a Delacroix pupil, made his Salon debut in 1847 and belonged to the Société d'aquarellistes français from 1879 to 1896. Fun fact: the moral is a warning about faces, 'Garde-toi, tant que tu vivras, de juger des gens sur la mine', and the fable's own victim of bad judgement is the mouse.
title_eng: The Cockerel, the Cat and the Young Mouse
title_original: Le Cochet, le Chat et le Souriceau (Fables de La Fontaine)
feline_symbolism: The moral, 'Garde-toi, tant que tu vivras, de juger des gens sur la mine', makes the cat the textbook case of a pleasant face hiding a predator.
image_credit: Jean de La Fontaine · This file comes from Gallica Digital Library and is available under the digital ID bpt6k5461375p/f309

title: Cat and Lantern (Neko to Chōchin)
description: Head and forepaws jammed into the open end of a paper lantern it has knocked on its side, a white cat with brown tabby patches, red collar and little bell kicks its hindquarters up, tail flicked. Kiyochika builds a domestic drama from a cat and a lantern alone. The lantern is unlit, a pale ribbed drum with a family crest, its bamboo handle rolled out across a deep blue ground. The colour is laid in soft, graded impressions rather than crisp outlines, shading the lantern's curve the Western way. It is a horizontal ōban-size sheet, roughly 24 × 36 cm.
context: Soft gradations of light and shade were the signature of Kobayashi Kiyochika (1847–1915), a former retainer of the shogunate, who began publishing his kōsen-ga, prints of Tokyo built on Western-style light and shade, in 1876. Cat and Lantern (Neko to chōchin) is dated 1877 and is one of his best-known animal subjects of those years. Fun fact: the Japanese caption on the Commons file, taken from a Tokyo ukiyo-e gallery, says the print needed 35 separate woodblocks, far more than a standard colour print of the time, which is how Kiyochika got those soft gradations.
medium: Woodblock print (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
collection: Smithsonian, Freer Gallery of Art and Arthur M. Sackler Gallery (Robert O. Muller collection)
image_credit: Kobayashi Kiyochika · https://ukiyo-e.gallery/current_event/

title: Cat with a Fish
description: A bright yellow cat with big black spots sits curled on itself, face turned square to us with huge turquoise eyes and a worried, scalloped brow, a fat blue-grey prawn clamped in its mouth and its red tail fan draped over its back. Kalighat painters worked fast on cheap paper, and it shows in the best way: one swelling outline for the body, flat washes of watercolour inside it, and black patches that read as both fur pattern and pure graphic design. Even the ears get red stripes. On the back someone wrote, in English, the bluntest possible caption: 'Cat caught a fish'.
context: Kalighat painters, who sold quick, colourful pictures to pilgrims at the Kali temple in Calcutta (now Kolkata), turned this cat into a sermon. The V&A reads the animal as a satire on a false ascetic, someone who has renounced the world yet cannot control his appetite, and notes that the picture is often taken as an illustration of a Bengali proverb. The museum dates the sheet to about 1890 (within 1885–1894) and records it as a gift from M. N. Varvill (IS.261-1955). Fun fact: the sheet carries its own English caption on the back, 'Cat caught a fish', which flattens the satire into a plain report.
feline_symbolism: The V&A reads the cat as satire on a false ascetic: a creature that has supposedly renounced the world but cannot control its appetite, with the fish as the giveaway.
image_credit: GIF IT UP India · https://www.flickr.com/photos/189116622@N04/50058561063/ , https://gifitup.net/dag-museums/

title: Kittens
description: Four silver tabby kittens have broken into a jewel box on a lace-edged table, and the evidence is everywhere: a string of pearls trails off the edge, a bangle, a cross and a brooch lie abandoned, and one kitten rolls on its back batting at the loot. Kittens is what the Atkinson calls this canvas, and what Couldery did better than almost anyone in Victorian London. His method was a miniaturist's, tiny strokes laid in the direction of the fur, so the stripes are built hair by hair. Ruskin said one of his cat pictures could not rightly be seen without a lens, and this is the surface he meant.
context: Miss Chatfield left this canvas to the Atkinson in Southport in 1919, where it is catalogued as SOPAG:135; Art UK lists the artist as 1832–1910. Horatio Henry Couldery, born in Lewisham, gave up cabinetmaking for the Royal Academy Schools, first exhibited at the Academy in 1861 and also illustrated children's books and greeting cards. Fun fact: his death is often given as 1893, when his career faded, but the death registration puts it at 4 February 1918 in Sydenham, so the 1910 on the museum's listing is wrong too.
image_credit: Horatio Henry Couldery · Art UK

title: The Cat (Pisica)
medium: Oil on canvas laid on metal
collection: National Museum of Art of Romania (MNAR), Galeria de Arta Romaneasca Moderna, Bucharest
description: A young grey-and-white cat lies twisted on its back across the lower left of the canvas, white belly up and paws flung out in every direction, eyes on something to the right. It is a small study, oil on canvas glued onto a metal support, and the handling is broad and quick: a dark muted ground, and the animal treated as a mass of light and shadow rather than a portrait of individual hairs. Only the face and the white chest get any finish; the hind legs dissolve into the brown. The metal backing is the detail most people miss.
context: Oil on canvas laid onto metal is an unusual support for a cat study, and it is how the Romanian National Art Museum's Modern Romanian Art Gallery describes this picture. Grigorescu (1838–1907) is remembered as one of the founders of modern Romanian painting, and the cat dates to his French years, between 1864 and 1867. It was reproduced in the museum's centenary album, with texts by Mariana Vida and Monica Enache, issued for the retrospective 'Grigorescu pictor al naturii' opened on 25 October 2007. Fun fact: in 2025 the exhibition 'Câini vs. Pisici' at Art Safari used this very cat to introduce a tour of Romanian artists and their pets.
image_credit: Nicolae Grigorescu · Grigorescu - Album comemorativ la 100 de ani de decesul lui artistului, editat de Muzeul Național de Artă al României cu ocazia expoziției retrospective „Grigorescu pictor al naturii” desfășurată la Galeria de Artă Româ

title: Cat and Butterfly (耄耋圖)
artist: Xugu (Zhu Huairen, 虛谷 / 朱懷仁)
submovement: Late Qing Shanghai School (Haipai) Literati Painting
medium: Hanging scroll; ink and color on paper
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: A white cat, drawn only as a broken, dotted outline with two blazing orange eyes, stands in the lower half of a tall hanging scroll, tail up, staring straight out, while a flutter of butterflies drifts above it past a bank of pale green chrysanthemums. Xugu painted with the side of the brush in dry, angular strokes, so the cat looks almost cut from paper, and a slatted fence and blue-tipped leaves frame it at right. A column of bold calligraphy runs down the upper right. The image is about 134 × 65 cm on ink and colour on paper, and the mounted scroll is over two metres tall.
context: Army officer first, Buddhist monk second, Shanghai picture-seller third: Xugu (c. 1823/24–1896), born in She County, Anhui, became one of the most individual of the late-Qing Shanghai painters. This scroll came to the Metropolitan Museum in 1986 as a gift of Robert Hatfield Ellsworth, in memory of La Ferne Hatfield Ellsworth (1986.267.52). Fun fact: cat-and-butterfly pairings were standard birthday pictures in China, because the words for cat (mao) and butterfly (die) sound like maodie, 'great old age'; the National Palace Museum makes the same point about the cat in a Xuande painting.
feline_symbolism: Cat and butterfly together make the rebus maodie (耄耋), meaning a person of seventy or eighty, so the picture wishes the owner a long life.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Woman with a Cat (Portrait of Madame Manet)
title_original: Femme au chat (Portrait de Madame Manet)
collection: Tate, London (purchased 1918), on loan to the National Gallery, London
description: A black-and-white cat sleeps curled in a woman's lap at the lower middle of the canvas, a dark island in a sea of pink, its white muzzle and chest the sharpest notes in the picture. She sits at three-quarter length, head propped on one hand, looking past us, and her dress dissolves into long, slashing strokes that go soft and unfinished at the edges. A blue-white curtain with a tie-back flickers at the left edge. The canvas is upright, 92.1 × 73 cm, and the cat is the anchor everything else orbits.
context: Zizi was the Manets' pet cat, and the National Gallery's note says Manet sketched and painted her several times, spending his densest brushwork on her fur and moody face. The sitter is his wife, Suzanne Leenhoff, who came into his life as his piano teacher; they married in 1863. The exact date is unknown, probably 1880 or later, which would make it his last portrait of her, and he may still have been working on it when he died in 1883. Tate purchased it in 1918 (N03295) and it hangs on loan at the National Gallery as L675.
title_eng: Woman with a Cat: Portrait of Madame Manet
image_credit: Édouard Manet · http://www.tate.org.uk

title: Cat in Summer Greenery (Katt i sommargrönska)
collection: Private collection (sold Bukowskis, Stockholm, auction 653, lot 604A)
description: Tabby-and-white kitten, standing square in a summer thicket and looking straight up at us: big round eyes, pink nose, white bib and two white front socks, its striped tail swinging out to the right. The picture is barely bigger than a postcard, 22 by 15.5 cm, upright, painted in oil on panel, and the greenery gets as much paint as the cat: long, wiry streaks of green, rose and dry brown, with a few pale leaves sliding in at the bottom. Look for the inscription at lower left, 'Bruno Liljefors Qvarnbo -84', which pins the picture to a specific place and summer.
context: Kvarnbo, just outside Uppsala, is where Liljefors settled after returning to Sweden from France in the mid-1880s, and where he found the motifs for his early, delicately observed studies of Swedish flora and fauna. The panel stayed in the artist's family until Bukowskis sold it in Stockholm on 7 December 2023, at a hammer price of 1.7 million SEK. Fun fact: that was also the moment the cat Jeppe entered his life. Liljefors told how a kitten dragged a shot capercaillie under a farmhouse bed, and he took the kitten home. Jeppe was plain earth-grey with no white, though, so this white-bibbed kitten is someone else.
image_credit: Bruno Liljefors · Bukowskis

title: White Cat, Black Cat (Chat blanc, Chat noir)
description: Row after row of small cats tumble across this sheet, read top to bottom like a film strip: a white cat sniffs at a mousehole, pounces, rears up with the mouse dangling from its paws, and then a black cat slinks in. The two arch their backs, square off and end in a boxing match on hind legs while the mouse scuttles off. There are no words at all, as the record notes, so Steinlen's line does every bit of the storytelling, with only his signature near the bottom. It is a photomechanical print, his pen drawing transferred photographically to a plate and run off with a weekly paper.
context: Lausanne-born Steinlen settled in Paris in 1881 and began frequenting Rodolphe Salis's Chat Noir cabaret in 1884. Salis also ran a weekly paper of the same name, launched in 1882, and Steinlen drew for it between 1884 and 1895, mostly stories in pictures starring cats. The BnF dates this sheet to 1884, lists it as no. 649-153 in Crauzat's catalogue of Steinlen's prints, and has digitised it on Gallica. Fun fact: these strips are usually called histoires sans paroles, stories without words, and this one obeys the label more strictly than several neighbours from the same year, which the BnF records as carrying French text.
submovement: Le Chat Noir journal illustration (histoires sans paroles)
feline_symbolism: The cabaret was named, so the story goes, after an old tomcat that moved in during building work, so any cat in its paper doubled as a house mascot.
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Illustrateur · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: How Love Comes to Cats (Comment l'amour vient aux chats)
description: Beside a chimney, a white cat lounges, then lunges at sparrows, slips off the roof and lands in the street at the feet of a black cat. Hissing turns into wrestling, wrestling into a moonlit stroll, and the last row delivers the punchline: a long line of kittens, black, white and patched, sitting in order of size. That, according to Steinlen, is how love comes to cats. The BnF classes the sheet as a humorous composition, and the only French text is the printed title at the bottom. It is a photomechanical print, a pen drawing photographed onto a plate for Le Chat Noir.
context: Rodolphe Salis's Chat Noir cabaret had its own weekly, launched in 1882, and Steinlen, who came to Paris from Lausanne in 1881, supplied it with drawn stories from 1884, the year the BnF gives for this print, until 1895. Most of them starred cats. The sheet is no. 649-116 in Crauzat's catalogue of Steinlen's prints, and the Bibliothèque nationale de France has published it on Gallica. Fun fact: Steinlen's reputation as the cat specialist of Montmartre, the one who drew them playing, sleeping and furious, started in these cheap weekly pages more than a decade before his famous 1896 Tournée du Chat Noir poster.
submovement: Le Chat Noir journal illustration (histoires sans paroles)
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Illustrateur · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: Horrible End of a Goldfish (Horrible fin d'un Poisson rouge)
description: Eight scenes around a goldfish bowl on a stemmed stand follow a black cat, drawn as a flat silhouette: it stares, paws at the glass, climbs up, fishes from the rim, falls in with a splash of hatching, and finally bolts, soaked, from the toppled bowl while the goldfish lies stranded in a puddle. The sheet, headed 'Le Chat Noir', comes from that weekly, and the only French text is the title along the bottom. It is a photomechanical print, so the line you see is Steinlen's pen drawing reproduced by photography, and a reader could get the joke before the coffee cooled.
context: Dated 1884 by the Bibliothèque nationale de France, this is one of the first batch of cat stories Steinlen drew for Le Chat Noir, the weekly paper of Rodolphe Salis's Montmartre cabaret. Salis launched the paper in 1882; Steinlen, in Paris since 1881, contributed from 1884 to 1895. The BnF catalogues the print as Crauzat 649-121 and has digitised it on Gallica. Fun fact: the goldfish's grim fate belongs to a long Steinlen habit of letting the cat win, with a fish, a mouse or a crow as the victim, which is partly why he became known in Montmartre as the specialist of cats.
submovement: Le Chat Noir journal illustration (histoires sans paroles)
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Illustrateur · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: The Cat and the Crow (Le Chat et le Corbeau)
description: Asleep on an upholstered chair, a white cat has a black crow perched on the chair back above it, and the rest of the sheet is pure escalation. The crow pecks, the cat wakes and swipes, the crow yanks its tail from under the seat, and the chase spills outdoors and up a tree, where the cat ends up dangling upside down from a branch while the crow looks on. The title puts the cat first, but the crow seems to get the last laugh. The BnF files it as a humorous composition; it is a photomechanical print from Le Chat Noir, Steinlen's pen drawing photographed onto a plate.
context: Crauzat's catalogue of Steinlen's prints numbers this sheet 649-111, the lowest among the cat stories in this group, and the Bibliothèque nationale de France dates it to 1884, the year Steinlen, a Swiss illustrator living in Paris since 1881, began frequenting Rodolphe Salis's Chat Noir cabaret. The cabaret's weekly paper, launched in 1882, carried his drawn stories from 1884 to 1895, and cats were the leading actors in most of them. Fun fact: Rutgers' French department adopted Steinlen's Chat Noir cats as an informal mascot and decorates its website with images from these stories.
submovement: Le Chat Noir journal illustration (histoires sans paroles)
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Illustrateur · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: The Avenging Nail (Le Clou vengeur)
description: A black cat chases a mouse to a row of barrels, climbs and dives in head first, leaving only its tail and back legs sticking out. Then a rabbit bursts out of a barrel instead, and in the last scene the cat perches on the rim while the rabbit bolts away, trailing a long wiggling line snagged on a nail: the avenging nail of the title. The BnF's subject headings list cats, a rabbit, mice, barrels and nails, and a printed dedication at bottom right addresses a lady surprised that rabbits have no innards. It is a photomechanical print from Le Chat Noir, Steinlen's own pen line reproduced by photography.
context: A textile mill in Mulhouse employed Steinlen as a trainee designer after his studies at the University of Lausanne, a training that does not obviously predict a career spent making Parisians laugh at cats and barrels. He reached Paris in 1881, and the Bibliothèque nationale de France dates this story to 1884, his first year in the orbit of Rodolphe Salis's Chat Noir cabaret in Montmartre. Salis's weekly, launched in 1882, printed Steinlen's picture stories from 1884 to 1895, and cats starred in most. The BnF catalogues the sheet as Crauzat 649-134. Fun fact: the print is dedicated, in type at bottom right, to a lady surprised that rabbits have no innards.
submovement: Le Chat Noir journal illustration (histoires sans paroles)
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Illustrateur · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: The Ancestors of Maigriou (Les Ancêtres de Maigriou)
description: Some thirty cats sprawl across a grey-toned sheet, and almost all of them are asleep: curled into rings, flat on their backs with paws in the air, stretched full length, or reduced to a single heavy black head at the corners. A couple wake up to stretch. Maigriou, a name that sounds like a cross between maigre (skinny) and a miaow, gets a family album rather than a tree, and the BnF's only subject heading is 'cats'. It is a photomechanical print from Le Chat Noir, Steinlen's pen line photographed onto a plate and printed on cheap paper, the format in which most Parisians first met his cats.
context: Next to 'Le Clou vengeur' in Crauzat's list (649-134), this sheet is no. 649-132, and the Bibliothèque nationale de France dates it to 1884. Both appeared in Le Chat Noir, the weekly that Rodolphe Salis launched in 1882 to promote his Montmartre cabaret, where Steinlen, in Paris since 1881, became a regular from 1884. He drew stories for the paper until 1895, mostly with cats in the lead. Fun fact: Steinlen kept drawing cats long after the paper folded, published a book of wordless cat designs, Dessins sans paroles des chats, and made cat figures in sculpture on a limited basis.
submovement: Le Chat Noir journal illustration (histoires sans paroles)
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Illustrateur · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: Shashthi, Goddess of Children, Standing on a Cat
description: Crouching flat beneath Shashthi, goddess of children, is a big white cat with black spots, its round eyes and almost human brows giving it a look of mild alarm. She has yellow skin and a red sari edged in white dots and carries a baby on her hip, while a second child stands on the cat's head, holding her hand. The cat takes the weight with the patience of divine transport. The painting is opaque watercolour on paper, done in the quick, broad strokes that made Kalighat pictures cheap and fast to produce, and her name, 'shashthi', is written by hand at the bottom.
context: Goddess on a cat: Shashthi, protector of children, rides a cat as her vahana, or mount, in Bengali tradition, which is why this Kalighat sheet stands her on a big spotted one. An unrecorded Kolkata painter made it about 1885 (the V&A allows 1880–1889), in opaque watercolour on paper, and wrote her name by hand at the foot. Fun fact: older images of Shashthi sometimes give the goddess herself a cat's face, so the animal under her feet has deep roots in her iconography.
title_eng: Shashthi, Goddess of Children, Standing on a Cat
feline_symbolism: In Bengali tradition the cat (marjara) is Shashthi's vahana, or mount, and older images sometimes show the goddess cat-faced.
image_credit: Unknown author Unknown author · https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O71571/painting-shashthi-goddess-of-children-standing/

title: Cat Watching a Spider
medium: Album leaf; ink and color on silk
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: Staring down at a spider in the lower left, a grey-and-white cat with a black cap of fur crouches at the corner of a folding screen, and the spider has, so far, not noticed the cat. The cat wears a bright knotted cloth around its neck, orange and turquoise patterned, the only loud colour on the leaf. Painted in ink and colour on silk, 37.5 by 27.9 cm, its Japanese title, Neko ni kumo zu, simply pairs the two animals. The fur is built from fine strokes and soft washes, while the spider needs only a few hard lines. It is an album leaf, meant to be held.
context: Accession numbers 14.76.61.20 and 14.76.61.73 both belong to the Met's Charles Stewart Smith Collection: two Meiji cats, one with a frog and this one with a spider. Ōide Tōkō (1841–1905) painted this leaf about 1888–92, in ink and colour on silk. Mrs Charles Stewart Smith and her sons Charles Stewart Smith Jr. and Howard Caswell Smith gave the whole collection to the museum in 1914, in memory of the collector. Fun fact: the Met's Japanese title for it, Neko ni kumo zu, simply means 'cat and spider', which is a fair summary of the plot.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0), via Wikimedia Commons

title: The Cat and the Fox (Katten och räven)
description: At the top of a very tall, very thin picture, a tabby-and-white cat clings to a branch and peers down, white paws gripping the bark and its ringed tail hanging below. At the bottom a red fox tips its head back, mouth open, eyes fixed on the cat above. The panel is absurdly narrow, 40.5 by 12.5 cm, closer to a Japanese hanging scroll than a Swedish salon picture, and it stacks the two animals into a vertical standoff. Between them there is only pale cow-parsley umbels and scratchy brushwork. Liljefors signed it in red at lower right and dated it 1885.
context: A chase has just stopped, not ended: the auction house reads the cat as hunted up the tree for safety, with the fox waiting beneath and the two predators still sizing each other up. The panel was sold at Bukowskis in Stockholm in May 1997 (no. 113) to a Swedish private collection, and again at Uppsala Auktionskammare on 11–14 June 2019, where it fetched a hammer price of 800,000 SEK. Fun fact: Liljefors came back from France in 1884 and spent much of his time in the countryside around Uppsala, which is where such moments of animal life turn up in his early work.
inventory_id: Uppsala Auktionskammare, International Quality Auction 11–14 June 2019, no. 912
image_credit: Bruno Liljefors · Uppsala Auktionskammare

title: Cat and Dogs Belonging to Queen Victoria
collection: Royal Collection Trust (Horn Room, Osborne House)
description: A tabby kitten perches on a wooden kitchen chair at right, draped with a brown cloth, and three royal dogs stand below and stare up at it: a dachshund, a smooth fox-terrier and a pug in a studded collar. The kitten holds the high ground, literally, and looks down with calm suspicion. Apple blossom drifts over the orchard, a cottage wall closes the background, and a besom broom leans against the chair at right. Barber signed and dated the canvas 1885. It measures 35.5 by 53.5 cm, the scale of a picture meant for a private room rather than a gallery wall.
context: Paul, Vic and Princess are the dogs, if the Royal Collection's reading of an 1886 inventory is right: the picture is probably the one recorded at Osborne House that year as 'a cat with Paul, Vic and Princess', Vic being the fox-terrier. The Royal Collection believes Charles Burton Barber (1845–1894) painted it for Queen Victoria, though it cannot be matched with certainty to the pictures she paid him for in 1885. It still hangs at Osborne, in the Horn Room, and was catalogued by Oliver Millar in 1992. Fun fact: the dogs get names in the royal records, while the kitten, the obvious star, stays anonymous.
title_eng: Cat and Dogs Belonging to Queen Victoria
title_original: Cat and Dogs Belonging to Queen Victoria
image_credit: Charles Burton Barber · Royal Collection

title: Tales for Sara: The Cat and the Ball of Yarn (Contes à Sara: Le Chat et la Pelote)
medium: Photomechanical print (impression photomécanique); engraved by Charles Gillot
description: Sixteen small scenes, read like a comic strip, follow a black cat from its first meeting with a ball of wool. The cat paws the ball off a shelf, dangles from the edge by the thread, stalks it, leaps, wrestles it, and then gets wound up so thoroughly that by the bottom row it has turned into a ball of yarn itself, with knitting needles still sticking out. There is no text at all, so the comedy lives in the cat's body language. It is a photomechanical print from Le Chat Noir, and the plate carries the credit 'Gillot sc.' for the firm that made the printing block.
context: Charles Gillot (1853–1903) engraved the block for this sheet, and the Bibliothèque nationale de France credits him in that role beside Steinlen as illustrator, dating the print to 1885 as Crauzat 649-196. Gillot's photomechanical relief process made it cheap to print line drawings next to type, which is how a weekly like Le Chat Noir, launched by Rodolphe Salis in 1882, could fill its pages with Steinlen's picture stories from 1884 to 1895. The series title 'Contes à Sara' (Tales for Sara) frames it as a bedtime story. Fun fact: Steinlen later published a book of his wordless cat designs, Dessins sans paroles des chats, so pages like this got a second life between covers.
title_eng: Tales for Sara: The Cat and the Ball of Yarn
title_original: Contes à Sara: Le Chat et la Pelote
submovement: Le Chat Noir journal illustration (histoires sans paroles)
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Illustrateur Gillot, Charles (1853-1903). Graveur · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: The Cat and the Guinea Pig (Le Chat et le Cochon d'Inde)
medium: Photomechanical print (impression photomécanique); engraved by Charles Gillot
description: A black kitten, a guinea pig and some tinned goods: the BnF's subject headings (cats, guinea pig, canned food) read like an inventory from a slapstick prop room. Across four loose rows the kitten sniffs, bristles, arches its back and bats at the plump white-and-patched guinea pig, which keeps escaping into toppled tins and finally pokes out of one at the far right. There is no text, so Steinlen makes it funny with line alone. The sheet is a photomechanical print from Le Chat Noir, with the credit 'Gillot sc.' for the engraving firm that converted his drawing into a printing block.
context: Two makers are named for this print by the Bibliothèque nationale de France, which dates it to 1885 and catalogues it as Crauzat 649-183: Steinlen as illustrator and Charles Gillot (1853–1903) as engraver. It ran in Le Chat Noir, the weekly that Rodolphe Salis launched in 1882 to accompany his cabaret, where Steinlen published drawn stories from 1884 to 1895, most of them led by cats. Fun fact: Gillot's name on the plate shows that these 'drawings' are really industrial products; his firm's photo-relief process is what made Steinlen's cats cheap enough to be read, laughed at and thrown away every week.
title_eng: The Cat and the Guinea Pig
title_original: Le Chat et le Cochon d'Inde
submovement: Le Chat Noir journal illustration (histoires sans paroles)
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Illustrateur Gillot, Charles (1853-1903). Graveur · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: Quilt Top, Crazy pattern
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: A crazy quilt is a patchwork with the rules removed: irregular scraps of silk, satin and velvet fitted together like broken crockery. Here the scraps are corralled into forty-two square blocks, seven rows of six, each patch edged with feather-stitch embroidery in yellow and red. The Met's subject tags list cats, birds, fans and horses. Fans and horseshoes are easy to spot, but the cat is a treasure hunt: in the fourth row, in the fourth block from the left, a small black velvet cat sits in profile on a red patch, with stitched eyes, across 154 by 132 cm of shine and nap.
context: Japanese pottery with cracked glaze and English art embroidery, both shown at the 1876 Philadelphia Centennial Exposition, are the usual suspects behind the crazy-quilt fashion of the late 1800s. An unrecorded American maker assembled this top around 1885 from silk, satin, velvet and cotton, and the Met catalogues it as a quilt top, the decorated face only. It came to the museum in 1989 as a gift of Tracey Blumenreich Zabar. Fun fact: strictly speaking crazy quilting is patchwork rather than quilting, since a crazy quilt rarely has the batting layer that defines a quilt.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Figure Dish
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: On the lid of this little covered dish lies a cat, head up and ears pricked, haunches rounded like a loaf. The base is moulded as a woven basket with a beaded rim and ribbed sides, so the cat looks as if it has settled into its own bed. It is pressed from opaque white glass, the material collectors call milk glass, and stands only 10.8 cm high and 14 cm long. Pressed glass is formed in a mould, so the cat's features were fixed by the mould-maker before a single dish was made. It comes in two parts, base and lid, hence the Met's 'a, b' number.
context: H. Sellers McKee, of the Pittsburgh glass-making family, helped found Jeannette, Pennsylvania, in 1888 and named it for his wife, Jeannette, and the town became known as 'the glass city'. The Met credits this dish to McKee and Brothers, which it dates 1856–89, and the dish itself to 1880–90, catalogued simply as a 'Figure Dish'. It is pressed opaque white glass, a gift of Mrs. Emily Winthrop Miles in 1946. Fun fact: the Pennsylvania town still carries a glassmaker's wife's name, which is more than most dish designers can say.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: A Frieze of Cats and Moons (Une frise de chats et de lunes)
title_original: Une frise de chats et de lunes
collection: Weisman & Michel Collection (David E. Weisman and Jacqueline E. Michel), private
description: Cats of every coat, black, tabby, calico and long-haired white, parade along a golden band and pick fights with full moons that all have faces. In the upper strip a white cat rears up and claws a pale moon that scowls and grimaces, while a piebald cat sniffs it from the other side; a pink moon looks on, appalled. A black cat arches its back at the far right like a punctuation mark. Painted in oil on canvas, this is a frieze of cats and moons, and the photograph shows it as intended: two long strips hung one above the other on a wall.
context: Two long strips of golden oil paint hold a procession of cats picking fights with moons. The frieze belongs to the American collection of David E. Weisman and Jacqueline E.
