Michel, nearly 200 works by artists who lived or worked in Montmartre, in which Steinlen holds a major place; it is dated 1885, a year after he joined the Chat Noir circle around Rodolphe Salis. The Musée Toulouse-Lautrec in Albi showed the collection, frieze included, in 'Montmartre, fin de siècle' from 4 May to 5 September 2021. Fun fact: the museum's own press release spells the artist 'Steinlein' in the caption to this very picture.
title_eng: A Frieze of Cats and Moons (Une frise de chats et de lunes)
submovement: Montmartre cabaret decoration (Le Chat Noir circle)
image_credit: Jl FilpoC · Own work

title: Cat Catching a Frog
description: Tail flung up in a tight curve, a tabby comes out of the reeds with one forepaw pinning a frog to the mud. The frog flails its legs and gapes; the cat's round yellow eyes never leave it. Kyōsai gives himself two very different bodies to play with: one all striped fur and coiled spring, the other slick, splayed and out of luck. The reeds on the left are dashed off in quick wet ink, and the grass blades at the bottom are tiny flicks of the brush. The leaf is ink and colour on silk, 35.9 by 27 cm, and was made to be looked at close up.
context: A double education shaped Kyōsai (1831–1889), briefly with the ukiyo-e master Utagawa Kuniyoshi and then in the Kanō school, which shows in his mix of polish and mischief. The Met dates this leaf to about 1887, and it came in the Charles Stewart Smith Collection, given in 1914 by Smith's widow and sons (14.76.61.20). Ōide Tōkō's 'Cat Watching a Spider' arrived in the same gift. Fun fact: Kyōsai's pupil Josiah Conder, the British architect who designed many Meiji-era buildings in Tokyo, started painting lessons with him in 1881, and was reportedly at his bedside when he died in 1889.
medium: Album leaf; ink and color on silk
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Julie Manet with Cat (L'Enfant au chat)
description: A white-and-tabby cat lies curled in Julie Manet's lap with its eyes squeezed shut and a grin that looks almost smug, the happiest face in the picture. Julie, eight going on nine, sits in three-quarter view in a cream dress with a yellow smocked yoke, her hair cut short with a fringe, one hand resting on the cat's back. A pink floral wallpaper and a red chair-back frame her. Renoir signed and dated the canvas at upper right: 'Renoir 87'. It is oil on canvas, 65 by 54 cm, and the cat takes up nearly as much of the composition as she does.
context: Dation, the French scheme that lets heirs settle inheritance tax with works of art, brought this portrait into the Musée d'Orsay in 1999 (RF 1999 13). Julie Manet (1878–1966), the only child of Berthe Morisot and Eugène Manet, later Madame Ernest Rouart, kept the picture herself, and it then passed to Julien Rouart. The Orsay's record lists a showing in Paris in 1888. Fun fact: the portrait was on public view in Paris a year after it was painted, then spent over a century with the sitter and her family before reaching a museum.
image_credit: Pierre-Auguste Renoir · KQGO9bsplWZeCg at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

title: Cat on a Flowerbed (Katt på blomsteräng)
description: Low in the bottom right corner of a summer meadow, half hidden by stems and dandelion clocks, a black-and-white cat sits with its ears pricked and its gaze turned off to the right. Liljefors gives the flowers almost as much attention as the animal: yellow daisies, pink clover and silver seed heads crowd the whole canvas. There is almost no horizon, only a sliver of red farm building in the top left corner. It is oil on canvas, 61 by 76 cm, signed lower right. Originally it shared a frame with a painting of red-backed shrike nestlings, the two composed to balance each other in form and colour.
context: Six paintings once hung together in a single frame, and the marks on the backs of the frames show how they were arranged. The set was split up at some point. Nationalmuseum acquired 'Nestlings of Red-Backed Shrike' and 'Four Bird Studies' in 1992 and bought the cat painting in 2013 (NM 7128), then reunited them in one frame in 2014, as the artist intended. Fun fact: the museum reads the starkly pared-down compositions and the multi-picture mounting as signs of Japanese art, which was fashionable in Europe in the later 19th century.
image_credit: Bruno Liljefors · Stockholms Auktionsverk

title: Self-Portrait with Cats for 'Les Hommes d'aujourd'hui', No. 349
description: Black and grey cats crowd in around Steinlen as he sits on a rush chair before a blank canvas: one arches on top of the easel, another rubs against his hand at left, and kittens tumble and fight at his feet. He looks away in profile, bearded, in a grey work jacket and pink shirt. The masthead credits the drawing to Jean Caillou, a pseudonym, and the corner inscription dedicates it 'à Steinlen son meilleur ami'. Each issue of the series profiled one personality, usually drawn by a colleague, so here the subject quietly does the job himself and disguises the byline.
context: Pierre et Paul wrote the text and 'Jean Caillou' signed the drawing, according to the masthead of this issue of Les Hommes d'aujourd'hui, a weekly series of caricature-portraits sold at ten centimes. The dedication in the corner reads 'à Steinlen son meilleur ami, Jean Caillou', and Caillou (pebble) is generally identified as a pseudonym Steinlen used for his own work, so the subject is quietly drawing himself. French Wikipedia confirms that Steinlen contributed to Les Hommes d'aujourd'hui. The sheet is held by the Bibliothèque nationale de France, which has digitised it on Gallica. Fun fact: the blank canvas on the easel is the only thing in the picture without a cat near it.
title_eng: Self-Portrait with Cats for 'Les Hommes d'aujourd'hui', No. 349
title_original: Les Hommes d'aujourd'hui, n° 349: Steinlen par Jean Caillou
image_credit: Théophile Steinlen · This file comes from Gallica Digital Library and is available under the digital ID btv1b53188733z

title: Jacquard-woven Picture
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: At the lower right corner a small white cat sits beside a saucer, entirely unbothered by history, while a woman in a bonnet and fichu sews a large starred flag on a porch. The woven caption reads 'Betsy Ross making the first United States flag', and a spinning wheel fills the left side. The picture is pocket-sized, 20.6 by 12.4 cm, and woven rather than painted: every tone comes from silk threads lifted and dropped by a punched-card Jacquard loom, which is why the cat's fur and the flag's stripes are built from the same dots of light and dark.
context: Paterson, New Jersey, is where the Met's record places the weaving, and Anderson Brothers is the only maker it names; the date is given as 1887 to 1890. Friends of the American Wing Fund bought the picture in 1984, and it sits in the American Wing rather than with the textiles of Europe. Fun fact: the loom signed its own work, since the caption 'Betsy Ross making the first United States flag' and the maker's name, 'Anderson Bros. Paterson, N.J.', are both woven into the bottom border of the silk itself.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0)

title: Portrait of E. P. Yaroshenko (Lady with a Cat)
title_original: Портрет Е. П. Ярошенко («Дама с кошкой»)
collection: Kaluga Museum of Fine Arts, Kaluga
description: With its back to us, a white cat sits upright in Elizaveta Platonovna Yaroshenko's lap, ears pricked toward her, while she smiles down at it and rests her left hand on its back. In her right hand she holds a paper knife, halfway through cutting the pages of the open book on her knees: the cat has interrupted her reading. She wears a dark dress with a white lace collar and cuffs, her braid neatly pinned. The room is nearly black, so the white cat, her face, her hands and the pale book are the lit points, like the light-and-dark tricks of the old Dutch masters.
context: Elizaveta Platonovna, born Stepanova in 1850, was married off at eighteen to a man three times her age, and took the step to escape her domineering mother. The failed marriage sparked a hunger for study: she left for St Petersburg, attended higher courses for women, studied law, and later went to the University of Bern, before a divorce and a second marriage to Vasily Yaroshenko, the painter's brother, an engineer who kept a laboratory on her inherited estate. The portrait came to the Kaluga museum in 1919 from that estate, Stepanovskoye (Pavlishchev Bor). Fun fact: the museum reads the paper knife as a sign that the book was hot off the press.
title_eng: Portrait of E. P. Yaroshenko (Lady with a Cat)
image_credit: Nikolai Yaroshenko · https://smallbay.ru/artrussia/yaroshenko_pictures.html

title: Cat and Kittens / after Henrietta Ronner
artist: After Henriëtte Ronner-Knip; published by W. Schaus, New York
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division (Popular Graphic Arts), Washington, D.C.
description: A big black-and-white mother cat crouches behind a green bowl of milk while three kittens drink and squabble around it: a black one at right, a patched one lapping with its tongue out, and a white one at the back mewing open-mouthed. A wicker basket and straw fill the background. Printed in colour from a stack of lithographic stones, the result passes at a distance for a small oil painting. The sheet measures 31.6 by 22.3 cm, and its yellow label announces 'Cat and Kittens, after Henrietta Ronner' from W. Schaus of Broadway. On the back is a pencilled stock number, 5341.
context: William Schaus, a dealer at 749 Broadway in New York, sold this as one of a series of 'fac-similes of water color drawings and oil paintings by eminent artists', as the yellow label stuck below the picture says, and the label's copyright line gives the year, 1867. Note how the label spells the artist 'Henrietta Ronner', the Americanised form of Henriëtte, and promises a facsimile of a painting that is itself not identified. The sheet now sits in the Library of Congress's Popular Graphic Arts collection (LCCN 2017650796).
title_eng: Cat and Kittens / after Henrietta Ronner
image_credit: Schaus, W. (William), publisher; Schaus, W. (William), copyright claimant; Ronner, Henriette, 1821-1909, artist · Library of Congress Catalog: http://lccn.loc.gov/2017650796 Image download: http://cdn.loc.gov/service/pnp/pga/12600/12657v.jp

title: Budding Artists
collection: Private collection (sold Bonhams, London, 26 September 2019, lot 19)
description: On a heavy old book, a calico mother cat sits in front of a battered portfolio and looks down at a tabby kitten gazing up at her. On the floor a ginger kitten and a black-and-white one tussle beside a dropped paintbrush, and another kitten scrambles through the legs of a carved chair at upper left. The joke is in the title, Budding Artists: the animals are the apprentices, and the studio clutter is theirs to inspect. The canvas is fairly large, 68.6 by 95.6 cm, signed and dated lower right, 'Ch. Van den Eycken. 1907'.
context: Provenance on the Bonhams lot page runs from the Willow Gallery in London to a private collector in France, and the canvas sold in London on 26 September 2019 for 16,937.50 pounds including premium. Its Belgian painter (1859–1923), a specialist in cats and dogs, worked in the same Brussels where Ronner-Knip had set the market for such pictures. Fun fact: the French collector bought it on New Year's Eve 2003.
image_credit: Charles van den Eycken · https://www.bonhams.com/auctions/25444/lot/19

title: View of a Roof with a Cat (Vue d'un toit avec un chat)
title_original: Vue d'un toit avec un chat
collection: Musee du Louvre, Departement des Arts graphiques, Paris
description: Ridged roof tiles run across the lower middle of a mostly empty sheet, with a tall chimney stack at left, a smaller one beside it and a gabled building behind at right. Tucked on the tiles just right of centre is the cat: a tiny pale shape, hunched and watching, easy to overlook. Redon sets it down as a view rather than a portrait, and the Louvre title, Vue d'un toit, avec un chat, puts the roof first and the cat second. The rest is blank sky and paper, with the initials 'Od. R.' at lower right. The inventory marks this side as the recto, so the sheet carries something on its back as well.
context: Chimneys, tiles and a speck of cat: the Louvre's graphic arts department holds this sheet as RF 40644, recto, under the title Vue d'un toit, avec un chat. Redon (1840–1916) is best known for his charcoal 'noirs' and lithographs of floating eyes and spiders, so a plain observation of a roof shows the other side of him, the draughtsman who looked hard at ordinary things. Fun fact: the animal is little more than a pale mark on the tiles, so the title is what tells you a cat is there at all.
title_eng: View of a Roof with a Cat
image_credit: Odilon Redon · https://arts-graphiques.louvre.fr/

title: Daubigny's Garden
title_original: Le Jardin de Daubigny (avec chat noir)
collection: Kunstmuseum Basel (Rudolf Staechelin Family Foundation deposit)
description: Slinking across the bottom left corner of Daubigny's garden, a black cat, painted in a few strokes of dark blue, heads for the left edge, a small dark shape on a lawn of swirling greens and yellows. Van Gogh used a double-square canvas, 56 by 101 cm, the stretched format of his final months, and filled it with a table and chairs, flower beds, a pale fence and a woman in black standing by the house. A church tower rises at right under a choppy green sky. The cat is the smallest figure and the easiest to miss, and it is the detail that tells this version apart from its twin.
context: Weeks before his death, in July 1890, Van Gogh painted the garden of the late landscapist Charles-François Daubigny at Auvers-sur-Oise. On 23 July he told his brother Theo it was 'one of my most carefully thought-out canvases'. This version is in Basel, on long-term loan to the Kunstmuseum from the Rudolf Staechelin Family Foundation. A second double-square version, now in the Hiroshima Museum of Art (F776), has the cat painted over. Fun fact: in 1929 the Berlin Nationalgalerie's new Friends' society bought that cat-less version for 240,000 reichsmarks, after director Ludwig Justi quietly checked its provenance, since its former owner Emile Schuffenecker was known to have made copies of Van Gogh.
image_credit: Vincent van Gogh · ArtDaily.com

title: Stalking Cat (Smygande katt)
medium: Oil on canvas laid on panel
description: Out of a snowdrift creeps a black-and-white cat, body pulled flat and long, eyes locked on two small mice at the lower left. The whole picture is painted almost in grisaille, white snow, grey shadow and dry black weed stems, so the cat's patches and the dark mice are the strongest marks on the canvas. It is an upright canvas laid on panel, 57.5 by 40.5 cm, a tall shape for a horizontal animal, which squeezes the stalk into a tight diagonal from upper right to lower left. The signature sits at lower left, 'Bruno Liljefors -90', the year shortened to two digits.
context: Jeppe was the black-and-grey striped wildcat-like tomcat that Liljefors used as a favourite model from the early 1880s; after a few years the animal vanished, and the painter wrote to his friend Anders Zorn that he truly mourned 'the noble animal'. Bukowskis tells this in a catalogue essay for another cat picture, and it fits here: the hunter who sat for hours watching foxes and hawks gave a stalking house cat the same flat-bellied attention. This canvas, laid on panel, is in a private collection and has been offered at auction in Sweden. Fun fact: the whole snowy scene is nearly colourless, yet the signature is a two-digit '-90'.
image_credit: Bruno Liljefors · Uppsala Auktionskammare

title: Pin Holder
title_original: Pin Holder: Anthropomorphic Cat at Brinsmead Piano
collection: Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum, New York
description: Tail stuck out behind, a grey tabby sits upright on a tiny piano stool and plays a grand piano with both front paws, head tipped back as if lost in the music. It is posed like a human player but wears nothing. The piano is a wood-grained grand with an open music stand and turned gilt legs, and its maker's name, BRINSMEAD, is lettered on the side: a tiny bit of brand placement in a sewing-table toy that doubles as a pin holder. Cooper Hewitt describes it as cast brass, gilt and then cold-painted, meaning the colours were applied without firing and can wear off with handling.
context: Brinsmead was a real London piano maker, so the cat is playing a recognisable product rather than a generic instrument. Cooper Hewitt dates the pin holder to the late nineteenth century and names no maker; small cold-painted animals of this kind are usually associated with Viennese workshops, but the record itself stops at 'unknown'. It entered the collection in 1949 as a gift of an anonymous donor (accession 1949-49-33) and sits in the Product Design and Decorative Arts department. Fun fact: the same donor gift includes the cat-and-kitten figure 1949-49-35, whose catalogue entry is blunter about what the tabby intends.
image_credit: Unknown artist Unknown artist · Catalog Photo

title: The Black Cat: The Cat on the Corpse
title_original: The Black Cat (Illustration for Edgar Allan Poe)
medium: Pen, brush and India ink over graphite
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: The black cat of Poe's story sits planted on top of the corpse's head, claws spread over the hair, one eye shut and the other a white slit glaring straight out. Beardsley gives it the full treatment: pure black ink against blank paper, a habit he took partly from Japanese woodcuts. The cat merges with the black ground, picked out only by a thin white contour and a speckled white blaze on its chest. Below, the dead woman's face is all white paper, eyes closed, earrings still on. The creature will not stay hidden.
context: Walled up with his victim, Poe's black cat ends the story sitting on the corpse's head and shrieking, which is exactly the moment Beardsley draws. The Met catalogues the drawing as pen, brush and India ink over graphite on a sheet of 25.4 × 16.2 cm, titled for an edition of Poe's Tales of Mystery and Imagination published in Chicago in 1895–96, and it came to the museum as a gift in 2020. Beardsley was art editor of The Yellow Book in 1894–95, the same years as his Poe set. Fun fact: the scan shown here has a ruled frame line round the edge, a sign that it reproduces a printed plate rather than the drawing itself.
title_eng: The Black Cat: The Cat on the Corpse
feline_symbolism: In Poe's tale the cat exposes the narrator's crime, so here it stands for guilt that cannot be walled up.
image_credit: Aubrey Beardsley (1872 - 1898) · Aubrey Beardsley

title: The White Cat (Le Chat blanc)
description: Arching into an impossible hump, its legs stretched long and thin like a table on stilts, a white cat with ginger patches on its head and back has its eyes squeezed shut and its tail curling up behind. Bonnard paints it in oil straight onto cardboard, 51.9 by 33.5 cm, and the brown of the support does much of the work in the sandy ground. Behind, dark green foliage and an orange tree trunk close off the space. The tall, narrow format is an odd choice for a horizontal animal, so the cat stretches upward to fit, which is half the joke.
context: Durand-Ruel in Paris showed this oil on cardboard in 1896, two years after Bonnard painted it in his Nabi years. It later belonged to the English collector Sir Michael Sadler, whose collection was exhibited at the Leicester Galleries in London in 1944, and then to M. and Mme Jacques Spreiregen in Nice. The French national museums bought it in 1982 and assigned it to the Musée d'Orsay. Fun fact: the number 74 in its inventory, RF 1982 74, coincides with its catalogue number in that 1944 Sadler exhibition.
image_credit: Pierre Bonnard · https://cdn.mediatheque.epmoo.fr/link/3c9igq/xvm189jq06ocbxc.jpg

title: Exposition Steinlen à La Bodinière
description: Fanning its whiskers against the pink-orange paper, a black cat stands upright in profile at the right of the sheet, while a calico curls in front of it, eyes half closed and tail wrapped round. Steinlen advertises his own exhibition, and the lettering spells out the offer in orange and grey: 'A La Bodinière, 18 rue St Lazare, Exposition de l'œuvre dessiné et peint de T. A. Steinlen', running from 10 April to 15 May 1894. The printer's line, 'Imp. Charles Verneau, 114 rue Oberkampf', runs up the right edge, and the sheet is a colour lithograph.
context: Poster-size cats were a cheap way to advertise a draughtsman who drew them for a living. This sheet announces a show of Steinlen's drawn and painted work at La Bodinière, 18 rue Saint-Lazare, from 10 April to 15 May 1894. The line at the foot says copies of the poster could be bought at Kleinmann's, 8 rue de la Victoire, and the printer was Charles Verneau of rue Oberkampf, the same printer who produced Steinlen's Chat Noir tour poster two years later. The Bibliothèque nationale de France holds an impression, digitised on Gallica. Fun fact: Verneau's mark, 'Déposé', shows that the design was registered like a trademark.
image_credit: Théophile Steinlen · This file comes from Gallica Digital Library and is available under the digital ID btv1b53074482g

title: Compagnie Française des Chocolats et des Thés
title_original: Compagnie Française des Chocolats et des Thés
description: Sitting low at the bottom left with its back to us, a dark tabby with a white chest stretches its nose toward the girl's bowl. Above it a dark-haired woman in a red blouse lifts a cup, looking down at the red-haired child, who leans over her own bowl, spoon in hand, beside an upturned tin of chocolate. The lettering fills the top, 'Compagnie Française des Chocolats et des Thés', and the printer's line at the foot reads 'Imp. Gourmont Frères, Paris'. The poster sells a hot drink by putting the family at the table, and the cat is the one member of it not allowed a share.
context: Chocolate and tea, but it is the cat that gets the best seat. The poster dates to 1895, as the Metropolitan Museum's impression records, and the Met's copy is a 1941 gift of the American sculptor Bessie Potter Vonnoh, listed there as a colour lithograph with a sheet of 79.6 × 59.7 cm. The image on this page, however, is the Bibliothèque nationale de France's digitised impression, shown on Gallica. Fun fact: in 1895 Steinlen was in the middle of a run of cat posters and covers, and this one turned the animal from a cabaret mascot into a member of the household.
title_eng: Compagnie Française des Chocolats et des Thés
image_credit: Théophile Steinlen · This file comes from Gallica Digital Library and is available under the digital ID btv1b9004763g

title: Cat Study
description: Two kittens, and nobody is leaping: a tortoiseshell-and-white kitten dozes in front with its eyes shut and a pink tongue-tip showing, while a black kitten with a white muzzle peers out over its back. This is a tiny oil sketch, 11 by 10 cm, about the size of a coaster, painted on canvas in 1895. The fur goes down in quick, scratchy strokes against a pink ground, the working note of a painter checking how an ear turns. The signature 'Henriette Ronner' is underlined at top left. Art UK lists it simply as 'Cat Study'.
context: Five paintings, all titled 'Cat Study' and made between 1895 and 1902, make up Hartlepool's Ronner-Knip holding; this is one of two dated 1895 (HAPMG 1947.5.4, with its companion 1947.5.5 close by). Tees Valley Museums, the group that runs Hartlepool's collections, notes that her cats show recognisable behaviour, such as the way they sit, look about and sleep against each other, and that studies often skip the background to catch the softness of fur. Fun fact: the pink wash here is the whole stage, and the picture is only 11 by 10 cm, about the size of a coaster.
image_credit: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip · Art UK

title: Cat Study
description: Two fluffy kittens lie side by side on a red cushion: a black-and-white one on the left with its eyes half lowered, and a tabby on the right staring straight out with wide green eyes, white front paws tucked neatly in front. A cat study in oil on canvas, 11.5 by 15 cm, small enough to hold in one hand. Ronner-Knip signs it 'Henriette Ronner 95' at top left, above a pale pink ground. The museum catalogues it with no more than the title 'Cat Study' and the date 1895, so the kittens do the talking.
context: Red cushion, pink ground, two kittens: the whole stage set fits in 11.5 by 15 cm. Hartlepool Museums and Heritage Service numbers it HAPMG 1947.5.5, next to its sibling 1947.5.4, and the Tees Valley Museums blog says her cats show recognisable behaviour, such as the way they sit, look about and sleep against each other. Ronner-Knip, born in Amsterdam in 1821, had lived in Brussels since 1850. Fun fact: she occasionally collaborated with the genre painter David Col.
image_credit: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip · Art UK

title: Cat and kitten Figure
collection: Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum, New York
description: A pale tabby with green eyes stands up on its hind legs, a darker striped kitten clamped face-down under one arm, and raises a stick high over the kitten's backside. The kitten's mouth is open in a red mew of protest and its legs dangle every which way. The whole drama is 6.8 cm tall: cast in brass and then painted, so the tabby stripes are brushwork laid over metal. The parent's face stays calm, almost smiling, which makes the raised stick read as a perfectly legible sentence.
context: 'As if about to spank' is how Cooper Hewitt's catalogue entry describes the tabby with its stick and its 'mewing kitten', about as much narrative as a design museum ever commits to an object label. The figure is dated late 19th to early 20th century, maker unknown, probably made in Austria, and came to the museum in 1949 as the gift of an anonymous donor (1949-49-35). Painted miniature animals of this kind are usually associated with Vienna and its trade in small cabinet and mantelpiece figures.
submovement: Austrian cold-painted miniature figures (Vienna bronze type)
image_credit: Unknown artist Unknown artist · Catalog Photo

title: Tournée du Chat Noir de Rodolphe Salis
title_original: Tournée du Chat Noir de Rodolphe Salis
submovement: Montmartre cabaret poster (Art Nouveau colour lithography)
description: Whiskers sprouting right through a red halo lettered 'Montjoye Montmartre', a black cat sits with its body in profile and its head swung round to fix us with two yellow eyes. The motto parodies the medieval French war cry 'Montjoie! Saint-Denis!', so the cat is both a saint and a battle standard. Its tail drops over the red band below and curls into the R of 'Rodolphe Salis'. The text could hardly be shorter: 'Prochainement Tournée du Chat Noir', which is to say 'coming soon'. The Rijksmuseum sheet is a full-size colour lithograph, 140 by 99 cm, printed by Charles Verneau, whose credit runs up the right edge.
context: Tin boxes, kitchen trays, tea-towel hooks and tiles: the fr Wikipedia article on this poster lists the everyday objects that now carry the cat, and notes that it turns up in films, series and in the video game Fallout, where one mission is to collect ten copies. The poster dates to 1896 and advertised a tour linked to the second Chat Noir cabaret, on the rue de Laval (now rue Victor-Massé), which closed in 1897 after Salis died. The Rijksmuseum's impression, RP-P-1969-78, carries the maker's 'Déposé' notice and was a gift of Mr Van Bergen of Zwolle.
title_eng: Tour of the Chat Noir with Rodolphe Salis
location: Zimmerli Art Museum at Rutgers University (Gift of Susan Schimmel Goldstein); Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam (RP-P-1969-78); Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam; Musée de Montmartre, Paris
feline_symbolism: The cabaret took its name from the stray black cats of Paris; the halo and mock war cry turn the cat into a tongue-in-cheek patron saint of Montmartre.
image_credit: Rijksmuseum · http://hdl.handle.net/10934/RM0001.COLLECT.418236

title: Laziness (La Paresse)
medium: Woodcut printed in black on ivory wove paper
description: Its tail curling away, a small white cat stands on the bed at the lower right while a nude woman sprawls face-down across the covers, her face buried in the crook of one arm and her other hand reaching down to touch it. Vallotton cuts it in pure black and white with no grey in between: the bedding becomes a riot of checks, lattices, zigzags and dots, and the body and the cat are bare white shapes cut out of the black. The image is only 17.8 by 22.2 cm, with 'La Paresse' lettered at lower left and the FV monogram at right. Nobody here is getting up.
context: Pure black and white did the work of colour, pattern and depth in Vallotton's hands. The Art Institute of Chicago's text explains that the woodcut, the oldest printmaking technique in Europe, had fallen out of favour as an artistic practice by the mid-19th century, and that Vallotton revived it, designing, carving and printing his own blocks, with simplified forms and contrasts of only black and white. Its impression of La Paresse (1947.454) came through the Joseph Brooks Fair Memorial Collection. Fun fact: Vallotton was perhaps best known in his lifetime for exactly these woodcuts, and the image you see here is the Bibliothèque nationale de France's digitised impression, not the Chicago one.
image_credit: Vallotton, Félix (1865-1925). Graveur · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: The Cat Show at the Crystal Palace (Illustrated London News)
medium: Pen drawings reproduced by process engraving, newspaper page
collection: Internet Archive, digitised copy of The Illustrated London News, vol. 109, no. 3001 (24 Oct 1896)
description: A huge long-haired tabby, 'Birkdale Ruffie', fills the middle band of the page, glaring out from a dark ground, while a frieze of show cats lines up above and a striped shorthair labelled 'Champion Xenophon' strides across the bottom left. This is The Illustrated London News for 24 October 1896, given over to Wain's prize winners from the Crystal Palace. Zaida sits top right among Persians and a Siamese. These are portraits, not caricatures: Wain is reporting which cat won and making each one recognisable to owners and breeders. Long Persian coats and dense short ones are rendered entirely in black line.
context: The Illustrated London News was where Wain's career started: he sold it his first cat drawings in 1884, and its 1886 Christmas number carried A Kitten's Christmas Party, the drawing that made him famous. From 1890 he rented a house at Westgate-on-Sea from the paper's managing director, Sir William Ingram. The same show appeared a day earlier in the Bromley & District Times, also drawn by Wain. Fun fact: Zaida, named at top right, was the chinchilla who rivalled Xenophon for top honours at shows, and for a time both were owned by Lady Gertrude Decies, according to the Cat-o-pedia history project.
title_eng: The Cat Show at the Crystal Palace
title_original: The Cat Show at the Crystal Palace
image_credit: Louis Wain · The Illustrated London News

title: Cats (Chats)
description: Piled up in the dark, three cats fill the sheet: a black cat sits upright at the back, a second black cat rests its chin on a flowered cushion with one pale eye open, and a tabby sprawls across the front with its paws stretched out like a dropped scarf. This lithograph measures 63.6 by 81.5 cm, the size of a small window. The BnF catalogues it simply as 'Chats' and the inscription 'Steinlen 96' can be found at lower left. Steinlen works almost entirely in black and brown crayon tones, rubbed and smudged, so the black cats nearly dissolve into the shadows around them.
context: Dozens of cats lived in Steinlen's house on rue Caulaincourt, so many that his contemporaries renamed it 'The Cat's Cottage' and an animal-protection society once rewarded him, according to Numéro's account of his career. Born in Lausanne in 1859, he settled in Montmartre in the 1880s and drew his neighbours' strays as readily as the street people of Paris. This large sheet is dated 1896 by its inscription and is held by the Bibliothèque nationale de France, which digitised it on Gallica; Wikimedia Commons gives its size as 63.6 × 81.5 cm. Fun fact: the household cats are the only models that never asked to be paid.
submovement: Art Nouveau decorative wall lithograph (Estampe murale)
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Lithographe · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: Cover for 1897 Calendar
medium: Color lithograph and commercial relief process
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: Its back to us and curled on the drawing table, a tortoiseshell cat rests its chin near a yellow sheet of paper, black and orange patches broken up by flecks of pink and green. Above it a man in an orange cap bends over his work, pipe clamped in his mouth, pen in one hand and ink bottle in the other, with three little ink pots lined up beside the cat. The Met's record tags a man, smoking and a cat. The sheet is 14 by 10 3/16 inches, colour lithograph with a commercial relief process, lettered 'Poster Calendar 1897' and 'Published by R. H. Russell & Son'.
context: Called the father of the American poster by some, Edward Penfield (1866–1925) designed this cover in 1896 for a poster calendar for the year 1897, published in New York by R. H. Russell & Son, as the lettering says. He was then art director at Harper's, where his posters helped bring the European poster craze to the United States. The Met acquired this impression in 1965 through the Elisha Whittelsey Fund (65.658.40(1)); a second Met impression, from the Leonard A. Lauder Collection of American Posters (1984.1202.123(1)), is catalogued as 'Poster Calendar 1897: Cover'. Fun fact: the Met's own subject tags for the sheet read 'painting, men, smoking, cats', which neatly sums up the scene.
image_credit: Edward Penfield · This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the Metropolitan Museum of Art . See the Image and Data Resources Open Access Policy

title: The Busybody
collection: Royal Museum of Fine Arts Antwerp (KMSKA)
description: A calico mother cat crouches on a stack of old folios and leans forward, nose out, to inspect four kittens sprawled across a heap of drawings below. The museum calls it 'De moeial', The Busybody, so the cats are minding something that is none of their business. A black-and-white kitten perches beside her, a grey one bats at the papers, and a ginger-and-white one stares at nothing in particular. A terracotta pot of brushes and a dried bouquet suggest a painter's studio. It is a sizeable canvas, 66.2 by 92.8 cm, signed and dated at lower left, 'Ch. Van den Eycken/ 1911'.
context: Antwerp's Triennial exhibition of 1911 hung this canvas as no. 250, and the museum bought it straight from the artist there, so it entered the collection (inv. 1707) the year it was painted. The title is Flemish for a busybody, a fair verdict on a mother cat nosing at her kittens' drawings. The record gives the inscription at lower left as 'Ch. Van den Eycken/ 1911' and offers the image as a free download.
image_credit: Charles van den Eycken · https://kmska.be/nl/meesterwerk/de-moeial

title: Brita, a Cat and a Sandwich (Brita, en katt och en smörgås)
collection: Private collection (sold Bukowskis, Stockholm, auction 609, lot 313, 7 June 2018)
description: Crouched in the grass at the front, head down over something on the ground, a small black-and-white cat is the lowest figure in the picture, while little Brita stands on the path behind it in a blue smock and bonnet, sandwich held up to her mouth. The title is a full inventory, and the order is probably the cat's. Behind them stand a red-boarded house with two white-framed windows full of potted flowers, sunflowers and a bed of red blooms, and a green gate swung open at the left. Larsson draws every shape in firm line and fills it with clear washes. The sheet is 47.5 by 68.5 cm, initialled 'CL' at lower left.
context: Four and a half million kronor was the hammer price when this sheet sold at Bukowskis in Stockholm on 7 June 2018, against an estimate of 3.5–4 million. The catalogue gives its history: watercolour and Indian ink, signed C.L., executed in 1898, owned by the Stockholm businessman Nils Stockhaus and then the Hans Erik Börjeson collection. It was shown at Liljevalchs in 1953 under the title 'En flicka, en katt och en smörgås' (A girl, a cat and a sandwich), at the Nationalmuseum in 1992, and in Turku and Helsinki in 2011–12. Fun fact: the family lived at Lilla Hyttnäs in Sundborn, given to Carl and Karin by Karin's father at the end of the 1880s, which is where his best-known family watercolours were made.
title_eng: Brita, a Cat and a Sandwich
title_original: Brita, en katt och en smörgås
submovement: Swedish Arts and Crafts domestic watercolour (Sundborn)
image_credit: Carl Larsson (Swedish, 1853-1919) · https://blog.daum.net/kmozzart/17177

title: Man with the Cat (Henry Sturgis Drinker)
collection: Smithsonian American Art Museum, Washington, D.C.
description: A ginger tabby sleeps flat out across Henry Sturgis Drinker's lap, at the lower left of the canvas, eyes shut and paws tucked, while his long hand rests beside it without quite touching. He sits back in a Windsor chair in a cream linen suit and purple tie, whiskers sweeping into a grey moustache, and looks at the painter steadily and a little warily. Beaux paints the suit in broad, fast strokes, all lilac and yellow shadows. The canvas is nearly life-size, 121.9 by 87.8 cm, signed at lower right. The cat is the one thing in the room that is completely relaxed.
context: The Smithsonian notes that Drinker was Beaux's brother-in-law, a railroad executive who later became president of Lehigh University. Beaux's portraits were so often compared to those of John Singer Sargent that, in a letter of the time, Bernard Berenson is reported standing before three of them and joking that the ordinary ones are signed John Sargent and the best are signed Cecilia Beaux. Wikipedia calls this probably her finest portrait. It reached the Smithsonian American Art Museum as a bequest of Henry Ward Ranger, through the National Academy of Design. Fun fact: this was not her first cat picture: Sita and Sarita (Jeune Fille au Chat), of 1893–94, is now in the Musée d'Orsay.
title_original: Man with the Cat (Henry Sturgis Drinker)
image_credit: Cecilia Beaux · -AGOOmzCCu5cNg at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

title: Celebrated Cats of the Fancy (Harmsworth Magazine)
medium: Halftone plate (black and white) from a magazine page
collection: Published in The Harmsworth London Magazine, London (1898)
description: Nine celebrities, all of them cats, each in its own roundel under the heading 'Some Costly Pets', with a price tag in the caption. Wain's plate for The Harmsworth London Magazine names its sitters like a team sheet: Xenophon, Ameer, Patrick Blue, Blue Boy, Rynda, Zaida, Banjo, Jemmy and Satan. There are Persians, British Shorthairs and two Siamese, one striding across the centre with its tail up. Each animal is drawn to be recognised by its owner. Look for number 1, 'Champion Zenophon', the striped tabby walking across the top left, valued at £100.
context: Xenophon, number 1 on the plate, was a blotched brown tabby shorthair reportedly found as a wild kitten in 1892, and he became one of the most decorated shorthairs of his day. Lady Decies took him over from Sam Woodiwiss in 1898 and renamed him Fulmer Xenophon; he died at her cattery in Birchington on 15 January 1903, and the cat weekly Our Cats announced it. Wain, president of the National Cat Club, was the obvious artist for a popular monthly's page of show champions. Fun fact: the caption prices the sitters, from 30 pounds for the Siamese Rynda to 160 for Zaida.
title_eng: Celebrated Cats of the Fancy (Harmsworth Magazine)
title_original: Affiche pour The Harmsworth London Magazine: Les Chats Célèbres
image_credit: Louis Wain · The Harmsworth London Magazine

title: Two Cats on a Cushion (Deux chats sur un coussin)
description: Curled into each other, two cats sleep: a striped tabby in front, nose tucked under a white paw and banded tail wrapped round, and a black cat behind with only its ears and one half-shut eye showing. In this impression there is very nearly nothing else. The BnF's catalogue title spells out the state: first state, 'with the cats alone', before the background curtain, the cushions and the date were engraved. So the cushion of the title is not here yet. The pair float on a pale plate tone crossed by stray scratches, with the signature 'Steinlen' in pencil in the margin below.
context: A cushion is missing from a print named after one. The BnF's catalogue title specifies a first state, with the cats alone and before the background curtain, the cushions, the signature and the date were engraved, so the sheet shows the moment when the cats were the whole idea. The library digitised this impression from its Steinlen holdings on Gallica, and the print is dated 1898. Fun fact: working states like this were prized by collectors because they show a plate being built up, which is why a nearly empty first state can be worth more attention than the finished version.
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Graveur · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: The Cats: Tsching, Batzar, and Blanc-Blanc (Les Chats: Tsching, Batzar et Blanc-Blanc)
title_original: Les Chats: Tsching, Batzar et Blanc-Blanc
collection: National Gallery of Art, Washington, D.C.
description: Wound into one round heap and seen from above, three sleeping cats fill the sheet, each head tucked into another's flank. Along the bottom left Steinlen has written their names, Tsching, Batzar, Blanc-Blanc, and under his signature at lower right sits a note that reads like 'vu de haut' (seen from above). It is charcoal on a small sheet, 22.6 by 29 cm. One stick does all the work: a hard contour on the cat at upper left, soft smudge across the flanks, and a ground scrubbed in with fast horizontal strokes. The palest cat, left largely as bare paper, takes the lower left of the heap.
context: Names turn a pile of fur into a household. The National Gallery of Art catalogues the sheet as charcoal, 22.6 by 29 cm, in the Rosenwald Collection (1943.3.8031), the gift that also brought the gallery a run of Steinlen's etchings and lithographs, and it transcribes the lower-left inscription as Tsching-Batzar-Blanc-Blanc. Steinlen, born in Lausanne and settled in Montmartre, published his album Des chats in 1898, around the time this sheet is dated. Blanc-Blanc means 'White-White', which is about the effort anyone puts into naming a white cat.
title_eng: The Cats: Tsching, Batzar, and Blanc-Blanc
image_credit: Théophile Alexandre Steinlen · This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the National Gallery of Art . Please see the Gallery's Open Access Policy .

title: Cats: Pictures without Words (detail of a plate)
medium: Photorelief etchings, bound in the book Des chats: dessins sans paroles (Paris: Ernest Flammarion)
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: Side by side on their hind legs, a black cat and a white cat rear up with front paws flung high at a small flying insect near the top of the page. The white one has its mouth wide open and is drawn in thin outline; the black one is a solid silhouette with a few scratches of light on its head. The picture is a detail from one page of Steinlen's wordless album Des chats. The line began as a crayon drawing, was transferred photomechanically to a zinc plate and printed in relief, a way of publishing a drawing without an engraver cutting it by hand.
context: Wordless was the selling point of Des chats, published in Paris by Ernest Flammarion in 1898. The Met catalogues its copy as a book of photorelief etchings, 44.5 by 30.4 cm, a gift of Mrs Edward C. Moën in 1961 (61.687.12), and credits Steinlen as 'Designer' rather than printmaker, because the plates reproduce his drawings photographically instead of being cut by hand. Photorelief etching turns a drawing into a zinc block that prints like type. The picture shown here is a detail from the Met's open-access photography of the book, shared through Wikimedia Commons.
title_eng: Cats: Pictures without Words (detail of a plate)
image_credit: Théophile Steinlen / Ernest Flammarion · This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the Metropolitan Museum of Art . See the Image and Data Resources Open Access Policy

title: Cat Arching Its Back (Chat faisant le gros dos)
description: A dark cat hunches along a bare plank floor, head lowered almost to the boards and spine humped into the big back of the title, tail trailing out behind. Steinlen scratched it straight into a zinc plate with a needle rather than biting it with acid, so the fur is all fine parallel strokes, with a few loose diagonal lines at upper right. The printed area is small, 14.1 by 7.5 cm, and wider than it is tall. His signature sits at lower right, a small red stamp below the image, and in the margin an unknown hand has added a cursive mark and the number '1.'
context: The title, the date and the catalogue number all come from somebody else's book. The BnF's note reads 'Titre d'après Crauzat' and 'Date d'après Crauzat : janvier 1898', so Ernest de Crauzat, who catalogued Steinlen's prints, named and dated this cat as his number 7. The only recorded state sits in a mounted volume of Steinlen's prints in the Département des Estampes et de la photographie (DC-385 (1)-FOL) and is digitised on Gallica. It was a busy cat year: Flammarion also published his wordless album Des chats in 1898.
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Graveur · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: Black Cat and Tabby Cat Grooming (Chat noir et chat tigré faisant sa toilette)
description: A striped tabby twists on its back in the foreground with one hind leg shot straight up, deep in its wash, while a black cat sits behind it almost lost in the dark hatching, only two pale eyes staring out at us. Steinlen etched the scene on zinc on a small upright plate, so the solid black coat and the barred one are both built from bitten line, with no colour to help. The printed image measures about 12 by 17.7 cm and exists in a single state. A pencil 'St.' signs it at lower right, and someone has written 'Pl. 4' in the lower left margin.
context: Number 20 in Crauzat's catalogue, May 1898: that is all the cataloguers had to go on, because the plate has no title of its own. The BnF's note says both the title and the date are taken from Crauzat, so the black cat and the tabby were named by a cataloguer, not by Steinlen. The impression sits in the same mounted volume as his arching-cat drypoint (DC-385 (1)-FOL), with 'Pl. 4' pencilled in the lower left margin by an unknown hand. Two cats, two techniques in one year: the drypoint scratches zinc with a needle, while this plate was bitten with acid.
title_eng: Black Cat and Tabby Cat Grooming
title_original: Chat noir et chat tigré faisant sa toilette
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Graveur · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: Cover for the Album 'Des chats' (Couverture de l'album Des chats)
description: Six cats crowd a fair-haired girl in a checked peach-and-white dress who holds out a shallow bowl: a grey tabby stretches up her skirt on its hind legs, a black cat arches against her ankles at lower left, a striped tabby, a calico and a long-haired black cat close in, and a ginger cat watches from the back with its tail up. Across the top run 'Dessins sans paroles' and 'des Chats par Steinlen'; at the foot is the publisher, Ernest Flammarion, 26 rue Racine, near the Odéon. It is a colour lithograph, 44.9 by 27.5 cm, and the BnF impression is a loose sheet.
context: Nobody has identified the monogram on this cover, which is odd for a sheet that prints 'par Steinlen' across its upper half. The BnF's note says so, and adds that the printer's name comes from Crauzat, who lists the cover as number 215. The album it wrapped, Des chats, dessins sans paroles, was published in Paris by Ernest Flammarion in 1898, the year the Met also gives for its copy. This impression is a colour lithograph, 27.5 by 44.9 cm, kept as a loose sheet in volume 4 of the BnF's mounted Steinlen collection, DC-385 (4)-FOL.
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Graveur · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: Two Cats Side by Side (Deux chats côte à côte)
description: Two temperaments share a patterned rug set against a wall and door frame: a lean, short-haired cat upright in profile, chin raised, gazing left, and a darker, fluffier cat hunkered down with its eyes shut. One is on duty, one is off. The plate is nearly square, 29.7 by 29.6 cm, and this etching is recorded as the seventh state, so Steinlen went back into it at least six times after his first proof. The BnF notes it is printed on calque, a thin tracing paper. It is signed in pencil at lower right, under a dedication beginning 'à E. de Crauzat'.
context: Seventh state, printed on tracing paper, dedicated to the man who catalogued Steinlen's prints: this impression was clearly a gift. The BnF names the dedicatee as Ernest de Crauzat (1866–1944), compiler of the catalogue of Steinlen's etchings and lithographs, and its reference field for this plate reads 'n.d.', with no Crauzat number given. The sheet lives in the reserve volume RESERVE DC-385 (A,1)-BOITE FOL. A man who spent years numbering other people's impressions ended up with a seventh state of his own.
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Graveur Crauzat, Ernest de (1866-1944). Dédicataire · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: Cat Nap
medium: Oil on paper laid down on panel
description: Sleep has won. A tabby-and-white cat lies on a pale green damask cushion, eyes shut, forepaws stretched out and one hind foot flipped so the pink pads face us, the posture of a cat that trusts the room completely. Ronner-Knip painted it in oil on paper, later laid down on a panel, 25.8 by 38.1 cm. There is no story here, no ball of wool or toppled vase, just one animal asleep, its white bib and legs set against loose, feathery green brushwork. Her signature, 'Henriette Ronner.', sits at lower left.
context: Amsterdam gave her a start under her father, Joseph August Knip, and Brussels gave her a market: after marrying Feico Ronner in 1850 she moved there, and from the 1870s her name meant playful, often long-haired cats in comfortable interiors. Late in life she watched live models in her studio, then folded paper figures into the poses she wanted before painting. This study was lot 251 in Christie's sale 17295 of nineteenth-century European and Orientalist art in 2019. Fun fact: the lot notice says the medium 'should read oil on paper laid down on panel', so even the cataloguers first misread the support.
image_credit: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip · https://www.christies.com/lotfinder/lot_details.aspx?intObjectID=6248915&lid=1

title: Making Music
description: A white-and-tabby mother cat watches four kittens who have found a guitar and are treating it as playground equipment: one pokes its face into the sound hole, one sits on the soundboard, one scrambles up a stack of music portfolios at right, and a fourth noses about behind them. A loose string curls off the instrument, sheet music spills underneath, red drapery hangs behind. Ronner-Knip painted the scene in oil on panel, about 32 by 45 cm, and signed it 'Henriette Ronner' at lower right. The joke is the title: the only music being made is the twang of a snapped string, and the performers do not look sorry.
context: Glasgow dealers J.B. Bennett & Sons, then a Dutch private collection, then the present seller in 2016: that is the provenance Christie's gives for this panel, which came up as lot 250 in sale 17295 in 2019. By then its painter, Amsterdam-born and Brussels-based from 1850, had been a cat specialist since the 1870s. Fun fact: the honours followed the cats, with the Order of Leopold in 1887 and the Order of Orange-Nassau in 1901.
image_credit: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip · https://www.christies.com/lotfinder/lot_details.aspx?intObjectID=6248914&lid=1

title: Tabbies in Hyde Park
medium: Process print (photomechanical), supplement to Hearth and Home, 6 August 1896
description: Eight cats pedal bicycles in a tight pack through Hyde Park, most of them white, grey or black rather than striped, several in baggy bloomers and one with a bow tie, while two dogs, one white and one black, race across the foreground. Wain plays it straight, as if reporting a sporting event. The image is wide, 30.4 by 50.6 cm, and it is a process print, a photomechanical reproduction of his drawing made for mass circulation. The printed lettering names it 'Tabbies in Hyde Park' and credits it as a supplement to Hearth and Home, 6 August 1896.
context: Supplements like this one earned Wain no royalties, because he sold his work together with the copyright cheaply, which left him in straitened circumstances in later life. Born in Clerkenwell in 1860, he sold his first cat drawings to The Illustrated London News in 1884 and was president of the National Cat Club by 1890. The sheet belongs to the Wellcome Collection (reference 39628i). Fun fact: Wellcome's catalogue files it under just two subjects, 'Cats' and 'Bicycle racing'.
title_original: A Group of Cats Engaged in a Cycle-Race in Hyde Park, London
image_credit: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/obf_images/c3/41/901eec22019691767711a4e63f9a.jpg Gallery: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/image/V0023074.html

title: Black Cats Howl as Witches Ascend into the Night (Metamorphosis)
medium: Colour process print after a lithograph
description: Black cats howl in the foreground, three of them with heads thrown back, and more prowl the rooftops at right, while naked witches on broomsticks stream up into a grey night over a city, the leader with one arm flung high. A thin red line of light runs along the horizon. The cats stay earthbound and loud; the women do the flying. The sheet is a colour process print, a photomechanical copy of a Steinlen lithograph, signed at lower right and laid on a mount lettered in pencil 'Metamorphosis' with the artist's name and the page number 23. The publication line reads only '(E. & W.)'.
context: Cats gathering at night to answer the Devil's call is genuine French folklore, the sabbat des chats, said to peak on the night of Mardi Gras, and Wellcome files this sheet under 'Cats: Folklore' as well as witchcraft and France. The Wellcome Collection holds the reproduction as 17285i and records neither a date nor a publisher beyond '(E. & W.)'. The original lithograph, drawn by Steinlen in Montmartre, is a separate object; this later colour copy is what survives in London.
title_eng: Black Cats Howl as Witches Ascend into the Night (Metamorphosis)
feline_symbolism: In French folklore cats held their own nocturnal sabbath at the Devil's summons, mirroring the witches'; Steinlen's howling black cats draw on that picture of the cat as the witch's companion and double.
image_credit: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/obf_images/0a/30/0003636e99003d3329dc4999eaa3.jpg Gallery: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/image/V0011894.html Wellcome Collection gallery (2018-03-23): https://wellcomecollection.org/works/bfdtqqhy

title: Sleeping Cat
medium: Relief plaque, brown-patinated metal (presumably bronze), signed Steinlen
description: Head tucked down and one forepaw folded over its face, a cat sleeps in a tight ball on a small rectangular plaque, its tail wrapped round so the whole animal reads as a single loop. The body swells out of the flat ground in low relief. The modelling is soft and lumpy, closer to thumb-pressed clay than to crisp casting, and polished highlights catch the ribs and the curve of the back against a brown patina. 'Steinlen' is incised at lower left.
context: 'Date supplied by cataloger' is the Boston Public Library's own note, and it explains the loose 'ca. 1900–1920'. The piece measures 16 by 12 by 6 cm and came as a gift in memory of Louis W. Black, through Hyman Swetzoff, on 5 November 1959. It is filed with the library's Steinlen collection of lithographs, etchings and other works, where it is the odd one out: a lump of sculpture among sheets of paper, which is how it ended up on the digital shelf beside prints of cats.
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre, 1859-1923 · This file was contributed to Wikimedia Commons by Boston Public Library as part of a cooperation project. The donation was facilitated by the Digital Public Library of America . Record in source ca

title: Portrait of a Woman with a Cat (Portret kobiety z kotem)
description: A red-and-white cat dozes on the lap of a woman in a deep red dress, eyes shut, one white forepaw stretched across her skirt while her hand rests on its back. The cat supplies the light note in a canvas built from reds and browns, white fur and ginger patches against a dress that nearly melts into the background. The sitter looks straight out, half smiling. On a canvas 100 by 69.8 cm, Pająkówna paints the stroking hand and the animal as one gesture, so the portrait is as much about a habit of touch as about a face. The sitter is not named in the museum record.
context: The dramatist Stanisława Przybyszewska was the painter's daughter, and the painter herself ended in Paris. Pająkówna (1864–1912, according to English Wikipedia) left Lwów with her daughter in 1907, lived in Vienna, Zurich and Munich, and settled in Paris in 1909. This portrait, dated 1898, belongs to the National Museum in Warsaw (MP 3944 MNW). The sitter is unnamed in the record, so the painting's quietest question is who she was.
title_eng: Portrait of a Woman with a Cat
image_credit: Aniela Pająkówna · National Museum in Warsaw

title: Mr. Louis Wain Gets the Election Fever
medium: Pen drawing reproduced by photomechanical process in The Sketch
collection: Published in The Sketch, 17 October 1900, p. 535, London; copy: New York Public Library (v. 31 (July 25-Oct. 17, 1900)), digitised in HathiTrust
description: Cats swarm a street plastered with election posters, and the slogans are the best part: 'Vote for Free Cats Homes and No Lethal Chamber', 'Vote for Tibbs, He Kisses the Babies', 'Vote for More Mousetraps', 'Vote for Better Cats Meat'. A striped cat up a ladder pastes another bill while a temperance meeting holds forth at the back. The title, 'Mr. Louis Wain Gets the Election Fever', casts the artist as the patient and leaves his cats to act out the symptoms. It is a black-and-white cartoon on page 535 of The Sketch for 17 October 1900, and every cat in it is a voter, a candidate or a heckler.
context: Pictures and copyrights went cheap: Wain sold both together, so reproduction in print paid publishers far better than it paid him, and The Sketch, a London illustrated weekly, ran this one in volume XXXI, issue 403. He had been president of the National Cat Club since about 1890, which makes a cat election a fair fit for a man with a feline constituency. Fun fact: a year later he launched the Louis Wain Annual, which appeared every year from 1901 to 1915 and again in 1921.
title_eng: Mr. Louis Wain Gets the Election Fever
title_original: Mr. Louis Wain Gets the Election Fever (The Sketch)
image_credit: Scan of the printed page from The Sketch, via Wikimedia Commons. Louis Wain died 1939; public domain.

title: Waiting Up!
medium: Pen drawing reproduced by photomechanical process in The Sketch
collection: Published in The Sketch, 26 December 1900, p. 386, London; copy: New York Public Library (v. 32 (Oct. 24, 1900-Jan. 16, 1901)), digitised in HathiTrust
description: Late at night, two white cats meet: one, in round spectacles, has sat up with her knitting, needles raised and the ball of wool rolled off across the floor; the other, fur on end and eyes like saucers, has plainly just crept in. The printed caption delivers the joke: 'Good Gracious, Mrs. Tabby; how you startled me! I thought you would have been in bed hours ago!' 'What! And leave you out on the tiles?' 'Waiting Up!' ran in The Sketch on 26 December 1900, the day after Christmas, as a single cartoon on page 386. Domestic comedy was Wain's staple: cats behaving exactly like the families who bought the paper.
context: At the turn of the century Wain was feeding cartoons to London's illustrated weeklies, and The Sketch printed a run of them between 1900 and 1902; this one is in volume XXXII, issue 413. He was about forty and supporting his mother and five sisters, which explains how much he drew and how little he kept. Fun fact: his cat career traces back to Peter, a black-and-white kitten who joined his household after his marriage in 1884 and comforted his wife Emily during her illness.
image_credit: Scan of the printed page from The Sketch, via Wikimedia Commons. Louis Wain died 1939; public domain.

title: Picture of a Cat
title_original: Picture of a Cat (The Sketch, July 18, 1900)
medium: Painted portrait reproduced by halftone in The Sketch
collection: Published in The Sketch, 18 July 1900, p. 554, London; copy: New York Public Library (v. 30 (Apr. 25-July 18, 1900)), digitised in HathiTrust
description: Head and chest only: a long-haired cat fills the frame, staring straight out with big pale eyes from a dark, smoky face set above an enormous pale ruff. No costume, no punchline: the published title is simply 'Picture of a Cat', and it appeared on page 554 of The Sketch on 18 July 1900. That plainness stands out in Wain's magazine work, where cats usually play out human comedies, and the fur here is built from loose, painterly strokes rather than his cartoon outline. His signature sits at lower left. What survives online is a small scan of the printed page, in black and white.
context: Plain cat portraits like this show the observer behind the cartoonist: Wain, president of the National Cat Club, wrote the domestic cat section of Hutchinson's The Living Animals of the World in 1901. The Sketch printed this one in volume XXX, issue 390. Fun fact: between 1900 and 1940 some 75 publishers issued more than 1,100 of his images as postcards, so a face like this could end up on a great many mantelpieces.
image_credit: Scan of the printed page from The Sketch, via Wikimedia Commons. Louis Wain died 1939; public domain.

title: Cat Study
description: On a pinkish cloth, three kittens pile together: a grey long-haired kitten in the middle looks straight at us with grey-green eyes, a white one with a ginger patch dozes behind at left, and a dark tortoiseshell-and-white kitten sleeps in front, one white paw stretched out. Oil on canvas, 15 × 20.5 cm, signed and dated 1901 at upper right. Hartlepool catalogues it simply as 'Cat Study', one of three small Ronner oils that arrived together under the numbers 1947.5.1 to 1947.5.3. Ronner was about eighty when she painted it, and even at the size of a postcard her study holds a whole litter.
context: The Order of Orange-Nassau reached her in 1901, the year of this study. The painter had trained with her father Joseph August Knip, moved to Brussels in 1850 and from around 1870 painted cats almost exclusively, often long-haired and playful, in bourgeois settings. The study is in Hartlepool Museums and Heritage Service (HAPMG: 1947.5.1). Fun fact: she watched live animals in her studio, then made paper sculptures in the poses she wanted and arranged them with furniture and fabric.
image_credit: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip · Art UK

title: Cat Study
description: A long-haired tabby-and-white cat lies tucked into a soft loaf on a pale cushion, eyes all but closed, chin sunk into a thick white ruff. Behind it the ground is a hot red, and the cat's own shadow climbs the wall as a big black shape, as though a second, darker cat were keeping watch. Another of the three small 'Cat Study' oils by Ronner-Knip in Hartlepool, this one 15 × 20 cm on canvas, signed and dated 1901 at lower right. At about the area of a paperback cover it was never meant for a salon wall, and the brushwork settles the animal in a few passes.
context: Queen Marie Henriette of the Belgians owned lapdogs this painter portrayed before cats took over her studio, a sign of how far her reputation travelled from Amsterdam via Brussels. After marrying Feico Ronner in 1850 she moved to Brussels, where her often-ill husband became her manager, and after 1870 cats were her near-exclusive subject. This study belongs to Hartlepool Museums and Heritage Service (HAPMG: 1947.5.2). Fun fact: her son Alfred and daughters Alice and Emma also became artists, and she often exhibited with them.
image_credit: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip · Art UK

title: Charlie Morton's Mascot: The Persian Cat of the Palace Theatre
medium: Pen drawing reproduced by photomechanical process in The Sketch
collection: Published in The Sketch, 6 November 1901, p. 102, London; copy: University of Minnesota (v.36 (1901/02)), digitised in HathiTrust
description: A huge, fluffy black Persian sits at a desk with a quill in one paw and an inkwell at its elbow, grinning at us with wide white-rimmed eyes, mid-letter. Wain's title names it the mascot of the Palace Theatre and the pet of 'Charlie' Morton, the theatre's manager, and the drawing filled a near-square block on page 102 of The Sketch for 6 November 1901. The mascot has been given a part to play, correspondent, rather than drawn as a plain show-cat portrait. Wain was a natural choice for the job: as president of the National Cat Club he knew long-haired show cats better than most illustrators.
context: Charles Morton (1819–1904), called the 'Father of the Halls', managed the Palace Theatre of Varieties in London from 1893, at the invitation of Sir Augustus Harris, until he retired shortly before his death. When this appeared he was 82, and his cat was evidently famous enough for a society weekly to send for the country's best-known cat artist. The Sketch printed it in volume XXXVI, issue 458. Fun fact: Morton worked almost to the end, and died in 1904 aged 85, three years after his Persian made the papers.
title_eng: Charlie Morton's Mascot: The Persian Cat of the Palace Theatre
title_original: 'Charlie' Morton's Mascot – The Persian Cat of the Palace Theatre
feline_symbolism: A theatre mascot was a good-luck charm, and Wain's title presents the cat in exactly that role.
image_credit: Scan of the printed page from The Sketch, via Wikimedia Commons. Louis Wain died 1939; public domain.

title: Homeward-Bound from the Seaside
medium: Pen drawing with printed green tint, reproduced in The Sketch
collection: Published in The Sketch, 25 September 1901, p. 406, London; copy: New York Public Library (v. 35 (July 24-Oct. 16, 1901)), digitised in HathiTrust
description: Five or six cats cram into a little cart pulled by two dogs, a shaggy one and a black-and-white terrier, galloping straight at us with dust flying off the wheel. One cat flourishes a whip, one waves a Union Jack, another a St George's cross, and the driver in the middle grins with the reins in hand. The title fixes the season: 'Homeward-Bound from the Sea-Side', printed on page 406 of The Sketch on 25 September 1901, as summer ended. A pale green tint washes road and sky. Wain's comedy works by transfer: the crowding and end-of-holiday high spirits belong to people, and he hands them to cats.
context: The Louis Wain Annual had just launched in 1901, and books such as The Dandy Lion (1901) and Cats (1902) were coming out beside the magazine work, which shows how busy his drawing board was when The Sketch ran this one in volume XXXV, issue 452. Fun fact: in 1907, six years later, Wain left for New York on a Hearst Newspapers contract and stayed until 1910.
image_credit: Scan of the printed page from The Sketch, via Wikimedia Commons. Louis Wain died 1939; public domain.

title: Hunting Picture (untitled cartoon)
medium: Pen drawing with printed green tint, reproduced in The Sketch
collection: Published in The Sketch, 18 September 1901, p. 364, London; copy: New York Public Library (v. 35 (July 24-Oct. 16, 1901)), digitised in HathiTrust
description: Muzzled hounds stand in for racehorses: two grinning cats ride them across a field like jockeys, reins in paw, while a bushy-tailed animal lies flipped on its back in the grass and a soaked, wide-eyed cat sits chest-deep in a stream in the foreground. The Sketch printed it on page 364 on 18 September 1901 with no title, only a note beneath: the editor had commissioned Mr. Louis Wain to draw a Hunting Picture, and 'This is the Cataleptic result!' The joke is on the commission itself. A week later the same paper ran Wain's 'Homeward-Bound from the Sea-Side' on page 406, so for two issues running his cats followed the English calendar.
context: 'He has made the cat his own': so ran H. G. Wells's statement on Wain, read out on the BBC in August 1925, and by 1901 the weeklies were treating him accordingly. Born in Clerkenwell in 1860, he had made his name with 'A Kitten's Christmas Party' in the Illustrated London News in 1886, and this untitled cartoon is one of several he drew for The Sketch that year (volume XXXV, issue 451). Fun fact: the printed note blames the 'Cataleptic' result on the editor's own commission.
image_credit: Scan of the printed page from The Sketch, via Wikimedia Commons. Louis Wain died 1939; public domain.

title: Pussy Bucks Up After the Dinner to the Cat's-Meat Men
medium: Pen drawing reproduced by photomechanical process in The Sketch
collection: Published in The Sketch, 23 January 1901, p. 28, London; copy: University of Minnesota (v.33 (1901)), digitised in HathiTrust
description: Two panels, two cats. On the left a fluffy white cat peeps coyly over an open fan; on the right a cat in an enormous bow tie struts toward us with a framed board under one arm and a small black case in the other paw. The cartoon, wider than tall, ran on page 28 of The Sketch on 23 January 1901 under one of Wain's best titles: 'Pussy Bucks Up After the Dinner to the Cat's-Meat Men'. The cat's-meat men, street sellers of meat for pets, have been given a dinner, and Pussy dresses up accordingly. The men who feed London's cats get fed, and the cats approve.
context: The cartoon appeared in volume XXXIII, issue 417, in the first month of the new century's first full year, with Wain president of the National Cat Club. He sold such drawings outright, along with their copyright, so reprints brought him nothing. Fun fact: in 1925 Ramsay MacDonald wrote that 'Louis Wain was on all our walls some 15 to 20 years ago', which suggests how widely images like this one travelled.
title_eng: Pussy Bucks Up After the Dinner to the Cat's-Meat Men
title_original: Pussy Bucks Up After the Dinner to the Cat's-Meat Men
image_credit: Scan of the printed page from The Sketch, via Wikimedia Commons. Louis Wain died 1939; public domain.

title: Cat on an Armchair (Chat sur un fauteuil)
collection: Musée d'Orsay, Paris (on deposit at La Piscine – Musée d'Art et d'Industrie André Diligent, Roubaix)
description: On the seat of a wooden armchair, a tabby lies curled with eyes shut, head up, forelegs stretched straight out in front, the pale cushion lit around it like a small stage. The ladder-back and the curve of the arm frame the animal at left and right, in a canvas wider than tall, 46 × 55 cm. The stripes on the flank go down in a few broad, dark strokes, and Steinlen's signature sits at lower left. Here the artist who drew cats for posters, magazines and albums gives one the dignity of oil paint. The chair is human furniture, and the cat has claimed it.
context: 'Between 1859 and 1923' is the Musée d'Orsay's date for this canvas, which is to say the artist's entire life. It came to the museum (RF 1970 5) as a bequest from Mme Roger Désormière in 1973, and the Commons photograph shows it on deposit at La Piscine, the art and industry museum in Roubaix. Wikidata is bolder and says 1902, so the catalogue here borrows that year for sorting only. An oil of a sleeping cat is the rarer kind of Steinlen, a printmaker's cat in paint.
image_credit: Théophile Steinlen · La Piscine [1]

title: Cat Study
description: Two kittens share this little canvas, not one: a white kitten with tabby patches on its head looks straight out with clear blue-green eyes, while a darker tabby sleeps against its shoulder at left, eyes shut. This is the smallest of Hartlepool's three Ronner 'Cat Study' oils, 12.5 × 15 cm on canvas, signed and dated 1902 at upper left, when the painter was eighty-one. Ronner kept making these to the end of her life, small oil notes of cats that sit somewhere between sketchbook and finished picture. Its sister studies, 1947.5.1 and 1947.5.2, are a year earlier.
context: Three consecutive accession numbers, HAPMG: 1947.5.1 to 1947.5.3, suggest the Hartlepool studies entered the collection together. From about 1870 the painter's finished pictures showed long-haired, often playful cats in well-off households, and small studies like this one were raw material. She died in Ixelles in 1909, seven years after dating this canvas. Fun fact: she showed at the Palace of Fine Arts at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago, so her cats crossed the Atlantic long before reproductions made them popular there.
image_credit: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip · Art UK

title: The Playwright
medium: Pen drawing with printed grey tone, reproduced in The Sketch
collection: Published in The Sketch, 4 June 1902, p. 258, London; copy: University of Minnesota (v.38 (1902)), digitised in HathiTrust
description: At a desk, a white cat pins its quill to the page and glares sideways through a monocle on a cord, mouth open as if a line has just gone badly wrong. 'The Playwright' appeared on page 258 of The Sketch on 4 June 1902, a single cartoon a little taller than wide, printed over a grey tone. The title promises literary ambition, a good joke in a weekly that lived on theatre gossip and first nights. Wain loved to give his cats a profession and the airs that come with it, and a dramatist was about as airy as professions got in Edwardian London.
context: By 1902 Wain had published Fun and Frolic (1900), The Dandy Lion (1901) and Cats (1902) as well as the first Louis Wain Annual, and his cartoons ran in The Sketch for at least three years; this one is volume XXXVIII, issue 488. Behind the productivity lay money worries: he sold work and copyrights cheaply and supported his mother and sisters. Fun fact: he also made brief ventures into animated film, drawing what Wikipedia calls the first screen cartoon cat, 'Pussyfoot'.
image_credit: Scan of the printed page from The Sketch, via Wikimedia Commons. Louis Wain died 1939; public domain.

title: The Sick Kitten
description: A kitten swaddled in a cloth gets its medicine: in this frame a child's hand brings a spoon to its mouth, close enough to fill the screen. In thirty-four seconds of film two small children nurse it, and the camera does something new for 1903: it moves in. George Albert Smith cuts from a wider view to a closer one, and he does it without the round black mask he had used in 1900 to tell audiences they were looking through a lens. The kitten is the reason the close-up exists, since the action that matters is too small to read from across the room.
context: Warwick Trading Company released the film in February 1903, after George Albert Smith had made, produced and shot it in Hove. It remakes his own lost 'The Little Doctor' (1901). Smith belonged to the loose group of Sussex filmmakers that the historian Georges Sadoul later called the Brighton School. Fun fact: Michael Brooke of BFI Screenonline reads the missing circular black mask, used in Smith's 1900 films to tell audiences a close-up was coming, as a sign that Smith thought viewers had grown sophisticated enough to tell a medium shot from a close-up without prompting.
dimensions: 35mm motion picture film strip (approx. 24 × 18 mm frame)
image_credit: George Albert Smith · http://www.screenonline.org.uk/film/id/443164/
rights_note: UK film of 1903: films made before July 1912 were protected only as series of photographs, and photographs taken before June 1957 went out of copyright 70 years after they were taken.

title: Cat with Detail Studies (Katze mit Detailstudien)
collection: Bavarian State Painting Collections (Bayerische Staatsgemäldesammlungen), Munich
description: Four long-haired tabby kittens tumble across this canvas, not the single cat the title 'Katze mit Detailstudien' might suggest. One lies on its back at left, paws curled, gazing straight up; two more heads tilt skyward at top right, and a fourth stares out at us from the lower right. The background is barely brushed in, so the weave shows through. It is small, 29.5 × 42.5 cm, and dated 1903. The museum's photograph is monochrome, so the colour of the fur is left to the imagination, and a sheet of studies like this suits a painter who worked almost entirely on cats.
context: Bought in 1914 at the Munich annual exhibition in the Glaspalast, from the artist's estate, this study reached the Bavarian State Painting Collections a year after Adam's death. He had trained in his father's photographic studio, studied at the Munich Academy from 1873 and set up as a painter in 1882, going on to the nicknames 'Katzen-Adam' and 'Katzenraffael'. Fun fact: in 1894 he published a small book, 'Vom Kätzchen', illustrated with photographs of his own paintings.
image_credit: Julius Adam, Katze mit Detailstudien, 1903 / Bayerische Staatsgemäldesammlungen – Neue Pinakothek München, CC BY-SA 4.0 (sammlung.pinakothek.de)

title: Invitation Card for Steinlen's Exhibition, 32 place Saint-Georges
description: A long black cat stretches across the top of the address panel like a draught excluder, head raised, ears pricked, and its tail drops down the right edge and curls into a hook. This side is the printed envelope, 12.1 × 9.2 cm, from Th.-A. Steinlen, 73 rue Caulaincourt, addressed in ink to Monsieur Beurdeley, 79 rue de Clichy, franked with a 15-centime stamp and postmarked Paris. Inside was the invitation to his exhibition at 32 place Saint-Georges in November 1903. Steinlen's red monogram sits top left.
context: Monsieur Beurdeley, 79 rue de Clichy, was asked to do Steinlen the honour of attending the opening: the BnF's title quotes the card's wording, 'de vouloir bien lui faire l'honneur d'assister à l'ouverture de l'exposition de tableaux, dessins', installed at 32 place Saint-Georges in November and December 1903. The envelope was printed with Steinlen's own address, 73 rue Caulaincourt, and a guard cat. It survives in volume 5 of the BnF's mounted Steinlen collection (DC-385 (5)-FOL), digitised on Gallica, because an exhibition invitation was worth keeping when the stationery was this good.
title_eng: Invitation Card for Steinlen's Exhibition, 32 place Saint-Georges
title_original: Carton d'invitation pour l'Exposition Steinlen chez Beurdeley
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Graveur Beurdeley, Alfred (1847-1919). Destinataire de lettres · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: Girl in a Birch Forest with Cat (Mädchen im Birkenwald mit Katze)
