description: Clutched to the girl's chest, a white cat with black patches and pale green eyes hangs over her arm, its striped tail and belly dangling below her hands. She stands in a dark green dress against a pale birch trunk, looking past us, while two small red-clad figures hover in the trees behind. The canvas is large and almost square, 98.9 × 80.9 cm, and the girl is cropped by the frame at head and feet. The birch stems were a Worpswede signature, and the cat's bright fur is the lightest thing in the picture.
context: Cropped heads and feet are part of the method here: the Paula Modersohn-Becker Museum's own text notes that in this picture, as in her other birch-wood children, the frame cuts head and feet, and neither features nor clothing are detailed. Paula Modersohn-Becker (1876–1907) worked in the artists' colony at Worpswede near Bremen and kept going back to Paris, where she studied Gauguin and Cézanne. The painting is no. 518 in her catalogue raisonné. Fun fact: the museum that holds it, opened in 1927 and designed by Bernhard Hoetger, is often called the first museum devoted to a woman artist.
title_eng: Girl in a Birch Forest with Cat
image_credit: Paula Modersohn-Becker · 1. Google Arts & Culture — xAExtzAT1yfw2w (page no more available) 2. Google Arts & Culture — cQFN1uw_6RxrMQ

title: Study of Eleven Cats (Studie van elf poezen)
collection: Netherlands Open Air Museum (Nederlands Openluchtmuseum), Arnhem
description: Kittens everywhere on one mahogany panel, and not all finished to the same degree. The Netherlands Open Air Museum notes that six are painted fully in oil while five stay as sketches, and the split is easy to see: fluffy brown tabbies curled asleep along the bottom, beside ghostly outline kittens drawn in thin brown line above. One small tabby head in the middle peers up with green eyes. Ronner signed and dated it 'HR 1904' at top left. It is a sampler of poses rather than a scene, here in a heavy gilt frame.
context: Cats are headstrong, so the Nederlands Openluchtmuseum says her many studies, in charcoal, pencil, pen and oil, were often dashed off at speed. Ronner-Knip concentrated on cats from about 1870 and was eighty-three when she signed this panel in 1904. The museum links the demand to the cat's new place in family life. Fun fact: it adds that even Queen Victoria ordered cat portraits. The panel is N.883, and its gilded frame and the fitting of the panel date from 1982.
feline_symbolism: The museum ties pictures like this to the nineteenth-century rise of the cat as a family pet.
image_credit: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip · Netherlands Open Air Museum

title: Cat Cleaning Itself (Tortoiseshell Washing Paw)
description: A tortoiseshell cat sits hunched with its head bent right down to its chest, deep in a wash, one front paw braced on the floor. Gwen John draws it in pencil and touches it with watercolour: olive and ochre patches on the back and head, while the white legs and belly stay as bare pencil line on pale paper. Grooming is the pose every cat owner knows and few artists bother with, because the animal folds into a knot of leg, tongue and fur. A few washes over the line are enough to name the cat.
context: Cats washed themselves on John's floor for four years: she acquired Edgar Quinet, a tortoiseshell, in 1904 and, Museum Wales says, 'frequently captured her adored cats in spontaneous drawings'. Tate's page gives this sheet as 'Cat', c.1904–8, and records it under N05155. Edgar Quinet vanished in 1908, John was devastated, and she wrote a poem about her loss.
image_credit: Photo © Tate (CC BY-NC-ND 3.0) · Gwen John
rights_note: Work in public domain (artist d. 1939). Collection photography © Tate, licensed under CC BY-NC-ND 3.0.

title: Reclining Cat (Liegende Katze)
collection: Private collection (sold Lempertz, Cologne, 15 May 2010, lot 1938)
description: With its chin pressed onto its own front paws and eyes nearly shut, a brown tabby lies flat on a grey-green cloth, its ringed tail stretched out behind. The canvas is long and low, 25 × 46 cm, and Adam lets the animal fill it. Look at the lower left: a loose green string trails off the cloth onto the floorboards, the toy that has apparently been given up on. It is signed and dated 'Jul. Adam 1905.' at upper right. Adam's reputation rested on fur and finish, and a plain study like this leaves nothing to look at but those.
context: At Lempertz in Cologne on 15 May 2010 this canvas fetched 12,600 euros including premium, against an estimate of 5,000 to 7,000. Adam turned to cats after a painting of two of them brought his first big success, and by the 1900s his cat pictures were known well beyond Germany, especially in the United States. In 1905, the year of this canvas, he won a gold medal at the Munich International Art Exhibition, though for other works. Fun fact: the auction house notes that in his lifetime he was called 'Katzenraffael', the Raphael of cats.
image_credit: Julius Anton Adam · lempertz.com

title: Cat car crash (postcard)
description: A motor car, a collision and a cat who wants names taken. The little red car has nosed into a grassy bank, its black-and-orange driver has been flung into a tree, and a striped passenger dangles upside down in a bush. At right a striped cat in a bowler hat raises a paw to his mouth and delivers the printed caption: 'Stop there till my mate comes, and I'll summons you both for furious driving and assault!' The card, from the Wrench Series, went to Ted Claxton, and '4/4/05' is written in ink below Wain's signature.
context: Postcards were Wain's widest audience: between 1900 and 1940, 75 publishers issued more than 1,100 of his images as cards. This one is printed in the Wrench Series, and the scan on Commons, uploaded by its owner from the original card, carries the date '4/4/05' and the recipient, Ted Claxton. That makes it a private, used object rather than a museum piece. Fun fact: Wain sold pictures together with their copyright, so however many cards were posted he earned nothing more.
image_credit: Louis Wain · Scan of original postcard in my possession

title: Clinique Chéron: Veterinary Clinic (Clinique pour chiens et chats)
description: Four cats own the top of this poster: a black-and-white one balanced on the young woman's shoulder, a black one pressing its head against her cheek, and a pale one and a tabby lounging on the sign beside the lettering, the tabby's tail hooked down its right edge. Below them three dogs, a white sighthound, a dark brown hound and a terrier on its hind legs, compete for her other hand. She wears a long orange-red dress with a small white sprig pattern. It is a colour lithograph printed by Ch. Wall, 197 by 140 cm, so the animals stood close to life-size on a Paris wall.
context: Téléphone 141 56, the poster announces under 'Sanatorium, Pension' and '8 rue des Moulins, avenue de l'Opéra': a veterinary clinic with boarding rooms, advertised on a sheet nearly two metres tall. The Rijksmuseum catalogues it as a colour lithograph printed by Ch. Wall in 1905 (Crauzat 511) and as a gift of P.F. Maas of Apeldoorn in 1968, number RP-P-1968-308. Steinlen had made the Chat Noir cabaret poster nine years earlier, and here the cats sit on top and the dogs queue below.
image_credit: Rijksmuseum · http://hdl.handle.net/10934/RM0001.COLLECT.362697

title: I Am a Cat (Wagahai wa Neko de Aru): First Edition Cover and Illustration
title_original: 吾輩は猫である (初版本装幀・挿絵)
artist: Hashiguchi Goyō (binding design); Nakamura Fusetsu and Asai Chū (illustrations)
description: On the cover of volume one, Hashiguchi Goyō boxed two pale cats sitting side by side in a black panel under the stamped title, a neat emblem for a narrator who sneers at his owner in fluent prose. The scan shown here is the National Diet Library's black-and-white copy of that first volume. Inside, the first volume came with uncut pages, so the reader had to slice each fold open with a paper knife to keep reading. The illustrations are by two painters trained in Western oils, Nakamura Fusetsu and Asai Chū, and Goyō added his own cat to the half-title of the second volume. Their cats are lighter and jokier than his.
context: Natsume Sōseki serialised the novel in the magazine Hototogisu from January 1905, and Ōkura Shoten and Hattori Shoten issued it as three volumes: 6 October 1905, 4 November 1906 and 19 May 1907. Sōseki, back from London, brought Western books and magazines to the design meetings and asked for a thoroughly Western look; the commission launched the young Goyō as a book designer and, later, as a woodblock printmaker. The book sold so well that from the 15th printing the binding switched from Japanese to Western style. A fun comparison from the Ghibli Museum's curator: Goyō's cat in volume two looks remarkably like Henry J. Ford's cat in Andrew Lang's Yellow Fairy Book.
title_eng: I Am a Cat: First Edition Cover and Illustration
medium: Letterpress book with multi-color woodblock cover design and monochrome woodcut illustrations
image_credit: National Diet Library Digital Collections (scan of vol. 1, 1905, via Wikimedia Commons)

title: Cat
description: Sitting upright and tall, with front legs straight as columns, a cat has its haunch bulging out to the left and its head dropped so the eyes look half shut. Gwen John gets it down in a few dark, decisive outlines on brown paper and leaves everything inside them bare. It is one of the run of small sheets in Cardiff she simply titled 'Cat', each one cat with no setting, drawn from life, probably in a few minutes, and left the moment the shape was down.
context: Four neighbours of this sheet in the NMW A 156xx run were checked, and A 15610, 15611, 15629 and 15632 were all bought by Museum Wales on 29 July 1976. John's tortoiseshell Edgar Quinet, named after her Paris street, disappeared in 1908; she was devastated and wrote a poem about her loss. The museum notes how often John drew her cats spontaneously, which is what these quick, contour-only sheets look like.
submovement: Modern British drawing, Gwen John's Paris cat studies
image_credit: Gwen John · https://museum.wales/collections/online/?field0=with_images&value0=1&field1=string&value1=%20Gwen%20&field2=category&value2=Drawing&page=1

title: Cat (verso)
description: Hunched and rounded, a cat seen from behind has its head turned toward the upper right, sitting in a thicket of crossing diagonal strokes that could be wicker or grass. This is the back of the sheet: the museum record shows two images, front and back, and John seems to have turned the paper over and drawn again. The lines are faint and the body is almost all bare paper. The sheet is small, 17.2 by 16.9 cm, nearly square.
context: Both sides of this sheet carry drawings, which is typical of a working drawing never meant for exhibition. Amgueddfa Cymru bought it on 29 July 1976 (NMW A 15632, charcoal, 17.2 × 16.9 cm) along with a long run of other 'Cat' drawings. John acquired her first cat in Paris in 1904, a tortoiseshell named Edgar Quinet after her street, and spent the next four years drawing it on whatever paper was at hand. It vanished in 1908.
submovement: Modern British drawing, Gwen John's Paris cat studies
image_credit: Gwen John · https://museum.wales/collections/online/?field0=with_images&value0=1&field1=string&value1=%20Gwen%20&field2=category&value2=Drawing&page=1

title: Cat
description: A tabby-and-white cat curled tight into an oval, seen from above, its white face and chest tucked against its flank at the left and the ears just poking up. Gwen John draws it in graphite and then lays dark brown-black stripes over the back in confident watercolour, picking out the white fur with opaque highlights against the brown paper. The sheet is only 111 by 137 mm, smaller than a postcard. There is no setting; the sleeping cat simply occupies the paper. This is a drawing made at close quarters from a living animal that was, for once, not going anywhere.
context: Edgar Quinet ran away in 1908, and Museum Wales records that John, devastated, wrote a poem about the loss. The tortoiseshell had come to her in Paris in 1904, named after the street where she lived, and the museum says she 'frequently captured her adored cats in spontaneous drawings'. Tate's page lists this work as 'Cat', c.1904–8, at T00156. At 11.1 by 13.7 cm it is smaller than a postcard.
submovement: Modern British drawing, Gwen John's Paris cat studies
image_credit: Gwen John · https://www.tate.org.uk/art/artists/gwen-john-1363

title: Portrait de Monsieur X (Pierre Loti)
title_original: Portrait de Pierre Loti (Portrait de Monsieur X)
description: Stiff and formal as the sitter beside it, a striped tabby sits bolt upright on a red stool in the lower left corner, yellow eyes fixed on us. The moustached man fills the rest of the canvas at half length, square to us, in a red fez and black coat, a cigarette held up in his right hand. Rousseau paints both with the same flat frontality, as if posing for an official photograph. Behind them a landscape opens up, with a leafy tree and smoking factory chimneys: the Kunsthaus calls the picture a 'portrait-paysage', the formula Rousseau favoured in his last years.
context: The sitter's name is the puzzle. Wilhelm Uhde published the picture in 1914 as 'Portrait of Mr. X (Pierre Loti)', after the naval officer and exotic-travel novelist Julien Viaud. In 1952 a Parisian man of letters, Edmond-Achille Frank, said he recognised himself in it, and the Kunsthaus says the sitter and date are still not fully settled. The provenance is the fun part: the satirist Georges Courteline bought it from Rousseau in 1906 and hung it in his 'Musée des Horreurs', a collection of bad and Sunday paintings kept as a joke. It then went through Paul Rosenberg and the Mendelssohn-Bartholdy collection in Berlin before the Kunsthaus bought it in 1940 for 22,000 francs.
image_credit: Henri Rousseau · Artbook

title: The Story of Miss Moppet: Miss Moppet Jumps upon the Mouse
medium: Watercolor, pen, and ink on paper
collection: Victoria and Albert Museum, National Art Library, London (printed book: The Story of Miss Moppet, Frederick Warne, 1906)
description: The moment of the pounce: 'And then all of a sudden, Miss Moppet jumps upon the Mouse!' The tabby kitten has spent the previous pictures with her head tied up in a duster, pretending to be ill so the mouse will come closer, and here the act drops. Potter draws her rump up and tail flicked high, front paws pinning a tiny mouse at lower left, the blue-and-white duster still knotted round her head and a pink cushion behind. The plates were reproduced from Potter's small watercolours, and the joke is the kitten's body turning from invalid to hunter in one page.
context: Christmas 1906 brought Miss Moppet to shops as a panorama, not a book: fourteen pictures on one strip folded accordion-style into a grey cloth wallet, a shilling a time, 10,000 copies in November and another 10,000 in December. Booksellers disliked it because the strips kept unrolling, and the story came back as a small book in 1916. Potter borrowed the kitten from a Windermere mason and called it 'an exasperating model'. Fun fact: in June 1976 Nicholas Garland parodied four of the panels in the New Statesman, with Margaret Thatcher as the kitten and James Callaghan as the mouse who escapes.
title_eng: The Story of Miss Moppet: Miss Moppet Jumps upon the Mouse
image_credit: Beatrix Potter · Project Gutenberg ebook of The Story of Miss Moppet , image taken from this HTML version , original text with this illustration is "And then all of a sudden—Miss Moppet jumps upon the Mouse!"

title: At the Play: An Exciting Moment
collection: Raphael Tuck & Sons postcard, set 9396 'Louis Wain's Cats' (card 3 of 6); Commons scan from a private collection
description: A theatre box crammed with cats in bows and collars, a big grey tabby in the middle staring straight out with yellow eyes, the rest gaping, grinning and clutching at each other. The caption tells you why: 'An Exciting Moment'. A pair of opera glasses has been abandoned on the blue velvet ledge beside a programme, and a cat at left hides behind a pink fan. Wain gets the comedy from treating a row of cat faces as human reactions. This is a horizontal Tuck 'Oilette' postcard; this copy carries a French stamp and a greeting beginning 'Bonne' printed across the top.
context: Set 9396, 'Louis Wain's Cats', shows a recorded first use of 1906 in Raphael Tuck & Sons' own database, and the set appears in the catalogues of 1908/09 and 1911/12. This is card 3 of six, labelled 'Oilette' and recorded as sold in the United States, Britain and France, which fits the French stamp on this copy. Wain had made anthropomorphic cats his trade since 1886, and some 75 publishers turned more than 1,100 of his images into postcards. Fun fact: he sold work with its copyright, so Tuck's fee was the end of his earnings from the image.
title_eng: At the Play: An Exciting Moment
title_original: At the Play: An Exciting Moment (Raphael Tuck & Sons)
image_credit: Louis Wain · own scan

title: At the Play
collection: Raphael Tuck & Sons postcard; Commons scan from the Carthalia collection (Andreas Praefcke)
description: Another box at the same imaginary theatre, this time hung with red curtains, and some eighteen cats packed in tiers like a school photograph. A white cat in spectacles peers over the crowd, a ginger one hides behind a green fan, and on the red ledge lie a discarded pair of pince-nez, a programme and a box of chocolates. Look at how the faces are drawn: real cat heads, whiskers and all, on bodies that lean and gesture like Edwardian theatregoers. Like its companion, it is a horizontal Tuck 'Oilette' card, printed in colour to look like a little oil painting.
context: Card 2 of 6 in Raphael Tuck & Sons set 9396, 'Louis Wain's Cats', has a recorded first use of 1906, and the Tuck database notes that the same images also appeared as cards C132 and C133. The scan on Commons comes from Andreas Praefcke's Carthalia collection of theatre postcards. Wain left for New York in 1907 on a Hearst contract, so the set belongs to his last London years before the move. Fun fact: TuckDB puts an estimated value of about 125 US dollars on a card from this set today.
title_original: At the Play: In the Theatre Box (Raphael Tuck & Sons)
image_credit: Louis Wain · own scan, https://www.andreas-praefcke.de/carthalia/id/5259

title: Untitled cartoon (cat with love letters)
medium: Pen drawing with printed green tint, reproduced in The Sketch
collection: Published in The Sketch, 27 March 1901, p. 399, London; copy: University of Minnesota (v.33 (1901)), digitised in HathiTrust
inv_number: The Sketch vol. 33, no. 426, HathiTrust umn.319510028004291
description: One bed, two white cats: the husband dozes against the pillow with a smug, sleepy grin, while his wife sits bolt upright beside him, eyes popping and mouth open in outrage. The printed caption below supplies the row: Mrs. Pussy has caught him talking in his sleep, and Mr. Pussy explains he was only quoting from the 'Love Letters of a Cat'. Wain's line drawings for the weeklies ride on outline, hatching and a black background that throws the white fur forward. The magazine printed it without a title, and his signature sits at lower left.
context: Untitled in print, this cartoon ran in The Sketch, vol. XXXIII, no. 426, on 27 March 1901, page 399, when Wain was the best-known cat artist in Britain and president of the National Cat Club. The Sketch was a London illustrated weekly, and its pages gave him a regular outlet alongside the annual he launched that year. Fun fact: in 1914 he produced a series of 'futurist' ceramic cats, which one reviewer called 'the latest thing in freak ornaments'.
image_credit: Scan of the printed page from The Sketch, via Wikimedia Commons. Louis Wain died 1939; public domain.

title: Cat and Plum Blossoms (梅に猫)
collection: Adachi Museum of Art, Yasugi, Shimane
description: Plainly losing a fight with sleep, a white cat with black patches on its head, back and tail sits curled up at the bottom left, paws tucked and eyes shut to slits. Thin plum branches dotted with white blossom reach in from the left above it, and a gnarled trunk climbs the right edge. Shunsō splits his methods: the trunk is built by letting ink bleed into damp silk, all soft blotted edges, while the cat's fur is laid in with fine hair strokes. The scroll is tall and narrow, 118 by 49.8 cm, and the warm, empty ground leaves the small round cat enormous room to doze in.
context: Mōrōtai, the 'vague style', was meant as an insult, and Hishida Shunsō (1874–1911) wore it anyway. He trained under Hashimoto Gahō at the Tokyo School of Fine Arts, helped Okakura Tenshin found the Nihon Bijutsuin in 1898, and built forms from graded colour instead of line. He painted this scroll in 1906 (Meiji 39); Japan's national art database lists it at 118.0 by 49.8 cm in the Adachi Museum of Art, Shimane. Fun fact: Shunsō reportedly disliked cats, yet Eisei Bunko curators count more than twenty cat works in his output, finished and unfinished.
submovement: Meiji Nihonga, Nihon Bijutsuin Morōtai (vague style) circle, Tokyo
image_credit: Hishida shunso (1874 - 1911) – Painter (Japanese) Born in Nagano. Died in Tokyo. Details on Google Art Project · BwGvjDB8VLU0zQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

title: The Tale of Tom Kitten: On the Garden Wall
medium: Colour-printed book illustration (reproduction of a watercolour)
collection: Internet Archive (University of Toronto library scan of The Tale of Tom Kitten, Frederick Warne, c.1907)
description: Tom Kitten pushes up through a bank of ferns in his tight blue suit and straw hat, wide-eyed and tail flailing out behind for balance, with a clump of pink flowers at his feet. This plate belongs to the garden-wall episode and follows the line 'Moppet's white tucker fell down into the road', when the kittens, dressed for their mother's tea party, scramble up the rockery and their clothes start to come apart. Potter keeps Tom small inside a real garden, with ferns and blossoms given as much care as fur. The joke is in the clothes: they are visibly the wrong garments for climbing.
context: Hill Top, the Cumbrian house Potter owned, is the model for the cat family's home, so this rockery sits in her own garden country. Frederick Warne issued the book in September 1907, and its plot turns on clothes: the Puddle-Ducks who walk off in them later get their own book, The Tale of Jemima Puddle-Duck. What survives here is the printed plate, not the original watercolour. The V&A holds about 2,400 Potter drawings, manuscripts and books from the Linder bequest of 1973, but I could not confirm that this original is among them.
title_eng: The Tale of Tom Kitten: On the Garden Wall
title_original: The Tale of Tom Kitten - Illustration from p. 38
image_credit: Beatrix Potter · Project Gutenburg ebook of The Tale of Tom Kitten

title: The Tale of Tom Kitten: illustration facing 'another, larger, book'
medium: Colour-printed book illustration (reproduction of a watercolour)
collection: Internet Archive (University of Toronto library scan of The Tale of Tom Kitten, Frederick Warne, c.1907)
description: Mrs Tabitha Twitchit leans round the bedroom door, paw raised, while her kittens go to ground: two pairs of ears poke up from behind the four-poster's crimson curtains and footboard, and a grey tabby in a blue bonnet sits with its back to us on the floor. This is one of the closing plates, facing Potter's aside: 'And I think that some day I shall have to make another, larger, book, to tell you more about Tom Kitten!' The kittens have lost their clothes to the Puddle-Ducks and been sent upstairs, and the wreckage is all here: frocks, a cap and a picture frame heaped on the floorboards.
context: Tabitha Twitchit's fib is the book's real punchline: she hides the muddy kittens upstairs and tells her tea guests they have the measles. Frederick Warne published it in September 1907, and one of the Puddle-Ducks that made off with the clothes turns up again in The Tale of Jemima Puddle-Duck. This plate is a printed illustration, so the old 'V&A holding' is unconfirmed: Leslie Linder left the museum about 2,400 Potter drawings, manuscripts and books in 1973, but I found no record tying this picture to them.
title_eng: The Tale of Tom Kitten: illustration facing 'another, larger, book'
title_original: The Tale of Tom Kitten - Illustration from p. 77
image_credit: Beatrix Potter · Project Gutenburg ebook of The Tale of Tom Kitten

title: The Tale of Tom Kitten: 'Now keep your frocks clean, children!'
medium: Colour-printed book illustration (reproduction of a watercolour)
collection: Internet Archive (University of Toronto library scan of The Tale of Tom Kitten, Frederick Warne, c.1907)
description: Under a slate-grey porch roof, three kittens step out into a garden of roses, snapdragons and hollyhocks, with Mrs Tabitha Twitchit watching from the doorway in a pink dress. This is the plate for her parting order, 'Now keep your frocks clean, children!'. Moppet and Mittens, in white pinafores, hold paws on the left; Tom stands in front in a tight blue suit with his back to us, arms held stiffly out. Everything is still clean, which is the point: next they fall on the path and Tom bursts his buttons. A small orange butterfly at right is already a distraction.
context: Moppet, Mittens and Tom are the kittens of the title, and the trouble starts the moment their mother sends them out with the order not to get dirty. Frederick Warne published the book in September 1907. The cat family's home is based on Potter's own house, Hill Top in Cumbria, so the porch and borders echo a real place. Lost clothes, a gang of passing Puddle-Ducks and a lie about measles follow within a few pages.
title_eng: The Tale of Tom Kitten: 'Now keep your frocks clean, children!'
title_original: The Tale of Tom Kitten - Illustration from p. 29
image_credit: Beatrix Potter · Project Gutenburg ebook of The Tale of Tom Kitten

title: 'Cats' Choker (Collier de chien aux chats)
medium: Rock crystal, gold, diamonds and enamel
description: Rock-crystal squares engraved alternately with cats and sprays of foliage are linked by gold mesh into a band about 34 cm long and only 5.4 cm high, sized to sit close around the throat. Laid on its side and curving gently, it shows three rows of plaques, and the engraving reads frosted white against clear stone, so the animals and their branches seem to float. Tiny diamonds hide the joints that let the squares flex, and white-enamelled gold borders the top and bottom. At this photographic scale the cats are small shapes in the squares; the grid of gold edges keeps everything rigid, and the figures repeat like a frieze.
context: Collier de chien, literally 'dog collar', is simply French for a choker, so a dog collar covered in cats is a joke the title makes for free. Calouste Gulbenkian bought it from Lalique himself in 1920, and the Calouste Gulbenkian Museum in Lisbon dates it c. 1906–08. The museum calls it perhaps one of the most elegant pieces by the artist in the collection, notes the shift to rectilinear lines, and says the play of light and transparency that Lalique pursued in glass is achieved here in rock crystal, an extremely difficult material to work.
image_credit: René Lalique · Museu Calouste Gulbenkian, Lisbon · Public Domain

title: Children Playing with a Cat
collection: Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, Los Angeles
description: Dozing with its eyes shut in the lap of a girl in a huge flower-trimmed blue hat, a grey-and-white cat sits at the lower left, while a naked baby on its mother's knee reaches over to pat it. The canvas is big for a late Cassatt, 81.3 by 100.3 cm, and wide enough for the group to spread sideways. The colour is the thing to notice: high-keyed lilac walls, a cobalt vase, a yellow dress laced with orange. The cat is the still centre of all that handling. Signed 'Mary Cassatt' at lower right.
context: Durand-Ruel, the Paris dealer, probably acquired the picture in 1908, according to the Sotheby's provenance, and the firm lent it to a 1913 Paris exhibition of three women painters. It then belonged to François Daulte, was sold at Sotheby's New York in 1998 and again in 2006, and came up a third time in 2020 from the collection of Richard and Betsy Porter. The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles now lists it among its Cassatts. Fun fact: it changed hands at Sotheby's New York three times in twenty-two years before ending up in a museum.
image_credit: Mary Cassatt · https://www.marycassatt.org/the-complete-works.html?q=&ps=96

title: Manor House in Jankówka (Meeting of the Cats)
title_eng: Manor House in Jankówka (Meeting of the Cats)
collection: Muzeum Narodowe w Kielcach (National Museum in Kielce)
description: On a sandy path in the bottom right corner, two cats meet: a grey tabby walking in from the left and a black cat arching its back and lifting its tail, the classic stand-off. The painting's original title is about them, not the house. Behind them a low white manor with a dark shingled roof sits in full summer, its porch smothered in creeper, fronted by a riot of pink and dark red dahlias, red flowers and tall sunflowers at upper left. The canvas is modest, 41 by 58 cm, and the cats are tiny in it, a family joke slipped into a landscape.
context: Autumn 1907 is when Mehoffer bought the Jankówka estate, between Dobczyce and Wieliczka in the Wieliczka Foothills, nudged by his friend the Wieliczka bookseller Jan Czarnecki. He restored the eighteenth-century wooden house, designed its interiors and laid out the terraced flower garden that appears in many of his pictures. The Muzeum Narodowe w Kielcach (inv. MNKi/M/1916) dates this oil 'after 1907'. Jadwiga Mehofferowa's notes give its first title, 'Spotkanie kotów' ('Meeting of the Cats'), and name the cats as the big striped Maciek and the small black Czarcik, who turn up in family photographs too.
image_credit: Józef Mehoffer · Muzeum Narodowe w Kielcach (National Museum in Kielce) · Public Domain

title: Summer: Cat on a Balustrade (L'Été: Chat sur une balustrade)
medium: Lithograph (brush, crayon and spatter with scraper) in pink/mauve, violet black and brown on cream wove paper
description: Stretched along the rail of a wooden balustrade, a striped tabby rests its chin on folded forepaws and stares left with wide yellow eyes, while one hind leg and the long tail drop off the rail into thin air. The Art Institute's medium line says brush, crayon and spatter on the stone, with highlights scraped back out, and the fur shows it: dark strokes crowding the flank and spatter softening the edges. A pattern of leaves is printed behind, so summer is in the warmth of the tone rather than in green or blue sky. The image is about 49 by 60 cm, big enough to hang like a painting.
context: Spatter and a scraper are both in the Art Institute of Chicago's medium line for this lithograph: brush, crayon and spatter on the stone, with lights scraped out afterwards, printed in pink/mauve, violet black and brown. The impression (1927.6372) came with the Charles Deering Collection, as did its companion Winter (1927.6371), and the Institute dates both to 1909. At 48.9 by 59.7 cm the image is large for a lithograph of a house cat on a fence.
image_credit: Théophile Steinlen · YgEQQ3J1MY30yw at Google Cultural Institute , zoom level maximum

title: Winter: Cat on a Cushion (L'Hiver: Chat sur un coussin)
medium: Lithograph in 6 colours (red, ochre, yellow, black, gray-brown, brown) from two stones, with scraping on stone, on ivory wove paper
collection: National Gallery of Art, Washington (impression shown); The Art Institute of Chicago (second impression)
description: Pink-red cushion, grey wall, one big tabby sprawled across both of them with its head up and yellow eyes wide open. One forepaw hangs over the cushion's edge with the claws showing, and a hind foot is turned up so that its pale pads face us. The Art Institute lists six colours printed from only two stones (red, ochre, yellow, black, grey-brown and brown), plus scraping on the stone, which is how the fur gets its sharp little lights. Steinlen's monogram sits beside the cat's head and his name at lower right. The image measures about 49 by 59 cm.
context: Six colours from only two stones: the Art Institute of Chicago's medium line makes the arithmetic plain, since each stone had to carry more than one colour, with extra lights scraped out on the stone. The Institute's impression (1927.6371) is in the Charles Deering Collection; the image shown here is the National Gallery of Art's impression (1986.4.1), whose sheet measures 45 by 57.7 cm, noticeably smaller than the Institute's 50.3 by 62.1 cm sheet, so impressions of one print can differ in trim. The Institute dates Winter and its companion Summer to 1909, and the NGA record cites Crauzat's 1913 catalogue, number 293.
dimensions: NGA sheet 45 × 57.7 cm; AIC image 49.4 × 58.9 cm, sheet 50.3 × 62.1 cm
image_credit: Théophile Alexandre Steinlen · This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the National Gallery of Art . Please see the Gallery's Open Access Policy .

title: Second Exhibition of Animal Artists (2e Exposition des artistes animaliers)
description: A tabby lolls across a pink cushion, one paw hanging over the edge and a pale pad turned up, and the cushion itself becomes the billboard: the lettering for the second exhibition of animal artists at the Cercle International des Arts, 97 boulevard Raspail, is printed straight onto it. Steinlen signs only with his monogram, beside the cat's head, and the dates run in red at upper left. It is a colour lithograph, 50 by 64 cm, small for a poster and printed by the Paris firm Affiches G. Frichot. The wide format lets the cat stretch the whole length of the sheet, its tail trailing off the bottom.
context: Same cat, same cushion, new job: the animal sprawled across the pink cushion here is the one from Steinlen's colour lithograph Winter: Cat on a Cushion, also dated 1909, with the lettering for the Second Exhibition of Animal Artists printed over the cushion. According to the poster the show ran from 30 March to 25 April 1909, open 9½ to 5½, at the Cercle International des Arts, 97 boulevard Raspail, near the rue de Rennes. The BnF holds this impression in its Estampes et photographie department (FT 5-DC-385), and Commons shows it digitised on Gallica.
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Lithographe · This file comes from Gallica Digital Library and is available under the digital ID btv1b10510621w

title: Still Life with Cat (Der Geist im Hausgestühl: Stillleben mit Katze)
title_original: Der Geist im Hausgestühl: Stillleben mit Katze
description: A tortoiseshell-and-white cat stretches along the bottom edge of a still life, eyes shut and chin lifted, its curled tail flicking up at the far left like a question mark. Above it the set-up is all Macke: a pale turquoise tabletop with two oranges and a lemon on a white cloth, a potted geranium with one red flower, a blue-striped stoneware jug, a green ginger jar. Pinned on the wall at upper left is a picture of costumed musicians with harp and cello. The cat is the only thing in the room not posed for the sitting, and it looks as though it wandered in to bask.
context: 'Der Geist im Hausgestühl', the spirit in the household furniture, is the title Macke gave this picture, and a dedication dated 18 February 1910 is recorded for it, addressed to his mother-in-law, Sophie Gerhardt. The Lenbachhaus in Munich holds it as FH 557, oil on cardboard, 69 × 74 cm. Fun fact: Macke painted it at the start of a career that ended when he was killed in Champagne in September 1914, at 27; he had barely four years of mature work, and the cat is one of the most relaxed things in them.
title_eng: Still Life with Cat on a Garden Bench
feline_symbolism: The dedication turns the cat into a playful household spirit, a joke on the domestic setting rather than a coded symbol.
image_credit: August Macke · https://sammlungonline.lenbachhaus.de/objekt/der-geist-im-hausgestuehl-stillleben-mit-katze-30036173.html

title: Melvin Vaniman with the airship America's cat mascot Kiddo, aboard the steamship Trent
artist: Bain News Service (George Grantham Bain Collection)
description: Kiddo, a short-haired tabby with a collar and bell, peers out of the bottom right corner of the frame, ears up and eyes level with the lens, held against the chest of Melvin Vaniman, chief engineer of the airship America. Vaniman, in a tweed cap and heavy turtleneck, gives the camera a tired, satisfied half-smile. The cat was a stowaway who had just survived days aloft over the Atlantic and a transfer to a steamer, and he looks about as impressed as cats usually do. The image survives as a 5 × 7 inch glass-plate negative, the standard format of a news agency that needed sharp pictures fast.
context: On 15 October 1910 Walter Wellman's hydrogen airship America left Atlantic City to try for the first air crossing of the Atlantic. Kiddo was found in the airship's lifeboat before take-off. After engine trouble and storms the crew and cat abandoned ship and were picked up by the Royal Mail steamer Trent, where this photograph was made. The negative is in the George Grantham Bain collection at the Library of Congress. Fun fact: the Smithsonian notes that Kiddo was the subject of the first wireless message ever sent from an aircraft: "Roy, come and get this ---damn cat."
title_eng: Melvin Vaniman with the airship America's cat mascot Kiddo, aboard the steamship Trent
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Washington, D.C.
feline_symbolism: The crew treated Kiddo as a mascot and credited his nine lives with their survival.
image_credit: unknown / * MVcatontrent.jpg : George Grantham Bain derivative work: DreamGuy ( talk ) · MVcatontrent.jpg

title: Marguerite with a Black Cat (Marguerite au chat noir)
collection: Centre Pompidou, Musée national d'art moderne, Paris
description: Sprawled across Marguerite Matisse's lap, a black cat forms a heavy dark lump draped over her right hand, one white-tipped paw showing at the edge. Marguerite, fifteen, faces us head-on in a blue pinafore over a white blouse. The pose is upright and hieratic, almost an icon's, and Matisse cuts the background down to two flat bands, sea green above and pink below, so nothing competes with her almond-eyed stare. The cat is the one soft, shapeless mass in a picture built from flat colour and firm outline. The canvas is 94 × 64 cm, signed and dated lower right, "Henri Matisse 1910".
context: Marguerite sat for her father about thirty times, and the Centre Pompidou counts this as one of the most stylised portraits. Marguerite (1894–1982) had a life-saving tracheotomy as a child, and the collar and brooch here hide the scar, as a black ribbon does in other portraits. The canvas stayed in the family: Marguerite married the critic Georges Duthuit, who compared it to Byzantine art and to Coptic frescoes from Bawit, and Barbara Duthuit gave it to the Musée national d'art moderne in 2013 in memory of Claude Duthuit (inv. AM 2013-544). Fun fact: it crossed the Atlantic early, shown at the 1913 Armory Show in New York under the plainer title "Portrait de Marguerite".
image_credit: Henri Matisse · https://images.navigart.fr/1000/4N/64/4N64871.jpg

title: Black Cat (Kuroki neko, 黒き猫)
submovement: Late Meiji Nihonga, Nihon Bijutsuin Morōtai circle (Bunten exhibitor, Tokyo)
medium: Hanging scroll; ink and color on silk
description: With its claws just showing on the bark, a black cat crouches on a lichen-spotted oak bough near the bottom of the scroll, its tail hanging off the far side, and it stares back at us with pale yellow-green eyes. Hishida builds the body with ink washes alone, no outlines for the fur: the black thickens and thins so the coat looks soft and the body has weight. Above it the oak leaves are something else entirely, flat ochre-gold shapes with patches of green, closer to a lacquer pattern than a botanical study, though a few are nibbled with insect holes. One leaf has already fallen near the bottom edge. Real cat, decorative tree.
context: Five or six days: that is all the time Hishida Shunsō reportedly spent on Black Cat. In 1910, a year before his death at 36, he had been preparing a folding screen for the fourth Bunten exhibition, gave up on it, and painted this scroll instead. His friend and patron Akimoto Shatei bought it first; in the Taishō period it passed to Hosokawa Morisato, founder of Eisei Bunko, who collected over twenty Shunsō works. It is an Important Cultural Property. Fun fact: its first full restoration in 2025 was part-funded by crowdfunding, which drew over 943 donors and 14.755 million yen.
image_credit: Hishida Shunsō (d. 1911), public domain · Eisei Bunko, Tokyo · via Wikimedia Commons

title: Two Cats, Blue and Yellow (Zwei Katzen, blau und gelb)
description: A blue cat twists into a knot in the foreground, one hind leg flung up in the air as it grooms, while a yellow cat lies stretched along the top of the canvas with its chin down, watching. The 74 × 98 cm landscape format gives them room. The colours are not a joke about fur. Blue and yellow were Marc's male and female principles, so the pair reads as a little diagram of his colour theory dressed up as a pet picture. Around them float a green ball, red fruit-like shapes and, tucked into the top left corner, a small white house. Signed lower left "Marc".
context: Barmen's Ruhmeshalle held it by 1927, in what is now Wuppertal. On 5 July 1937 it was confiscated in the Nazi campaign against "degenerate art", under the confiscation number EK 16133, one of around 130 Marc works stripped from German museums. It came to the Kunstmuseum Basel in 1939 and is inventory 1746 there. Marc painted it in 1912 in Sindelsdorf. Fun fact: blue and yellow here are his male and female principles, so a picture that looks like two cats playing is also a small diagram of his colour theory.
feline_symbolism: In Marc's 1910 colour scheme blue was the male principle and yellow the female, so the two cats can be read as a paired, gendered couple.
image_credit: Franz Marc · cgfa.sunsite.dk/marc/marc2.htm

title: Three Animals: Dog, Fox, and Cat (Drei Tiere: Hund, Fuchs und Katze)
description: A dark grey cat sits upright at the right edge and looks straight out at us, the only one of the three animals paying attention. In front of it a big white dog pads across the canvas, nose down and eyes nearly shut, and behind them a red fox lies curled asleep with its white-tipped muzzle on its paws. The canvas is 80 × 105 cm. Marc reduces them to interlocking curves and shares colour among them, so the fox's red bleeds into the ground and the cat half dissolves into green and yellow. Signed lower left "Marc". Painted in oil, with tempera according to one catalogue listing.
context: Dog, fox and cat lie peaceably together here, a small utopia of the kind Marc thought humans had lost; he painted it in 1912, the year of the Blaue Reiter almanac, when he was trying to show animals as they might experience the world. The canvas belongs to the Kunsthalle Mannheim, according to the catalogue data on Commons and Wikidata. Fun fact: the fox is one of Marc's favourite animals, and he painted a Blue-Black Fox in 1911; here it shares space with two domestic animals that would normally chase it.
title_eng: Three Animals: Dog, Fox, and Cat
image_credit: Franz Marc · www.zeno.org

title: The White Cat (Cat on a Yellow Cushion)
description: A white tomcat sleeps curled into a near-perfect circle, nose buried against one forepaw and head pillowed on a lumpy yellow cushion. The Moritzburg files it as Die weiße Katze, while the longer name Kater auf gelbem Kissen (tomcat on a yellow cushion) is also in circulation, and the cushion is as much the subject as the cat. White fur on yellow is a hard pairing because there is so little contrast, so Marc pushes the body into a tight, rounded shape and lets grey shadow and outline do the separating. Behind both he lays a hot red ground scattered with yellow star shapes. Oil on cardboard, 488 × 600 mm, signed lower right "Marc".
context: Sindelsdorf, the Bavarian village where Marc worked in 1912, is where this picture was painted. It belongs to the Kunstmuseum Moritzburg in Halle (Saale), which collected Marc before 1933 and lost much of its modern collection to the Nazi confiscations of August 1937; this painting was not among the casualties. Fun fact: the cushion is doing theory. In Marc's colour letter to Macke of December 1910, yellow was the female principle, gentle and cheerful, so a sleeping cat on a yellow cushion is about as calm a statement of his system as he made.
title_eng: The White Cat (Cat on a Yellow Cushion)
feline_symbolism: Yellow was Marc's colour of the gentle female principle, which suits a cat sunk in rest.
image_credit: Franz Marc · The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

title: Cat with Kittens (Katze mit Kätzchen)
collection: Kulturstiftung Sachsen-Anhalt, Kunstmuseum Moritzburg Halle (Saale), Grafische Sammlung
description: A ginger mother cat, striped in quick red strokes, curls in a loose ring around her two kittens: a solid black one clambering up her chest with its paws out, and a white one stretched along her belly at the bottom. Marc works on a small sheet of cardboard, 35 × 30 cm, in mixed media rather than straight oil, and leaves the brown card showing all round. The size and the support suggest something quicker and more private than his exhibition canvases. Instead of a row of sweet faces, the litter is one compact whorl of colour: red, black and white.
context: Halle's museum-digital record lists a cardboard study called Katze mit Jungen (Cat with Young) as tempera, oil and pencil, inventory MOIIH00356, and dates it only 1900–1916. It was acquired in the 1920s together with the White Cat, and the record says it was detached from that painting, which implies the two pictures were once physically joined. This catalogue entry gives 1912 and the Hoberg/Jansen number 186, and I could not confirm that the Commons image is that same sheet. Fun fact: if the match holds, the red mother, black kitten and white kitten share a pedigree with a famous neighbour, the sleeping White Cat of the same year.
image_credit: Franz Marc · https://www.pubhist.com/person/2580/franz-marc-1880-1916-german-painter-and-printmaker

title: Portrait of the Artist's Wife with a Cat (Portret żony z kotem)
description: A lean black cat sits bolt upright at the far end of a green sofa, ears tall and yellow eyes catching the light, claiming a whole third of the picture for itself. Michalina Krzyżanowska leans back in the opposite corner, arms folded in a shimmering pale gown, her hair piled high, looking past us with mild patience. The canvas is nearly square and big, 114 × 124 cm, a public exhibition size for a private subject. Krzyżanowski was known for dramatic light and greys and blacks in his portraits, but here the wall behind is a flat electric blue, and the cat and the dark floor carry the black.
context: Kyiv, St Petersburg and Munich were the schools of Konrad Krzyżanowski (1872–1922): he studied at the St Petersburg Academy under Repin and Kuindzhi and then with Simon Hollósy, whose school he followed to Nagybánya. Back in Warsaw he ran a private painting school and taught at the Warsaw School of Fine Arts from 1904 to 1909. In 1906 he married Michalina Piotruszewska, a former student, whom he painted many times. This 1912 portrait is in the Muzeum Śląska Opolskiego in Opole, inventory MSO/S/228. Fun fact: Krzyżanowski was expelled from the St Petersburg Academy after clashing with the rector over its teaching system.
title_eng: Portrait of the Artist's Wife with a Cat
image_credit: Konrad Krzyżanowski · culture.pl

title: Woman with a Cat (La Femme au chat)
description: Planted on the dining table, a white cat stares straight back at us, front paws on the cloth, while the woman beside it in a dark green blouse smiles and does nothing whatsoever about it. The table is a big pale oval that tips up towards the viewer, with a plate of food left within easy reach of the cat, a bowl of green grapes and an orange in the foreground, and a hot red wall behind. Bonnard signs at upper right. Everything is soft and warm except the cat, whose narrow face and alert ears make it the sharpest thing in the room.
context: Marthe, Bonnard's companion and later wife, is usually named as the woman here, and the table-with-a-view was one of his favourite devices, tipping the cloth up so that fruit, plates and pets all crowd the lower half. The painting is dated 1912 and catalogued at the Musée d'Orsay as RF 1977 84, according to Commons and Wikidata. Fun fact: the plate on the cloth in front of the sitter is almost empty, which gives the cat a motive.
image_credit: Pierre Bonnard · Musée d'Orsay (via Wikimedia Commons)

title: Paris Through the Window (Paris par la fenêtre)
license: © Estate of Marc Chagall / ADAGP, all rights reserved
description: With a human face, a cat sits on the window ledge at lower centre, haunches down, between the striped window frame and the rooftops of Paris, with the Eiffel Tower rising pink and grey behind it. The cat is the hinge between the room and the city. The canvas is big and almost square, 136 × 141.9 cm, and the window frame, striped in red, yellow and blue, takes over the left half. Flowers sit in a pot below the sill, the only other domestic thing here. Bottom right, a man with a two-coloured double face looks both ways at once, and above the tower a parachutist drifts down.
context: Apollinaire was one of Chagall's early champions, and this canvas has been shown in his company: it appeared in the Musée de l'Orangerie exhibition "Apollinaire, le regard du poète" in Paris in 2016, and Chagall's Homage to Apollinaire dates from the same year as the painting, 1913. Chagall (1887–1985) made it during his first stay in Paris, a few years after arriving from Russia. It belongs to the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York (accession 37.438). Fun fact: the man at the bottom right has two faces, one blue and one pink, so he can look at the cat's side of the window and the room's at once.
collection: Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York
image_credit: © Estate of Marc Chagall / ADAGP. Photo: Aerra Carnicom. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from upload.wikimedia.org and is not stored on this site.

title: Four Playing Cats (Vier spielende Katzen)
description: Four cats tumble across a wide, low canvas of 44.5 × 66.5 cm: a dark brown one arches over the middle, a green one coils at lower left with its tail hooked into a spiral, and pale grey-white bodies crowd in from the right, one with its eyes squeezed shut. The horizontal format suits a pile-up, and Marc strings the bodies out so the eye slides along the curves from one cat into the next. By 1913 his forms were more faceted than in his earlier cat pictures, and here the backgrounds break into blue and green wedges behind the play.
context: Verdun, 4 March 1916, is where Marc was killed, aged 36, only three years after this picture. In 1913, his most productive and most fractured year before the war, prismatic, Cubist- and Futurist-influenced forms entered his animal paintings. It belongs to the Staatsgalerie Stuttgart. Fun fact: the number 2384 attached to the image online appears to be the Staatsgalerie's inventory number, while the catalogue raisonné page for the picture is 210.
image_credit: Franz Marc · https://www.staatsgalerie.de/sammlung/sammlung-digital/nc/suche/Franz%20Marc/_/_/person/werk/auflistung/record.html

title: Two Cats (Zwei Katzen)
description: Locked in a slow circle, two cats fill the sheet edge to edge: a tortoiseshell in the foreground, all dark crosshatching patched with ochre, twists to look back over its own shoulder, while a ginger-and-white cat behind lowers its head to sniff at it. Marc draws fur with fast, scribbled lithographic line and lets a few flat tones of brown and orange do the colouring. The scratchy swirls in the background are the same marks as the fur, so the cats almost dissolve into the floor. Signed in the stone 'Lit. F. Marc' at lower left.
context: Munich in 1909 was where Marc spent his time drawing animals from life, before colour turned symbolic in his work and before the Blaue Reiter almanac of 1912. Prints like this were where he worked out how to make an animal's body and its surroundings move together. The Lenbachhaus, which holds the largest public collection of Blaue Reiter art, acquired the sheet by purchase in 1964. Fun fact: this entry used to describe a 1913 painted postcard, but its image was always this print, so the record now follows the picture.
image_credit: Franz Marc · Copied from an art book

title: Two Cats at Rest (Deux chats au repos)
inv_number: BnF Estampes DC-385 (3)-FOL; Gallica btv1b10510756r (Crauzat: non décrit)
description: At rest, side by side: a black cat lies curled with its eyes shut, while a lean, short-haired companion sits bolt upright in profile, eyes half closed, keeping the watch. No furniture, no story, just two bodies of fur in etched line, with plenty of empty paper above them. The plate is almost square, about 29.3 × 29.5 cm at the platemark. This impression is signed in pencil at lower right and carries the note 'pour E. de Crauzat', so the sheet doubles as a small gift.
context: Two states of this plate survive at the BnF, a first state and this later one, which Steinlen signed in pencil and dedicated 'pour E. de Crauzat'. Unlike its two 1914 companions in the same album, the sheet carries no engraved date, so 'c. 1914' rests on the company it keeps. The BnF's reference field reads 'non décrit': the 1913 catalogue of Steinlen's prints by Ernest de Crauzat, the dedicatee, does not list it. The same black cat and lean pale cat seem to model again and again, from the 'Two Cats Side by Side' etching to these late plates.
inventory_id: BnF Estampes DC-385 (3)-FOL; Gallica btv1b10510756r (Crauzat: non décrit)
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Graveur Crauzat, Ernest de (1866-1944). Dédicataire · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: Two Sleeping Cats (Deux chats endormis)
inv_number: BnF Estampes DC-385 (3)-FOL; Gallica btv1b10510770w (Crauzat: non décrit)
description: On a fluffy white cushion, two cats sleep curled into one heap: a black cat behind, ears up and face buried, and a pale, short-coated cat in front with its chin tucked over a paw. The horizontal plate, 15.3 × 25.3 cm, suits animals stretched out rather than sitting up. The margins carry three kinds of handwriting: Steinlen's signature and 1914 bitten into the plate at lower left, his pencil signature with 'pour E. de Crauzat' at lower right, and '4e état' scribbled in the bottom left margin, the artist keeping score of his own revisions.
context: Anyone wanting to follow the plate through its states has the BnF to thank: it holds a second state and this fourth, the latter marked '4e état' in the artist's own hand, bottom left. This impression is dated 1914, engraved in the plate beside the signature, and dedicated 'pour E. de Crauzat', the compiler of the Steinlen print catalogue that appeared in 1913. The BnF's reference field reads 'non décrit': a plate dated 1914 simply came after the book. The sheet is mounted in DC-385 (3)-FOL.
inventory_id: BnF Estampes DC-385 (3)-FOL; Gallica btv1b10510770w (Crauzat: non décrit)
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Graveur Crauzat, Ernest de (1866-1944). Dédicataire · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: Two Cats on a Ledge (Deux chats sur un rebord)
inv_number: BnF Estampes DC-385 (3)-FOL; Gallica btv1b10510771b (Crauzat: non décrit)
description: A slim, pale cat sits upright on a ledge with its tail curled along the edge, gazing down, while a black cat crouches beside it, chin forward, peering over the drop. The black cat's shadow lands on the wall behind like a third cat. The etching is small and nearly square, 19 × 17.5 cm, with bitten line and white paper. The margins are busier than the image: signature and 1914 etched top right in the plate, a pencil signature and 'pour E. de Crauzat' bottom right, and '4e état' bottom left in Steinlen's own hand.
context: Where the signature goes shows how Steinlen composed: on this plate he etched 'Steinlen 1914' high at top right, clear of the ledge, while on its companion Two Sleeping Cats the same inscription sits low at the left. Both are fourth states, marked '4e état' in his hand and pencilled with a dedication to Ernest de Crauzat. The BnF lists this one as 'non décrit' in Crauzat's catalogue, which came out in 1913, a year before the plate was dated. It is mounted in the album DC-385 (3)-FOL.
inventory_id: BnF Estampes DC-385 (3)-FOL; Gallica btv1b10510771b (Crauzat: non décrit)
image_credit: Steinlen, Théophile Alexandre (1859-1923). Graveur Crauzat, Ernest de (1866-1944). Dédicataire · Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: Portrait of Michalina Krzyżanowska with Cat
collection: National Museum in Warsaw (Muzeum Narodowe w Warszawie)
description: Gazing up at her with its head tipped back, a brown tabby sits upright on Michalina Krzyżanowska's lap, her hand resting lightly on its flank. She sits at half length in a huge yellow fur stole and stares out at us, unbothered. Her husband paints her in oil on a canvas 87 × 78.5 cm, large enough to make the sitting feel like an occasion. Critics place him among Poland's early expressionists, a painter of charged portraits of women. Look at the acid-green wall: faint squaring lines still show through the loose paint.
context: Volhynia, her family's home, is where war pushed the Krzyżanowskis from Warsaw in 1915, the year of this version of a portrait Konrad Krzyżanowski painted of his wife many times. Trained in Kyiv, St Petersburg and with Simon Hollósy in Munich, he co-founded a Warsaw painting school, and Michalina had been his pupil before they married in 1906. The National Museum in Warsaw holds the canvas (MP 5 MNW). Fun fact: during the Second World War, Michalina worked for the Polish underground under the code name "Mrs Mouse", an alias that sits nicely beside this picture.
title_eng: Portrait of Michalina Krzyżanowska with Cat
image_credit: Konrad Krzyżanowski · cyfrowe.mnw.art.pl

title: Jane Cowl with Buzzer the Cat
title_eng: Jane Cowl with Buzzer the Cat
artist_dates: American (born Germany), Berlin 1869–1942 New Milford, Connecticut
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Washington, D.C.
description: Buzzer, a striped tabby, is held up at face height in a white-gloved hand, ears pricked and staring straight into the lens, while the Broadway actress Jane Cowl tilts her head and looks down at the cat with half-closed eyes. The Library of Congress catalogue gives the cat equal billing in the title. What survives is a 5 × 7 inch glass negative, so every print is a modern positive pulled from a fragile plate. Genthe's soft, low-contrast light melts her feathered hat into the curtain behind, but keeps every whisker sharp.
context: Studio negatives of actors and dancers make an odd home for a cat, but the Library of Congress dates this one to between 1912 and 1914 and gives Buzzer the title billing beside the Broadway actress Jane Cowl (1884–1950). Arnold Genthe, born in Berlin in 1869, worked as a photographer in San Francisco and then New York, where his portrait studio photographed actors, dancers and writers. The record files the plate under the subject heading "Genthe, Arnold, 1869–1942: animals and pets". Fun fact: the Library bought Genthe's negatives from his estate in 1942 or 1943, so a studio cat entered a national collection in the same boxes as the stars.
title_original: Cowl, Jane, Miss, with Buzzer the cat, portrait photograph
image_credit: Arnold Genthe · This image is available from the United States Library of Congress 's Prints and Photographs division under the digital ID agc.7a13339 . This tag does not indicate the copyright status of the attached work. A normal copyrigh

title: Study of the Cat Raminou (Étude du chat Raminou)
description: Raminou, Valadon's own cat, sleeps curled into a tight oval, eyes shut and front paws tucked under, alone on a small panel, 38.1 × 32.4 cm, painted in oil on plywood. The bare wood is left showing all around him, its grain running across the picture like a rug he happens to lie on. That cheap support suits a sketch made at home, fast and for herself. The title is written below the cat with her name: "Mon Raminou / Suzanne Valadon". The possessive is the detail to look for: Valadon labelled this one as hers.
context: Dr Robert Le Masle left this panel to the Musée national d'art moderne in 1974 (AM 1974-118), and since 3 April 1975 it has been on deposit at the Musée des Beaux-Arts de Brest. The record dates it 'vers 1917' and gives the inscription 'Mon Raminou / Suzanne Valadon'. Fun fact: in 2015 it travelled to Paris for the Musée de Montmartre exhibition on the rue Cortot studio of Valadon, Utrillo and Utter, where it was catalogue no. 33.
collection: Centre Pompidou, Musée national d'art moderne, Paris (on deposit at the Musée des Beaux-Arts de Brest since 1975)
submovement: Montmartre independent figuration (rue Cortot studio, Paris)
image_credit: Suzanne Valadon · Cette œuvre fait partie de la collection du Musée des Beaux-Arts de Brest .

title: Merchant's Wife at Tea (Купчиха за чаем)
description: A well-fed brown-and-white cat walks along the terrace railing at right and arches its head against the merchant's wife's shoulder, tail curled high, while she sips tea from a saucer with her little finger raised. Around them is a feast on a square canvas, 120 × 120 cm: a samovar, a cut watermelon, rolls, pretzels, grapes and apples, laid out on a white cloth. Behind the terrace, a provincial town shows a bazaar, church domes and a neighbouring couple also at tea.
context: Illness had taken away Kustodiev's ability to move by 1918, and the State Russian Museum's text calls his memory of provincial Russia a 'wonderful land of memories', which explains why the town behind the terrace feels remembered rather than observed. The museum received the canvas in 1925 from the State Museum Fund in Leningrad (Ж-1868), and its keyword list gives 'cats' alongside church domes and watermelons.
submovement: Mir iskusstva (World of Art) circle genre painting
feline_symbolism: The pampered cat doubles the sitter: its borrowed features make it a furry echo of her sleek, well-fed contentment.
image_credit: Boris Kustodiev · GgFFUJTfMEA_Xg at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

title: Interior of an Egyptian Harem (Wnętrze egipskiego haremu)
collection: Private collection (sold Dorotheum, Vienna, 19 June 2018, as 'Traute Zweisamkeit')
description: Folded into a neat loaf at the end of the bed, a tabby cat sits right beside the woman's hip, eyes half shut, the most at-home creature in the room. She sits on a red-covered bed with her chin in her hand and a feather fan in her lap, looking bored, while a warm square of light from an unseen opening falls across the painted walls. The bed end is carved with two dark lion heads, and lotus flowers stand in a blue vase at left. Bakałowicz paints in oil on a small wood panel, 33 × 47.5 cm, and signs it "St. Bakalowicz MCMXIX, Roma".
context: Lion-headed bed supports like these, Valentin Boyer argues in a 2020 article, trace back to drawings in the Cairo Museum's 1914 general catalogue and to bed supports in Turin. Stefan Bakałowicz (1857–1947), a Warsaw-born painter working in Rome, signed this panel in 1919. It is in a private collection and was sold at the Dorotheum in Vienna in June 2018 as "Traute Zweisamkeit". Fun fact: Boyer notes that Bakałowicz avoids pyramids and other clichés, relying on quiet motifs such as lotus bouquets, footstools and cats to signal Egypt.
feline_symbolism: Boyer counts the cat among the discreet, recurring motifs Bakałowicz uses to make a room read as Egyptian without resorting to cliché.
image_credit: Stefan Bakałowicz · Boyer V. Entre rêverie et authenticité – une immersion dans l'Égypte ancienne avec le peintre Stefan Bakałowicz : [фр.] // Studies in Ancient Art and Civilisation. — 2020. — Vol. 24. — P. 277—298. — doi:10.12797/SAAC.24.

title: Woman with a Cat (Femme avec un chat)
description: Staring out with two round eyes, a small black cat sits curled on the woman's lap while her tubular hand rests on an open book beneath it. She is a nude assembled from spheres, cones and tubes, grey and polished like engine parts, with a sheet of black hair and a blank oval face. The cat gets the same geometric shorthand: a dark lozenge with ears. Léger sets them in a yellow armchair against a grid of black, white and ochre panels and a yellow-and-black harlequin pattern, on a canvas 130.8 × 90.5 cm. Signed and dated lower right.
context: Two nearly identical versions of this subject came out of Léger's studio in 1921, part of a run of female figures thought to be studies for Three Women (Le Grand Déjeuner, 1921–22). This larger one belonged to Gottlieb Reber in Switzerland until 1958, then to Samuel and Florene Marx, and reached the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 1994 as a gift of Florene M. Schoenborn (1994.486). Fun fact: the smaller twin, 97.5 × 70.5 cm, went the other way through the market, from the dealer Paul Rosenberg to the Hamburger Kunsthalle, which bought it in 1967.
title_eng: Woman with a Cat (Femme avec un chat)
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: Fernand Léger · Metropolitan Museum of Art

title: Drawing by Louis Wain (cat)
medium: Pen, black ink, and colored crayon on wove paper
collection: Wellcome Collection, London (papers of Noel Gordon Harris, PP/NGH/58)
description: Both forelegs flung out, a shaggy cat lunges at us with claws spread, grinning under a huge round nose and squinting with glee. It is a Louis Wain cat drawn rather than painted, signed "Louis Wain." below, and it survives in an unlikely place: a folder of poems, notes and drawings in a psychiatrist's papers, one of two Wain cat drawings in the file. Wellcome's cautious caption is "Drawing of cat (?)". Along the bottom edge runs a handwritten line, "Keep your mouth shut, and let me open your mind for you", with "caught!" squeezed in above.
context: Noel Gordon Harris (1897–1963), psychiatrist and later president of the Royal Medico-Psychological Association, kept this drawing in his papers, which his daughter Joyce Griffith gave to Wellcome's Contemporary Medical Archives Centre in 1985 (PP/NGH/58, file dated c. 1930s–1940s). Harris took a post at Springfield Mental Hospital in 1923; Wain was certified and admitted to Springfield's pauper ward in 1924, before a public appeal moved him to Bethlem. Fun fact: that overlap may be how the drawing reached Harris, though the file does not say so.
image_credit: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/obf_images/e8/8a/eb8541ffe2fa2b205a23b10daec9.jpg Gallery: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/image/L0018572.html

title: Reclining Nude with Cat (Liegender Akt mit Katze)
submovement: German Expressionist colour woodcut (Kirchner's Davos years)
medium: Colour woodcut on folded book prospectus
collection: National Gallery of Art, Washington, D.C.
description: While she stretches out across the block with one arm behind her head, a black cat curls at the far right end of the couch, a dark lump by the nude's feet. Kirchner cut the scene into a woodcut barely the size of a playing card, 6.2 × 9.4 cm, and printed it in orange, violet and maroon. The sheet it sits on is a folded book prospectus, 26.5 × 32.4 cm unfolded, headed "Ernst Ludwig Kirchner, Das graphische Werk, von Gustav Schiefler", with a column of German sales text below. Every gouge that reads as a bold slash is a few millimetres long.
context: Sixty-two by ninety-four millimetres is the block's size, and the sheet that carries it is a folded book prospectus. The woodcut entered the National Gallery of Art in Washington in 2007 as a gift of Ruth Cole Kainen, a major donor of German prints (accession 2007.75.2). Fun fact: this is not a grand exhibition print but publicity printed onto a prospectus, which shows how closely Kirchner was involved in how his work was published and sold. The NGA record does not say which book the prospectus advertised, and I could not confirm it.
image_credit: Ernst Ludwig Kirchner · This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the National Gallery of Art . Please see the Gallery's Open Access Policy .

title: Tabby Cat (Madara Neko, Important Cultural Property of Japan)
description: A brown-striped tabby with white patches twists itself into a tight curl to groom, head bent back over its flank, one white forepaw pushed out towards the lower right, turquoise eyes glancing sideways at us. It floats alone on a field of honey-coloured silk with nothing to compete with it, apart from a small signature seal at the upper left. Seihō made his name with animals studied from life, and the Yamatane Museum's account is that this one was a cat he met by chance in Numazu, then watched and sketched closely. The fur is a mass of fine, layered strokes, with the pale underside left almost bare.
context: A chance meeting in Numazu, Shizuoka, set this picture going: Takeuchi Seihō (1864–1942), the leading Kyoto painter of the age, was captivated by a cat he came across there and painted Hanbyō in 1924 (Taishō 13). The Yamatane Museum of Art in Tokyo owns it, it is an Important Cultural Property, and the museum counts it among its most popular works. Fun fact: Yamatane built a whole 2020 special exhibition around the picture, showing it in public for the first time in about four years alongside 17 other animal paintings by Seihō.
submovement: Taishō Nihonga, Kyoto school (Takeuchi Seihō circle), animal painting
image_credit: Takeuchi Seihō · [1]

title: Panther (Panthère)
description: A panther walks along a low plinth, head dropped below the line of its shoulders, tail trailing almost to the floor in one long curve. Pompon reduces it to the forms he trusted: a continuous back, smooth flanks, no fur, no fuss. From 1905 he deliberately simplified his animals, polishing surfaces and suppressing detail, so light does the work that carved hair would do in a 19th-century animal bronze. The paws are rounded knobs, the ears two shallow bumps. In stone it looks heavier and calmer than a bronze would, a big cat made to be walked around.
context: Fame came late to François Pompon (1855–1933). For decades he was a praticien, the craftsman who turned other sculptors' models into marble, working for Rodin, Camille Claudel and Falguière, and he was 67 when his Ours blanc caused a stir at the 1922 Salon d'automne. French Wikipedia lists a Panthère of 1925 among the sculptures at the MuMa, Le Havre's museum of modern art. Fun fact: the same MuMa list names a second big cat by him, a Panthère noire, alongside the white bear, a hen and a red partridge.
collection: Musée d'art moderne André Malraux (MuMa), Le Havre
image_credit: François Pompon · photo by Pymouss

title: Cat and Flowers (Neko to Hana)
submovement: École de Paris Japanese Expatriate Modernism
collection: The Museum of Modern Art, Saitama (MOMAS)
description: Head turned so one yellow-green eye and a fan of whiskers catch the light, a black cat sits on a windowsill beside a pot of flowers, back half to us. Behind it the window glows yellow and orange, crossed by dark mullions. Tanaka draws in pastel on a sheet 35 cm wide and 47 cm high, so the composition stands upright. The museum's tags list pencil and coloured pencil alongside the pastel, and the fur is built from dense, scribbled black strokes over tan paper. Known first for figures and nudes, Tanaka gives the cat the same close attention. Signed lower right.
context: Seattle came before Paris. Tanaka Yasushi (1886–1941) left Saitama Prefectural Urawa High School in 1904 and travelled alone to Seattle to study painting, where his nudes drew notice. In 1920 he moved to Paris with his wife, showed at the Salon d'Automne and elsewhere, and died there without ever returning to Japan. The Museum of Modern Art, Saitama, which holds this sheet, dates it broadly to 1920–40. Fun fact: his career runs Saitama to Seattle to Paris, and the drawing has made the return trip he never did.
image_credit: Tanaka Yasushi · The Museum of Modern Art, Saitama (MOMAS) · Public Domain

title: Two Children with a Cat (Dwoje dzieci z kotem)
collection: Muzeum Narodowe w Warszawie (National Museum in Warsaw)
description: In the bottom right corner, half hidden among long blade-like leaves, a tabby cat sits bolt upright and stares out with the same flat calm as the children. They fill a canvas 100 × 82.5 cm: a dark-haired toddler in a brown smock clasps his hands, a fair older child stands behind, and a white hen perches on the fence at left. Makowski's children are a recognisable cast, stiff, doll-like figures who seem carved rather than born, with something of Polish folk toys about them. The scene is outdoors, thin trees, picket fence and brick houses, in the warm, still light he admired in the old Dutch masters.
context: Classical philology came before painting for Tadeusz Makowski (1882–1932): he read it at the Jagiellonian University, then studied painting at the Kraków Academy under Jan Stanisławski and Józef Mehoffer before moving to Paris in 1908, where he stayed for life. Cubists around Henri Le Fauconnier admired his early work; later he turned to carnivals, fairs and above all children. The National Museum in Warsaw holds this canvas (MPW 2700 MNW), dated around 1920. Fun fact: he kept a diary from 1912 to 1931, published in Warsaw in 1961.
submovement: École de Paris (Polish circle), folk- and Dutch-inflected figure painting
image_credit: Tadeusz Makowski · National Museum in Warsaw

title: The Falsehood of Woman: Self-Portrait with Maryla Grossmanowa (Fałsz kobiety)
title_eng: The Falsehood of Woman (Self-Portrait with Portrait of Maryla Grossmanowa)
title_original: Fałsz kobiety, z autoportretem (Portret Maryli Grossmanowej)
medium: Pastel on paper mounted on canvas
collection: Muzeum Narodowe w Warszawie (National Museum in Warsaw)
description: A long-haired grey-brown cat crouches in the lower left corner, eyes narrowed, as if it has seen this act before. Above it Witkacy, in a brown suit, grins at us while painting a grotesque grinning face on a canvas, and Maryla Grossmanowa reclines at right in a red dress and pearls, hand to cheek, against a rocky seascape. A huge pastel, 115.5 × 184 cm, on paper laid down on canvas. Top left: "Ignacy Witkiewicz 1927 I (T.A)" and coded notations; bottom right: "Witkacy / NP1 X 1922 / NP1 II 1924". Witkacy logged what he had, or had not, been taking while he painted.
context: After 1925 Witkacy ran his portrait business as "The S.I. Witkiewicz Portrait Painting Company", with grades ranging from largely representational likenesses to expressionistic ones and ones made under narcotics, and the motto "The customer must always be satisfied". This sheet, dated January 1927, is marked T.A, a Type A. The National Museum in Warsaw bought it (Rys.W.11538) and showed it in 2022 in "Witkacy. Seismograph of the Acceleration Age". Fun fact: his mnemonics were so thorough that some pictures record nothing stronger than a cup of coffee.
image_credit: Stanisław Ignacy Witkiewicz · cyfrowe.mnw.art.pl

title: Standing Anthropomorphic Cat with Decorative Patterns
description: On its hind legs stands a cat whose body is not fur but pattern: a magenta face with diamond-crossed green eyes and a tiny heart for a nose, curling yellow acanthus ears, and a blue bow-like flourish where the chest should be. The colours are mainly yellow, purple and blue, set on a green ground worked with rows of red decoration. Wain painted it in gouache on a small sheet, 18.8 × 12.6 cm. Pencilled on the back are the words "Early Greek", his label for the style of the patterns. A cat after ancient vases, by way of a wallpaper sample book.
context: Springfield, Bethlem and Napsbury were the three hospitals of Wain's last years, after his sisters had him certified in 1924, and Wellcome Collection dates this gouache broadly to 1925/1939. He kept painting there, decorating wards at Christmas and making both old-style cats and abstract, patterned designs. Fun fact: the famous sequence that supposedly charts Wain's decline into schizophrenia was assembled in 1939 by the psychiatrist Walter Maclay from undated pictures bought in a shop, and critics now point out Wain was painting conventional and patterned cats side by side.
title_eng: Standing Anthropomorphic Cat with Decorative Patterns
title_original: A cat standing on its hind legs, formed by patterns supposed to be in the "Early Greek" style
image_credit: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/obf_images/1f/9f/b6cb7095a1247632a85b8738f449.jpg Gallery: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/image/L0026932.html Wellcome Collection gallery (2018-03-21): https://wellcomecollection.org/works/bvxdmx8m

title: Three Cats Performing a Song-and-Dance Act
description: On a green lawn, three cats in top hats perform a song-and-dance number. At left a white cat in a scarlet suit kicks up a leg, waving a cane and a feathery plume; a tabby in white trousers and a yellow topper follows, cane tucked to its chest; the third, in pale pink with a green waistcoat and red hat, brings up the rear with an umbrella and an open-mouthed "oh". Behind them rise bushes of blue and white blossom. Music hall transplanted to the garden, in gouache on a sheet 17.7 × 22.6 cm, signed "Louis Wain" lower left. One umbrella among the canes: someone missed the memo.
context: H. G. Wells wrote in 1925 that Wain "invented a cat style, a cat society, a whole cat world", and this gouache shows that world still going strong. Wellcome Collection dates it to 1925/1939, the years of Wain's confinement in Bethlem and later Napsbury Hospital, where he kept painting and decorated the wards at Christmas. Pictures like this undercut the old story that his work simply dissolved into abstraction as his illness advanced: here are the dressed-up, jolly cats that made him famous in the 1880s and 1890s.
title_eng: Three Cats Performing a Song-and-Dance Act
title_original: Three Cats Performing a Song and Dance Act
image_credit: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/obf_images/2f/45/1297a2e55598c2ba91e267c1f500.jpg Gallery: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/image/L0026312.html Wellcome Collection gallery (2018-04-05): https://wellcomecollection.org/works/asen9ww3

title: Kaleidoscopic Cat II
collection: Bethlem Museum of the Mind, Beckenham, Kent
description: Enormous green-rimmed eyes, pupils slid to one side, stare out of a ginger-and-white face with ears up and fur bristling outward in quick red-brown strokes. The cat itself is still very much a cat; the ornament lives behind it, a green field of blue-green scrolls and small red stars crowding in around the ears. The image's own title files it under "kaleidoscope", the word that has stuck to Wain's most patterned pictures, but here the pattern is only starting to creep in. Look for the faint signature at lower left. The reproduction comes from the Bethlem Museum of the Mind.
