context: Certified in 1924, Wain moved to Bethlem Hospital after a public appeal, and in 1930 went to Napsbury, painting throughout. In 1939 the psychiatrist Walter Maclay arranged undated Wain pictures bought in a Campden Hill shop into a sequence said to chart a schizophrenic decline. Critics now note Wain painted conventional and patterned cats side by side, and later commentators link these designs to 1960s psychedelic art. Fun fact: the date is still unresolved; Wikidata gives 1910, well before his hospital years.
image_credit: Louis Wain · Bethlem Museum

title: Norman
description: A turquoise cat's head fills a blue ground, and its fur has stopped behaving like fur. White lines run across the face and broad ruff in pointed arches, loops and little hooked crockets, beaded with pink and red dots, the vocabulary of a church window rather than a tabby coat. Two huge yellow eyes and a red, cross-shaped nose hold it together, and three white sprigs rise from the crown like finials. Wellcome's cataloguer saw tracery and crockets in those lines. The sheet is small, about 18.5 by 12 cm, in flat, opaque gouache, with a single pencilled word on the back: "Norman".
context: Springfield Hospital in Tooting took Louis Wain (1860–1939) in June 1924; he moved to Bethlem in 1925 and to Napsbury in Hertfordshire in May 1930, and he kept painting in all three. Wellcome Collection can only date this gouache to 1925–1939, somewhere inside those hospital years. For a long time the catalogue called it "A cat in 'Gothic' style", a title that went straight into books and on to Wikipedia. In February 2025 Wellcome retitled it "Norman", taking the name from the pencilled word on the verso, so the cat now goes by what the back of the sheet says rather than what a cataloguer thought it looked like.
image_credit: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/obf_images/cd/03/9030e9bf472c799c9b492cc2ba5e.jpg Gallery: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/image/L0026931.html Wellcome Collection gallery (2018-03-21): https://wellcomecollection.org/works/nww85e9p

title: Three Cats Singing
description: Mouths open and eyes rolled up toward something out of frame, three cats sing in profile like a church trio caught mid-verse: a brown tabby at left and two blue-grey cats beside it. Each grips an open red-covered book in its paws. Behind them, pink daisies and red pompom flowers crowd a yellow-green background, colours the Wellcome cataloguer called "equally lurid", a fair warning for anyone expecting Victorian browns. The sheet is gouache, about 17 by 23 cm, so the paint lies thick and matt, and Wain has signed it plainly at lower right: "Louis Wain."
context: Singing, card-playing and tea-drinking cats were a staple of late Victorian illustration, and Wain did not stop making them after his family had him certified in 1924. He spent a year at Springfield, five at Bethlem, and his last years at Napsbury, where he died in July 1939. Wellcome Collection holds this gouache with a broad date of 1925–1939, so it belongs to the hospital decades, though no record says which ward it was painted in. Curator Bryony Benge-Abbott, writing for Wellcome in 2020, argues that work like this undercuts the old story of steady psychotic decline: alongside the patterned cats, Wain went on producing exactly the comic anthropomorphic scenes that had made him famous.
image_credit: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/obf_images/b7/4f/26d89e691250b47be288293a4f76.jpg Gallery: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/image/L0026168.html Wellcome Collection gallery (2018-04-05): https://wellcomecollection.org/works/gbcecf7t

title: Cat and Bird (Katze und Vogel)
description: Broad as a full moon, a cat's face takes up almost the whole canvas, built from simple shapes: almond eyes with green vertical pupils, a long thin nose ridge, whiskers drawn as fine curving lines. On its forehead, between the eyes, perches a small pink bird, as if the cat is thinking about it. The palette stays muted, warm ochres and orange-browns over chalky white with touches of green, so the one bright note is the nose, a red heart. Above the bird hangs a small dark circle. Oil and ink on a prepared ground, 38 by 53 cm.
context: Whose thought is that bird? William Rubin read the picture through Gestalt psychology: the bird is not sitting on the cat but inside its head, a thought the cat is unwilling to let go of. Klee made it in 1928 while teaching at the Bauhaus in Dessau. According to the provenance summarised on Wikipedia, he consigned it to Alfred Flechtheim's Berlin gallery in 1929, and in 1934 it was sold to Franz Herbert Hirschland, whose daughters inherited it. MoMA acquired it in 1975 (300.1975) through the Sidney and Harriet Janis Collection Fund and a gift of Suzy Prudden and Joan H. Meijer in memory of F. H. Hirschland.
medium: Oil and ink on plaster-primed gauze mounted on plywood
collection: The Museum of Modern Art, New York
feline_symbolism: Following Rubin's reading, the bird is the cat's own fixation made visible, and the red heart-shaped nose has been read as a sign of desire.
image_credit: Paul Klee · Own work

title: Portrait of Ludwik Kotulski, with Patient and a Cat
title_eng: Portrait of Ludwik Kotulski, with Patient and a Cat
title_original: Portret Ludwika Kotulskiego, z pacjentką i kotem
collection: Muzeum Sztuki w Łodzi (Museum of Art in Łódź)
location: Muzeum Sztuki w Łodzi (Museum of Art in Łódź)
description: Across Kotulski's lap and forearm lies a black cat, its dark body almost swallowed by his charcoal-grey coat. He sits bald and pensive, a finger at his lips, while behind him a woman's face, described as his patient, peers over his shoulder out of a sweep of white, and at left a winged, twisting yellow-and-pink creature clutches a pedestal. The sheet is brown paper nearly a metre across, in pastel, unusually wide for a portrait. Lower right runs the book-keeping: "NP 17 / T.B / 1928 III" and the signature.
context: From around 1925 Stanisław Ignacy Witkiewicz ran his portrait practice as a mock business, the S.I. Witkiewicz Portrait Firm, with a printed set of rules and five price-graded types from A to E. Type B, marked "T.B" here, meant an accurate likeness with a slight push on the sitter's characteristic features. Witkacy also logged his own habits on the sheets: "NP 17" means he had not smoked for seventeen days when he made this one in March 1928. The pastel was bought by the Museum of Art in Łódź in 1973 from a private collection sold through Desa, and it was shown in the museum's big Witkiewicz exhibition in 1980. It is catalogue number I 768 in the Witkacy catalogue raisonné.
image_credit: Stanisław Ignacy Witkiewicz · https://www.digi-art.pl/pl/p/Witkacy-Portret-Ludwika-Kotulskiego/3386

title: Black Cat Hissing (Neko)
collection: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
description: Back arched and front legs stretched low, a black cat hisses with claws spread and its mouth wide on a pink tongue and white fangs. A red collar with a small gold bell and a blue-and-pink tied cord are the only bright notes besides one yellow eye. In a colour woodblock print a large area of black is a technical dare: it has to be printed evenly from a carved block, by hand, so the few details, whiskers, teeth, claws, must be carved precisely or vanish. A grey shadow pools beneath the animal, on warm cream paper.
context: Souvenir prints for foreign buyers were the job when the publisher Watanabe Shōzaburō hired Takahashi Shōtei (1871–1945) in 1907, starting with ten landscapes after Hiroshige. Shōtei had trained under his uncle Matsumoto Fūko, who gave him his art name, and he also signed as Hiroaki and Kōmei. He designed around five hundred prints for Watanabe before the 1923 Great Kantō earthquake, whose fire destroyed the workshop and every woodblock in it. LACMA, which lists the artist as Takahashi Hiroaki, dates this impression only to the second quarter of the 20th century.
image_credit: Rawpixel Ltd · Black Cat Hissing 20th century print in high resolution by Hiroaki Takahashi. Original from The Los Angeles County Museum of Art. Digitally enhanced by rawpixel.

title: Psychedelic Cat
collection: Bethlem Museum of the Mind, Beckenham, Kent
description: A single white cat crouches and grins, its fur outlined in flame-like red-orange strokes, round red-brown eyes rimmed in blue, a wide pink smile. The cat stays recognisable; the pattern is around it, concentric zigzag bands of purple, blue, green, yellow and red radiating out to the edges like an electric aura. That is the manner that later earned Wain's late cats the nickname "psychedelic", the creature reading as much as an emblem as a pet. The Commons file credits the picture to Bethlem Museum of the Mind and gives no title, size or medium, so even what it is painted on goes unrecorded there.
context: Eric Guttmann and Walter Maclay, the psychiatrists behind the Guttmann-Maclay Collection, assembled their Wain pictures in the 1930s, and the Bethlem Museum of the Mind in Beckenham now holds a group of them. Their arrangement of Wain's cats into a supposed clinical progression, "from conventional to psychedelic" in the museum's words, shaped how these pictures were read for decades. Wain was certified in June 1924, spent a year at Springfield, five at Bethlem and the rest of his life at Napsbury, dying in July 1939. Fun fact: the Commons file's date of 1875 is impossible; it would have Wain painting this as a teenager, years before his first published drawings.
image_credit: Louis Wain · Bethlem Museum

title: Cat (Kot)
collection: Muzeum Górnośląskie w Bytomiu (Upper Silesian Museum, Bytom)
description: A long-haired cat sits in three-quarter view, body turned away, head swung round to face us with a dark mask, tufted ears and two orange eyes. Those eyes are the only colour on the sheet, which is the point: Goryńska's prints lean on a crisp contour, what the Bytom museum calls her "perfect, drawn line", and lay colour on chosen areas only. Fine cut lines build a white ruff, a grey flank and a huge plumed tail sweeping round the front paws. Pencilled 1930 at lower left and signed at lower right, the sheet is titled simply Kot, "Cat": no anecdote, just the animal as a problem of shape.
context: Cats came first for Wiktoria Goryńska (1902–1945): the Bytom museum notes that her early animal subjects included a whole series of cats. Born in Vienna, she trained at the Kunstgewerbeschule there and moved to Warsaw in 1918, where she studied under Tadeusz Pruszkowski and Władysław Skoczylas and joined the Ryt Association of Graphic Artists. She was also one of the first Polish women to fence competitively and wrote about the sport. In the occupation she served as an underground courier under the pseudonym "Leti"; deported after the Warsaw Uprising, she died at Ravensbrück on 29 March 1945.
image_credit: Wiktoria Goryńska · muzeum.bytom.pl

title: Two Cats (Shuang Mao Tu)
description: Under a leafy branch, two cats share a rock: a long-haired white cat with black patches sits up and stares straight out, while a calico companion curls asleep behind it. The hanging scroll is more than a metre high and barely half a metre wide, ink on paper with touches of blue and ochre wash, stacked vertically: leaves above, cats in the middle, the rock in broad wet ink below. The key is the inscription at upper left. Xu explains the cats are a couple, "lifelong partners", painted to mark their union. Two square seals close it: "Beihong" and a motto, "always believe it to be good".
context: A lady called Yishan, according to the inscription, left her cats at Xu's "humble home" in the new capital, and a friend named Tan Junwan was the first to wish the pair a happy union; Xu painted the scroll to commemorate the match, signing it late in the jiaxu year, 1934. In other words, this is a wedding portrait for two cats, with a guest list. Xu Beihong (1895–1953) trained in Paris from 1919, came home determined to graft Western drawing onto Chinese brush-and-ink painting, and from 1927 taught at National Central University in Nanjing, then the capital. He later headed the Central Academy of Fine Arts, whose CAFA Art Museum is credited with the scroll.
image_credit: Xu Beihong (徐悲鴻) · CAFA Art Museum, Beijing · Public Domain

title: The King of Cats (Le Roi des chats)
license: © Estate of Balthus, all rights reserved
description: Leaning against the painter's shin, tail up, a tabby cat is the only soft thing in the room. Balthus stands above it in a tight jacket and a swagger pose, in a cramped space with bare walls and hard light that MCBA compares to a prison cell. The furniture amounts to a stool and a whip. Propped against the wall, a canvas carries the title in English: "A Portrait of H. M. The King of Cats, painted by Himself", with the year in Roman numerals. Oil on canvas, 78 by 49.7 cm, painted in muted colours and thick paint.
context: Mitsou (1921), a picture story drawn by an eleven-year-old Balthus about a cat he found and lost, was published with a preface by Rilke, so the King of Cats had a long pedigree by 1935. That year the 27-year-old painted himself in Paris, and he also signed letters to his future wife, Antoinette de Watteville, as the King of Cats. The Musée cantonal des Beaux-Arts in Lausanne received the canvas in 2016 as a gift from the Fondation Balthus Klossowski de Rola (inv. 2016-048). MCBA's curators point to a borrowed source: the pose, bare setting and restrained palette lean on Manet's Portrait of Théodore Duret (1868).
feline_symbolism: MCBA reads the cat as Balthus's alter ego and the picture as an allegory of a wild self that has to be tamed daily, hence the whip; in his memoirs he wrote of a secret, mysterious belonging to the world of cats.
image_credit: © Estate of Balthus / MCBA Lausanne. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from mcba.ch and is not stored on this site.

title: Professor Pulverstone Had a Litter of Kittens… (Profesor Pulverstone okocił się…)
title_eng: Professor Pulverstone Had a Litter of Kittens…
location: Muzeum Tatrzańskie im. Dra Tytusa Chałubińskiego w Zakopanem
description: Five kittens tumble at lower left, one of them dark, freshly delivered by Professor Pulverstone, who sprawls above them with a big four-legged body and a shaggy, bearded human head. The caption explains he "okocił się ze zdziwienia": gave birth to kittens out of sheer astonishment on seeing two of his monsters, which he believed were figments of his imagination, start to flirt coarsely. The monsters cavort on a table at top, labelled "owe potwory". His wife, with some hesitation, voices a mock-French "désintéressement" at right, and a tame seal called Rózia gets her own label. Pencil on paper, about 22 by 32.5 cm, with "Kopia N7" circled at top.
context: All Souls' Day, 2 November 1936, is written across the top left ("w dzień zaduszny, 2 XI"), three years before the artist's suicide in September 1939. A note beside it reads "Kopia N7", suggesting he repeated the composition. Drawings like this, populated with invented scholars and their household beasts, ran alongside the portrait business that paid his bills. The sheet belongs to the Tatra Museum in Zakopane, the town where Witkacy grew up. The title verb okocić się is normally used only of a cat giving birth, which is the whole joke.
image_credit: Stanisław Ignacy Witkiewicz · https://witkacykatalog.com/pl/katalog/126674

title: Cat Catching a Bird (Chat saisissant un oiseau)
description: Claws out like white hooks, a striped cat stands rigid on a dark ridge, tail up, with a black bird clamped sideways in its jaws. The bird's chest is torn open in a red wound, its wings splayed, and the cat's flattened head, white-rimmed eyes and bared teeth look less hungry than furious. Picasso does not soften it. The title says it plainly, Chat saisissant un oiseau, and the horizontal canvas, 81 by 100 cm, gives the struggle room to spread sideways. The date 22-4-39 is written in white at upper left against the grey-blue sky.
context: Dated in the sky at upper left, 22-4-39, this was painted a few months before the Second World War began, and it is tempting to read the cat's violence as a comment on the times, though the picture carries no political label. The French state's POP database lists it in the Musée national Picasso, Paris (inv. MP178), and flags Picasso as an artist still under rights, with the work entering the public domain only in 2044. That is why this page links to the picture rather than storing a copy.
image_credit: © Succession Picasso. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from uploads2.wikiart.org and is not stored on this site.

title: Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird
title_original: Autorretrato con collar de espinas y colibrí
medium: Oil on canvas mounted to board
collection: Harry Ransom Center, The University of Texas at Austin
description: Over Kahlo's left shoulder, a black cat with pale, staring eyes and pricked ears peers out of the dark leaves, its head level with her chin. It is easy to miss, because everything else is louder: Kahlo faces us head-on, a necklace of thorns cuts into her throat and trails across her chest like roots, and a dead black hummingbird hangs from it with wings spread stiff. Behind her other shoulder a spider monkey fiddles with the thorns. Two dragonflies hover above her head and two butterfly clips sit in her hair. Oil on canvas on masonite, about 61 by 47 cm.
context: Soon after finishing it in 1940, Kahlo gave this painting to the photographer Nickolas Muray, with whom she had had an affair that ended around the time of her divorce from Diego Rivera. The Harry Ransom Center in Austin acquired it in 1965 as part of Muray's collection of Mexican art, and catalogues it as 66.6. The Center counts it among the 55 self-portraits she painted in her lifetime and notes that scholars have offered political, cultural and religious readings of it. Common ones take the hummingbird as a love charm and the monkey as a stand-in for Rivera, though the black cat is left unexplained.
title_eng: Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird
feline_symbolism: The black cat is usually read as a sign of bad luck and death, a fitting neighbour for the dead hummingbird.
image_credit: Harry Ransom Center, The University of Texas at Austin (Acc. 66.6) · © Banco de México Diego Rivera Frida Kahlo Museums Trust / ARS, New York
rights_note: Copyrighted by Banco de México Diego Rivera Frida Kahlo Museums Trust / ARS, New York. Served directly by the holding institution (Harry Ransom Center, Acc. 66.6). Hotlinked; no local reproduction stored.

title: The Cat (Le Chat)
description: A bronze cat stands four-square on a slab base, tail cranked stiffly up behind, head turned to look out past us, ears pricked. About 55 cm from end to end, only 18 cm wide and 36 cm high, the proportions are all length, the body a long low bridge between the legs. The surface is lumpy and gouged, every push and scrape of the model kept, because lost-wax casting reproduces the wax or plaster closely, surface and all. Look at the edge of the base for the foundry's stamp, "CIRE PERDUE C. VALSUANI", lost wax, C. Valsuani, the Paris foundry that cast it.
context: Lost-wax casting keeps every thumbprint, so the cast bronze in Paris is a fair record of what Picasso did to the clay. The Musée national Picasso dates this cast to 1943, in the German occupation, and an older date range of 1941–1943 probably reflects the gap between modelling and casting, which the record does not spell out. It is catalogued as MP324 and entered the national collection in 1979 by dation, the French arrangement that lets heirs pay inheritance tax in works of art. Because Picasso's rights run until 2044, the museum's own record still marks this cat as a protected work.
image_credit: © Succession Picasso. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from popcorn-prd-perf-assets.s3.gra.io.cloud.ovh.net and is not stored on this site.

title: Lt Cdr R. H. Palmer Plays with Peebles, the Ship's Cat, on HMS Western Isles
title_original: Peebles, Ship's Cat of HMS Western Isles
artist: Ministry of Information Photo Division (official photographer)
description: Peebles, a shaggy black ship's cat, stands at the clasped hands of an officer who bends double on the deck of HMS Western Isles at Tobermory on the Isle of Mull, with water and low hills behind. The man is Lieutenant Commander R. H. Palmer of the Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve, in cap and braided sleeve, and the cat is in the middle of the frame, tucked against his arm. The IWM caption says Peebles was clever enough to shake hands with people entering the wardroom, and that here he is jumping through the hoop made by Palmer's arms. Black-and-white official photograph.
context: Cats were routine on Royal Navy ships, and the Ministry of Information Photo Division, the wartime unit that supplied images for press and propaganda, photographed this one at the Tobermory anti-submarine training base in 1944. The Imperial War Museum holds the print as D 20280, and the Commons file title places it in 1944. The comic part is the caption: Palmer is the hoop, not the photographer, and the cat is the performer. The picture sits among IWM's images of daily life afloat at Tobermory.
title_eng: Lt Cdr R. H. Palmer Plays with Peebles, the Ship's Cat, on HMS Western Isles
collection: Imperial War Museum, London (Ministry of Information Second World War Official Collection)
submovement: British Ministry of Information official photography
image_credit: Ministry of Information Photo Division photographer. Imperial War Museums, D 20280 (Crown copyright expired; public domain).

title: Girl with a Kitten (Kitty Garman)
license: © The Lucian Freud Archive, all rights reserved
description: Gripped by the neck, a tabby kitten dangles from Kitty Garman's fist, and it is hard to say which of the two looks more alarmed. Its pale green eyes echo her olive-green ones, and its striped body and white paws hang limp below her knuckles. Freud crops in close: her face and very large eyes take up much of the canvas, every strand of brown hair drawn with a fine brush and almost no showy handling. The picture is small, about 41 by 31 cm, so the hard focus feels concentrated rather than grand. Her gaze slides off to the right; the hand does the talking.
context: Eight portraits of Kitty Garman, Freud's first wife, date from 1947 to 1951, and this is the first, painted when he was 24 and shown the next month at the London Gallery in a two-man show with John Craxton. Stephen Freud, the painter's brother, owned it first; the collector Simon Sainsbury later owned it and bequeathed it to Tate in 2006, and it was accessioned in 2008 as T12617. The kitten earns its place in the title: Tate's catalogue and Art UK's essay both treat the animal's wary stare as a match for the sitter's own.
submovement: Early Lucian Freud: post-war British linear realism
feline_symbolism: Commentators read the clutched kitten as a mirror of the sitter's own wariness; Freud left no statement to that effect, so treat it as interpretation.
image_credit: © The Lucian Freud Archive. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from uploads6.wikiart.org and is not stored on this site.

title: Dalí Atomicus
license: © Philippe Halsman Archive / Magnum Photos, all rights reserved
description: Flying across the frame, three black cats hang in the air, one arching high above the water, two tumbling below in a tangle of legs and tails, while a sheet of water from a thrown bucket arcs past them and Salvador Dalí hangs in mid-jump, brush raised, moustache waxed upward. A chair floats at left, where an assistant's arm sneaks in at the very edge of the frame. Leda Atomica hangs at right on wires, with a step stool below it. The cats are real and so is the water. Look at the easel in the middle: its frame is empty, a window onto the bare studio wall.
context: Four on the count was when Dalí jumped: Philippe Halsman made the picture in his New York studio in 1948 with a 4x5 twin-lens camera of his own design, and on three, assistants (his wife Yvonne and daughter Irene among them) threw the cats and the water. MoMA's record says it took 28 tries, while other accounts say 26, over five or six hours, with Halsman developing between takes while the cats were caught and dried. Life magazine published it in 1948 together with some of the failed takes. Fun fact: the title nods to Dalí's Leda Atomica, which he had been working on since 1945 and which is itself about objects suspended without touching.
collection: Museum of Modern Art (MoMA), New York
submovement: Surrealist studio photography (Halsman and Dalí collaboration)
image_credit: © Philippe Halsman Archive. Photo: Library of Congress / MoMA. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from upload.wikimedia.org and is not stored on this site.
rights_note: Public domain in the United States due to non-renewal of original copyright registration (Library of Congress Prints & Photographs LC-H9- 09633); hotlinked for compliance in international jurisdictions where photographer copyright persists (Philippe Halsman d. 1979, life + 70).

title: Oscar, cat from the German battleship 'Bismarck'
title_original: Oscar, the Cat from the German Battleship Bismarck (Unsinkable Sam)
description: Black-and-white fur sits on a floating plank of wreckage with open sea around it, the cat glancing back over its shoulder with wide green eyes. This is a pastel, so the coat is built from soft dragged strokes of chalk rather than lines, and the white bib, white toes and black body stand out against teal water. Bare buff paper shows at the edges, and a curling wave rises in the foreground. The framed sheet measures 785 by 610 mm. The plank carries the story: it restages the moment the cat was supposedly fished out of the sea after the Bismarck went down.
context: Three sinkings are credited to this cat in the legend: the Bismarck in May 1941, then HMS Cossack in October and Ark Royal in November, hence the nickname Unsinkable Sam. Royal Museums Greenwich describes the sheet as a framed pastel of a black-and-white cat on floating wreckage, one of the survivors of a ship that lost all but 114 of about 2,200 crew, and credits it to the animal painter Georgina Shaw Baker (1860–1951). The Bismarck survivor story rests on thin evidence, and Wikipedia reports that historians doubt it, so the pastel is best read as a picture of a legend.
title_eng: Oscar, cat from the German battleship 'Bismarck'
image_credit: Georgina Shaw Baker · https://prints.rmg.co.uk/cdn/shop/products/T0772.jpg

title: The Cat (Le Chat)
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
license: © Succession Alberto Giacometti, all rights reserved
description: One straight line of bronze does for head, spine and tail, held up on four legs as thin as matchsticks: the cat is about 81 cm long and only about 14 cm deep, so seen end-on it almost disappears. The surface keeps the pinches and gouges of the plaster it was cast from, and the rough slab of a base is as lumpy as the animal. Look at the head, a small rounded wedge with a pricked ear, and at the tail, held level behind like a ruler while the legs bend mid-stride.
context: Giacometti showed the plaster of Le Chat at the Galerie Maeght in Paris in 1951, and bronzes followed in an edition. The Met dates its cast 1954 and received it in 1998 as part of the Jacques and Natasha Gelman Collection (accession 1999.363.24), where it is listed at 28.6 × 81.3 × 14 cm and weighs 23 lb. Other casts are in the Fondation Maeght and the Giacometti-Stiftung. The Met's rights line shows the work still under copyright, which is why the image here loads from the Fondation Giacometti instead of being stored.
feline_symbolism: Sotheby's reads the cat, like the companion Dog, as a stand-in for Giacometti himself; that is a cataloguer's interpretation.
image_credit: © Succession Alberto Giacometti. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from www.fondation-giacometti.fr and is not stored on this site.

title: Chat Malicieux (Mischievous Cat) Clip Brooch
license: © Van Cleef & Arpels, all rights reserved
description: Winking from a lapel, a cat has a body that is a single oval cabochon of black onyx, while the head, ears, tiny paws and big plumed tail are worked in textured yellow gold, every hair chased in. One eye is a cabochon emerald under a curved brow set with diamonds; the other is shut, a single gold slit. A ruby makes the nose, and fine gold wires fan out as whiskers. Examples run from about 3.3 cm for the petit model to about 5 cm for the large one, small enough to wear every day, which was the whole idea.
context: December 1953 is when Van Cleef & Arpels' own collection site dates the first sketch of this winking cat, and the name 'Chat malicieux' (mischievous cat) came later. It belongs to the firm's animal jewels, an iconography it had explored since the 1940s. Surviving examples are dated unevenly by the trade: Sotheby's gives one as stamped 1959, another house says circa 1955, and an Artcurial example is circa 1970, which says the design stayed in production for years. Fun fact: because the model was made across decades, a 'vintage' piece needs its date stamp checked before the label is trusted.
medium: 18-karat textured yellow gold, carved black onyx, cabochon emeralds, round diamonds, and ruby
collection: Van Cleef & Arpels Heritage Collection, Paris
image_credit: © Van Cleef & Arpels / Sotheby's. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from sothebys-md.brightspotcdn.com and is not stored on this site.

title: Sympathy (Simpatía / La rabia del gato)
collection: Colección Eduardo F. Costantini, Malba (Museo de Arte Latinoamericano de Buenos Aires)
license: © Estate of Remedios Varo, all rights reserved
description: Knocked-over glass, spilled water, and a cat in mid-twist on a red tablecloth: the liquid runs off the table edge and spreads across the floor into a puddle that becomes a small sea. Instead of scolding, the woman strokes the cat, and sparks leap from its orange fur, link up into a little electrical web and reach her hair, which bristles in the same flame-orange spikes. The cat's hind legs kick skyward. Varo painted it in oil on Masonite, about 96 by 85 cm, using decalcomania (paint pressed and lifted) for the watery surfaces. Look at the floor under the table: small orange tufts poke out beneath the woman's dress.
context: At Christie's New York in May 2019 this picture sold for about 3.1 million dollars, reportedly to Eduardo Costantini, founder of Malba in Buenos Aires, and Malba's own collection site now lists it as Colección Eduardo F. Costantini, on view at the museum. Varo painted it in Mexico City in 1955 and showed it that year in the group show 'Seis pintoras'. She described the scene herself: the cat causes chaos, and the caress sets off sparks that give the woman a permanent wave. The alternative title, La rabia del gato, translates as the cat's rage.
feline_symbolism: Christie's and the critic Nancy Vosburg read the cat as Varo's alter ego, noting how her own almond-eyed face resembles a cat's.
image_credit: © Estate of Remedios Varo. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from uploads4.wikiart.org and is not stored on this site.

title: The Whittington Stone Cat Monument
description: A stone cat sits on top of a weathered milestone, looking out over the traffic at the foot of Highgate Hill. Jonathan Kenworthy carved it in 1964 from Kellymount limestone; in daylight it now reads as a speckled grey, barely darker than the lichen-stained Portland stone tablet below. The shapes are smooth and simplified, a cat reduced to haunches, chest and ears, its head turned sharply over one shoulder towards the road. A ring of iron railings with scrollwork and spearhead finials, red paint flaking through the black, keeps the ensemble at arm's length. The faded inscription on one face retells the legend.
context: Third-year student Jonathan Kenworthy of the Royal Academy Schools carved the cat in Irish Kellymount limestone in 1964, according to his family, which makes the most photographed part of the monument the newest: it arrived 143 years after the 1821 tablet. The stone marks roughly where, in the legend, young Dick Whittington turned back after hearing Bow Bells promise he would be Lord Mayor. The real Richard Whittington (c. 1354–1423) was a mercer who served as mayor several times and left his money to charity; the cat belongs to the later story. Historic England lists the stone at Grade II (list entry 1298038).
medium: Kellymount limestone cat (1964) on Portland stone tablet (1821)
feline_symbolism: In the legend the cat is the source of Whittington's fortune.
image_credit: Felipe Tofani · https://www.flickr.com/photos/gastaum/53873083708/

title: Monument to Dr. Samuel Johnson's Cat Hodge
description: Hodge sits on top of a copy of Johnson's Dictionary, upright and self-satisfied, ears pricked, a small dark bronze silhouette against the red brick of Gough Square, with a pair of empty oyster shells beside him. The cat is life-size, and he looks across the square towards the house where his owner worked. The pale stone plinth carries his name in capitals above a black plaque with the line 'a very fine cat indeed'. Look into the oyster shells: visitors drop coins in them for luck, and on special occasions someone ties a pink ribbon of the kind used on barristers' briefs around a shell or around Hodge's neck.
context: Boswell's Life of Johnson (1791) supplies the oysters: Johnson bought them for Hodge himself, so that the servants would not come to resent the cat. Jon Bickley made the bronze statue, modelling it on his own cat, Thomas Henry, and it was unveiled in September 1997 by Sir Roger Cook, then Lord Mayor of London. It faces 17 Gough Square, where Samuel Johnson lived and compiled much of the Dictionary. The inscription flatters Hodge more than Johnson did: Boswell records him adding, 'but I have had cats whom I liked better than this'.
title_eng: Monument to Dr. Samuel Johnson's Cat Hodge
medium: Cast bronze figure on Portland stone pedestal with open oyster shells
collection: Gough Square, City of London, England
dimensions: Life-size cat figure (approx. 50 cm) on 110 cm stone plinth
submovement: British Contemporary Public Sculpture & Literary Commemoration
location: Gough Square, City of London, England
image_credit: ceridwen · From geograph.org.uk

title: Monument to the Cat of Kazan (Kot Kazansky)
license: © Estate of Igor Bashmakov, all rights reserved
description: Belly up and paws in the air, a very plump cat sprawls on a little cushioned bench under a canopy held by twisted columns, in the middle of a pedestrian street. The metal is toned dark, so the whole thing reads like oversized folk ironwork against the shopfronts of Bauman Street in Kazan. The cat's head is tipped back and its face is creased in what looks like deep contentment, one paw hooked over its chest. It is plainly too comfortable to move for anyone passing by.
context: Thirty Kazan cats are said to have been sent to St Petersburg by an imperial decree of 13 October 1745 under Empress Elizabeth, to catch mice in the unfinished Winter Palace; the Hermitage cats still live there. The Kazan sculptor Igor Bashmakov made the monument, installed in 2009 on Bauman Street at the corner of Musa Jalil Street. The 'Cat of Kazan' also comes from an eighteenth-century Russian lubok (popular woodcut print). Kazan has other cat monuments too, including one at the Raifa Monastery.
title_eng: Monument to the Cat of Kazan (Alabrys)
collection: Bauman Street, Kazan, Republic of Tatarstan, Russia
submovement: Contemporary Russian Public Sculpture & Urban Folklore
image_credit: © Estate of Igor Bashmakov. Photo: Vadim Indeikin, CC BY-SA 3.0. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from upload.wikimedia.org and is not stored on this site.

title: Bolognese
artist_dates: Contemporary collage artist and illustrator, based near Valencia, Spain
medium: Hand-cut paper collage (paper, glue and scissors)
image_credit: © Lola Dupré. Shown with credit and a link to the artist; images load from loladupre.com.
attribution: “Bolognese”, 2026, by Lola Dupré (loladupre.com). Hand-cut paper collage, 12 × 16 in (30.5 × 40.6 cm).

title: Ophelia
artist_dates: Contemporary collage artist and illustrator, based near Valencia, Spain
medium: Hand-cut paper collage (paper, glue and scissors)
image_credit: © Lola Dupré. Shown with credit and a link to the artist; images load from loladupre.com.

feline_symbolism: The cat next to Judas is read as a negative sign tied to the betrayal, though it also works as a simple observation of a cat waiting for scraps.
title: The Last Supper (Cenacolo di San Marco)
collection: Museo Nazionale di San Marco, Florence
location: Small refectory (Refettorio piccolo), Museo di San Marco, Florence
image_credit: Francesco Bini · Own work (Wikimedia Commons, Wiki Loves Monuments), CC BY-SA 4.0
description: On the patterned floor beside Judas's stool, a small grey cat sits bolt upright, exactly where scraps are most likely to fall. Judas sits on the near side of the table with his back to the viewer, holding the bread Christ gave him. Behind the long white table, with its embroidered cloth ends, the apostles sit two by two in calm conversation, John asleep against Christ. Above their heads the wall opens onto a garden of orange trees, cypresses and a palm, with birds in the sky and a peacock perched at the right. A Latin line runs along the back wall under the arches, taken from Christ's promise in Luke that they will eat and drink at his table in his kingdom.
context: Three Last Suppers by Ghirlandaio survive, and this is the last of them, reusing the Ognissanti layout of a table set into a real vaulted room. The Dominicans of San Marco commissioned it for the small refectory (refettorio piccolo), where guests of the convent rather than the friars ate. Domenico was busy and probably supplied only the design, leaving most of the painting to his brother Davide and his brother-in-law Sebastiano Mainardi. Italian scholarship reads the cat beside Judas two ways at once: a negative symbol, and a plain domestic touch, a cat waiting for food. Fun fact: a few years earlier Cosimo Rosselli had put a fighting cat and dog right by Judas in the Sistine Chapel, also in this catalogue.

feline_symbolism: The lion belongs to Jerome's legend, the beast he cured of a thorn; the sleeping cat is the domestic counterpart, a sign of the quiet of the scholar's study.
title: Saint Jerome in his Study
submovement: Venetian-period Early Renaissance oil painting (Antonello da Messina, Netherlandish-influenced)
image_credit: National Gallery, London (public-domain artwork), via Wikimedia Commons
description: Just left of two potted plants, on the front edge of the raised platform that holds Jerome's study, a small grey cat sleeps, so pale and tiny you could take it for a cushion. Jerome himself sits in his wooden cell in the middle of a huge Gothic hall, reading, his cardinal's hat put down on the bench beside him. Everything is laid out for slow looking: books and a jar on the shelves, a towel on a peg, a crucifix, sunny countryside through the windows. A partridge and a peacock stand on the stone ledge at the front, next to a brass bowl, and down the shadowy aisle at the right Jerome's lion pads towards us. So the picture has two felids, the saint's lion in the gloom and an ordinary house cat asleep in the light.
context: A doll's house is how the National Gallery describes the effect: a fictive stone wall pierced by a broad archway lets us peek into Jerome's study. Antonello made the panel in Venice in the 1470s (about 1475), most probably for an important patron he was keen to impress and delight. In 1529 it belonged to Antonio Pasqualino in Venice, and the Gallery bought it in 1894 after it had passed through the Baring collection. The partridge on the ledge stands for truth and the peacock for immortality. Fun fact: the Venetian writer Marcantonio Michiel, who saw it in Venice, described it in 1519 as a work by Jan van Eyck.

feline_symbolism: A cat carrying off prey inside the Garden of Eden hints that violence and appetite are already present before the Fall.
title: The Garden of Earthly Delights
image_credit: Museo del Prado high-resolution image (Prado in Google Earth), via Wikimedia Commons
description: Paradise is not safe for small animals. At the foot of the left wing, below God presenting a freshly made Eve to Adam, a spotted cat strolls off with a small dark creature hanging from its jaws, something with legs and a tail that looks more like a lizard than a mouse. Around it Eden is already slightly off: odd hybrid creatures, a bird-like thing reading a book in a dark pond, and in the background a lion tearing into its prey. The centre panel fills with naked people, giant fruit and birds, and the right wing is a night-time hell of musical instruments turned into instruments of torture. Closed, the wings show the world on the third day of Creation in grey.
context: No date, no title: the triptych is undated, and 'The Garden of Earthly Delights' is a modern name for it. Bosch is thought to have painted it in 's-Hertogenbosch between about 1490 and 1510, and it is usually read as a warning against the temptations of the flesh. The Eden wing is full of animals that would have been exotic to its first viewers, including a giraffe and an elephant, and Wikipedia's account singles out the cat with its lizard-like prey. The painting later belonged to Philip II of Spain, went to El Escorial, and has been in the Prado since 1939. Fun fact: even before the Fall, the predators in Bosch's Paradise are already at work.

title: Madonna of the Cat (Madonna della Gatta)
collection: Museo e Real Bosco di Capodimonte, Naples
image_credit: Sailko · Own work (Wikimedia Commons), CC BY-SA 3.0
description: Down in the lower right corner, a tabby-and-white cat crouches low in the shadow of the old woman's skirts and stares straight out of the picture, eyes glinting. Everyone else is busy with each other. Mary holds the Christ Child on her lap as he reaches towards the infant John the Baptist, who leans in from the left; beside her sits an elderly woman, usually named as St Elizabeth, chin on her hand. In front of them stand an empty wooden cradle with a cushion and a plate of food, and John's reed cross lies on the floor with its scroll trailing. It is a pyramid of figures straight out of Raphael's circle, and then that cat.
context: Vasari called it 'il quadro della gatta', the painting with the cat, when he saw it in Mantua in 1566, and the nickname stuck. Giulio Romano, Raphael's chief assistant, painted the panel in 1522–23, probably for Federico Gonzaga while still in Rome. By the late sixteenth century it belonged to Barbara Sanseverino in Parma; the Farnese took it into their collection in 1612, and it reached Naples around 1737 with Charles of Bourbon. Fun fact: the same cat is said to recur in Giulio's erotic painting The Lovers of 1524–25.

title: The Last Supper
image_credit: Sailko · Own work (Wikimedia Commons), CC BY 3.0
description: Peering into the picture, a white cat with a tabby head slips out from behind an apostle's bare leg at the bottom right corner. Under the table a dog lies curled asleep beside a metal basin and a glass carafe. Above them the supper is pure commotion: thirteen men crammed round a white cloth, John fast asleep with his head on his crossed arms, apostles leaning, gesturing, rubbing their faces, one with his chin in his hand. These are farmers and labourers with sunburnt faces and dirty feet, and what looks like a lamb's head lies on a platter at the centre of the table.
context: Battista Erizzo, a Venetian nobleman, commissioned the canvas in 1546, and the balance was paid in 1547 and early 1548, which is why the Galleria Borghese dates it to the late 1540s. By 1700 it was in the Borghese collection in Rome, and the Italian state bought it in 1902. The gallery notes how Bassano absorbed compositions by Raphael, Dürer and Leonardo while refusing to idealise the apostles; the sleeping John comes from Dürer's engraving of 1523. Fun fact: in 1993 the picture travelled to the Kimbell Art Museum in Fort Worth, home of Bassano's Supper at Emmaus.

title: The Feast in the House of Levi
title_eng: The Feast in the House of Levi
submovement: Venetian High Renaissance Monumental Decorative Painting
image_credit: Photograph by Oakenchips, light correction by Paolo Villa (Wikimedia Commons), public domain
tags: feast in the house of levi
description: Beside a seated dog on the chequered floor, in front of the central arch, a grey cat lies stretched in the shadow, easy to miss among the crowd. Neither animal pays any attention to Christ, who sits in the central arch above them. Veronese builds a palace for the party: three huge arches, columns, balustrades and staircases, with a pale dream of a city behind. Turbaned guests, halberdiers on the stairs, servants with flagons and a dwarf jester with a parrot fill the loggias, all of them busy with the feast and not with the sacrament.
context: A fire in 1571 destroyed Titian's Last Supper in the refectory of the Dominican convent of Santi Giovanni e Paolo in Venice, and Veronese's huge canvas was made to replace it. About three months after he finished it in 1573 the Holy Office summoned him, accusing him of heresy for the bleeding servant, the dwarf jester with a parrot and the German-style halberdiers. Rather than repaint, he changed the subject: an inscription now cites Luke 5, the feast Levi gave for Jesus. Fun fact: asked to justify the soldiers, Veronese reportedly defended a painter's freedom to add ornament, comparing it to the licence given to poets and madmen.

title: The Last Supper
collection: Basilica di San Giorgio Maggiore, Venice
location: Presbytery, Basilica di San Giorgio Maggiore, Venice
image_credit: Sailko · Own work (Wikimedia Commons), CC BY 3.0
description: Front paws on the rim, back legs braced, an orange cat has climbed the side of a wicker basket in the foreground and is peering in, one more servant raiding the kitchen. Nobody stops it: the woman bending beside it is busy with her own errand, and the dishes are all going the other way. Tintoretto turns the Last Supper into a dark, crowded hall, the table running away from us on a steep diagonal, Christ near the middle giving bread to an apostle in a burst of light. Above them a lamp throws out flame, and its smoke turns into a swarm of ghostly angels. Servants carry fruit and plates on the right, unaware that a sacrament is happening behind them.
context: San Marcuola (1547) and San Felice (1559) had each set the table straight across the picture, as Leonardo had. For this one, painted 1592–94 for Palladio's church of San Giorgio Maggiore, where it still hangs in the presbytery, Tintoretto swings the table into the depth of the room and lets the everyday and the miraculous share the same light. It is among his last works, since he died in 1594. Fun fact: the Benedictines of San Giorgio had commissioned Veronese's Wedding at Cana for their refectory in 1562, so the same monastery ended up with two famous banquets, each with a cat in the foreground.

title: Allegorical Female Figure with Music Book, Gamba and Cat
title_original: Allegorische Frauengestalt mit Liederbuch, Gambe und Katze
title_eng: Allegory with Music Book, Gamba and Cat (Music)
image_credit: Bayerische Staatsgemäldesammlungen – Alte Pinakothek München, CC BY-SA 4.0
description: Sitting at the woman's feet at the lower right, a large fluffy white cat is hunched up like a loaf with its eyes shut, either asleep or pointedly ignoring the music. She stands naked against a dark wood that opens to a pale sky, reading from a small black book held up in one hand while the other holds a viol by its neck, its body resting on the ground. Baldung paints her very simply, a long, pale, softly modelled figure on a tall narrow panel, with nothing to tell us what she means except the book, the instrument and the cat.
context: Nobody has solved this picture, and the Pinakothek says so plainly: its meaning remains unsolved to this day. The figure is presumed to be a personification from humanist thought, and proposals include Music and Prudence, the Temperaments, planetary deities, the Virtues, the Liberal Arts or a Christian reading. The museum pairs it with a companion panel of a woman with mirror and serpent, and says the two were probably part of a series; both came from the Electoral Gallery in Munich. Fun fact: the museum's own title lists the cat alongside the music book and the gamba, so this is one of the few cats in German painting that is officially part of an unsolved puzzle.

feline_symbolism: Here the cat stands for respectable, constant love, the girl’s faithfulness to the young man painted on the other side of the panel.
title: Girl Making a Garland (reverse of Portrait of a Young Man)
collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of J. Pierpont Morgan, 1917 (Open Access, CC0)
description: On the windowsill at the right, a white cat sits upright, its tail hanging down over the ledge, watching the girl at the next opening. She sits in a yellow dress, eyes lowered, working a garland of small blue flowers, her long hair loose and a pearl band round her head. Behind them is a dark wooden lattice, and a white scroll twists through the air above, lettered MIT VERGIS MEIN NIT PINT ICH, roughly 'with forget-me-nots I bind'. On the dark wall at the right sit a monogram of the letters AD and the date 1508. Turn the panel over and a young man looks out from the other side.
context: Forget-me-nots are the whole message here: the scroll says the girl binds her garland with them, a plea to be remembered. The panel is double-sided, with a Portrait of a Young Man on the front and this girl on the reverse (ca. 1508, oil on poplar, 17.8 × 14 cm). Hans Süss von Kulmbach, born around 1480, worked in Nuremberg and died there in 1522, and the Met's own Journal ran a 1992 article on this panel under the title 'The Bride and the Cat'. J. Pierpont Morgan gave it to the museum in 1917. Fun fact: the wall carries an AD monogram of the Dürer type, yet the Met catalogues the panel under Kulmbach.

title: Joseph Interpreting the Dreams of His Fellow Prisoners
title_original: Joseph legt de dromen van zijn medegevangenen uit
title_eng: Joseph Interpreting the Dreams of His Fellow Prisoners
artist: Master of the Story of Joseph
collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Harris Brisbane Dick Fund, 1953 (Open Access, CC0)
tags: master of the story of joseph
description: Paying no attention to the prophecy delivered over its head, a tabby cat curls on the chequered floor under the little round table, right by a prisoner's foot. Joseph, in a blue doublet and a red turban, points at the two men he shares a cell with: the butler, in red with striped hose, flinging up his hand, and the baker in brown, who has more reason to look worried. Their dreams float above them in two glowing circles, the baker carrying baskets on his head while birds peck at them, and the butler standing by a vine. It is a very comfortable prison, with a bed, a jug, bread rolls and a pewter plate, and an old man looking in through the arched doorway.
context: Genesis 40 supplies the plot: in Pharaoh's prison Joseph tells the butler he will be restored to office in three days, and the baker that in three days he will be hanged, and both things come true. The Met dates this round panel to about 1500 and gives it to the Master of the Story of Joseph, an anonymous Netherlandish painter named after the subject; it came with the Harris Brisbane Dick Fund in 1953 (53.168). Fun fact: the Met's own description points out the butler's fashionably striped hose and the grumpy cat curled at his feet, so the one creature in the room ignoring every omen is, officially, in a mood.

feline_symbolism: The emaciated cat that leaves a mouse alone is a visual joke on ruin: the household has fallen so low that even its cat has given up.
title: Sorgheloos ("Carefree") in Poverty
medium: Colorless glass, vitreous paint and silver stain
collection: The Cloisters, Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, The Cloisters Collection, 1999 (Open Access, CC0)
description: Stretched flat on the floor at the bottom left, all ribs and limp legs, a thin cat lies at the man's feet while a mouse sits nearby and nobody bothers to chase it, which is the clearest sign of how bad things have got. Sorgheloos, whose name means Carefree, sits on an upturned tub in a bare kitchen, warming himself at a fire of a few straws, with a pitiful dog sitting up by the wall. The shelves hold pots and a pan, a basket sits on top of the cupboard, and through the window Poverty herself is seen gathering more straw. The whole scene is painted in grey-brown line on clear glass, with silver stain giving the warm yellows of the tub, the fire and his cap.
context: Sorgheloos is the Netherlandish Everyman who spends everything and ends up with nothing, and roundels like this one followed him down the road in a series. The Met notes that his only companion here, besides a pitiable dog and cat, is Poverty, who gathers straw for his fire outside. The glass is colourless, painted with vitreous paint and silver stain, 22.5 cm across and dated 1510–20, and it entered the Cloisters Collection in 1999 (1999.243). Fun fact: in another roundel of the story, now in Toledo, Sorgheloos is shown with a companion called Lichte Fortune; by this scene the fair-weather friend has vanished, and Poverty has taken her place.

title: Girl with a Cat
collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Harris Brisbane Dick Fund, 1933 (Open Access, CC0)
description: Slung across a young woman's forearm, a big striped tabby fills the bottom of the print, one paw dangling as only a thoroughly relaxed cat can manage. She is shown half-length in profile, wrapped in a hood and a heavy cloak, looking down and away with a calm, rather serious face. Vermeyen builds everything from loose, quick, crisscrossing lines that suit soft fur and folds of cloth, and leaves the background as plain hatching, so only her profile and the cat compete for attention.
context: Jan with the Beard, or Barbalonga: Vermeyen collected nicknames for a beard said to have been a metre long. Beyond the whiskers he was a painter, printmaker and designer of woven wall hangings for the Habsburg regents Margaret of Austria and Mary of Hungary, and he travelled with Emperor Charles V on the 1535 campaign to take Tunis, later turning it into a famous set of designs for weavers. His etchings are rare, and this one, dated 1546, survives in very few impressions. The Met's came through the Harris Brisbane Dick Fund in 1933.

title: Study of a Sleeping Cat
culture: Flemish, active in Rome and Turin
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of Paul Jeromack, in honor of Robert Tuggle, 2013 (Open Access, CC0)
description: Alone on an otherwise empty sheet, a grey tabby is curled up with its chin tucked towards its front paws, eyes shut, one hind leg stretched out behind. The body is built from short parallel strokes of black chalk that follow the stripes along the flank, while the face is worked in softer, denser touches so it looks like it is breathing. There is no ground line, no furniture and no second figure, only a few stray marks below. At the bottom, an old hand has written "jean miel" in brown ink next to the number 101. The whole sheet measures just 8.3 × 9.6 cm, smaller than a postcard.
context: Bieco ('squint') and Honingh-Bie ('honey bee', a pun on Miele, honey): those are the two Bentvueghels nicknames recorded for Miel, who belonged in Rome to the Netherlandish artists' club whose members took names. The Met catalogues the drawing as attributed to him, a Flemish painter who worked in Rome from the 1630s until 1658, belonged to the Bamboccianti (Dutch and Flemish artists who made small pictures of Roman street life), and then served as court painter to Charles Emmanuel II of Savoy in Turin. In 1648 he became the first northern artist admitted to the Accademia di San Luca. The sheet came to the museum in 2013 as a gift of Paul Jeromack in honour of Robert Tuggle.

title: Pussy's Return
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Bequest of Adele S. Colgate, 1962 (Open Access, CC0)
description: A tabby mother cat strides along a gravel path towards the viewer, tail held high, yellow eyes fixed on something out of frame. Kittens bunch up at her heels, and another dashes down the path from the garden gate far behind. To the right a trellis is smothered in pink roses and vine leaves; in the distance stand a white clapboard house with a chimney and a tree-lined yard. The colour was laid on by hand over the lithograph, so the roses and the sunlit path are the brightest passages. The publisher’s imprint runs along the foot of the sheet.
context: A bookkeeper's career sits behind the firm's name. James Merritt Ives was hired in 1852 by Nathaniel Currier, on the recommendation of Currier's brother Charles, and became a partner in 1857, when N. Currier, Lithographer, turned into Currier & Ives. The Met dates this cat-family scene loosely to 1868–78 and holds it from the 1962 bequest of Adele S. Colgate. Fun fact: Ives came to the business as a bookkeeper, not an artist, and through a family tie: his wife Caroline was the sister-in-law of Charles Currier.

title: Lobster Sauce
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Bequest of Adele S. Colgate, 1962 (Open Access, CC0)
description: A fat striped tabby sprawls against a dark wooden wall, eyes bulging and teeth bared in a snarl, a forepaw hooked into the claw of a dark lobster that lies across its belly. A huge fish takes up the whole right side of the picture, its tail rising to the top edge and its head pointing at the viewer. On the left stand a glass pepper shaker and a small dish, and a horn-handled knife lies at the bottom corner. Almost everything is in grey and black, with colour kept for the cat’s open mouth. The title is lettered below, with the credit “Lith. & pub. by N. Currier”.
context: At 38 × 53.5 cm the image is roughly three times the area of the Currier & Ives kitten print Pussy's Return, which makes it a loud sheet for a shop wall. The Met dates it 1846–56, the years when Nathaniel Currier still worked under his own name, before James Merritt Ives joined as partner in 1857 and the firm became Currier & Ives. It came to the museum with the Adele S. Colgate bequest of 1962. Fun fact: the Met's subject tags for the print are simply cats, fish and lobsters, so the cat is the joke and the seafood is its audience.

title: Kitty in Clover
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Bequest of Adele S. Colgate, 1962 (Open Access, CC0)
description: A girl with long fair hair sits on a patterned floor with her knees drawn up, a small white kitten held against her cheek. Her eyes are closed and she is smiling. She wears a dress with a lace-trimmed hem and sleeves, and buttoned boots; an open alphabet book lies on the floor at her feet, with ABC legible on the page. The print is a toned monochrome lithograph (the Met’s record gives no hand-colouring), and the lettering beneath includes the firm’s printed copyright notice for 1872.
context: The lettering under the picture carries a copyright notice entered in 1872 'in the office of the Librarian of Congress at Washington', which dates the sheet precisely: after the 1870 revision of the law, copyright registration moved from local federal courts to the Library of Congress. Currier & Ives published sentimental child-and-pet subjects like this in large numbers in the 1870s. This sheet came to the Met in the Adele S. Colgate bequest of 1962. Fun fact: 'in clover' is an old idiom for living in comfortable luxury, so the title says the kitten has it made.

title: Three Black Cats in the Snow
title_eng: Three Black Cats in the Snow
title_original: Design for a heading for children's writing-paper
image_credit: © Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Drawing by Louis Wain (d. 1939); image loads from the V&A.
description: On a snowy ledge against a deep blue night, three black cats sit in a row, two turned inward as if mid-argument, the third showing us its back. Their tails curl into matching question marks and Wain has pricked the snow with grey paw prints. The cats are solid silhouettes, picked out with a few white lines for fur and a flash of yellow or green in the eyes. The painted panel is stuck to the top of a larger blank sheet, and a few stray paw prints wander down onto it, as if the cats had walked off the picture.
context: Children's writing-paper once opened with pictures like this: the V&A record calls it a design for a heading, drawn by Wain for Raphael Tuck & Sons Ltd and dated ca. 1920, within a range of 1915 to 1924. The drawing is signed 'Louis Wain', has a blue border, and is attached to a larger sheet, which is where a child's letter would have gone. It entered the museum in 1962 as E.30-1962, and the museum's dimensions come from its printed accessions register for that year.

title: Pussy Cat Pussy Cat
submovement: Studio still-life photography (Royal Photographic Society collection)
collection: Victoria and Albert Museum, London (Royal Photographic Society Collection)
image_credit: © Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Photograph by E. Heimann; rights not cleared, image loads from the V&A.
description: A coiled wire spring sits in a pool of light and throws a huge shadow on the wall behind it. The shadow is a cat: spiral body, a round face with a heart-shaped nose, whiskers and triangular ears. At lower right a tiny, real toy cat arches its back and stares up at its giant double. The print is signed in white ink at lower right. The V&A calls it a mounted black-and-white photograph of a cat figurine with the silhouette of a stylised cat behind.
context: A nursery-rhyme line gives the picture its title, and the V&A records that it was assigned by the photographer: "Pussy cat, pussy cat, where have you been?". The museum dates the bromide print to ca. 1957 (within 1952–1961) and holds it in the Royal Photographic Society Collection, acquired in 2024 with help from the National Lottery Heritage Fund and Art Fund. The record names only "E. Heimann" and notes a signature on the print, so nothing further about the maker is claimed here. The trick is simple lighting: from the side, a wire spring throws a giant cat on the wall, and the little toy cat has to face it.

title: Concentration
submovement: Pictorial portrait photography (Royal Photographic Society collection)
collection: Victoria and Albert Museum, London (Royal Photographic Society Collection)
image_credit: © Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Photograph by Oliver J. Berg; rights not cleared, image loads from the V&A.
description: Seated three-quarters on, a black cat turns its head down and to the left, one pale eye catching the light. The background is a smoky brown that the cat melts into; only the sheen along its back and shoulder, and a few whiskers, separate fur from dark. The print is soft and low in contrast, so the cat looks like a charcoal drawing as much as a photograph. The title, assigned by the photographer, names what the cat is doing.
context: Concentration is the title assigned by the photographer himself, according to the V&A record, which dates the mounted bromide print only "ca. early 20th century". The V&A gives no dates or biography for Oliver J. Berg, so the year 1925 here is just a sorting midpoint. The print belongs to the Royal Photographic Society Collection at the V&A, acquired with the generous assistance of the National Lottery Heritage Fund and Art Fund, and digitised with support from The William Brake Foundation. Fun fact: the accession number RPS.354-2023 dates the acquisition to 2023, and the V&A still lists the photographer simply as Berg, Oliver J.

title: Cat Spies on Birds near a Sleeping Dog
title_eng: Cat Spies on Birds near a Sleeping Dog
title_original: Kat bespiedt vogels bij een slapende hond
image_credit: Henriëtte Ronner · Rijksmuseum, Jonkheer P.A. van den Velden Bequest, The Hague
description: A big brown dog sleeps in his kennel with his chin and one paw hanging over the sill, chained to a stone. A few sparrows are feeding from the bowl of scraps right in front of him. Under the kennel floor, almost hidden, a black-and-white cat lies in the shadow with its head turned toward the birds, only its face and a paw showing at the left. The watercolour is signed 'Henriëtte Ronner' at lower right, and three living things share the picture without disturbing one another.
context: The record can't say when this was painted, only 1831–1892, so the catalogue sorts it at the midpoint, 1862. The sheet is a brush drawing in colours, 309 × 520 mm, from the Jonkheer P.A. van den Velden Bequest in The Hague, and its inventory number begins RP-T-1892, which suggests it was in the Rijksmuseum by 1892. Ronner (1821–1909), who spent her career in Brussels, became best known for her cats. Here the drama is the watching, not the pounce: the cat has not moved, and the dog has not woken up.

title: Inlay for a Plate in the Form of a Feline
title_eng: Inlay for a plate in the form of a feline
culture: Scythian-style, Iran (said to be from Ziwiye)
submovement: Iron Age Iran (Ziwiye Treasure), Scythian-style gold appliqué
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of Nasli Heeramaneck, 1964 (Open Access)
description: Barely bigger than a postage stamp, this gold feline lies flat on its belly, forelegs tucked under a heavy head, hindquarters curled into a round haunch. Its shoulder and thigh are marked out as raised, rounded fields, and the feet end in tight spirals like unrolled watch springs. A pair of ears and one large, ringed eye sit on a blunt, flattened face. The Met catalogues it only as a crouching feline and names no species, so we leave the leopard question open and enjoy the pose: compact, watchful, ready to spring from a thumb-sized perch.
context: Two plaques in the Met were probably once inlaid in a silver plate, now in the Iran National Museum, Tehran, whose fragments were first reported in 1949 and attributed to Ziwiye in the Zagros Mountains. The Met is frank about the shakiness of that label: many objects sold as Ziwiye cannot be tied to the site, and forgeries abound. Small gold plaques like this one were usually sewn onto clothing, so setting them into a vessel shows Scythian taste meeting the court style that later became Achaemenid Persian art, itself built from Assyrian, Babylonian and Urartian sources.

title: Kelermes Panther (Gold Shield Plaque)
submovement: Scythian Animal Style, Kuban gold (Kelermes kurgans)
collection: The State Hermitage Museum, St Petersburg
image_credit: Photo: Sailko, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
description: Gold, hammered out of one sheet, a panther leans down and forward with its head dropped almost to its forepaws, as if sniffing a trail. The back is a single sweeping curve from ear to haunch. The face is blunt, with a round inlaid eye and a flat ear shaped like a leaf. Behind the hind legs a broad band of tail sweeps down to the ground, packed with small crouching beasts of prey, so the tail is also a crowd. Its flat, open-backed outline suggests something meant to be fixed to another surface rather than held.
context: Iron scales were found round the gold panther at Kelermes, in the Kuban, according to Ellis Minns's survey Scythians and Greeks, which is a main reason it is read as a shield ornament. Scytho-Siberian animal style liked to exaggerate the ears, eyes, claws and nostrils of beasts of prey and to let body parts turn into other animals, so a tail made of smaller cats is par for the course. The Hermitage's Scythian collection page lists the panther among its Kuban gold of the 7th century BCE.
note_for_lead: Commons filename says 'kurgan chertomlyk' but object is the Kelermes panther (Hermitage). Hermitage digital-collection record page not retrievable (SSL error); source_url is Hermitage Scythian collection page that names the Kelermes Panther. Image 1555x744 (<1600). Verify inv. number if possible.

title: Ipuy and Wife Receive Offerings from Their Children (facsimile)
title_eng: Ipuy and Wife Receive Offerings from Their Children (substantially restored)
artist: Norman de Garis Davies (copyist of an unknown Deir el-Medina tomb painter)
culture: Ancient Egyptian (New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty); facsimile by the Met Egyptian Expedition
date_display: original ca. 1290–1224 BCE; Met facsimile acquired 1930
submovement: Ramesside Deir el-Medina Tomb Painting (TT217), preserved as a Met Egyptian Expedition facsimile
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, Rogers Fund, 1930 (Open Access, CC0)
description: Under the lady's chair, in the bottom left corner, a small spotted cat sits bolt upright and stares out of the picture. She is dressed for the occasion: the Met's 1983 book on its facsimiles says she wears a collar and a silver earring. Her kitten has found a better seat, up on the lap of the tomb owner, the sculptor Ipuy, who sits in the middle of the scene holding a flower. The couple on their tall chairs receive offerings from their children, one of whom carries a jar and wears a leopard-skin garment with the tail hanging down the front. The leopard here is only a costume; the cat and kitten are the living animals.
context: A pampered cat in a collar and a silver earring, with a cheeky kitten on its master's knee: that is how the Met's 1983 book on its facsimiles sums up this scene. The book adds that this copy, unlike all others in the collection, renders a badly damaged picture and was painted to look as it did when fresh. It also notes that tomb artists often placed a favoured pet beneath a chair, perhaps so that the deceased would feel at home. The original is in the tomb of the sculptor Ipuy (TT 217) at Deir el-Medina, about 1275 BCE.
feline_symbolism: A household pet placed under the chair, a convention of Theban tomb painting that kept familiar company with the dead.

title: Animals Seated under a Chair, Tomb of Anen (facsimile)
title_eng: Animals Seated under a Chair, Tomb of Anen
artist: Norman de Garis Davies (copyist of an unknown Theban tomb painter)
culture: Ancient Egyptian (New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty); facsimile by the Met Egyptian Expedition
submovement: Theban Eighteenth Dynasty Tomb Painting (TT120, reign of Amenhotep III), preserved as a Met Egyptian Expedition facsimile
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, Rogers Fund, 1930 (Open Access, CC0); image via Wikimedia Commons
description: Against a yellow ground, a big red-and-black tabby sits side-on between two striped chair legs, its long ringed tail dragging round the base on the left. Its forelegs are wrapped around a goose that has pushed its head up beside the cat's chest, and no one seems alarmed. Overhead a grey-green monkey leaps across the gap from one chair leg to the other, tail streaming. Flaking pigment has left pale blotches across the middle, including over the cat's face. The Met titles the sheet Animals Seated under a Chair and files it as a facsimile of a Theban tomb scene.
context: Wilkinson and Hill's 1983 book on the Met's facsimiles finds a joke in this very scene: a household cat, they write, might be shown eating a fish or even "embracing" a goose, while a monkey leaps over their heads. The Met catalogues the sheet as a full-size (1:1) tempera copy of a painting in Anen's tomb at Thebes, from the reign of Amenhotep III, acquired with the Rogers Fund in 1930. The book adds that Egyptian artists included such details when decorum allowed, but never so that they upstaged the main figures.
feline_symbolism: A household cat shown at ease beneath the chair, one of the domestic touches Theban painters allowed themselves.

title: Cat Figurine, Middle Kingdom
submovement: Middle Kingdom Faience Figurines of Desert Animals (Dynasty 12 burial equipment)
medium: Blue faience with black spots, paint
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, Purchase, Edward S. Harkness Gift, 1926 (Open Access, CC0)
description: Bright turquoise and barely longer than a matchbox, this cat creeps forward over a slab-like base with its head low and its front legs bent, as if it has just spotted something. Black glaze spots dot the back and the tail is held down behind. Its ears are pricked and the face is a flat little triangle with dark eyes. In the Met's photograph it shares the frame with a pale faience dog (left) from the same group of animal figurines, lying down with paws forward. The cat is the one on the right.
context: At about 4,000 years old, this is among the earliest cats in the catalogue, and the Met is careful about what it is: cats, it notes, were not yet fully domesticated in the Middle Kingdom. Faience figurines of wild animals had been left in temple precincts since the Early Dynastic Period, and in the Twelfth Dynasty they came back as burial equipment, with new species added. The Met's curators suggest that controlled images of desert animals may have assured the dead of safety. The Met lists the figure in a 2015 exhibition catalogue entry titled "Wildcat Stalking".
feline_symbolism: A stalking wildcat among the protective desert animals placed in Twelfth Dynasty burials.

title: Cat Coffin (Sycamore Fig)
culture: Ancient Egyptian (Late Period to Ptolemaic Period)
submovement: Late Period–Ptolemaic Carved Wooden Animal Coffins (temple votive offerings)
collection: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland
image_credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Gift of the John Huntington Art and Polytechnic Trust, 1914.806 (Open Access, CC0)
description: Carved in sycamore fig, a cat sits bolt upright facing us, front paws together, ears up and eyes open. The carver left the fur as fine parallel cuts across the chest and back, and the toes are marked out one by one on the big front paws. The tail curls round the base on the left. Photographed against a blue gradient, the wood glows orange-brown. It is only 20 cm tall, a coffin for a very small animal or its remains.
context: Wooden cat coffins like this were left in temples as offerings, and the Art Institute of Chicago explains the logic of a similar one: the mummified animal's soul was a messenger between worshippers and the gods, carrying requests about illness or wrongs done. Cleveland dates its example loosely, giving 664 to 30 BCE or 664 to 330 BCE, which shows how hard such pieces are to pin down without an excavation context. The cat form suggests an offering to Bastet, a goddess the Art Institute describes as revered for her motherly qualities.
feline_symbolism: A cat-shaped container for a votive animal mummy, presented to Bastet.

title: Arched Sistrum with Hathor Head and Cat
submovement: Thirtieth Dynasty Cult Rattles (Hathor-Bastet temple music)
collection: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland
image_credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Gift of the John Huntington Art and Polytechnic Trust, 1920.1990 (Open Access, CC0)
description: Look to the top of the handle, just above the woman's head, and a tiny cat sits upright on the little shrine-shaped block that carries the frame. Below it is the main face of the instrument, a woman with cow's ears and a heavy striped wig, who is the goddess Hathor, set on a plain handle. Above the cat, a narrow arch of bronze rises, with a crossbar that once held strung metal discs and now carries a few corroded stubs. Most of the sistrum's height is arch and handle; the cat is one small, easily missed detail.
context: A sistrum is a rattle, and Cleveland explains why this one carries a cat: the rustle of the metal discs was thought to soothe the nerves of goddesses, especially Hathor and Bastet, so the instrument is decorated with a Hathor head and with a cat, the image of Bastet. Women played them as members of temple choirs, in the museum's account. Cleveland dates it to the 30th Dynasty, 380 to 343 BCE.
feline_symbolism: The cat is the image of Bastet, placed on a rattle meant to soothe the goddess.

title: Mummified Cat
culture: Ancient Egyptian (Late Period to Ptolemaic Period)
image_credit: The Walters Art Museum, Baltimore, Gift of the heirs of Mrs. Frances Eaton Weld, 1947 (CC0); image via Wikimedia Commons
description: Wrapped from rounded head to tail in strips of pale linen, this cat is a slim bundle about 32 cm long, photographed upright against black. There is no painted face and no modelled ears, only a bulge at the top for the head and a tight collar of bandage below it. The linen runs in bands that change direction and thickness down the body, some patched where the cloth has thinned. The Walters says an X-ray shows the neck unbroken, the forelegs pressed to the body and the hind legs folded together, so the cat itself is there, but hidden.
context: Cat mummies went in the greatest numbers to Bastet at her cult centre, Bubastis, in the eastern Delta. The museum explains that since the Late Period the Egyptians gave animal mummies to the gods as gifts, and that the animals were bred near the temples for the purpose. Its curators also record a less dignified afterlife: some cat mummies were exported to Europe in the nineteenth century to be used as fertiliser. This one reached the Walters in 1947, a gift of the heirs of Mrs. Frances Eaton Weld.
feline_symbolism: A votive offering to Bastet, whose cult centre Bubastis received the largest number of cat mummies.

title: Base of a Funerary Kouros (Kerameikos Base) with Cat and Dog Fight
title_eng: Base of a Funerary Kouros with a Cat and Dog Set to Fight
submovement: Late Archaic Attic marble relief statue bases (Kerameikos cemetery, ca. 510 BCE)
medium: Pentelic marble, with traces of red ground paint
image_credit: Photo: Francesco Bini, 2023, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0. Object: National Archaeological Museum, Athens (Hellenic Ministry of Culture).
description: Two seated young men in long cloaks sit facing each other on stools, each holding a cord. On the left one has a dog on a lead; on the right the other has a cat, and the two animals are being pushed together for a scuffle. The cat is the small creature at bottom centre-right, between the stool legs, back arched and tail curled up behind it. Two standing onlookers lean in from the outer edges, one on each side. The red paint left in the background makes the pale marble figures read almost like a red-figure vase painting.
context: The block was found in 1922, built into the Themistoklean Wall at the Kerameikos, the fortification Athens raised right after the Persian invasion of 480 BCE out of whatever the nearby cemetery could spare.
