The Hellenic Ministry of Culture reads the scene as athletes at rest in the gymnasium while a dog and a cat are set against each other. The Cambridge cast catalogue adds a nice sideline: the wrestling side of the same base has one of the first foreshortened feet in Western art, so this one block holds a technical breakthrough and a very early pet scrap.

title: Marble Statue of a Panther
submovement: Hellenistic Greek marble animal statuary (Dionysiac panthers)
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Bequest of Nanette B. Kelekian, in honor of Joan R. Mertens, and in celebration of the Museum's 150th Anniversary, 2020. Open Access (CC0).
description: Long, low and stripped of its legs, a marble panther stands side-on with its head lifted and its ears pricked. The body is one smooth, stretched line from shoulder to hip, the neck rises at a steady slope, and the face looks straight ahead with a round eye and a short, blunt muzzle that has lost its surface. Look for what is missing: there is no mane, which helps tell a panther from a lion. The stone has gone cream and brown with age, and the Met shows it in three views.
context: Ninety-seven centimetres of marble came to the Met by bequest in 2020, given in honour of the curator Joan R. Mertens to mark the museum's 150th anniversary. The Met dates it only to the Hellenistic period, 323–31 BCE, and lists no findspot. Spotted cats of this kind belong to the retinue of Dionysos in Greek art, which may be why a sculptor bothered to carve an animal at this size. Here the spots are gone, but the animal's long, low line is still unmistakably cat.

title: Pair of Bronze Cista Feet with Panthers Attacking Cranes
title_eng: Pair of Bronze Cista (Toiletries Box) Feet with Panthers Attacking Cranes
submovement: Praenestine bronze cista fittings (Latium, Late Classical-Hellenistic)
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of Ernest Erickson Foundation, 1988. Open Access (CC0).
description: Each of these two small bronze feet ends in a clawed paw at the bottom, with a flat, fan-edged plate above it. On that plate a panther crouches and has a crane pinned beneath it, the bird's wings splayed out below the cat's body. The two feet are a matching pair, so the same predator, same victim and same fan-shaped frame appear twice, one on each. Only about eight centimetres high, they look like jewellery for furniture. The panther sits right at the top of each foot, curved over the bird.
context: A cista was a lidded toiletries box, and Praeneste (modern Palestrina), south-east of Rome, was the best-known place for making engraved bronze ones in the late fourth century BCE. These feet are the supports that kept such a box off the table, and the Met catalogues the pair as Praenestine, about 350–300 BCE, 8.3 cm high, a gift of the Ernest Erickson Foundation in 1988. Each foot ends in a clawed paw, which makes the whole box look like a small animal on the move. A panther on every foot means a box that looks fierce from the floor.

title: Terracotta Head of a Panther
submovement: Early Imperial Roman terracotta with Dionysiac grape motifs (1st century CE)
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Rogers Fund, 1912. Open Access (CC0).
description: A pale clay panther head, a little over twenty centimetres tall, snarls to the left with its lips drawn back from the jaw. The ears are pricked and the eye is a plain, wide-open almond. Folds of skin crease the cheek and bridge of the nose, and the whiskered muzzle swells out in front. Clusters of grapes sit above the ear and beside the neck, so this is a Dionysiac cat. Behind the head a broken fin of clay shows where it was once fixed to something larger.
context: Rogers Fund bought the head for the Met in 1912, and the Met files it as Early Imperial Roman, first century CE, 20.6 centimetres high. The grape clusters by the ear and neck tie the animal to Dionysos, who is often shown with panthers. What the head was fixed to is not stated in the open record, but the clay flange at the back shows it was never meant to stand alone.

title: Pair of Earrings with Heads of Lynxes
title_eng: Pair of Gold Earrings with Heads of Lynxes
submovement: Hellenistic Greek gold animal-head hoop earrings (4th–3rd century BCE)
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Purchase, 1898. Open Access (CC0).
description: Two gold hoops, each barely the size of a thumbnail, finish in a tiny cat head with a short snout and small ears. Fine wire is wound in tight bands along the curve of each hoop, tapering to a thin hook at the other end. The heads sit at the top of the pair, both facing to the left. At this scale the sculptor has given the animals a tilt of the skull and a rounded muzzle rather than fine detail, and the Met names them as lynxes.
context: Classical writers believed a lynx's urine hardened into a gemstone called lyngurium, a belief that, according to Wikipedia, lingered in medieval lapidaries until the seventeenth century. Even if the goldsmith never thought of that legend, a lynx on an ear is a neat joke about precious stones. The Met bought the pair in 1898 and dates them to the fourth or third century BCE. Each one is only about 2.5 centimetres long.

title: Black-Figure Band Skyphos (Drinking Cup): Sirens, Stags, and Panthers
title_eng: Black-Figure Band Skyphos with a Siren, Stags and Panthers
submovement: Attic black-figure Little-Master (band) cups, ca. 540 BCE
image_credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art. Open Access (CC0).
description: A drinking cup with a narrow painted band sits just under the rim, and that is all the decoration it needs. At the centre of the band on each side a siren spreads her wings and turns her head left. A grazing stag stands on either side of her, and then, at the outer ends of the frieze, a black panther faces inward. To find the cats, follow the band to the two ends beside the handles. Inside, the bowl is plain apart from one dot ringed by circles.
context: Collectors call cups like this Little-Master cups, after the fine, small-scale decoration, which the painter kept to a narrow frieze above the bend of the bowl. This one has no human drama at all, just a siren, stags and panthers in order, repeating on the other side. Cleveland dates it to about 540 BCE, lists it as a bequest of Maud Eells Corning, and gives its overall size as 13.1 by 29.9 centimetres. The panthers are small, but they are the animals that bracket every scene.

title: Pebble Mosaic of Dionysos Riding a Panther (House of Dionysos, Pella)
submovement: Macedonian pebble mosaic floors of Pella (House of Dionysos, late 4th century BCE)
image_credit: Photo: Carole Raddato, 2012, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0. Object: Archaeological Museum of Pella (Hellenic Ministry of Culture).
description: Spread across a dark pebble floor, a cream-coloured spotted cat stretches out with a young god perched side-saddle on its back. Dionysos holds up a staff trailing ribbons in one hand, and the ribbons flutter out above his head. The animal fills the lower and central part of the panel: long legs, a small head turned to the left, dark dots over the flanks and a tail that curls up behind. A border of larger, rounder pebbles frames the scene.
context: Pebbles, not cut tesserae, built this floor, which comes from the andron, the men's banquet hall, of Pella's House of Dionysos and dates to the late fourth century BCE. The Pella museum label calls the animal a panther, though the solid black spots and long legs would also suit a cheetah, so the species is open. Dionysos is a regular passenger on big cats in Greek art, which is why a spotted animal is not as odd in a banquet room as it first sounds.

title: Tomb of the Leopards, Tarquinia: Confronted Leopards above the Banquet
title_eng: Tomb of the Leopards (Tomba dei Leopardi)
submovement: Etruscan painted tombs of Tarquinia, Monterozzi necropolis (Late Archaic to Early Classical, ca. 470 BCE)
medium: Fresco (painted plaster on rock-cut tomb walls)
collection: Necropolis of Monterozzi, Tarquinia (Parco Archeologico di Cerveteri e Tarquinia)
image_credit: Photo: Sailko, 2017, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0. Monument: Necropolis of Monterozzi, Tarquinia (UNESCO World Heritage Site).
description: Two spotted leopards pace towards each other along the gable of a small rock-cut tomb, their heads meeting over a slender sprig of leaves. Dark dots cover their pale coats, and a thin red outline picks out ribs and legs. Beneath them, running across the wall below, wreathed banqueters recline on couches while servants wait on them. The leopards sit in the triangle of wall just under the painted chequered roof, directly above the feasters, so look up when you enter the chamber.
context: Leopards were not part of the Etruscan environment, so the painters probably took the image from Greek art, which in turn borrowed the hunting-leopard motif from Egypt, as Wikipedia summarises the scholarship. The Tarquinia visitor site dates the tomb to 473 BCE and says it was found in 1875, while Wikipedia gives 470–450 BCE. In the 1920s D. H. Lawrence called the walls "a dance of real delight". The chamber is only about 3.5 by 3.3 metres, so the leopards loom over the guests at close range.

title: Book of Hours, W.102: Blue Cat Beating a Cymbal (fol. 78v)
title_eng: Book of Hours (Walters W.102), fol. 78v: cat with a cymbal
submovement: English Gothic Book of Hours Marginalia (Late 13th-Century Drollery Cycle)
medium: Ink and pigments on medium-weight parchment
dimensions: Not given on the Walters object page
image_credit: The Walters Art Museum, Baltimore (CC0). Image loads from the Walters website.
description: Blue, striped and rather pleased with itself, a cat stands upright on its hind legs in the bottom right corner of the page and holds a small square instrument up in one paw. It is drumming, or clashing a cymbal, depending on whom you ask. The performance happens beneath the last line of a dense block of Latin prayers, with a few red-and-blue penwork tendrils wandering down the left margin. The cat has a scrap of green ground to stand on, which is about all the stage it gets, and its tail swings out behind it. The text above is far bigger than the cat.
context: Walters curators describe W.102 as a finely illuminated and iconographically rich English book of hours from the end of the thirteenth century, and say the margins of its Hours of Christ Crucified carry the funeral of Reynard the Fox. A museum-education blog places the cymbal-playing cat on this folio and dates it to about 1300. The main artist also worked on a Bible in the Bodleian (Auct. D.3.2) and a psalter at Trinity College, Cambridge (O.4.16). Nobody knows who the patron was: a woman prays in many initials, yet the Office of the Dead mentions "freres" (brothers).

title: Manuscript Leaf with the Pièta, from a Book of Hours (Cat with a Mouse in the Border)
title_eng: Manuscript Leaf with the Pietà, from a Book of Hours
title_original: Feuillet d'un livre d'heures avec la Pietà
submovement: North French Late Gothic Book of Hours Border Illumination (Bestiary Border)
medium: Tempera, ink, and shell gold on parchment
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. The Friedsam Collection, Bequest of Michael Friedsam, 1931 (Open Access)
description: Gold-ground borders crowd round a small Pietà, and in the right-hand border, about halfway down beside the Virgin's blue mantle, a grey cat lies on a green mound with a mouse clamped in its jaws. Its round head, pale muzzle and wide eyes look straight out at you, and its long tail trails off the mound. Owls, a wading bird and an elephant carrying a tower sit on the same strip above it, while a lion, a dog and wild men wrestle along the bottom. The cat is the neatest thing in the margin: it has finished its job and is waiting to be admired.
context: Barely 13 cm of parchment held all of this: the Met measures the illumination at 12.8 by 8.6 cm, which puts the cat at around a centimetre and a half long. The Met's own subject tags for the leaf list cats, dogs, owls, camels, elephants and lions, a bestiary in the margin of a prayer. This single page came to the museum in the 1931 bequest of Michael Friedsam, and its North French origin is dated only to the last quarter of the fifteenth century.

title: Ivory Pyx with the Triumph of Dionysos in India (Leopards Pulling the Chariot)
title_eng: Ivory Pyx with the Triumph of Dionysos in India
title_original: Πυξίς με τον θρίαμβο του Διονύσου στην Ινδία
submovement: Early Byzantine Ivory Carving (Justinianic Dionysiac Pyxis)
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. Gift of J. Pierpont Morgan, 1917 (Open Access)
description: Cut from a single section of elephant tusk, the drum-shaped box wraps a procession round its side. At the lower centre of the main face a spotted leopard, dotted with drilled holes, stretches flat out in a gallop, mouth open, hauling a chariot on a pair of straps. Another head shows behind it in the team, and a figure above them throws one arm up. The felines are carved in the same shallow relief as the figures but their bodies are the longest, smoothest lines on the box. Lion-like manes are absent, and the spots make them leopards, which the Met tags them as.
context: Dionysos riding in his chariot over his conquest of India is how the Met reads the scene, a story told by the fifth-century Egyptian poet Nonnos of Panopolis. Pyxides like this were cut from cross-sections of tusk: ancient owners kept valuables in them, and later Christians used some to hold the consecrated host. A Dionysiac subject on a box from the age of Justinian shows how long the old myths stayed in fashion. The catalogue gives a mid-500s date, a possible Syrian origin, and a note that it was said to have been found in Rome.

title: Northumberland Bestiary: Cats and a Mouse (Ms. 100, fol. 33r)
submovement: English Gothic Bestiary Illumination (Transitional First/Second Family Bestiary)
medium: Pen and ink, tinted drawings, body colour and translucent washes on parchment
collection: J. Paul Getty Museum, Los Angeles
image_credit: The J. Paul Getty Museum, Los Angeles, Ms. 100 (2007.16), fol. 33r. Digital image courtesy of the Getty's Open Content Program
description: Inside a ruled frame in the upper half of the leaf, two cats share the space. The one on the left sits up on its haunches like a small person and holds a limp brown mouse in both front paws. The other, a long pale cat with blue-grey shading and a tail that sweeps out behind it, prowls to the right with its head up. Just outside the frame, in the top right corner, another mouse leaps in the margin. Underneath, a brown mouse runs inside a big circle that grows out of a red-and-blue initial, so the page is a full cat-and-mouse set.
context: The mouse chapter of this bestiary draws on Isidore of Seville, one of the Isidore excerpts that make the Northumberland book a transitional case between the two main families of English bestiaries. The Getty dates the manuscript to about 1250 to 1260 and counts 74 parchment leaves, roughly 21 by 15.7 cm. From 1776 it stayed at Alnwick Castle until 1990, when Sotheby's sold it for £2.97 million, and the Getty acquired it in June 2007. Folio 33 is the mouser page, and the museum's own caption is a plain mouser with a mouse ready to pounce on another.

title: Feline Mortar and Pestle
culture: Peru, North Highlands, Pacopampa(?), Chavín style
image_credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, In memory of Mr. and Mrs. Henry Humphreys, gift of their daughter Helen, 1957.494. CC0 (Open Access).
description: Small enough for a palm, a stone feline stands on four stubby legs with its head turned straight at us, ears pricked and round eyes incised. Its back is hollowed into a shallow trough, ringed with a maze of incised steps and keys, and a fat cylindrical pestle lies along the top, carved with spirals and circles. More circles are scratched onto the flanks and legs. The cat is the whole object: the body is the bowl, the pestle is a kind of load it carries, and the grimly neat face gives away nothing about what was being ground.
context: Eleven centimetres is far too small for grinding maize, so Cleveland's curators propose that the set crushed pigments or plant hallucinogens used in rites aimed at spiritual insight. They suggest it may come from Pacopampa, a northern highland site where elites took on Chavín deities and worshipped them alongside local ones. In the museum's words, such small sculptures illustrate the appeal and the spread of Chavín religion, so a pocket-sized stone cat in the far north belongs to a very large story.
feline_symbolism: Chavín feline deity, linked to ritual power and altered states.

title: Ceremonial Mace (Club) Head: Feline (Jaguar?)
image_credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, In memory of Mr. and Mrs. Henry Humphreys, gift of their daughter Helen, 1949.469. CC0 (Open Access).
description: Mouth wide open, a speckled grey-and-pink stone feline snarls out of a block of rock no bigger than a loaf of bread. Bulging eyes sit under heavy brows, two round ears stand up behind them, and a stepped, squared-off frame runs around the muzzle like a visor over the teeth. The back of the head slopes into a smooth, rounded boss where the stone was meant to be mounted. Seen from the front, it looks half animal, half helmet, and fully prepared to bite.
context: Heads like this were probably slotted onto wooden shafts, and Cleveland lists the possible jobs: chiefly insignia, group emblems, ceremonial weapon heads, or all three at once. The wood has vanished, but the stone survived because these objects were eventually buried in elite graves. The museum's own title keeps a question mark after the word jaguar, and its text adds that a mace head of this kind with a bird may show a male curassow.
feline_symbolism: Jaguar as emblem of chiefly authority.

title: Vessel: Jaguar(?)
submovement: Pataky Polychrome Ceramics (Southern Nicoya, Costa Rica)
image_credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, James Albert and Mary Gardiner Ford Memorial Fund, 1969.108. CC0 (Open Access).
description: Tall as a bread bin and twice as lively, this pot turns into a jaguar standing on its hind legs. The head pokes from one shoulder with its mouth open and tongue showing, while a curved strap loops out beside it. The belly is a smooth orange swell, and the legs are covered with dense panels of dark patterning, ending in striped feet. A band of tiny figures runs around the neck. The animal is not painted onto the pot: the pot is the animal.
context: According to the museum, Pataky artists excelled at animals that join a modelled head to a flat, boldly patterned vessel chamber, which then doubles as the body. The meanings of these animals are, in the museum's words, unstudied, though it seems important that many strike human poses, since creatures mixing human and animal traits often carry mythic weight. The title keeps its question mark: the museum does not claim to know for sure that this is a jaguar.
feline_symbolism: Animal with human traits, possibly mythic.

title: Jaguar Bowl
image_credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Gift of Phyllis Sloane in memory of Rose White, 1998.87. CC0 (Open Access).
description: A bowl shaped as a jaguar crouching around its own rim perches on a flared red pedestal. The face leans over the front with a wide grin of teeth and a lolling tongue, a forepaw with spread claws on either side, and banded loops curling up at the sides. Below, the foot is incised with fine linear patterns over a dark red surface. Nothing about the beast looks relaxed, yet something about it also looks like it is enjoying itself.
context: "Comically fierce" is the museum's own phrase for this jaguar, and the probable origin it gives is the southern highlands of Colombia. The bowl is shaped as the animal crouching around its rim, set on a pedestal foot, and the record lists it as resist-painted earthenware dated 850 to 1500, a span of 650 years. In resist painting, a design is kept free of the surrounding colour so the base shows through. The fangs mean business and the grin does not agree.
feline_symbolism: Jaguar as powerful, comically ferocious guardian.

title: Feline
image_credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, In memory of Mr. and Mrs. Henry Humphreys, gift of their daughter Helen, 1960.264. CC0 (Open Access).
description: Like a doorstop with opinions, a stone feline sits bolt upright, facing front with its forelegs straight and its toes marked by short carved grooves. The head is round, with small ears set high, wide-open eyes and a muzzle that sits in a faint, almost amiable line. The reddish-brown stone is pitted and speckled all over, and the body is stripped down to a simple tall form rather than a naturalistic crouch. At about 23 centimetres, it is small enough for a table, serious enough for a shrine. The overall impression is of a cat that has been asked to hold still for a very long time and has agreed to, on its own terms.
context: Dealer John Wise of New York handled the piece in 1958, Cleveland's provenance shows, and it reached the museum in 1960 as a gift in memory of Mr. and Mrs. Henry Humphreys. The museum labels it simply "Feline", and so does this catalogue. For context, the Aztecs called the jaguar ocelotl and regarded it as king of the animals; their military had a class of ocelotl warriors who dressed like the animal. The record does not give the sculptor, workshop or findspot, which is typical for pieces that reached museums through the dealers of the 1950s.
feline_symbolism: Ocelotl, the jaguar as king of animals and emblem of warriors.

title: Crouching Feline
submovement: Wari Middle Horizon Lapidary Work (Peruvian highlands)
image_credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, In memory of Mr. and Mrs. Henry Humphreys, gift of their daughter Helen, 1955.58. CC0 (Open Access).
description: Barely the length of a finger, a pale stone feline sits on its haunches with two turquoise chips for eyes. Its mouth is open, with a hole through the throat and another bored through the body. The forepaws are folded on the knees with the claws incised as three short strokes each, and the tail runs down into a tapering point beneath, like a peg. The ears are pricked and the face is almost grinning.
context: Jewelry, not sculpture, is how Cleveland classifies it, and the culture line carries a question mark: Peru, Wari (?), 6th to 10th century. The stone and turquoise pieces measure 7 by 2.3 cm, and the holes bored through the throat and body look made for a cord, though the record does not say how it was worn. That is an inference, and the turquoise eyes are the sure thing: two small blue chips that make a pebble-sized animal look back at whoever holds it.
feline_symbolism: Feline as elite emblem of Middle Horizon Andean power.

title: Feline Pendant
culture: Isthmian Region, Panama–Costa Rica, Veraguas-Chiriquí style
image_credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Severance and Greta Millikin Purchase Fund, 2015.11. CC0 (Open Access).
description: Thumb-sized and rosy gold, a jaguar crouches with its front paws splayed flat and its tail thrown up behind. One round eye is ringed with a raised line, and the ears are laid back. Clamped crosswise in its fanged mouth is a rod-like limb with a knob at its end. Everything has been reduced to a few strong shapes, as in a cartoon, and the polished surface gives off a warm glow. Seen from the side, the gap between its bared teeth and that bar is the whole drama.
context: "A nasty precious" is how Cleveland describes the pendant: nasty because the jaguar holds a severed limb, probably human, in its fanged mouth, precious because of the polished gold. The museum credits the warm, rosy colour to copper in the alloy, and notes the cartoon-like essentials of the design. Cast goldwork of this kind was made across the isthmus connecting Panama and Costa Rica between the 11th and 16th centuries.
feline_symbolism: Predatory jaguar with severed limb; power over life and death.

title: Jaguar Pendant
image_credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Gift of Mr. and Mrs. James C. Gruener, 1990.163. CC0 (Open Access).
description: Lying along the ground like a cat on a warm floor, a small gold jaguar has its long tail swept up into a hook at the end. The head is lifted, crowned with a pointed ear and a toothy band along the muzzle, and the forelegs lie straight ahead. A pair of loops under the chest hold the whole animal as a pendant. The metal is smooth and gleaming apart from the beaded detail on the mouth. Despite the small size, the proportions are lean and long, closer to a stalking cat than a plump charm.
context: The pendant has a tidy ownership trail in Cleveland's records: it passed through Stendahl Art Galleries in Los Angeles, which sold it in 1965 to James C. and Florence C. Gruener of Cleveland. James Gruener (1903–1990) bequeathed it to the museum in 1990. The museum dates it broadly to 800–1500 and gives its style as Veraguas, after the western Panamanian province. Unlike the Veraguas-Chiriquí piece in this catalogue, this one carries no severed limb, just the animal at rest.
feline_symbolism: Jaguar as emblem of status and power in the Isthmo-Colombian area.

title: Feline Vessel
culture: Central Andes, North Coast, Moche people
submovement: Early Moche Darkware Ceramic Sculpture (North Coast of Peru)
image_credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, John L. Severance Fund, 2010.4. CC0 (Open Access).
description: Burnished to a dull gunmetal grey, a feline crouches with its forepaws stretched out in front and its hind legs flung flat behind, mouth open on fangs and lines of whiskers. Big round eyes and large ears give it an alert, slightly startled look. A looped stirrup spout rises from its back where a tail would be, and the claws are cut out one by one on every foot.
context: Kiln chemistry is the real subject. The museum calls this darkware vessel early Moche and says it shows the move from earlier North Coast cultures, which used smudge firing and pigment applied after firing, to Moche potters with higher-oxygen firing and slips applied before it. The record adds that the Moche were known for their fine animal representations, and it stops at the word feline, naming neither jaguar nor puma. Dated 200 to 850 CE, it measures 17 by 14 by 19.8 cm.
feline_symbolism: Feline as Moche symbol of power.

title: Male Feline-Shaped Container
submovement: Moche Cast Copper-Alloy Metalwork (North Coast of Peru)
image_credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund, 1973.164. CC0 (Open Access).
description: Ears flaring and lips pulled back from its teeth, a stocky reddish-brown feline stands on four short legs. Its body is a box with a hinged-looking lid across the back, and the sides are incised with wavy, interlocking lines. The tail curls round at the rear. Small holes pierce the sides of the box, and the cast metal has the grainy surface of old copper. Compared with the polished ceramic felines of the same coast, this one is gritty and blunt.
context: A label word most museums skip: male. Cleveland records this little animal as cast copper alloy, 7.7 by 10.2 cm, from the north coast of Peru in the Moche style, and dates it across seven centuries, 50 to 800 CE, so the date range is bigger than the object. The lid on the back means it opens, but the catalogue entry says nothing about what it held, and it calls the animal a feline rather than a jaguar. The ears, the bared teeth and the incised pelt carry the personality instead.
feline_symbolism: Feline as Moche symbol of power; container for something precious.

title: Jaguar Pendant
image_credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Gift of John Wise, 1953.273. CC0 (Open Access).
description: A slim bar of pale green jade, about the length of a hand, has been carved into a jaguar seen from the side. At the right end the snout juts out with its jaw and tooth line cut in short grooves, while curling scrolls and a ringed circle fill the long body. The edges are worn smooth and one end is slightly chipped, as if the stone had been handled for centuries. Read quickly, it is a swirl; read slowly, it is a cat.
context: Classic Maya times, 250–900 CE, is the span in Cleveland's record, which credits a gift from John Wise in 1953 and gives the jade bar's size as 4.4 by 12.6 centimetres. In many Mayan languages the jaguar was called balam or bolom, and it stood for the bravery and strength of warriors and the elite, while also being associated with the underworld. Jade, a stone prized across Mesoamerica, was a fitting material for such a status symbol. Cleveland does not say what the scrolls represent, so they are best taken as the carver's shorthand for the cat's body.
feline_symbolism: Balam, the Maya jaguar, symbol of warriors, rulers and the underworld.

image_credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art. The Cleveland Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0).
title: Feline Incense Burner
submovement: Seljuq Khurasan cast-bronze zoomorphic incense burners
medium: Copper alloy, cast, engraved, chased, and pierced
collection: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland
description: Two pointed ears, each capped with a small ball, rise above a wide-open mouth and a round, staring eye. The feline stands square on four stout legs, its neck and flanks worked into lacework, and a long tail curls up from the rump and ends in a flared tip. The head is a separate casting that lifts off, so hot coals and incense can be dropped into the hollow body. Bands of engraved Arabic circle the neck and run along the spine. The whole animal is filled with holes on purpose: perfumed smoke was meant to drift out through the pierced palmette pattern.
context: Which cat is it? The label says the beast may represent a caracal, a type of lynx, and adds that felines were favoured in Persian art. Animal-shaped vessels became popular in Iran in the 1000s and 1100s, especially as incense burners. The inscription quotes Qur'anic verses telling worshippers to set work aside, attend prayer, then disperse to seek God's bounty, and Cleveland suggests the drifting scented smoke may have worked as a sensory reminder of that teaching. So a cat-shaped object doubled as a gentle nudge toward the mosque.
feline_symbolism: Possibly a caracal; felines were favoured subjects in Persian art.

image_credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art. The Cleveland Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0).
title: A Woman with Two Children Encounters a Leopard (Tuti-nama, Thirtieth Night)
title_eng: A woman with two children, having abandoned her home, goes into the forest where she encounters a leopard
artist: Anonymous artist of the court of Akbar
submovement: Early Mughal manuscript painting under Akbar (Cleveland Tuti-nama atelier)
medium: Gum tempera, ink, and gold on paper
dimensions: Overall: 20.3 x 14 cm; painting only: 15.6 x 10.2 cm
collection: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland
description: Gold sky, pink cliffs and blue-grey boulders frame a family on the run: a woman in an orange blouse and patterned wrapped skirt, two small naked children clutching her hands, bottom left. Up on the pink ledge at upper right, the leopard has just crept into view. It is a pale, long-bodied animal with black rosettes and a tail that arcs over its back, and its head is lowered toward the group. A leafy bush and some flowering stones in front of it give the woman a little cover.
context: Her husband had beaten her, the Cleveland label explains, so the woman fled with her children into the wilderness. The leopard fancied a child for dinner, but she offered one child and half of her own body, claiming a lion had already staked a claim to the other half. Fearing the lion, the leopard bolted. The gold sky and pink-and-blue rock come from painting styles of north-western Iran, while the woman's dress, a tied blouse and wrapped skirt, is Indian: a blend typical of Akbar's early court workshop, according to the museum.
feline_symbolism: The leopard is a predator outwitted by a quick-thinking mother.

image_credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Dudley P. Allen Fund. The Cleveland Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0).
title: Antelope and Deer Hunt
submovement: Mughal Allahabad court painting for Prince Salim (Govardhan)
medium: Gum tempera and gold on paper
dimensions: Image: 20 x 11.8 cm; overall: 37 x 25.3 cm
collection: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland
credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Dudley P. Allen Fund
description: A hillside of green turf is full of fleeing animals: a ram, a blackbuck, a hare, a spotted deer with branching antlers, a pale doe. At the centre, a cheetah in a red collar has leapt on a dark antelope and has its jaws at the animal's throat, long spotted body stretched out and tail flicking behind. Two men with sticks drive game down from the rocks above, one in an olive coat at upper left, one in a plum robe at upper right. The signature, Govardhan, sits at lower right.
context: The cheetah catching the blackbuck, Cleveland points out, was a much-repeated image, and the hunt works as a metaphor in Persian literature, the protagonist finally getting what he wants. Here it may nod to Prince Salim, a keen hunter who set up a rival court in Allahabad between 1600 and 1605, defying his father Akbar and hoping for the throne. Salim lured some imperial artists away, among them the young Govardhan, who later rose to high rank under two emperors. The grey antelope in the foreground, Cleveland adds, is a nilgai, Asia's largest antelope.
feline_symbolism: The hunting cheetah as a metaphor for achieving a desired goal, per Cleveland.

image_credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund. The Cleveland Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0).
title: Lampas with Scenes of Wild Animals
title_eng: Lampas with scenes of wild animals
submovement: Safavid court silk lampas with animal combats
medium: Silk and gilt-metal thread: lampas, brocaded
collection: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland
credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund
description: Rows of gold and white animals fill a green silk ground, scattered among small flowers. The cheetahs are the spotted ones in the alternating rows, each with its body stretched across the back of a deer and its jaws at the neck. Between them, lions seize wild asses, so the pattern is really two kinds of hunt woven side by side. Deer and antelope bound in the gaps. The fragment is cut at a slant along one edge, which is why some rows end in half an animal.
context: Cheetahs in one row attack deer, while in the alternating row lions seize wild asses: Cleveland's label needs one sentence to describe the whole pattern. The piece is a lampas, a silk structure with extra gilt-metal threads brocaded in gold, dated to the late 1500s or early 1600s in Safavid Iran. Cheetahs were hunting partners at the Persian court: the Met's catalogue of a turquoise rider figure explains that specialist keepers trained them and carried them behind the saddle, so the woven chase would have read as a courtly scene.
feline_symbolism: Courtly hunting cheetahs as emblems of the royal chase.

license: Artwork public domain; image © Victoria and Albert Museum, London
image_credit: © Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from framemark.vam.ac.uk and is not stored on this site.
title: Akbar Hunts Blackbuck with Trained Cheetahs
title_eng: Akbar hunting black buck with trained cheetahs
submovement: Akbar's ketabkhana, illustrated Akbarnama (La'l and Sanwala)
medium: Opaque watercolour and gold on paper
description: Down a stony gully at the centre, a cheetah has pinned a dark blackbuck, its spotted body arched across the animal's back while other antelope scatter up the rocks at left. Akbar, upper right, reins in a dark red horse among riders and white horses. At the bottom a cart drawn by white oxen stands empty: the cheetah was released from it. A second cheetah, blindfolded and held by its keeper, waits among the horsemen at the upper right.
context: Cheetahs went to the hunt by cart and were blindfolded until the moment of release. The V&A reads this scene closely: the freed cheetah brings down a fully grown male blackbuck, the second cheetah waits blindfolded with its keeper, and the naturalist Divyabhanusinh identifies two other cheetahs as sub-adult males. The event is dated to 1572, but the painting was made about 1592 to 1595 for the Akbarnama. A Persian note beneath credits the composition to La'l and the painting to Kesav Khord, a different name from the V&A's Sanwala.
feline_symbolism: Trained hunting cheetah as an imperial status animal.

license: Artwork public domain; image © Victoria and Albert Museum, London
image_credit: © Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from framemark.vam.ac.uk and is not stored on this site.
title: Akbar Assists in Capturing a Cheetah
title_eng: Akbar assists in capturing a cheetah
submovement: Akbar's ketabkhana, illustrated Akbarnama (Tulsi and Narayan)
medium: Opaque watercolour and gold on paper
description: A crowd of men in turbans surges across a green hillside, and in the middle of them a spotted cheetah is being lifted out of a pit, legs in the air and its pale belly and long tail exposed. A second cheetah sits in a wooden cage at the right edge, and an empty cage stands behind the tree line at the top. Two Persian captions break into the picture, one across the upper right and one lower right, and dark pits yawn at the bottom corners.
context: Dug pits were the tool of choice. The V&A says the scene shows the first time Akbar watched cheetahs being captured so that they could be tamed and used in hunting. The historian Abu'l Fazl called their capture the most remarkable of all the arts of the hunt in Hindustan, since the animals had to be lured into specially dug pits without being injured. The illustrated manuscript was made in the royal ketabkhana, passed from Akbar to Jahangir and Shah Jahan, and was bought by the museum in 1896 from the widow of Major General John Clarke.
feline_symbolism: Cheetah capture as a prized skill of the royal hunt.

license: Artwork public domain; image © Victoria and Albert Museum, London
image_credit: © Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from framemark.vam.ac.uk and is not stored on this site.
title: Falconer with Companion and a Hunting Cheetah
title_eng: Falconer with companion (Small Clive Album, p. 74)
submovement: Jahangir-period Mughal album page (Small Clive Album)
medium: Opaque watercolour and gold, and probably silver, on paper
dimensions: Painting 22 x 11 cm; page 35.5 x 23.5 cm
description: Two men stand in a rocky meadow in front of a dark tree: a bearded elder in a yellow coat and a younger man in a mauve jama, who holds a grey peregrine on his glove and offers it a morsel. Seated between them, at ground level, a hunting cheetah looks back over its shoulder at the young falconer, spots drawn one by one on its pale coat. Golden hills and a streaky orange-to-blue sky rise behind, with domed buildings and two palms at right. The page is framed by a border of red poppies and pink lilies.
context: Thought to be a gift from the Nawab of Avadh to Lord Clive in 1765 to 1767, the Small Clive Album holds 56 leaves of Mughal paintings, drawings and flower studies, and this is page 74. The V&A points to the Persian-style dress and the Persian-looking modelling of the rocks and tree, set against the more usual Mughal streaky sky, and notes that the faces are painted so finely that individual hairs show. The album was sold from Powis Castle at Sotheby's in January 1956, and this page is a gift of John Goelet.
feline_symbolism: Hunting cheetah as a trained courtly companion.

license: Artwork public domain; image © Victoria and Albert Museum, London
image_credit: © Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from framemark.vam.ac.uk and is not stored on this site.
title: Princess Chasing a Cat That Has Stolen Her Parrot
title_eng: Princess chasing cat to save parrot
submovement: Late Mughal single-page genre painting, ca. 1740
medium: Opaque watercolour and gold on paper
description: Against a flat, dark ground under a thin strip of orange dusk, a woman in a pleated pink skirt, red-and-green choli and gauzy veil leans forward with one hand lifted, a thin cord trailing from the other. Ahead of her to the left, a long white cat with an orange-tipped tail bounds off across the grass with a green parrot gripped in its jaws. The chase runs left across an otherwise empty field, and the princess's orange slippers barely touch the ground.
context: Compare this with the V&A's Akbarnama cheetahs, painted a century and a half earlier for an emperor: the cat here is a household thief, not a royal hunting animal. The museum catalogues the scene simply as a princess chasing the cat that has run off with her pet parrot, and dates it, with a hedge, to about 1740 and probably Mughal. It was purchased with Art Fund support in 1955. The picture leaves the ending open, which for a parrot is the worrying part.
feline_symbolism: The pet cat as a household predator.

title: A Hunter Shoots a Leopard (Anwar-i Suhaili)
title_eng: A Hunter Shoots a Leopard; Illustration to the Anwar-i Suhaili
submovement: Illustrated Anwar-i Suhaili (Lights of Canopus) single-folio painting, India, ca. 1570 to 1575
medium: Opaque color and gold on paper
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: Howard Hodgkin Collection, Purchase, Florence and Herbert Irving Acquisitions and other funds, 2022. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. Open Access (CC0).
description: Pink crags and a green slope set the stage as the leopard lunges across the right half of the picture, its mouth open and its coat rosetted with black spots. Blood marks its side and muzzle where a hunter, drawing a blue bow at the far left, has hit it. In front of the leopard a pale animal lies torn and bleeding on the grass. Two lines of Persian text run over the rocks and a third is set into the foreground.
context: Provenance reads like a relay race. The Met's record traces this small folio to the Hon. Mountstuart Elphinstone in England around 1815, then Sotheby's in 1938 and 1986, when it went to the collector Howard Hodgkin, who held it until his death in 2017. His trust sold it to the museum in 2022, and it was shown in the 2024 exhibition Indian Skies: The Howard Hodgkin Collection of Indian Court Painting. The painting itself is 13.3 by 17.8 cm and shows a hunter shooting a leopard for an Anwar-i Suhaili manuscript.

title: Leopard Bearing the Lion's Order to Fellow Judges (Kalila wa Dimna)
title_eng: "Leopard Bearing Lion's Order to Fellow Judges", Folio 51 recto from a Kalila wa Dimna
culture: Indian (Gujarat), probably after an Egyptian original
submovement: Gujarat illustrated Kalila wa Dimna manuscript, second quarter of the 16th century
medium: Ink and opaque watercolor on paper
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Alice and Nasli Heeramaneck Collection, Gift of Alice Heeramaneck, 1981. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. Open Access (CC0).
description: Five lines of Arabic script sit above a garden of cartoon-bright blossoms. The leopard crouches at the left edge, pale grey with dark rosettes, one paw at the base of a tall cypress-like tree and its head turned toward the animals at the right. Three of them sit in a row, a dark-grey one, a red-orange one and a yellow one, all with upright ears, while a fourth peeks out behind them. Pomegranates, rosettes and swirling leaves fill every gap.
context: Dimna, the Iago of jackals, has lied his way into disaster, and here the leopard sits in judgment on him. The Met's essay tells it: Dimna turned the lion-king against the ox, the ox died, and the sorrowing king ordered a trial, which ends with the jackal condemned to starve. A hare turns away in disgust. The Met places this folio in Gujarat, probably based on an Egyptian original, and dates it to the second quarter of the 16th century; it came with the Heeramaneck gift of 1981.
feline_symbolism: The leopard as the lion's court official in animal-fable literature.

title: Mounted Hunter with Cheetah
submovement: Jazira or Iran, turquoise-glazed molded stonepaste figural vessels (Seljuq period)
medium: Stonepaste; molded in sections, glazed in transparent turquoise, underglaze-painted in black
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: Harris Brisbane Dick Fund, 1966. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. Open Access (CC0).
description: A rider in a tall pointed cap sits on a stocky horse, one arm raised with a mace and a shield slung on his back, the turquoise glaze pooled blue-green over his coat and the horse's trappings. The cheetah is the small crouching shape on the horse's rump behind him, tucked against the saddle. The horse stands on a rectangular base on four short legs. Pale clay shows through where the glaze has worn thin, and the figure is hollow, with an opening at the top of the rider's cap. His face is a plain molded profile with a heavy nose.
context: Armed for battle, yet the small cheetah behind him says hunter. That is the Met's reading of this figure: a mace in his right hand and a shield on his back, but a cat riding pillion. The catalogue entry explains that cheetahs, caracals and other wild felines were trained by specialist keepers (yuzdar) and carried on their masters' horses for hunting hares and gazelles. It also cites a Shahnama passage about a royal hunt with three hundred horsemen leading cheetahs. The figure was bought in 1966 through the Harris Brisbane Dick Fund.
feline_symbolism: The hunting cheetah as a rider's companion.

title: Picture of a Cat, a Bird, and a Crabapple
title_eng: Picture of a Cat, a Bird, and a Crabapple
submovement: Suzhou multicolour woodblock wall prints (Jiangnan, Kangxi–Yongzheng)
medium: Multicolour woodblock print; ink and colour on paper
collection: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland
image_credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund, 2025.60 (CC0)
description: Pink crabapple blossoms crowd a twisting branch, and a blue-crested bird with green and blue wings sits on it with its tail swept down to the left. The cat is at the bottom right, tucked among blue-washed rocks at the foot of the tree: a white cat patched with black and orange-yellow, crouched compactly, mouth open, looking up toward the bird. The colours are laid in flat areas, rust-red for the trunk, blue for the stone, green for the leaves, with the outlines holding everything in place. The cat is the smallest thing in the picture and the only one that seems to be paying attention.
context: A sheet like this was made to be pinned to a wall. Cleveland's note says that in the 1600s printing boomed in Jiangnan cities such as Nanjing, Suzhou, Hangzhou and Huizhou, moving from colour-printed illustrated books to single sheets hung in urban homes. Each colour came from its own carved block, so a print this tidy needed a whole set. The museum dates it loosely to the Kangxi or Yongzheng reign, 1662 to 1735, and acquired it in 2025 with the J. H. Wade Fund.

title: Black Cat and Narcissus
submovement: Late Qing flower-and-animal painting on hanging scrolls (Zhu Ling, active ca. 1820–1850)
medium: Hanging scroll; ink and colour on paper
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Rogers Fund, 1956 (Open Access, CC0)
description: Curled on a pale rock slope in the upper third of the tall scroll, a black cat with a white chest and bib turns its amber eyes straight out at us. Ink is laid thick for the fur and left bare for the bib. Below it a broad wash of pink-orange rock fills the middle, and at the foot a clump of narcissus with white, yellow-hearted flowers and long blue-green leaves grows among small stones. A twig of pink blossom enters from the right. The painter's inscription and seal sit top right, above the cat's head, so the writing hangs over the picture like a lid.
context: Three collectors' marks are recorded on this scroll, which is one way to read its history: an appraisal seal of Wang Weiyuan, a mark reading 'collection of the Song family of Shangqiu', and another reading 'treasured by the She family'. The Met's record gives the artist's inscription as 'Huanghua Daoren Ling painted this at Yuanpu, a traveller's lodging', so the cat was painted while Zhu Ling was away from home. The Met lists him as active around 1820 to 1850 and files the picture under the Qing dynasty; it came to the museum through the Rogers Fund in 1956.

title: Cat
submovement: Late Qing professional flower-and-animal painting on hanging scrolls (Wang Li)
medium: Hanging scroll; ink and colour on paper
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of Robert Hatfield Ellsworth, in memory of La Ferne Hatfield Ellsworth, 1986 (Open Access, CC0)
description: Seen from behind, a white cat sits on a grey-washed rock in the lower half of the scroll, its round back to us and its black head turned up and to the left with one yellow eye showing. A thick black tail swings down across the white flank and out over the rock's edge. Above the cat the paper is given over to dense columns of small calligraphy, ending in a red seal at the lower left of the text. The cat is a single pale mass held between black head and black tail, and everything else is rock and writing.
context: Seventeen columns of calligraphy fill the top of this scroll, and they read like a cat handbook. The Met's translation of the inscription ranks kittens by litter size ("if only one, it is a dragon; if two, they are tigers; if three, they are cats; and four, they are rats") and names a white cat with a black tail and spots on its head "the iron stick beating the cherries". That is close to the animal below: white body, black head, black tail. The Met catalogues the scroll as by Wang Li (1813 to 1879), undated, a gift of Robert Hatfield Ellsworth in 1986.

title: Treatise on Cats (Tamra Maew): two royal cats recommended for breeding
title_eng: Treatise on Cats (Tamra Maew), Or. 16797, f. 3v
artist: Anonymous Thai court painter and scribe
submovement: Central Thai concertina manuscript painting (samut khoi), Rattanakosin period
medium: Paper folding book (samut khoi), ink and colours
image_credit: The British Library, Or. 16797 f. 3v, via Wikimedia Commons (public domain)
description: Stacked one above the other, a pair of cats stand in profile, each on its own low wooden platform inside a scalloped cartouche. The upper cat is white with a black saddle across its back, black marks around the face and a raised tail, set against rose-red. The lower cat is dark grey with a white chest and white socks, glancing back over its shoulder against buff, its long tail trailing behind. Thai script runs beside each cat, describing the breed and what it will bring its owner. The British Library's caption calls this pair royal cats recommended for breeding.
context: Up to 100,000 tamlueng: that is the price the British Library's catalogue puts on a pair of very expensive royal cats in this manuscript, and near the end it lists an unlucky spirit cat with yellow eyes that would set the owner's house on fire. Cat treatises, called Tamra Maew, are said to go back to the Ayutthaya period (1351 to 1767), though the surviving copies all date from after the Burmese sack of 1767, and many were folded concertina-style. The Public Domain Review opens its feature with the Siamese cat Siam, sent to the White House in 1878, which did not survive long.

title: Lime Pot in the Shape of a Cat
title_eng: Lime Pot in the Shape of a Cat
submovement: Khmer Angkor-period glazed stoneware animal-form lime pots (Buriram kilns)
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Purchase, The Vincent Astor Foundation Gift, 2007 (Open Access, CC0)
description: A plump grey-green pot, just under nine centimetres tall, has been turned into a cat sitting upright. Two big round eyes with dark glazed pupils stare out above a nose and a wide, upturned incised smile, and two small pointed ears stand at the top. A band of incised lines runs around the neck like a collar, and short toes are cut into the base so the body appears to rest on its paws. The small opening for the lime paste is on top of the head, between the ears. The glaze is thin and pale, and gathers darker in the incised lines.
context: Filed plainly as a lime pot from Buriram Province, now in Thailand but then part of the Khmer Empire (802 to 1431), it is dated by the Met to the 11th or 12th century. For a pot that charming, the opening is tiny, just 2.5 cm across at the rim, on a base 5.4 cm wide and a body under nine centimetres tall, so it was clearly made to be handled. The Met bought it in 2007 with the Vincent Astor Foundation Gift.

title: Dreaming Cat
submovement: Early Edo monk-poet ink painting with kyōka (comic verse), Kyoto
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of Sue Cassidy Clark, in honor of John T. Carpenter, 2019 (Open Access, CC0)
description: A round striped cat sits tucked up, chin on its chest, eyes closed, a mound of grey brushwork with a ringed tail wrapped across its front and two stiff ears. It sits at the right of the sheet, and almost all of the rest is left bare. At the left, a column of cursive script carries a comic poem and the signature of the painter, who called himself 'Old Man of Jeweled Clouds'. Dark outlines and paler washes inside them make the body look fluffed out and heavy at once.
context: Zhuangzi once dreamed he was a butterfly. The Met reads this cat as a joke on that story: instead of showing the philosopher slumped asleep, as other Japanese artists did, Shinkai painted a rotund sleeping cat. The poem hinges on the word fukami-gusa, read first as part of 'fast asleep' and then as an old name for peonies, so the verse quietly conjures peonies and butterflies. Shinkai was a Buddhist monk of the early Edo period who, the Met says, studied tea with Kobori Enshu and comic verse with Matsunaga Teitoku. The scroll is cited in the Japan Society's 2015 catalogue List of Cats.

title: Cat with Poems: Pictorial Parody of Priest Saigyō's Legend
title_eng: Cat with Poems: Pictorial Parody of Priest Saigyō's Legend
medium: Hanging scroll; ink and colour on paper
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Rogers Fund, 1971 (Open Access, CC0)
description: Huge brush-written characters run down the middle of a tall scroll, with columns of smaller poems scattered to either side, and at the very bottom left a striped cat sits looking out to the left. Its body is pale with soft orange-brown stripes along the back and a banded tail that curls out behind it. The cat is tiny next to the lettering, but the bold writing leans over it. The painter signed at the bottom left corner, beside the cat, so artist and animal share the same corner.
context: "Everything human is Saigyo's horse." The Met records that the large inscription varies that saying, attached to the twelfth-century priest-poet Saigyo, and that here the horse has become a cat: "Everything human is Saigyo's cat". That swap is the parody in the title. The painter, Matsumura Goshun (1752 to 1811), signed and sealed at the bottom left, right beside the cat. The Met bought the scroll in 1971 through the Rogers Fund from the New York dealer Roland Koscherak.

title: Tiger (Leopard) on Display (Nishi Ryōgoku ni oite kōgyō)
title_eng: On Display in West Ryōgoku: a Leopard
submovement: Late Edo / Bakumatsu sensational-news woodblock print (Yoshitoyo, Utagawa school)
medium: Woodblock print (nishiki-e); ink and colour on paper
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Bequest of William S. Lieberman, 2005 (Open Access, CC0)
description: A spotted leopard rears up inside a cage of black lattice and red posts, mouth open, one forepaw raised and its long tail whipping up the right-hand side. A rooster flaps at the top left, and another lies at the bottom among its scattered feathers. A blue-edged panel at the top right carries a printed inscription. The coat is printed as rings of dark rosettes on yellow, the claws drawn out like hooks. The big cat takes up almost the whole sheet, so the cage looks too small for it.
context: Japanese customs officials reportedly refused to pass the first tigers imported after Yokohama opened in 1859 because they were not on the import list, until the Dutch consul suggested simply letting one loose. So says the minister Rutherford Alcock, quoted by the MIT Visualizing Cultures entry on this very sheet, which reads Yoshitoyo's picture as a leopard attacking a rooster, more ferocious than other Ryogoku portraits of the exhibited animal. Kanagaki Robun's inscription on it says the tiger and leopard roar so that rooftiles shake. The Met titles it Tiger (Leopard) on Display.

title: Cat Seen from Behind
submovement: Meiji Maruyama-school naturalist painting (Kawabata Gyokushō, Tokyo)
medium: Album leaf; ink and colour on silk
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Charles Stewart Smith Collection, Gift of Mrs. Charles Stewart Smith, Charles Stewart Smith Jr., and Howard Caswell Smith, in memory of Charles Stewart Smith, 1914 (Open Access, CC0)
description: Turning its head over one shoulder so that only a black face with long whiskers shows, a grey cat sits with its back to us, wearing a pink ribbon tied in a bow at the neck. Two big ears, one black and one grey, stick out. The body is a soft grey wash that fades to white at the belly, and the tail curls up at lower right. One white front paw is drawn with a sharp stroke. The signature and a red seal are at the upper right, in the blank silk. Nothing else is in the picture.
context: Nine Lives was the title of a 1949 exhibition of the cat in history and art at the Cooper Union Museum in New York, and the Met's record lists this leaf in it. The Met dates the leaf to about 1887 to 1892 and files it in the Charles Stewart Smith Collection, given in 1914 in memory of Smith, who had died in 1909. Its maker, Kawabata Gyokusho (1842 to 1913), trained under Nakajima Raisho, a Maruyama-school painter. The bow shows the cat was someone's pet, painted as a household animal.

title: Dead Leopard
submovement: Colonial India albumen photography (big-game hunt trophy photograph)
collection: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland
image_credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Purchase from the Karl B. Goldfield Trust, 2018.224 (CC0)
description: An adult leopard lies on its side across the centre of an oval-masked photograph, its head at the right, its spotted flank facing the lens and its long tail stretched out to the left. It has been laid on a bed of dry grass and leaves in front of a dark tangle of bamboo-like foliage. Every rosette on the coat is sharp, and the face is turned half toward the camera. The oval vignette gives the print the look of a portrait, and the leopard is its only sitter. It sits on a mounted sheet of cream paper.
context: Vulnerable today, the Indian leopard was no one's conservation worry when this print was made: Cleveland notes that nineteenth-century hunters would not have fretted about sustaining its population. The museum's label says the trophy has been laid out so that its sharp teeth and long tail show, and that elaborate big-game hunts were a prestigious pastime for Indians and colonials under the British Raj. The photographer is unknown, and the albumen print is dated to the 1880s or 1890s.

title: Letter H from Il Perfetto Scrittore, with putti, cats and dogs
title_eng: Letter H from Il Perfetto Scrittore
title_original: Lettera H, da Il Perfetto Scrittore
artist: Andrea Marelli (engraver), after Giovanni Francesco Cresci
submovement: Roman Mannerist Ornament Printmaking (Cresci writing-book alphabets)
image_credit: Victoria and Albert Museum, London (E.2718-1910). Sixteenth-century print in the public domain.
description: Both lower corners of this framed capital H hold the same little drama. At bottom left, a large cat sits upright on a scroll bracket while a second, smaller cat tangles with a plump curly-haired putto. At bottom right, a putto lies on his belly holding a small cat up on its hind legs, claws raised, to bait a heavy dog on the opposite scroll. The letter itself is a knotted, rope-like capital, flanked by bearded satyr-herms and capped by two flying putti. Look low: the animals sit right on the bottom edge of the frame.
context: A knot alphabet is not the usual place to look for cats, yet this engraved H comes from one. Andrea Marelli cut the plates for Giovanni Francesco Cresci's Il Perfetto Scrittore (Rome, 1570), and the V&A says this is one of 21 plates from a suite of 23 in the book's second part. Its catalogue describes the border plainly: a letter H in a strapwork border with a satyr-herm on each side, and a putto holding a cat to bait a dog in each lower corner. Writing-masters sold lessons in handwriting; the engraver supplied the fun for the margins.

title: Supper at Emmaus
title_eng: Supper at Emmaus (The Pilgrims of Emmaus)
image_credit: Musée du Louvre, Paris (INV 146). Photograph of a public-domain painting via Wikimedia Commons.
description: Two small girls in gold-patterned silk sit on the pavement at the bottom of the canvas, hugging a large brown spaniel between them. The cat is easy to miss, down in the lower centre-right: a small dark grey cat with a red collar, tucked into the shadow behind the girls' skirts, just left of a kneeling boy in black who holds a little white dog. Above this corner, Christ breaks bread at a white-clothed table under a pedimented doorway, while a Venetian family in silks and velvets crowds in from the right. Four great columns stand behind the whole scene.
context: Contemporary Venetians stand around the miracle as if sitting for a group portrait, which makes the Gospel supper feel like a very grand dinner party. The Louvre gives the canvas as 242 by 416 cm, inventory INV 146, and its provenance starts with Victor Amadeus I of Savoy, listed in his Turin inventory of 1635, before the picture passed to Marshal Créquy and then to Louis XIII. Wikipedia adds that two copies of the children with the dogs, one of the girls and one of the boys, hang in the museum at Dijon, acquired in 1799. The cat stayed behind in the shadows of the original, collared and unbothered.

title: The Annunciation (etching)
submovement: Urbino Late Renaissance Etching and Engraving (Barocci)
image_credit: Art Institute of Chicago, The Joseph Brooks Fair Collection (1942.528). CC0 public domain designation.
description: Head on a cushion and one paw tucked under its chin, a cat sleeps curled up in the bottom left corner while the archangel Gabriel and the Virgin have their great exchange a few feet away. The cat is drawn with short, nervous strokes that make its fur look rough against the smooth sweep of the angel's robe. The Virgin kneels with her hands raised, a lily in the angel's grip, and through the window behind them runs a view of a hill town with towers. Heavy curtains hang above.
context: Only one etching by Barocci survives, and this is it. The Art Institute calls it his most famous print and says the plate reproduces the altarpiece commissioned by the Duke of Urbino for the basilica at Loreto, painted between 1582 and 1584. Barocci published the plate himself, and it was found in his studio when he died. In the eighteenth century it entered the Calcografia in Rome, which kept the popular image in circulation. The plate measures 43.8 by 31.1 cm, a generous stage for a cat the size of a thumb.

title: Madonna and Child with a Cat
title_eng: Madonna and Child with a Cat
title_original: Madonna col Bambino e un gatto
artist: Master of the Pala Sforzesca (attributed to, or circle)
submovement: Milanese Late Quattrocento Devotional Painting (Pala Sforzesca circle)
image_credit: Walters Art Museum, Baltimore (37.455), acquired by Henry Walters, 1913. Photograph supplied by the museum to Wikimedia Commons; the painting is in the public domain.
description: Down on the patterned carpet, almost touching the Christ Child's bare foot, a small grey cat in a red collar sits on the patterned carpet at the bottom left corner. A loose red thread is looped around the foot, and the cat reaches a paw toward it, playing the oldest game there is. Mary's long left hand rests on the cat's back as she looks down at her son, who sits on a white cushion with a puzzled, knitted brow. Behind them a river town with towers and a Roman arch fills the landscape. The Virgin's mantle carries the words GRACIA PLENA along its edge.
context: Leonardo's Madonna of the Cat drawings, from about 1478, are the touchstone. The art historian Ilse Friesen notes that other artists put cats in Holy Family scenes, but Leonardo placed the animal unusually close to the figures' heart, a liberty church authorities might have judged harshly, since in fifteenth-century Italy cats were linked with the devil and witchcraft. Here a Milanese follower puts the cat just as close, at Mary's hand and the Child's foot, wearing a thin red collar and batting at a loose red thread.

title: Candelabra grotesque with four children with a cat and a dog
title_eng: Candelabra grotesque with four children, a cat and a dog
title_original: Candelabro grottesco con quattro fanciulli, un gatto e un cane
submovement: Italian Renaissance candelabra grotesque ornament engraving, ca. 1490 to 1515
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, Harris Brisbane Dick Fund, 1923 (23.39.9). Open Access, CC0.
description: Four naked children crowd round a stone basin at the very bottom of this tall, thin engraving. The cat sits upright at the lower left, bushy tail trailing on the ground, with both forepaws raised to the handle of a cup that a child, seen from behind, is holding out over the basin. Another child blows into a pipe beside the cat. On the right a long-bodied dog stands on its hind legs next to a coiled snake. Above them the panel climbs in a stack of urns, foliage and a mask-faced bust, with two more children at the top.
context: Two museums, two names. The Met gives this tall strip to Giovanni Antonio da Brescia and lists it as one of twelve candelabra grotesques, dated 1490 to 1515. The V&A holds the same design as plate 9 of a set of twelve ornamental panels, gives the name Giovanni Pietro da Birago as engraver and designer with Brescia in its short title, and dates it about 1505 to 1507. Its description is blunt: an ornamental panel with four children, a cat and a dog. Both museums agree on who is in the basin corner.

title: Studies of a Gentian, Moth, Birds, Cats, Interlacing Motif, and Greek Frets
title_eng: Studies of a Gentian, Moth, Birds, Cats, Interlacing Motif, and Greek Frets
title_original: Studi di genziana, falena, uccelli, gatti, intreccio e greche
submovement: Sienese Mannerist Decorative Draftsmanship (Belcaro grotesque circle)
medium: Pen and two colors of brown ink, brush and watercolor over leadpoint or black chalk (recto); pen and light brown ink over leadpoint or black chalk (verso)
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, Purchase, Gift from the family of Howard J. Barnet, in his memory, 2001 (2001.451a, b). Open Access, CC0.
description: Sharing the right half of the sheet with a big death's-head hawk moth, a pair of cats sit low: a front-facing head in pale brown ink, whiskers fanned out and eyes level with the viewer, and a full cat in profile with ears up and tail curling beneath it. More small heads are sketched in outline above them. The moth itself is black and orange and spreads across the middle, among a purple gentian, a blue-green bird, a brown bird, a chick, a Greek key and a braid of interlace.
context: Model-book pages were a working designer's stock of motifs. The Met says the range of delicately drawn animals, insects and ornaments suggests this sheet was once part of a sketchbook or model book, and ties the imagery to the artist's fresco cycle at the Villa Belcaro near Siena, painted 1530 to 1540. It singles out the lively pen line of the two cats and the little strutting barnyard fowl, and the moth, a death's-head hawk moth, drawn and painted with striking naturalism. The sheet could be raided for a frieze.

title: De Humana Physiognomonia: a boy and a cat (pp. 88–89)
title_eng: On Human Physiognomy: a boy and a cat
submovement: Neapolitan Late Renaissance Natural Philosophy Illustrated Book (Della Porta)
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, Harris Brisbane Dick Fund, 1937 (37.36.2). Open Access, CC0.
description: Two plates share this open spread. At left, below a bald old man facing a long-eared ass, a small oblong plate pairs a curly-haired boy with a cat. The boy looks straight out with a narrow, small-featured face; the cat, drawn in the same size, has its ears pricked and its whiskers splayed. The printed line above the plate reads "Hac tabula felis, & parvae faciei detegitur imago", roughly: this plate shows the cat and the image of a small face. On the facing page a monkey sits beside a man with a lined, bony face.
context: Character, Della Porta argued, shows up in how a face resembles an animal's, so his book lines human heads up with beasts. The Linda Hall Library lists greyhounds, bulls, monkeys, cats, asses and lions among the comparisons. Here the caption names the small face, and the boy's narrow, small-featured head is matched with a cat's. The Met holds the 1586 edition published by Giuseppe Cacchi (accession 37.36.2), where each plate measures only 8.9 by 14.9 cm. The cat was never asked what it thought of the comparison.

title: The Kitchen
submovement: Cremonese Late Renaissance Kitchen and Market Genre Painting (Campi)
image_credit: Photograph by Francesco Bini (Wikimedia Commons, 2014, CC BY-SA 4.0) of a painting in the Pinacoteca di Brera, Milan (inv. 476). The painting is in the public domain.
description: Under the busy kitchen table at the bottom right, a grey tabby has claimed a wooden plate and sits hunched over it, nose down on a heap of scraps. A small white-and-brown spaniel in a blue collar, tail up like a plume, has dropped into a play-bow and is yapping straight at it. Above them a cook in a yellow skirt prepares a bird, a woman leans over a board at the centre, and an old woman sits with a rolling pin, while a boy at left sits on the floor puffing into an inflated bladder. A butchered carcass hangs at upper left and pewter plates are stacked on the right wall.
context: A butchered ox, a child puffing into an inflated bladder and a cat squaring up to a dog: the museum's own text calls the ox and the bladder-blower examples of a taste for the grotesque. The Brera lists the canvas as 145 by 220 cm, oil on canvas, in room XV under inventory number 476, and dates it 1590 to 1591, though the Commons file for the photograph gives 1578 to 1581. Campi, a Cremonese painter who died in 1591, made kitchens and markets his speciality, and the cat and the spaniel are painted as carefully as the cooks.

title: The Visitation of Saint Elizabeth (Madonna of the Cat), Palatine Gallery
title_eng: St Elizabeth's Visit to the Mother and Child and St Joseph, with St John the Baptist and St Zachary, known as the Madonna of the Cat
title_original: La visita di Sant'Elisabetta alla Madonna e al Bambino, detta Madonna della gatta
submovement: Urbinate Counter-Reformation Altar and Devotional Painting (Barocci, late period)
collection: Palatine Gallery, Palazzo Pitti, Florence (Gallerie degli Uffizi)
license: Image © Gallerie degli Uffizi; painting in the public domain
image_credit: Gallerie degli Uffizi, Palatine Gallery, Florence (inv. 1890 n. 5375). Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from datocms-assets.com (the Uffizi's image host) and is not stored on this site.
description: Right in the middle of the canvas, on the edge of the bed where Mary sits propped against a cradle, a grey-and-white cat is curled into the pink folds of her dress with its head up, as if just woken. The household is in the middle of a visit. Joseph, in yellow, draws back a heavy curtain at left to let in Elizabeth and her young son John the Baptist; old Zachary peers in at far right. Through the window behind, the towers of the ducal palace of Urbino stand on their hill. Joseph's tools and a sewing basket lie on the step in the lower left.
context: The nickname comes from something hidden in the folds of Mary's dress. The Uffizi says the cat is nestled there almost as if woken by the guests, and that the painting was probably commissioned by Francesco Maria II della Rovere and tied to Pope Clement VIII's visit to the Marche in 1598, though the birth of the duke's heir around 1605 is also proposed. It reached Florence in 1631 in the dowry of Vittoria della Rovere, and in 1663 to 1664 it was woven into a wall hanging by Pietro Fevère. Finestre sull'Arte reports it back on view at the Pitti after more than a decade of absence.

title: Sinte Aelwaer
title_original: Elck dient Sinte Aelwaer met grooter begheert die van veel menschen wordt gheeert
image_credit: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam. Public domain.
description: A woman with a halo rides side-saddle on a grey donkey across a patch of grass, wearing a red skirt and a feathered turban. Her right arm is raised high, and in that hand, up in the top left of the picture, dangles a small grey cat held by the scruff like a banner. A piglet is tucked under her other arm, a magpie perches on her head, and a rat sits on her shoulder. Printed text fills the margins on the left and below. The colourist has given the cat the same pale grey as the donkey, so the two animals echo each other across the sheet.
context: Sinte Aelwaer is an invention: the Rijksmuseum calls her a made-up pseudo-saint and patron of quarrelsome people, and reads her animals as attributes. The cat stands for cunning, the piglet for laziness and malice, the magpie for lying and gossip, and the rat perhaps for gossip or for the death that strife leads to. According to the poem, the noise of these creatures signals discord. The record credits Cornelis Anthonisz. as printmaker, Jan Ewoutsz of Amsterdam as block-cutter and printer, and a print by Albrecht Dürer as the model for the composition.

title: The Steps of Life (Levenstrap)
artist: Anonymous woodcutter after Jörg Breu the Younger
submovement: Augsburg Woodcut Broadsheet (Breu the Younger circle)
image_credit: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam. Public domain.
description: A stone staircase crowded with men of nine ages fills the top half of this big woodcut, from a small boy at far left to a bent greybeard, with a skeleton drawing a bow at the summit. Under the steps, nine arched niches each hold an animal. In the lower right, in the second niche from the end, a shaggy cat lies curled up with its tail wrapped around its body, just left of the donkey in the last niche. Below the arch, the Last Judgement plays out in two scenes.
context: A goat, pig, cow, lion, fox, wolf, dog, cat and donkey: that is the Rijksmuseum's list of the nine animals under the stairs, each matched to a stage of life. The sheet, 494 by 660 mm, is printed from four blocks, and a gravestone in the Last Judgement scene carries the year M.D.XXXX, which dates it to 1540. Death in the shape of a skeleton with bow and arrow threatens from the top. Here the cat gets the sleepy, almost-finished end of the staircase, which is not a bad deal compared with the wolf.

title: Discordia (The Bad Household)
artist: Crispijn van de Passe the Elder after Maarten de Vos
submovement: Late Netherlandish Mannerist Moral Engraving (de Vos–van de Passe)
image_credit: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam. Public domain.
description: Three well-dressed couples are brawling in a dining room, with furniture, plates and a candelabra knocked about. At the bottom of the print, a child and a cat both take a bite of a roast turkey that has spilled onto the floor. The cat is at the lower centre-right, head down at the bird, while the grown-ups ignore the theft. A dog tugs at a woman's hem at the lower left. In the open doorway behind them, servants run off with their own spoils.
context: Discordia is the bad half of a pair: the Rijksmuseum describes a companion print of a good household. The margin quotes Proverbs 17 in Latin, "Melior est buccella sicca cum gaudio quam domus plena victimis cum iurgio", roughly "better a dry crust with joy than a house full of feasting with strife", followed by a motto. The signature reads "M. de Vos figuravit" and "Crisp. Vande Pass sculp. et excud.", meaning de Vos designed it and van de Passe engraved and published it. The same turkey the cat enjoys is the moral: when the household fights, the pets feast.

title: Gula (Gluttony)
image_credit: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam. Public domain.
description: A braided young woman sits on a wild boar and holds a long pole with a flag in both hands. Top left, a helmeted coat of arms leans in the corner under an owl, and the shield on it shows a cat curled up asleep, its round head resting on its paws. The flag on the pole carries a porcupine. An obelisk stands behind her on the right, and two lines of Latin run along the bottom edge. The cat is small, about the size of a thumbnail on the original sheet.
context: Gluttony rides a boar, as you would expect, but the surprise is the heraldry: a shield in the top corner showing a cat, with an owl perched above it. The Rijksmuseum describes this as the fourth of seven prints in the series, dated 1552 and carrying Aldegrever's AG monogram. The sheet is only 103 by 63 mm, a little taller than a playing card, and the cat on the shield is correspondingly tiny. A sleeping cat is an oddly gentle emblem for a deadly sin.

title: The Witches' Sabbath
image_credit: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam. Public domain.
description: Naked women crouch around a cauldron at night, one at right stirring with a ladle while another at left reaches up into the smoke, and a third flies across the top of the sheet on a goat, holding a pitchfork and a pot. Skulls, antlers and pitchforks litter the foreground. At the lower right, tucked between a tree trunk and the seated witch's hip, a shaggy cat sits hunched with its back to us, its tail curling out along the ground. It is easy to miss among the antlers.
context: Two impressions, two printings: the Met's copy of this 1510 Baldung is a chiaroscuro woodcut in two blocks, printed in gray and black, a second state on a sheet of 38.9 by 27 cm, while the Rijksmuseum's impression, 378 by 257 mm, shows black line only. The Rijksmuseum's description is blunt about the cat: it simply sits at the right. Among smoke, skulls and flying hags, the cat is one of the few quiet things on the sheet.
