title: Woman Spinning
submovement: Early Netherlandish Woodcut (Lucas van Leyden attribution)
medium: Woodcut, hand-coloured in pink and orange, with brush additions
image_credit: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam. Public domain.
description: A woman in a huge feathered hat sits on a stone seat and spins thread from a distaff, a small dog sleeping across her lap. A cat is at the bottom left corner, curled into a tight round on the pavement beside the hem of her skirt, its head turned back toward its tail. Pink wash on her dress and orange on the hat make her stand out against the plain brick wall. The print is trimmed, and the missing corners have been redrawn in brush.
context: Missing corners on this sheet have been patched in with a brush: the Rijksmuseum notes that the print was cut down, pasted onto a larger leaf and completed by hand, and that the woodcut was hand-coloured in pink and orange. It gives the work to Lucas van Leyden only as "attributed to" and dates it simply to the 1500s. The sheet measures 238 by 153 mm. The dog on the lap and the cat on the floor make a neat pair: the lap pet and the floor pet, one on either side of the thread.

title: The Fall of Man
image_credit: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam. Public domain.
description: Adam and Eve stand close under the tree of knowledge, both holding the fruit they have just picked while the serpent coils above their heads. Animals fill the garden around them. At the bottom right, at Eve's feet, a cat lies curled up with its eyes half shut and its tail laid along its body, just in front of a dog sitting upright. A sleeping lion fills the lower left corner, and a boar looks on behind Adam. The cat is the only creature that has not noticed anything is wrong.
context: Handwriting does some of the work here. Below the image someone has written "Année 1559", and on the back a note reads "v.der Heyden / Petrus a Merica", while the Rijksmuseum credits Pieter van der Heyden as printmaker on the strength of what is mentioned on the object. The record lists the animals as a lion, boar, dog, cat and peacock, and the plate measures 270 by 205 mm. The impression was bought with the support of the F.G. Waller-Fonds. Of all the creatures in this garden, the cat looks least like a witness to the first sin.

title: Nature drives out with a fork, yet always returns (Cat Catches a Mouse)
title_eng: Nature drives out with a fork, yet always returns (Cat Catches a Mouse)
title_original: Natura furca expellas tamen usque recurret
artist: Theodor de Bry after Jean Jacques Boissard
culture: German (Frankfurt am Main) after French design
submovement: Frankfurt Emblem Book Engraving (de Bry workshop)
medium: Engraving, plate 39 from an emblem book
image_credit: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam. Public domain.
description: On a table covered with a white cloth, a spotted cat has caught a mouse. With one paw it holds the mouse and with the other it has knocked over a lit candle, which lies flat and sparks along the cloth. The onlookers react with raised hands and open mouths: three at left, four at right. The cat is long and low, tail curled, and faces the viewer. A Latin motto runs across the top of the print and the plate number, 39, sits at the lower left.
context: Tiny but loud: this plate measures just 65 by 80 mm. The Rijksmuseum records it as plate 39 from Denis Lebey de Batilly's Emblemata, published in Frankfurt by Theodor de Bry in 1596, after a drawing by Jean Jacques Boissard. The Latin motto, NATURA FURCA EXPELLAS TAMEN USQUE RECURRET, is the proverb that nature driven out with a pitchfork still comes back. The moral is that a cat will be a cat, even in front of a ring of alarmed gentlemen and a fallen candle.

title: The Gluttonous Couple
artist: Anonymous engraver after Joos van Winghe, with reference to Hans Holbein
submovement: Late Netherlandish Mannerist Genre Engraving (van Winghe)
dimensions: Sheet 275 × 414 mm (printed from two plates on two sheets)
image_credit: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam. Public domain.
description: A stout woman in a headscarf passes a slice of fish across a small table to her heavy husband, who slumps in a chair with his cheek on his hand and a big glass in front of him. Hams hang from the wall behind and a bed with drawn curtains fills the right side. In the centre foreground, a striped cat sits upright with its back to us, facing the table and watching the fish, while a dog sleeps on the floor on the left. The couple gets all the attention but the cat has the sharper eyes.
context: Rogier Bontemps is written on the edge of the bed curtain, according to the Rijksmuseum, which credits Joos van Winghe as designer and a painting by Hans Holbein as the source. The print is dated 1593 and was printed from two plates on two sheets, which explains the wide format of 275 by 414 mm. Four-line Latin verses run in two cartouches below, and in the front left of the room a dog and a cat share the floor.

title: Childhood (Pveritia)
artist: Crispijn van de Passe the Elder
submovement: Late Netherlandish Mannerist Engraving, Ages of Man series (van de Passe)
image_credit: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam. Public domain.
description: Two naked boys hold a cat up between them, one clutching it round the middle from the front and the other kneeling to grab its hind legs. The cat is upright in the middle of the print with its ears flat, mouth open and claws out. Behind them are a house with a smoking chimney and a landscape where more children play games. A four-line Latin verse and the maker's credits run below, and the title PVERITIA is printed in the sky.
context: PVERITIA is Latin for childhood, and the sheet belongs to a series titled Aetates Hominum Secundum Anni Tempora, roughly the ages of man according to the seasons of the year. The Rijksmuseum's note is brief: two children hold a scratching cat while other children play in the background. It credits Crispijn van de Passe as designer, publisher and engraver and gives the Latin verse to Karel van Utenhove. Whatever the verse says about the age, the cat has plainly not signed up for it.

title: The Cat Clavichord (Cat Concert)
medium: Engraving with four verses in German
image_credit: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam. Public domain.
description: Five fools sing and play around a wooden clavichord, while a sixth drinks wine from a flask at the far left. The keyboard is a box with a row of small animal heads poking out of the top, including cats with their ears back and a dog. The player at the right pushes keys, a lute-playing fool leans in over the group, a boar growls in time at the front, and a goat watches from the right. A grapevine trellis fills the background. Four verses in German run along the bottom.
context: Plucking paws and pulling tails is how the Rijksmuseum says this instrument was "played": a cat clavichord, or cat organ, with cats and a dog housed in the box. The record gives the print to Hans Kellerthaler of Dresden only as "attributed to", and dates it to 1575 to 1611, the span of his working life. Four four-line German verses run along the foot of the sheet, and a boar grunts along at the front. It is a concert for people who enjoy being out of tune, and the animals in the keyboard have no say in the programme.

title: Hunting Wild Cats
artist: Philips Galle after Johannes Stradanus (Jan van der Straet)
submovement: Antwerp Hunting Series Engraving (Galle after Stradanus)
image_credit: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam. Public domain.
description: Hunters in a wooded valley push spotted cats out of the trees with long poles and let the dogs deal with them on the ground. At the lower left two cats rear up against a hound at the foot of the trunk, while a third lies pinned beneath a dog at the centre. At the top of the tree a smaller animal clings to the branches, waiting to be poked out. On the right two riders with swords trot past, and a man in a wide hat drives his pole into the foreground. A Latin couplet runs along the bottom.
context: Forty-three plates of hunting, fowling and fishing make up the series, and this is the one where the quarry is cats. The Rijksmuseum records the design by Jan van der Straet, mentioned on the sheet as working in Florence, and Philips Galle as printmaker and publisher in Antwerp in 1578, with a Latin caption describing how the cats are poked out of the trees and left to the dogs. The spots on these "cats" look closer to a leopard than a house cat, which is part of the charm of Renaissance natural history.

title_original: Een huisvrouw op een binnenplaatsje bij het schoonmaken van vis
image_credit: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam (CC0)
title: A Housewife in an Inner Courtyard Cleaning Fish
title_eng: A Housewife in an Inner Courtyard Cleaning Fish
submovement: Dutch kitchen-yard genre (Potuyl, Amsterdam/Dordrecht circle of Rembrandt followers)
description: Fish scales, cabbage, mushrooms and a copper pot crowd the foreground of a back yard, where a young woman in a white cap gutting a fish on a barrel lid is the obvious star. The real drama is down on the ground at lower left, beside a little bench. A grey-and-white cat has crouched over a dropped fish, hunched low, ears flat, wolfing it down before anyone notices. Behind the woman, through the open fence, two children and a dog wander along a village lane. Rakes, baskets and a wheel lean against the shed wall, so the whole picture feels like a lived-in corner rather than a staged set.
context: A Paris sale of 20 February 1914 catalogued this little panel as the work of Adriaen van Ostade, and it fetched 3,900 francs under that name, as the Rijksmuseum's provenance notes record. Only later did it settle with Hendrik Potuyl, a painter of kitchen and peasant scenes who died in 1652. Mrs Kessler-Hülsmann gave it to the museum in 1940. The museum's own description is brisk: by the bench at left, a cat eats from the fish. It is a cat getting away with lunch.

title_original: Een hond en een kat bij een half geslachte ree
image_credit: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam (CC0)
title: A Dog and a Cat near a Partially Disembowelled Deer
title_eng: A Dog and a Cat near a Partially Disembowelled Deer
submovement: Dutch hunting still life (Jan Baptist Weenix, Utrecht/Amsterdam)
description: A roebuck hangs by one hind leg from the dark, its belly slit open, while a knife and a heap of innards lie on the stone ledge below. On the right a lean black-and-white hound lunges toward the carcass with its mouth open. High on the left, standing on a fold of green curtain and almost swallowed by the shadow, a small grey cat faces the dog. Both animals are pointed at the meat, and at each other, which makes the cat the one quiet piece of live action in an otherwise motionless still life.
context: Signed "Gio. Batti. Weenix", the Italian form of his name, at lower left, this canvas is large: 180 by 162 cm, and with its frame the museum's data puts it at 46 kg. The record gives the scene as a still life of a gutted roe deer hanging by one leg, a knife and removed organs on the table, a barking dog at right and a cat at left by the curtain. The Rijksmuseum dates it 1645 to 1660. The cat has the best seat in the house and the least interest in the knife.

image_credit: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam (CC0)
title: Children with a Mousetrap
submovement: Leiden Fijnschilders (Fine Painters), Gerard Dou circle
description: Three children share a stone window arch, hung with a striped curtain. A fair-haired boy in front holds a little wooden mousetrap high in his left hand and, with his right arm, clutches a small grey cat against his chest. The cat is the one who looks worried, wide-eyed, wedged under his elbow and a long way from any mouse. A girl next to him points up at the trap, and a boy behind her is crying. A flowerpot stands on the sill at lower left. Everything is finished in the glassy, polished style of the Leiden school.
context: Gerard Dou's nephew painted this: Wikipedia notes that Domenicus van Tol's works "often draw comparison" with his uncle's, and that he was a fijnschilder, a fine painter, who joined the Leiden guild in 1664. The Rijksmuseum dates the panel only to 1660 to 1676 and records his signature "D. V. Tol" on the window sill. The museum's title names the trap, but the only mouser in the picture is the one in the boy's arm.

image_credit: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam (CC0)
title: The Parrot Cage
submovement: Leiden merry-company and household genre (Jan Steen)
description: A woman reaches up to a birdcage hanging from the ceiling, its little door standing open, while behind her two men play backgammon and a third watches. At the far left another woman fries oysters over the fire. Down on the floor in the lower left corner, a small boy sits with his legs stretched out and feeds a cat from a spoon. The cat sits up on his lap, plainly more interested in the spoon than in the household drama. A discarded oyster shell and a pewter dish lie scattered on the tiles in front of him.
context: Oysters, backgammon and a parrot: the museum gives the full title as Interior with a woman feeding a parrot, two men playing backgammon and other figures, known as "The Parrot Cage", and the cat does not make the headline. The record mentions it only in passing, a boy on the floor feeding it with a spoon, while the cage hangs from the ceiling with its door open. The panel is signed "JSteen" at lower right, and the Rijksmuseum dates it to about 1660 to 1670. The spoon-fed cat is the household's quietest luxury.

image_credit: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam (CC0)
title: The Anaemic Lady
submovement: Dordrecht domestic genre and doctor-visit pictures (Hoogstraten, Rembrandt and de Hooch influences)
description: A pale young woman in a gold bodice and white skirt sits slumped, hands clasped, with her feet on a foot-warmer, while a bearded doctor behind her holds a flask of her urine up to the window light. A silent man in a brown cloak stands by. On the floor at lower right, tucked against the table leg and the heavy red carpet, a small grey tabby sits upright and watches. Its eyes are on the room rather than the patient, as if it has already guessed what is wrong with the sitter. A staircase and a distant fireplace recede through the doors on the left.
context: "Anaemic" is a loose rendering of the Dutch bleekzuchtig, roughly "pale-sick". The Rijksmuseum notes the foot-warmer and the cat at right as the supporting cast, and the picture is signed "S.v.H." at lower right. Wikipedia says that Hoogstraten imitated Pieter de Hooch in two works, this doctor's visit being one of them, and that one of his perspective boxes, a peepshow with a convincing view of a Dutch house, is displayed at the National Gallery in London. The painting is on loan to the museum from the City of Amsterdam (A. van der Hoop Bequest).

image_credit: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam (CC0)
title: Cat Concert
submovement: Amsterdam mezzotint (Jan van Somer, satirical genre prints)
description: From a velvety black ground, a man in a floppy hat sits on a bench with a cat clamped across his lap, its tufted face turned to the viewer and its mouth open mid-yowl. Children crowd in at the left, one holding a smoking pipe aloft. A woman at right waves one hand and holds up a sheet of music in the other, as if conducting. A tankard stands on a round table at lower right. The cat itself, fur on end, is the loudest thing in the room.
context: Blunt is the museum's summary: a man holds a cat under his arm and makes it cry out, and the cat yowls and breaks wind in the face of the person showing the sheet of music. The sheet is dated only 1655 to 1700. Jan van Somer, a Dutch printmaker given as active from about 1645 to after 1699, worked in mezzotint, whose deep velvety darks suit a candle-lit farce like this. Jacob Gole made a related print with the identical museum description.

image_credit: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam (CC0)
title: Cat Concert
submovement: Amsterdam mezzotint (Jacob Gole, satirical genre prints)
description: A snarling tabby, ears up and fangs bared, pokes its head out at the lower left. Its striped body is tucked under the arm of a man in a plumed hat and stretched across his chest like a fiddle, with its tail clamped between his teeth and a long stick laid across it as a bow. A child leans over a ledge behind them, pointing. At right a woman in a lace collar squeezes her eyes shut against the noise and holds out a sheet of music. A wine glass and a tankard stand at the bottom edge.
context: Same plot, different plate: this sheet carries the same museum description as Jan van Somer's Cat Concert, a man making the cat caterwaul while it breaks wind in the face of the person holding the music. The record dates Gole's activity only to 1670 to 1724 and gives the cut-down sheet as 149 by 186 mm. Mezzotint lifts highlights out of a roughened dark plate, which is why the cat's whiskers and teeth glow against the black. The tabby is both instrument and critic.

image_credit: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam (CC0)
title: Man with a Cat and a Mouse
title_eng: Man with a Cat and a Mouse
artist: Cornelis Danckerts I, after Dirck Waerden
submovement: Amsterdam moralising print (Danckerts publishing house, after Dirck Waerden)
description: Perched on the shoulders of a ragged man, a fat cat has its claws in his face, tail curling up behind. The man screws up his face and opens his mouth to yell. With one hand he warns the viewer off, and between the fingers of the other he dangles a mouse by its tail. The cat is after the mouse and does not care what it steps on. The background is nothing but fine vertical hatching, which pushes the cat and man into hard relief.
context: Two lines run below: "Ons Gooßen kryt met luyder keelen / De Nicker mach met katten Speelen." The Rijksmuseum summarises the verse as being about Goossen, who cries out because the cat is playing, and the credit lines name Dirck Waerden as designer and C. Danckerts as the one who cut the plate. The museum gives the date only as between 1613 and 1656. The sheet entered its collection with the support of the F.G. Waller-Fonds.

image_credit: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam (CC0)
title: Rommelpot Player with a Cat
artist: Jan van Somer, after Adriaen Brouwer
submovement: Amsterdam mezzotint after Flemish peasant genre (Brouwer)
description: Inside a dark round frame, a young man in a loose shirt scrapes at a rommelpot, a friction drum made from a pot with a stick through a membrane, held against his belly. A second man in a feathered cap leans over his shoulder, laughing and singing along, one hand up in the air. Behind the first man's shoulder on the left, a striped tabby perches with its small pointed face peering forward, watching both of them. The signature "Somer fe." runs along the lower margin.
context: Only 122 by 123 mm, this round vignette makes the figures, cut off at the waist, feel like a keyhole view into a tavern corner. The Rijksmuseum credits the composition to a painting by Adriaen Brouwer and the mezzotint to Jan van Somer, whose name is printed on the sheet ("Somer fe."). In the museum's summary the cat is simply an extra on the first player's shoulder while a second man sings along. It dates the sheet loosely to 1655 to 1700.

title_original: Aap dwingt een kat de kastanjes uit het vuur te halen
image_credit: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam (CC0)
title: The Monkey Forces a Cat to Pull the Chestnuts from the Fire
title_eng: The Monkey Forces a Cat to Pull the Chestnuts from the Fire
submovement: Amsterdam animal-fable print series (Gole, after Francis Barlow)
description: In a plain room with a leaded window, a ring-tailed monkey grips a striped cat by the front paw and presses it toward a blazing hearth. Chestnuts lie on the logs in the fire, and thick smoke rolls up the chimney. The cat is the one being dragged: ears back, mouth open in a snarl, body twisted in the monkey's arms. Through the open door on the right, a peaceful landscape with a tree and a tower shows what is going on outdoors, which is nothing at all. The margin line reads "F.B. delin." and "J. Gole exc.".
context: "Cat's paw" is the idiom for someone used by another to do a risky job, and this is the scene behind it: La Fontaine's fable of the monkey who makes the cat fish roasting chestnuts out of the fire. The Rijksmuseum records the sheet as one of a series of ten prints of different animals. The margin line "F.B. delin." credits the design to Francis Barlow, the English animal draughtsman, while "J. Gole exc." names the Amsterdam publisher. Gole's name sits where a publisher's would, so the sheet advertises who sold it as well as who drew it.

medium: Brown and grey wash on vellum
image_credit: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam (CC0)
title: Stable Interior with Eight Figures
submovement: Rotterdam stable-interior and peasant drawings (Cornelis Saftleven)
description: The wash is laid on in pale browns, so the barn looks sunlit and dusty. At left two men and two women crowd around the fire. In the middle of the sheet, on a low stool just behind a woman's skirts, a plump tabby sits hunched with its head turned toward the group. To the right two pigs sleep in the straw with two boys, and further back a goat and a sheep wait by a fence. A jug and its fallen lid lie in the foreground, and a basket and barrel are stacked on the far right.
context: Five drawings went to the Rijksmuseum in 1891 from H. Cremers of The Hague for 73 guilders in all, and this barn scene was one of them, according to the provenance notes. They trace it, with a question mark, to Dutch sales of 1750 and 1769 that describe a Saftleven on vellum in wash. The sheet is dated 1651 and measures 255 by 334 mm, brown and grey wash on vellum with a framing line in brown ink. The cat on its stool has a better view of the fire than the pigs do.

title_original: De Vrede maant de kerken tot verdraagzaamheid
image_credit: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam (CC0)
title: Peace Urges the Churches to Tolerance
title_eng: Peace Urges the Churches to Tolerance
submovement: Low Countries allegorical and confessional satire painting (anonymous, early 17th c.)
description: Holding a palm or olive branch, a woman in a red-orange dress sits at the left of a dinner table while the guests quarrel over food. In the centre sits the pope in his tall tiara, a bowl of porridge in his hand and two cats curled in his lap, one gazing out at the viewer. Calvin sits at the left, a roast calf in front of him, and Luther plays the lute at the right. At lower right an Anabaptist crouches to dip his bread in a pan by the fireplace. Painted verses on the walls speak for each guest.
context: The pope's painted verse blames his bitter porridge: it is flavoured with orange peel, he says, so his cats do not lick it as they usually do. Calvin's verse above his roast calf also mentions the "sappe van Oraignen", the juice of oranges. The museum describes Peace urging the confessions to tolerance, with Charity and her children in a picture on the wall at right. Its provenance notes record that the canvas was bought at an anonymous sale in France by Louis J. Bosman of Brussels, and it came to the Rijksmuseum as a gift of J.W. Bosman.

title: A Cat Stealing Fish
submovement: Neapolitan Baroque still life (Recco family workshop)
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: A wicker basket has been knocked on its side on a stone ledge, and a long silvery fish, red crustaceans and a round clay pot have slid out of it. A striped tabby has climbed up behind the spill. It stands at the top of the canvas, just right of centre, one forepaw hooked over the basket, and it looks straight out at the viewer with wide eyes, caught in the act. Down on the rock lie a red mullet, a bream and a shelled sea creature, and at left a big copper basin leans on its rim, glowing against the dark.
context: Naples bought its still lifes by the dozen, and the Recco family workshop supplied many of them: Giuseppe, born in 1634, was the son of Giacomo Recco, one of the founders of the genre there. The Met acquired this canvas by purchase in 1871, within a year of the museum's own founding, which gives it the accession number 71.17. The dark, lamp-lit setting is typical of Neapolitan still life, and here it makes the cat the only living thing in the room.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, Purchase, 1871 (71.17). Open Access, CC0.

title: The Beggars: Old Woman and Cats
title_eng: The Beggars: Old Woman and Cats
submovement: Lorraine etching, Callot's Les Gueux (The Beggars) series
description: Perched side-on on a three-legged stool, an old woman bends forward in a bulky robe and headcloth, a walking stick propped behind her shoulder. A dark cat is clutched against her chest, held in the crook of her arm. A second cat lies curled up on the ground beneath the stool, tucked in beside a round woven basket, its head down and its back turned to us. Callot builds the folds of her skirt out of dense parallel lines and leaves the background paper bare, so the two animals read as small dark knots in a pale sheet.
context: Barely fourteen centimetres tall, the plate belongs to a set of 25 etchings of beggars and vagrants that Callot made around 1622 to 1623. The set goes by several names: Les Gueux, Les Mendiants (The Beggars), Les Baroni and Les Barons. Cleveland's provenance for this impression includes the collector's stamp of Friedrich August II of Saxony, Dresden (Lugt 971), so a king-era print collection once held the old woman and her cats. The cats are drawn with the same care as their owner, as part of her household.
image_credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, The Jane B. Tripp Charitable Lead Annuity Trust (2008.34.25). Open Access, CC0.

title_original: Le Chat guettant l'oiseau en cage
title: The Cat Watching the Bird in the Cage (Lux Claustri, plate 10)
title_eng: The Cat Watching the Bird in the Cage
submovement: Lorraine etching, emblem book Lux Claustri (The Light of the Cloister)
medium: Etching and letterpress; second state of two
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: On a stone ledge in the foreground a round-bellied cat sits with its back to us, ears pricked and tail trailing behind, gazing up at a wooden cage that sticks out from a brick wall at the right. The bird inside is only a dark smudge behind the bars. Past the ledge the etching opens onto a hillside, a small walled town and a few birds in the sky. Above the picture a motto is set in type, and below it come a Latin couplet and four lines of French, so the whole sheet works like a small riddle.
context: "Captiva, sed secura" runs across the top: captive, but safe. The French verse says the prisoner bird sings without fear of the cat that never stops eyeing it, just as a monk, whatever the demons say, chants psalms and blesses his chosen prison. The Latin couplet speaks for the cat: leave the cage and you will fall to my claw. Plate 10 comes from Lux Claustri, a small book of emblems about monastic life, and the Met describes the sheet as etching with letterpress. The National Gallery of Art dates its impressions of the print to 1628, while the Met gives 1621 to 1635.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, Bequest of Edwin De T. Bechtel, 1957 (57.650.348(10)). Open Access, CC0.

title_original: Les Vierges folles sommeillent en attendant l'époux
title: The Foolish Virgins Sleeping
submovement: Parisian etching, Bosse's Wise and Foolish Virgins pair
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: Firelight and window light fall across the floor of a grand salon hung with patterned wall coverings, framed pictures and a mantelpiece of vases. Five young women in 1630s dress doze on stools and chairs or fuss with a hand mirror. The cat is in the foreground, lower left of centre, a grey tabby sitting on the sunlit boards with its back to us, its body a tidy round and its ringed tail stretched out behind. It is the only creature in the room not pretending to have anywhere else to be, and it fits the mood: the whole sheet is about waiting and doing nothing.
context: Four lines of verse run under the picture and open with "Ces Vierges au lieu de veiller", These virgins, instead of keeping watch. Bosse took the Gospel parable of the foolish bridesmaids who let their lamps run dry and played it out in a fashionable seventeenth-century interior. The Met records the etching as ca. 1635, first state of two, bought with the Harris Brisbane Dick Fund in 1926, and holds the matching sheet of the wise virgins, which also has a cat on the floor. The Met gives Bosse's birthplace as Tours and his death as 1676 in Paris.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, Harris Brisbane Dick Fund, 1926 (26.49.12). Open Access, CC0.

title: The Wise Virgins Resting Whilst Awaiting the Arrival of the Husband
submovement: Parisian etching, Bosse's Wise and Foolish Virgins pair
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: Night has come. A crescent moon shows through the barred window at upper left, and the room is lit by a fire at right and by oil lamps lined up on a small altar with a cross and an open book. Five women sit close together in the middle of the room, three of them reading from one volume. At the very bottom of the picture, a little right of centre, a dark cat sits hunched with its back to us on the lit floorboards, ears up, tail curling away. The fire has picked it out and left it alone, a black shape sitting up while everyone else keeps vigil.
context: Five oil lamps stand burning on the altar, which is the point of the picture: these are the bridesmaids of the parable who came prepared. A printed title, "Les Vierges sages", and verse beginning "Nul vain objet ne peut distraire", no idle thing can distract them, sit under the plate. The Met sheet (26.49.9, Harris Brisbane Dick Fund, 1926) is trimmed at the sides. Bosse puts a cat on the floor in the foreground of both this and the foolish virgins, yet the Gospel parable mentions no cat, so each one is his own addition.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, Harris Brisbane Dick Fund, 1926 (26.49.9). Open Access, CC0.

title: A Peasant Family
submovement: French 17th-century peasant genre (Le Nain brothers), small cabinet picture on copper
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: Six figures are crowded in front of a bare stone fireplace: a boy in an orange-red jacket, hands in his pockets, at left; a taller boy in grey behind him; a small child in a floppy hat playing a pipe; a bearded man seated with a wicker-covered flask between his knees; and a girl in a red bodice at right. The cat is low in the picture, left of centre, on the grey floor between the red-jacketed boy's boots and the seated man's feet. It is white with grey patches and sits with its head turned, ignoring the music, in a warm patch near the hearth.
context: About 38 by 30 centimetres and painted on copper rather than canvas or wood, this is a picture meant to be held close. The Met says the Le Nain brothers are famous for portraying rural life with sensitivity, without the ridicule of earlier peasant images, and notes that the work has been attributed to both Antoine and Louis; it is now given to Antoine. It entered the museum in 2023 as a gift of Michel David-Weill and is shown in Gallery 622. A white-and-grey cat is the only member of the household not posing.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, Gift of Michel David-Weill, 2023 (2023.605). Open Access, CC0.

title: The Lacemaker
submovement: Roman genre painting by a Danish artist (Monsù Bernardo, Bamboccianti milieu)
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
description: A girl in a mustard bodice and blue apron sits on the floor with a half-made piece of lace in her hands, her head bowed over it. Behind her a rush-seated chair carries the lace pillow, a bolster stuck with a fan of bobbins, and a basket of yarn sits in the lower left corner. The cat is at the far right, standing at the edge of the chair in the shadow: grey and white, front paws planted, mouth open and eyes fixed on the girl. Its face is the brightest thing on that side of the canvas, and it seems about to speak.
context: A Danish painter who worked in Rome under the nickname Monsù Bernardo, Bernhard Keil is said by the Met to have trained in Rembrandt's studio before leaving the Dutch Republic in 1651 for Italy. The Met dates the picture to about 1665, shows it in Gallery 630, and received it in 1971 with the bequest of Edward Fowles. The lacemaker's quiet work is the subject, and Keil adds a restless extra: a cat at the edge of the chair that clearly has its own plans for the evening.
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, Bequest of Edward Fowles, 1971 (1971.115.2). Open Access, CC0.

title: The Wedding at Cana
submovement: Bolognese late Baroque history painting with genre detail (Crespi)
description: Christ sits at the left in red and blue beside his mother, while at right a servant in silk and a kneeling page hand the steward the first cup of the miraculous wine. The cat is in the bottom right corner, on the stone floor beside a gilded wine jug and the boot of a standing guest. A grey-and-white tabby lies on its back with its hind feet tucked up, one forepaw batting at the jug and its face turned to us. At the opposite corner a spotted dog sleeps against Christ's sandal, so the two animals bracket the feast.
context: A tower of gilt and silver plate rises behind the guests, one of the luxurious accessories that the Art Institute says Crespi packed into the picture along with smaller interactions between characters. Its catalogue entry credits the painting with joining the Venetian tradition of colour and grandeur to the close observation of figures typical of Crespi's native Bologna. The canvas is about 1.9 by 2.5 metres and dated about 1686, and it came to Chicago through the Wirt D. Walker Fund in 1956. The cat and the dog are the unscripted guests, and they behave like it.
image_credit: Art Institute of Chicago, Wirt D. Walker Fund (1956.129). Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

title_eng: Strolling Actresses Dressing in a Barn
title_original: Strolling Actresses Dressing in a Barn
title: Strolling Actresses Dressing in a Barn
collection: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland
image_credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Milton Curtiss Rose, 1959.310 (CC0)
description: Two small cats scramble over a heap of stage props in the bottom foreground, left of centre, batting at a golden orb beside a gilt lyre. Above them a leaky barn is full of goddesses getting dressed: Diana, Juno and Flora hitch up their gowns, a ghost and two devils wait their turn, and wine is going round. Laundry hangs from a line under the rafters, an eagle costume lies by the bed, and a monkey sits on the costume pile at the lower right. The cats have found the only game in the room that needs no rehearsal.
context: Crown, orb and lyre: the royal props in the foreground are the print's argument. Cleveland records that Hogarth meant the engraving as a protest against Robert Walpole's Licensing Act of 1737, which gave the government power to heavily censor the stage, and a large crown beside a playbill points at the law. The troupe is preparing a play called The Devil to Pay in Heaven, and the shabby backstage is made messier by a heavy consumption of wine. A note from Wesleyan's collection singles out the kittens in the foreground among the entertaining details.

title: Seated Woman with a Cat
artist: Jean-Michel Moreau the Younger (Moreau le Jeune)
submovement: French late-Rococo portrait drawing (Moreau le Jeune)
medium: Brush and gray and black wash
collection: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland
image_credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Bequest of Muriel Butkin, 2008.396 (CC0)
description: Looking down at the floor, a grey-and-white cat stands on a small table at the left edge of the sheet, tail curling up behind it, while its owner looks out at us. She sits in an armchair in a frilled cap and a lace-trimmed shawl, hands folded in her lap, with framed prints on the wall behind her, one of them a harbour crowded with tall ships. Everything is brush and grey wash, soft enough that the cat's striped coat and the sitter's bonnet seem to be made of the same material.
context: A collector's stamp in the lower left corner of the sheet reads Goncourt: Edmond and Jules de Goncourt, the nineteenth-century writers who championed Moreau le Jeune, once owned the drawing. Cleveland suggests the sitter may be a relative of the poet Louis Gresset (1709–1777), and notes that Moreau drew a similar portrait of Gresset, now at the Snite Museum of Art. Moreau was a draftsman, illustrator and engraver who became Dessinateur et Graveur du Cabinet du Roi, so he spent his days drawing for the court. This small sheet shows him drawing for himself.

title: A Boy with a Cat—Morning
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Marquand Collection, Gift of Henry G. Marquand, 1889 (public domain, Open Access)
description: In a dark wood at first light, a boy in a pale, torn shift and dark sandals stands scratching his head. The cat is at the lower left, beside his feet at the edge of the shadows: a grey-brown tabby stepping out of the grass and looking off in the same direction as the boy. A crumpled red cloth lies on the ground to his right, and a yellow gleam of sky shows between the trees. The boy's clothes are little more than loose flicks of white paint.
context: Henry G. Marquand gave the canvas to the Met in 1889, a century after it was painted. The museum notes the boy's shift is painted in bold, loose strokes that suggest its ragged condition. It is dated 1787, the year before Gainsborough died in London, and the Met holds a second picture of poor children from the same year, Cottage Children (The Wood Gatherers). Both show poor children outdoors rather than commissioned sitters.

title_eng: Cat Surveying Fish and Fowl on a Table
title_original: Cat Surveying Fish and Fowl on a Table
title: Cat Surveying Fish and Fowl on a Table
submovement: French Enlightenment kitchen still-life drawing (Chardin circle)
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Bequest of Harry G. Sperling, 1971 (public domain, Open Access)
description: Ruff bristling and back arched, a cat stands on a kitchen table at the right of the sheet, face turned toward a spread of food. A plucked bird hangs at the back, a dish sits in the middle, a fish lies along the front edge, and a flat fish rests at far left. The chalk is quick and loose, with the cat drawn in a handful of scribbled strokes and the lettering Chardin fecit 1753 written along the bottom of the sheet.
context: Black chalk, a signature and a date of 1753 look like a clear case, yet the Met catalogues the sheet only as attributed to Chardin, and the lettering reads "Chardin fecit 1753" along the bottom. It came to the museum in the Harry G. Sperling bequest of 1971. The subject fits the artist: Chardin had already painted a cat stalking fish and game on a kitchen table in the 1720s, as in The Ray at the Louvre. A cat among the fish and fowl was clearly a motif he returned to.

title: Harlequin with Bird and Cat
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, The Jack and Belle Linsky Collection, 1982 (public domain, Open Access)
description: Harlequin sits on a rocky stump in his lozenge-patterned jacket, blue breeches and a slouch hat, holding a small bird up in one raised hand. A wicker cage waits behind his hip. The cat crouches at bottom left on the base, grey and white, with its ears forward and its head tipped up toward the bird. A single blue flower sits on the base at the right. The pose is a joke set up in porcelain: the bird is out of its cage, and the cat has noticed.
context: Crossed swords painted on the underside of the unglazed base identify the Meissen factory mark. The Met catalogues the model to Johann Friedrich Eberlein, a Meissen modeler who died in 1749, and dates it 1743. Meissen was the first European maker of hard-paste porcelain, and its stage figures borrowed the stock characters of the commedia dell'arte. The Met's Linsky Collection holds several of them, including Columbine and Pantalone by Johann Joachim Kändler.

title_eng: Snuffbox in the form of a cat
title_original: Snuffbox in the form of a cat
title: Snuffbox in the form of a cat
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, The Jack and Belle Linsky Collection, 1982 (public domain, Open Access)
description: Looking back over its shoulder with wide, round eyes, a grey-striped cat curls on a green mound of painted grass, as if it has just heard its name. The grey stripes on its back and tail are painted hair by hair, with two soft grey patches on its flanks, and a band of gold runs around the base. The whole animal is the box: the porcelain cat sits in a gold mount only 6.7 cm long, small enough to sit in a palm.
context: Gold turns a toy into a snuffbox. Christie's collecting guide describes the gold-mounted Meissen box as a luxury object of the mid-eighteenth century, made after the factory had moved on from its early chinoiserie phase of the 1720s. The Met dates this example to about 1745 and records the materials as hard-paste porcelain and gold, with the object given to the museum in the Jack and Belle Linsky Collection in 1982. Meissen, founded in 1710, was the first European maker of hard-paste porcelain.

title: Seated cat
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of Irwin Untermyer, 1964 (public domain, Open Access)
description: Ears cocked and chin lifted, a cat sits upright on a scrolled base painted green, white and purple, its tail wrapped round its haunches and its mouth set in a faint smile. The coat is dabbed with orange and purple patches that run together like watercolour on damp paper, and fine painted whiskers cross the muzzle. Orange and purple dabs also mark the forehead and cheeks, which gives the face an almost tortoiseshell mask. The round eyes give it the look of a thoughtful, slightly smug household cat.
context: Four inches (10.2 cm) is all it measures, and the Met dates it to about 1760 under the Derby Porcelain Manufactory, active from 1751 to 1785. It came to the museum with the collection given by Irwin Untermyer in 1964. The company now called Royal Crown Derby says the Huguenot André Planché settled in Derby in 1745 and made soft-paste vases and figurines there, which is the tradition this soft-paste cat belongs to.

title_eng: Bonbonnière in the form of a tabby cat
title_original: Bonbonnière in the form of a tabby cat
title: Bonbonnière in the form of a tabby cat
artist: Unknown (British enamel workshop, possibly South Staffordshire or Birmingham)
submovement: English Painted Enamel on Copper (South Staffordshire / Birmingham bonbonnières)
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of Mrs. James M. Kellogg, in memory of her husband, 2023 (public domain, Open Access)
description: Chin down and shoulders hunched, a striped cat crouches over a patch of mustard-green turf with its front paws drawn in under its chest. Its body is painted in thin brown-red stripes on a pale ground, its eyes are wide and dark, and a small dark creature, apparently its catch, lies right under its chin. The cat forms the lid of a little sweetmeat box: it is only 4.5 cm long. A thin metal rim runs round the base, and the box opens along it.
context: Rolling copper into thin sheets, instead of the far costlier gold, is what made boxes like this affordable. The Met notes that by the middle of the eighteenth century this technology let enamellers in London, South Staffordshire (Bilston and Wednesbury) and Birmingham turn out small luxuries. The museum dates the box to about 1770 to 1780, gives its size as 3.2 by 4.5 cm, and received it in 2023 as a gift of Mrs. James M. Kellogg, in memory of her husband.

title: Cat
submovement: Staffordshire Creamware and Coloured-glaze Pottery Figures
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Rogers Fund, 1912 (public domain, Open Access)
description: Honey-yellow all over, a cat sits bolt upright on a flat oval base with its ears pricked and its eyes ringed in brown. Two dark lines of glaze run straight down from the eyes like trails of tears, and brown splashes mark the back and flanks. The tail curls round the base, and the modelling is simple and rounded: a chunky, solemn animal with a long-suffering face. Nothing about the piece is fussy, and its charm is all in that downturned mouth and the sorrowful stripes under the eyes.
context: Six inches (15.2 cm) of lead-glazed earthenware, and the Met catalogues it simply as British, Staffordshire, ca. 1780, with the Rogers Fund purchase in 1912. Dealers who handle similar Staffordshire cats describe the type as early creamware figures decorated in underglaze oxide colours on a hollow base, and Christie's has sold one of about 1780 seated on an oval green base and sponged in green and ochre. The same colour palette of earth oxides, rather than painted enamels, is what gives the cat its yellow body and brown streaks.

title: Animal Locomotion, Plate 720: Cat, Galloping
submovement: Chronophotographic motion studies (Muybridge, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia 1884–87)
medium: Collotype after electro-photographic negatives, plate from the portfolio Animal Locomotion, Vol. X: Domestic Animals
collection: Boston Public Library, Rare Books Department
image_credit: Boston Public Library, via Digital Commonwealth (No Copyright – United States).
description: Twenty-four photographs of one cat, laid out in four rows of six on a dark mount, catch a gallop frame by frame. In the top row the animal is stretched long and low, its head to the left. Down the rows it bunches up, back arched and paws gathered under it, then flings itself out flat again. Behind it runs the thin grid of horizontal and vertical lines Muybridge used as a measuring scale, so every frame can be compared with the next. The sequence is a plain record of what a galloping cat does, one slice at a time, with no attempt to make it graceful.
context: Plate 720 sits in Volume X, Domestic Animals, of the 1887 portfolio Animal Locomotion, which the Boston Public Library holds in its Rare Books Department. The set ran to 781 plates, and only 221 of them show animals; most of those are horses. Muybridge sold subscribers any 100 plates they chose for $100. Full sets cost $600 and sold so badly that reportedly only 37 complete ones were produced. A cat plate was therefore a small corner of a very expensive project. The Library's catalogue lists the plate as a collotype and notes the 1887 copyright line printed under the image.

title: Animal Locomotion, Plate 716: Cat, Walking, Changing to Galloping
title_eng: Animal Locomotion, Plate 716: Cat, Walking, Changing to Galloping
title_original: Animal locomotion. Plate 716 (Cat; walking; change to galloping)
submovement: Chronophotographic motion studies (Muybridge, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia 1884–87)
medium: Collotype after electro-photographic negatives, plate from the portfolio Animal Locomotion, Vol. X: Domestic Animals
collection: Boston Public Library, Rare Books Department
image_credit: Boston Public Library, via Digital Commonwealth (No Copyright – United States).
description: Four rows of six small photographs follow one cat as it strolls from left to right, tail held up like a question mark. In the top rows the walk is calm and even, one paw lifting at a time. By the lowest row the pace has quickened: the body stretches, the tail drops to follow it, and the stroll turns into a trot and then a gallop. A fine grid of lines on the backdrop lets you measure how far each leg travels between frames. Viewed together, the grid squares show a cat changing gear without any visible effort.
context: A caption printed under the mount reads "Animal Locomotion, Plate 716", with Muybridge's 1887 copyright line. The Boston Public Library's catalogue gives the subject as "Cat; walking; change to galloping" and files it under Volume X, Domestic Animals. Muybridge made the pictures at the University of Pennsylvania, and the portfolio was issued in eleven volumes numbered from 1 to 781. It lists 514 plates of men and women in motion against only 221 of animals. That makes a pet cat one of the rarer sitters in a project that was mostly about people and horses.

title: Concert of Cats
artist: Rudolph Ackermann (publisher), lithograph by an amateur after a design credited to P. Breughel
submovement: Regency amateur lithography and humorous prints (R. Ackermann's Lithography, London 1817)
image_credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Mr. and Mrs. Lewis B. Williams Collection, 1940.1090 (CC0 Open Access).
description: Most of them singing, a crowd of cats gathers round an open music book on the right. A tall grey one at the top left plays a trombone. Others sit up on their haunches with their mouths wide open, one of them in spectacles, while a few sit calmly in the foreground, facing the page. The notes in the book are drawn as little mice, and one real mouse sits among them. A violin, a pipe and a pile of books lie on the floor in front, and a bird looks out from a round opening at the upper right, understandably keeping its distance. It is a very small, very crowded print.
context: Credited to "P. Breughel" and to "an Amateur" who etched it on stone, the lettering gives the imprint as R. Ackermann's Lithography, July 1817. Cleveland catalogues it as a lithograph and records the culture only as "England(?)". Ackermann ran a print shop and publishing house in London and was an early champion of lithography in Britain, so the date fits a moment when amateurs were being urged to try the new technique. Neither named maker can be pinned down from the lettering, and whoever the amateur was, he gave each singer a different face.

title: Interior, Little Girl with Cat
submovement: Paris colour etching revival (Alfredo Müller, Montmartre, 1890s)
dimensions: Not given in the museum record
image_credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Bequest of Elizabeth Carroll Shearer, 2016.226 (CC0 Open Access).
description: Holding out one hand, a girl in a purple dress with a ruffled white collar crouches on the floor, eyes lowered to a dark brown cat sitting in front of her. The cat is turned away from us at the lower left, curled round, with its tail laid out on the boards. Behind them a pitcher stands on a covered table by an open door that looks onto a sunlit garden, and a leaded window with diamond panes fills the upper right. Light falls across the floor in a soft yellow patch. The girl and the cat both seem to be waiting to see who will move first.
context: Diamond window panes, a pitcher and a draped table furnish a quiet room in which almost nothing happens. Alfredo Müller was born in Livorno to a Swiss family and settled in Montmartre after his father's bank failed. In Paris he came to know Renoir, Pissarro and Cézanne, and he became known as an etcher in colour. Cleveland holds this sheet as an etching and aquatint with hand colouring, which means each impression was finished by brush and may differ slightly from the next.

title: Six Etchings: Head of a Kitten
title_eng: Head of a Kitten (from Six Etchings)
submovement: Etching by a patron of the Impressionists (Dr. Gachet, Auvers-sur-Oise, 1890s)
medium: Etching and drypoint on wove paper
image_credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Gift of Elizabeth Carroll Shearer in memory of Robert Lundie Shearer, 2002.142.2 (CC0 Open Access).
description: Face dropped onto its tucked front paws, a tabby kitten has its eyes shut, one hind foot poking out at the right. Dark hatched lines make the stripes across its forehead, and a few sparse strokes sketch the curve of the back, so the rest of the body fades into bare paper. The ears are flattened slightly as it settles. A small monogram sits at the lower right of the plate. At the bottom of the sheet, in the margin, there is a round stamp of a cat's face.
context: A round cat-face stamp appears in the bottom margin of the sheet, an owner's mark of the Gachet family. A related print at the Wellcome Collection carries the same stamp and is said to certify the provenance from Paul-Ferdinand Gachet and his son Paul-Louis. Gachet was the physician who looked after Vincent van Gogh in Auvers in 1890. He was also a friend of Pissarro, Renoir, Manet and Cézanne, and an amateur artist himself. Here the doctor is the artist, and the kitten is drawn in sleep, which no real kitten would ever allow for long.

title: The Cat in the Studio
submovement: Danish genre painting in Paris, pre-Impressionist interiors (David Jacobsen, 1855–69)
collection: SMK – Statens Museum for Kunst, Copenhagen
image_credit: SMK – Statens Museum for Kunst, Copenhagen (public domain, SMK Open).
description: Crouched over a blue-rimmed plate on bare floorboards, a big grey-brown cat with a white chest tears into a scrap of pink meat. Its whole body is one round, heavy shape, nose down, ears flat to the plate. Around it sits a painter's working room: a paint box open on a stool with a small landscape in its lid, a yellow-lined pot at the left, and framed canvases leaning against a grey wall at the right. A few crumbs lie on the boards. The artist signed in the lower right corner and dated it 1860.
context: Camille Pissarro shared a studio with Jacobsen in Paris after returning there in 1855, according to Cleveland's catalogue text for a Pissarro drawing. This little oil was lent to Ordrupgaard's 2017 show on Pissarro's time on St Thomas. It joined the SMK collection in 1918, and a 1908 catalogue of Danish Jewish artists lists it simply as "Katten", the cat. The cat has the room to itself, and the painter's tools seem to be there only to show whose room it is.

title: Reclining Cat
submovement: Danish Golden Age drawing (Eckersberg circle, Copenhagen, 1840s)
collection: SMK – Statens Museum for Kunst, Copenhagen
image_credit: SMK – Statens Museum for Kunst, Copenhagen (public domain, SMK Open).
description: Hatched in soft pencil, a short-haired cat lies tucked up with its forepaws laid in front of it, chin low and eyes open. Dark patches mark the ears, the cheek and the back, with a small black shape at the tail end. White fur is left as bare paper and the body is built from loose diagonal hatching, so the whole animal looks warm and slightly puffed. The face is the most finished part, with whiskers and a calm, half-interested stare. The sheet is only about the size of a postcard.
context: Rheumatic fever at the age of eleven is one of the first facts about Købke, who later trained for four years under Eckersberg. SMK dates this cat to 1845–46, two or three years before he died of pneumonia at 37, and acquired the sheet in 1887. In pencil on a scrap about 81 × 136 mm, a Golden Age painter has caught a house cat in the middle of a long, serious doze.

title: Two Sleeping Cats
submovement: Danish Golden Age pen drawing (Skovgaard, Lundbye circle, Copenhagen, 1840s)
medium: Pen and black ink on paper
collection: SMK – Statens Museum for Kunst, Copenhagen
image_credit: SMK – Statens Museum for Kunst, Copenhagen (public domain, SMK Open).
description: On a broad stone ledge, two cats have fallen asleep in a heap, one with its chin on the other's back. The nearer cat lies stretched out along the front edge, ears folded flat. The cat behind it curls up with its face turned in against the first. A window with a dense cross-hatched pane takes up the right-hand side, and a plain wall block rises at the left. Everything is in thin pen lines with almost no shading, so the animals look pale against the paper. The artist wrote the date, 10 December 1843, in the lower right corner.
context: A card-sized sheet and a few strokes of ink were enough here for Skovgaard, who is better known for monumental Danish landscapes. SMK catalogues a second cat drawing by him, Reclining Cat with Her Kitten, carrying exactly the same inscription: 10 December 1843. So he drew at least two cat studies on one day. Skovgaard was a leading figure of the Danish Golden Age and a lifelong friend of the animal painter J. Th. Lundbye, who died in 1848.

title: The Cats (with a pencil study of a cat's head and two magpies)
title_original: Kattene. Foroven blyantsstudie af et kattehoved og to skader
submovement: Danish National Romantic animal drawing (Lundbye, Copenhagen, 1840s)
medium: Pen and black ink, with pencil studies at the top
collection: SMK – Statens Museum for Kunst, Copenhagen
image_credit: SMK – Statens Museum for Kunst, Copenhagen (public domain, SMK Open).
description: Four cats gather around a barrel at the bottom of the sheet. Two of them lean over its rim, one with its head right inside the barrel and the other balancing with a long curled tail. A third cat sits on a step in the middle with its back to us, watching. The fourth stands at the left, facing the viewer with ears pricked. A pencil sketch of a cat's face sits in the top-left corner, and a long-tailed bird, drawn in faint outline, floats above the whole group.
context: Four cats, a barrel and a bird in pencil: SMK catalogues the sheet as "Kattene" (The Cats), with a pencil head study and magpies at the top, 182 by 138 mm, signed with a monogram in pen and black ink left of centre. Lundbye, who lived only from 1818 to 1848, grew up in Kalundborg, and SMK's biography notes that his father resisted his drawing in an almost brutal way before he got into the Academy in Copenhagen. Cats were a recurring subject for this animal painter, and this sheet shows why: four different attitudes in one small heap.

title: Playing Kittens: Two Kittens Playing with a Ball
title_eng: Playing Kittens: Two Kittens Playing with a Ball
title_original: Legende kattekillinger. To killinger, der leger med en bold
submovement: Danish naturalist sculpture of the Thorvaldsen succession (J. A. Jerichau, Copenhagen, 1860s)
collection: SMK – Statens Museum for Kunst, Copenhagen
image_credit: SMK – Statens Museum for Kunst, Copenhagen (public domain, SMK Open).
description: Two white marble kittens tumble together on a carved cushion. The one in front is crouched low with its head up, ears pricked, and both front paws wrapped around a small round ball. Behind it the second kitten stretches out on its side and stares at the same ball, its long body and tail curling away to the right and back. The cushion is rough and lumpy, with a stone base under it. A white block of marble has been turned into something soft, and the two animals seem about to bat the ball in opposite directions.
context: Thorvaldsen's studio in Rome was where Jerichau started out, working there for about a year after graduating in 1837, and his early Hercules and Hebe (1846) is strongly Neoclassical. He later moved toward a more dynamic, realistic style, and made The Panther Hunter in the same year. A pair of pet kittens is a long way from either, yet SMK dates this marble to 1861 and acquired it in 1938. The stone has been persuaded to look soft, and the ball has the full attention of both animals.

title: May Belfort
image_credit: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam, gift of the Instituut voor de Opleiding van Tekenleraren (public domain).
description: A young woman in a long orange-red gown stands slanting across the sheet, as if about to step out of it. A white ruffled cap with a big bow sits on her head, and a black frilled collar frames her face. In the crook of her arms, at chest height, she holds a small black cat; its head tucks under her chin and its thin tail hangs down against the red skirt. Olive-green lines sketch a brick wall behind her, and her name is spelled out in tall green letters along the bottom edge, with the artist's monogram in the corner.
context: A baby's frills and a black kitten were May Belfort's stage costume. The V&A notes that Toulouse-Lautrec showed her several times holding a small black cat as a reference to her signature song, and a published account says she appeared dressed as a baby with a black kitten, performing "Daddy Wouldn't Buy Me a Bow-Wow". The Rijksmuseum titles this 1895 colour lithograph poster "May Belfort with a cat in her arms".

title: Sleeping Cat
image_credit: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam, M.C.J. Breitner-Jordan Bequest, Zeist (public domain).
description: One cat sleeps curled on a flat surface, head at the left, chin down and eyes closed, the near ear folded forward. Soft pencil strokes, quick and loose, model the striped back and rounded haunch, and a few long lines mark the ground it lies on. The head is the most carefully drawn part, with just a few strokes for the cheek and ear. Everything else is quick shorthand. A small brown stain sits to the right of the cat's tail, and the sheet carries the stamps of the Rijksmuseum and of Breitner's studio.
context: A "1949" in the object number marks the year this sheet entered the Rijksmuseum, from the estate of Breitner's widow, according to the museum's record trail, and the artist's own studio stamp is still on it. Breitner worked from life in notebooks and loose sheets like this one, catching cats asleep because sleeping cats stay put. He is generally counted as an important Amsterdam Impressionist, and this sleeping cat is a small, quiet side of that reputation.

title: Reclining Cat on a Cushion
title_original: Liggende kat, op een kussen, naar links
submovement: Dutch Biedermeier-era amateur drawing from life (Jean Bernard, Amsterdam, 1800s–1820s)
image_credit: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam, gift of the heirs of J. Bernard van IJsseldijk (public domain).
description: A plump tabby sits like a loaf on a square cushion that rests on a stool, with its head turned to the right and half-lowered. Black chalk gives every layer of fur its own small flicks, so the coat looks thick and slightly ruffled. Dark patches mark the cheek, shoulder and flank, while the cushion is shaded in a few heavy strokes. A frame line has been ruled round the sheet, and the artist's signature sits at the lower right corner. The drawing is only about the size of a postcard.
context: The Rijksmuseum records the day this tabby sat for Bernard as 2 November 1828, five years before his death. The same collection holds other cat drawings by him from 1815 and 1825, so the cushion cat was one of a long line. The sheet is black chalk and measures 144 by 200 mm. Chairs, stools and cushions recur in these studies, and the cats are drawn with the patience of someone who looked at them for a long time.

title: The Cat
submovement: British etching and aquatint (Nevinson, Slade-trained printmaker)
dimensions: Sheet: 40.1 x 25.5 cm; platemark: 17.6 x 13.6 cm
image_credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Gift of Mrs. Malcolm L. McBride, 1948.433 (CC0)
description: Black against a pale window, a cat sits with its back to us and both ears pricked, watching whatever is going on outside. Everything else in the room has gone to soot: a heavy curtain on the left, a dark ledge along the bottom, and what looks like a stack of books on the right. Through the glass, bare trees are scratched in with fine lines, so the garden seems drawn by a much lighter hand than the interior. The cat is the whole point, a solid silhouette with only the ears and the curve of the back sharply drawn. Aquatint, the process that lays down grainy areas of tone, gives the blacks their velvet depth.
context: Nobody expects a velvet-black cat from the man who painted the machine-gun picture La Mitrailleuse. Nevinson trained at the Slade School alongside Stanley Spencer and Mark Gertler, flirted with Futurism, and became one of the best-known British war artists of the First World War. He also made etchings and lithographs, which is the craft behind this quiet sheet. Cleveland dates it only to "the 1900s", which sits oddly with an artist born in 1889, so read the date as the museum's loose label. The print is signed in the lower margin and came to Cleveland in 1948 as a gift of Mrs. Malcolm L. McBride.

title: The Parrot and the Cat (Sketch for "Good-Night" by Eleanor Gates)
title_eng: The Parrot and the Cat (Sketch for "Good-Night" by Eleanor Gates)
submovement: Edwardian magazine illustration (Golden Age of British illustration)
medium: Black ink wash with graphite on paper
image_credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Gift of Mrs. Ralph Perkins in memory of Coburn Haskell, 1946.158 (CC0)
description: Hackles up, a black cat arches on the left half of the sheet, back humped, tail curled, mouth open in a hiss with its pale eyes locked on the enemy. The enemy is a parrot swooping in from the upper right, wings flung wide, and Rackham has let it dissolve into loose blots and streaks of grey wash so it reads more as a storm than a bird. A dark smudge lower right looks like a fallen wing or tail feather. The cat itself is built from darker, wetter wash over faint graphite lines, with the fur ragged where the brush ran dry. It is the sketch stage of a magazine picture, drawn fast and without fuss.
context: Buenas Noches was the title of the Eleanor Gates short story this sketch served, one of six Rackham pictures that ran with it in Scribner's Magazine in February 1906, according to Cleveland. The museum says the sketch shows the climax, where Loretta the parrot faces her enemy Tomasso the cat to protect her friend Tony the canary, in the same poses as the finished illustration. Rackham is remembered for lavish colour books made as Christmas gifts, but he also did commercial work such as bookplates, greeting cards and magazine pictures. The sheet reached Cleveland in 1946 as a gift in memory of Coburn Haskell.

title: Honorable Mr. Cat
submovement: American Japonisme colour woodblock printing (Helen Hyde, Japan-based)
medium: Color woodcut on cream Japanese paper
dimensions: Image/block: 17.6 x 18.3 cm; sheet: 26.5 x 28 cm
image_credit: Art Institute of Chicago, Gift of Mrs. Edwin F. Gillette and Mrs. Hallie Hyde Irwin, 1920.1479 (CC0)
description: Pencil-thin diagonals of rain slant across the whole block, and under a big paper umbrella a small child hurries along, hugging a black cat to her chest. The cat is carried like a bundle: its head is tucked into the child's shoulder beside a pink bow, and its hind legs dangle straight down her skirts. A green bamboo fence makes the wall behind, a grey reflection stretches across the wet street under her wooden sandals, and the sleeve and hand of an adult at the left edge hold the umbrella handle. The cat is the point of the picture, carried like a parcel.
context: Berlin and Paris came first, then Japan: Helen Hyde, an American, went there to learn colour woodblock printing and stayed until 1914. Biographies note that she took lessons from Kanō Tomonobu, described as the last master painter of the old Kanō school. Her subjects were mostly women and children, and the English title here, "Honorable Mr. Cat", hands the animal a courtesy title it plainly has not earned by behaviour. Chicago holds the print as a 1920 gift from two donors, one of them Mrs. Hallie Hyde Irwin.

title: The Black Cat, for Edgar Allan Poe's "Selected Tales of Mystery"
title_eng: The Black Cat, for Edgar Allan Poe's "Selected Tales of Mystery"
dimensions: Image: 21.3 x 14.9 cm; sheet: 35 x 27.5 cm
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of Margaret Murray and Michael Blodget, 2018 (public domain, Open Access)
description: Brickwork has been split open in the dark, and in the gap near the top of the picture a dark blue-grey cat squats with its mouth wide in a shriek. Cream patches of flaking plaster crowd around the hole, the bricks are laid in brick-red, mauve and ochre, and the lower corner sinks into purple shadow. The cat is small, and sits in the one patch of blue-black, which is exactly why the eye goes straight to it. The image is a watercolour and gouache design for the ending of a horror story, pasted on a mount with the title pencilled at the lower right.
context: Poe's "The Black Cat", first printed in 1843, ends when a murderer who has bricked his wife's body into the cellar wall is given away by a wail from behind the plaster: he had walled up the cat with her. That is the moment Byam Shaw paints. The Met dates the drawing to 1909 and links it to an edition of Poe's Selected Tales of Mystery. Byam Shaw was a painter, illustrator and teacher, and in 1903 he made a family pastel with the title My Wife, My Bairns and My Wee Dog John. The Met received this sheet in 2018 from Margaret Murray and Michael Blodget.

title: Og Katten var Herre i Huset og Hønen Madame (And the Cat was Master of the House and the Hen the Lady)
title_eng: And the Cat was Master of the House and the Hen the Lady
title_original: Og Katten var Herre i Huset og Hønen Madame
submovement: Funen Painters (Fynboerne) pen illustration, Faaborg and Kerteminde circle
image_credit: SMK, Statens Museum for Kunst, KKS1976-56 (public domain, CC0 via open.smk.dk)
description: On the rumpled bed at the right-hand side, a cat lies stretched out with its back to us, plainly in charge of the room. At the left a stiff little bird, hen-like and wide-eyed, sits upright on a wooden chair beside a window drawn in slanted lines. Syberg builds the cottage from dense pen hatching, with a few quick pencil lines still showing beneath. At the bottom he has written out the caption in Danish, "Og Katten var Herre i Huset og Hønen Madame", with the number 37 at the right.
context: Hans Christian Andersen's "The Ugly Duckling" has a stretch where the frozen duckling takes shelter with an old woman, her cat and her hen, and the title line here is the story's own joke: the cat is master, the hen is the lady. SMK dates the set to 1928, records the caption and the number 37 in pen below the drawing, and cites a 1975 book of the drawings, Den grimme ælling, where this sheet appears as figure 53. Syberg belonged to the Funen Painters, a Danish group of artists around Faaborg and Kerteminde.

title: Self-Portrait with Cat
medium: Oil on commercially woven cotton fabric
collection: Harvard Art Museums / Busch-Reisinger Museum, Cambridge, Massachusetts
image_credit: Harvard Art Museums/Busch-Reisinger Museum, Museum purchase, BR50.12; public-domain photograph via Wikimedia Commons
description: A green-faced man in a dark orange coat with black lapels fills the foreground, his left arm lost in a spray of small green strokes and a tall stem of blue bell-shaped flowers rising beside his head. The cat sits at the far left, black and upright on a shelf in front of a blue-framed picture, so small beside the man that it is easy to miss until you spot its two pointed ears. The walls are red fading to orange-pink. The paint is laid on thickly in broad strokes, and the support is a red-and-white checkered cloth instead of a canvas.
context: Checkered cotton is an unusual thing to paint on, and Harvard calls it a rare support for Kirchner. The picture dates from his years at Frauenkirch near Davos, where he settled for good in 1917 after a wartime breakdown, and Harvard notes that its heavy paint still has the energy of his prewar work, before he moved to large flat planes of colour. In 1937 the Nazi authorities removed it from the Folkwang Museum in Essen, and the Busch-Reisinger bought it in 1950.

license: © Edward Steichen / Estate of Edward Steichen, all rights reserved
image_credit: © Edward Steichen / Estate of Edward Steichen / Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from framemark.vam.ac.uk and is not stored on this site.
title: The Cat
submovement: Photo-Secession Pictorialism (Steichen's platinum prints, New York 1902)
collection: Victoria and Albert Museum (Royal Photographic Society Collection), London
description: Emerging from a brown-black gloom as a soft pale curve, a curled-up nude woman lies with a black-and-white cat in front of her, bottom left of centre, bending its head down to the floor. The cat is the one crisp patch of light in the picture: white chest and paws against dark fur, while the woman dissolves into the grain of the print. Everything is blurred on purpose, the edges melting into shadow, as though the camera had been replaced by a smudge of charcoal. The mount around the print is a warm tan, and the photographer's name is written at the bottom.
context: Pencil on the tissue mount reads "STEICHEN, MDCCCCII", the year given in Roman numerals as if it were a monument inscription, according to the V&A record. The print is a platinum print measuring 139 by 170 mm, and it entered the Royal Photographic Society's holdings in 1930 as part of the Alvin Langdon Coburn Gift, now kept at the V&A. Steichen went on to serve as chief photographer for the Condé Nast magazines Vogue and Vanity Fair from 1923 to 1938.

license: © John Nash / Estate of John Nash, all rights reserved
image_credit: © John Nash / Estate of John Nash / Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from framemark.vam.ac.uk and is not stored on this site.
title: Cat and kitten
submovement: British wood-engraving revival (John Nash, post-war London group)
description: Asleep in a tight ring on a plaid blanket, a tabby cat has one ear folded flat and one white paw poking out at the bottom edge. A second, smaller sleeper is tucked in against it. Nash cuts the fur as thousands of tiny curved lines, thick on the dark stripes and thin where the light hits, and then sets the animal against the broad black-and-white bars of the blanket so the whole print vibrates. It is a small print with a lot of patience in it.
context: No formal art training lay behind these thousands of tiny curved cuts: John Nash began as a newspaper reporter in 1910, and his brother Paul, a Slade student, encouraged him to draw. The V&A lists this print as "Cat and kitten", dated about 1920, and it came in with the 1929 accessions of the Department of Engraving, Illustration and Design, published by the Board of Education the following year. Nash later became better known for landscapes and botanical illustration.

license: © Ethel Mars / estate, all rights reserved
image_credit: © Ethel Mars / estate / Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from framemark.vam.ac.uk and is not stored on this site.
title: A White Cat
submovement: American colour woodcut in Paris (Mars and Squire circle, ca. 1904–10)
description: Paper left bare does the work of fur here: a white cat lies stretched out on a golden-ochre bed with its head up and its eyes closed, and the only drawing is a few dark flecks along the back, the legs and the underside. Behind it, a block of salmon pink fills the upper corner like a wall. The woodcut is built from three flat areas, pink, ochre and cream, with grainy printing that shows the texture of the block. The cat takes up nearly the whole sheet, front paws extended and tail tucked at the lower left.
context: Seven centimetres by ten: this print would vanish into a coat pocket. The V&A dates it only to circa 1900–1910, records it as a gift from the artist, and carries a 1910 accession number. Ethel Mars, an American illustrator, travelled to Europe from 1900 with her lifelong partner, the artist Maud Hunt Squire, and the pair lived mostly in Paris. A white cat printed in three flat colours is a very economical way to fill a small block.

title: To studier af en kat der vasker sig (Two Studies of a Cat Washing Itself)
title_eng: Two Studies of a Cat Washing Itself
title_original: To studier af en kat der vasker sig
submovement: Danish post-Gauguin decorative painting (Ludvig Find, Copenhagen)
medium: Brush and black ink on paper
image_credit: SMK, Statens Museum for Kunst, KKS1975-45 (public domain, CC0 via open.smk.dk)
description: Each drawn in a handful of loose black brush strokes, two cats at their toilette share one narrow sheet. The upper cat twists its head down to lick its flank, one front paw hanging in the air and its long tail swinging off to the left. Below it a second cat curls in a tight ball with its muzzle tucked in, one black patch over the eye and the tail thrown out behind. Find leaves almost the whole paper bare so the white fur is just the paper itself. A small signature and the year "08" sit in the margin between the animals.
context: Postcard-sized and dashed off in black brush, this sheet is signed in the margin "Fin(d) 08", with the d of the name in brackets as SMK transcribes it. It measures 194 × 130 mm and came into the collection in 1975. Find was born in 1869 and died in 1945. Leaving the paper bare for the white fur is the economy of the drawing: a cat mid-wash, a cat mid-sleep, and not a stroke more than needed.

title: Forgangen nat vor sulten kat (Last Night Our Hungry Cat)
submovement: Danish narrative etching (H. N. Hansen, Rome carnival series, 1900)
image_credit: SMK, Statens Museum for Kunst, KKS6104/2 (public domain, CC0 via open.smk.dk)
description: Night has fallen on the Roman Forum: two fluted columns with leafy capitals climb the upper left, a railed walkway crosses a ruined wall, and a huge stone figure of a woman looks down from the right under scattered stars. Two tiny figures with a lantern cross the walkway. The cats are down in the black at the lower left, where a tabby sits upright among the brush with its eyes on the visitors, and two more pairs of eyes glow in the dark along the bottom edge. The plate is signed and dated 1900, with the title written in the margin beneath it.
context: Eight etchings, one rhyme: this sheet belongs to a set titled Variations on a Theme, Last Night Our Hungry Cat, made from the Rome carnival, and SMK catalogues each plate with a line of Danish doggerel. Read in order, the lines run from the hungry cat to a young and tasty mouse, then a rat that makes the cat let the mouse go, then a nose "quite long", and end with "both escaped happily from the cat's claw". The monogram on this plate reads "HNH. Roma Febr. 1900", and SMK acquired the whole series in 1911.

title: Prowling Cat
submovement: British wood-engraving revival, Society of Wood Engravers circle (London, 1930s)
description: Black fur is built from thousands of short flicks of the gouge, and two bare white slivers of paper make the eyes, so the cat seems to glare out of its own shadow. It walks from left to right across a bright strip of ground, shoulders low, one forepaw lifted, while a thicket of broad-leaved plants and spiky grass stands dark behind it. The margin carries the pencilled title with the edition number, 21 of 50, the signature, and the date 1938 in the top corner.
context: Claude Flight taught Eileen Mayo to cut lino over the telephone in 1927, and her first print, Turkish Bath, was shown at the Redfern Gallery's First Exhibition of British Linocuts. Cats stayed on her subject list for good: the curator Peter Vangioni called the pair in her 1931 linocut Cats in the Trees "domestic tigers". The V&A record gives only the technique, a woodcut, the date 1938 and the donor, Dr R. Gainsborough.
license: © Eileen Mayo estate, all rights reserved
image_credit: © Eileen Mayo estate / Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from framemark.vam.ac.uk and is not stored on this site.

title: Cat in Cherry Tree
