submovement: British wood-engraving revival, Society of Wood Engravers circle (London, late 1940s)
description: Cherry blossom crowds the top and left of the block, five-petalled flowers cut as small clean stars against dark leaves. A black cat picks its way along a knobbled branch, front paws gripping, head turned up and back toward a bright break in the foliage where short rays fan out behind its ears. The long tail drops in a smooth curve at the right. Below the image Mayo pencilled the title, the edition number 3 of 80, and her signature.
context: Sixteen years earlier Eileen Mayo had sent cats up a tree, in the 1931 linocut Cats in the Trees; here she came back to the idea in wood. The year after this woodcut she moved to Paris to study with Fernand Léger, and later she emigrated to Australia. The V&A's record notes only that the woodcut is signed and numbered 3/80, with sizes taken from its Circulation register. The print is tiny, 8.9 × 10.2 cm, so the cat and the blossom share a block smaller than a postcard.
license: © Eileen Mayo estate, all rights reserved
image_credit: © Eileen Mayo estate / Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from framemark.vam.ac.uk and is not stored on this site.

title: Battersea
submovement: Picture Post photojournalism (London, post-war humanist reportage)
description: Rain has turned the yard to black glass, and a cat crosses it in the foreground with its tail hooked high, a soft dark shape against the shine. Further back, under a brick wall, a man in a long coat leans in toward a woman, and a lamp somewhere out of frame throws their shadows huge across the bricks. The cat sits at bottom left, closest to the lens, and the couple are small and half-lost in mist at upper centre.
context: Stray cats were everywhere in 1951, when Picture Post ran Thurston Hopkins's essay Cats of London. The Blitz had left many cats homeless, and they bred more or less wild in the bomb sites, living on scraps. Hopkins lured them into the camera's view with a little food. The V&A notes that this frame, Battersea (1950), did not make it into that first big feature, possibly because of its 'sexually charged' undertone, and says Hopkins left Picture Post in 1957.
license: © Thurston Hopkins estate, all rights reserved
image_credit: © Thurston Hopkins estate / Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from framemark.vam.ac.uk and is not stored on this site.

title: The Black Cat (illustration to Poe)
submovement: British Surrealist-inflected book illustration (London, Second World War)
medium: Pencil on thin paper, mounted on a support sheet
description: A thin young woman with shoulder-length wavy hair, eyes closed, is sandwiched between two stone walls, the front one smashed away unevenly so she is visible down to the waist. On the top of her head a black cat is crouched with its back arched, fur on end, tail up, jaws wide open in a snarl. Droplets of blood run from her hairline across her forehead. The cat sits at the top centre of the sheet, directly above her face.
context: Edgar Allan Poe's 'The Black Cat' first appeared in the Saturday Evening Post on 19 August 1843. Its narrator walls his murdered wife into the cellar, and the police find her only because the cat, accidentally bricked up with the body, shrieks. This drawing was made for a 1945 anthology of weird tales, Come Not Lucifer, published by John Westhouse. Rolf Brandt, trained as an actor and brother of the photographer Bill Brandt, came to London from Hamburg in the early 1930s.
license: © R.A. Brandt estate, all rights reserved
image_credit: © R.A. Brandt estate / Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from framemark.vam.ac.uk and is not stored on this site.

title_eng: Orlando Goes to Sea (Oronsay menu cover)
title_original: Orlando Goes to Sea (Oronsay menu cover)
title: Orlando Goes to Sea (Oronsay menu cover)
submovement: British picture-book lithography, Orlando the Marmalade Cat (Hale, 1938–1972)
medium: Colour-printed folded menu card after an illustration by Kathleen Hale
description: Red hull, pink funnel, a pennant reading ORLANDO GOES TO SEA: the ship is called The Saucy Puss. Orlando himself, a big ginger cat, stands at the wheel at the far left. On a red ladder in the middle, his wife Grace, a cat with brown markings, cooks in a saucepan on top of the funnel. Their three kittens play around the deck, one climbing the rigging, one writing, one fishing from a porthole, while a cow and a hen share the ship.
context: Passengers on the Orient liner Oronsay got a cat with dinner on Monday 26 October 1953. The V&A says the card was one of a series of six drawings on the same theme. Kathleen Hale invented Orlando to entertain her children at bedtime, and in 1941 Orlando's Evening Out became the first fictional picture book published by Puffin. A ballet of Orlando was staged at the 1951 Festival of Britain.
license: © Kathleen Hale estate, all rights reserved
image_credit: © Kathleen Hale estate / Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from framemark.vam.ac.uk and is not stored on this site.

title_eng: Orlando Sails to the Arctic Regions (Oronsay menu cover)
title_original: Orlando Sails to the Arctic Regions (Oronsay menu cover)
title: Orlando Sails to the Arctic Regions (Oronsay menu cover)
submovement: British picture-book lithography, Orlando the Marmalade Cat (Hale, 1938–1972)
medium: Colour-printed folded menu card after an illustration by Kathleen Hale
description: Ice has frozen the ship's red bow into a snow-capped wedge, and the cat family has gone skating beside it. Orlando, the ginger one, whirls at left with a penguin in a feather boa, while his wife Grace in her fur coat and the kittens glide round in pink skates. More penguins slide in from the distance, and a cow wrapped in a purple quilt looks on. At the top a white hen sits in a nest under an iced-over parasol, which the V&A says is wrapped in a tea cosy.
context: Chapter 3 of the Oronsay series is lettered "Orlando Sails to the Arctic Regions" along the foot of the card, and the V&A says it was the cover of a children's tea party menu for Tuesday 27 October 1953. In the picture the hen sits on a hot-water bottle in a tea cosy, because the Arctic is cold. The V&A has two of the six drawings, a gift from Mrs Pamela Griffiths, whose late husband collected them as a passenger on board. The first Orlando book, published in 1938, was among the earliest picture books made with photolithography.
license: © Kathleen Hale estate, all rights reserved
image_credit: © Kathleen Hale estate / Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from framemark.vam.ac.uk and is not stored on this site.

title: White Cat
submovement: Chicago Surrealist-tinged WPA easel painting (Federal Art Project, Illinois, late 1930s)
image_credit: © Gertrude Abercrombie estate / Smithsonian American Art Museum. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from ids.si.edu and is not stored on this site.
description: A hard, empty room in lilac and navy: a panelled door at right, a wainscot of vertical boards, a small landscape in a heavy frame on the wall, with a tiny figure under a bare tree. Mid-floor, a low table carries a white tray and one blue vase. The cat is bottom right, white and small, sitting where the door meets the floorboards, turned toward the table with its tail curling out onto the dark boards. It is the only living thing in the room, and it has the best view of the vase.
context: Tags on SAAM's record link the painting to the Federal Art Project in Illinois, and the museum acquired it by transfer from the General Services Administration in 1971. Gertrude Abercrombie was a Works Progress Administration painter from 1934 to 1940, later called 'the queen of the Bohemian artists' of Chicago. She was close to the jazz scene, and Dizzy Gillespie performed at her 1948 wedding to the critic Frank Sandiford.
license: SAAM states: public domain (free of copyright restrictions)
collection: Smithsonian American Art Museum, Washington, D.C.

title: Young Cat Sleeping
submovement: WPA Federal Art Project lithography (New York City, 1930s)
medium: Lithograph on paper mounted on paperboard
image_credit: © Mabel Wellington Jack estate / Smithsonian American Art Museum. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from ids.si.edu and is not stored on this site.
description: Everything is dark except the cat. It lies curled into a tight comma on a black ground, chin tucked on its forepaws, eyes closed, whiskers fanned out over its tail. The light strokes that build the fur follow the curve of the body, thickest along the haunch and thinnest where the face turns. The plate is signed and dated 'M. W. Jack '37' at lower left, and the title and her full signature are pencilled below. The cat fills the lower two thirds of an almost square sheet, and the black above it presses down like a lid.
context: Two federal agencies handled this print before the museum did. A stamp at lower left ties it to the Federal Art Project in New York, and the credit line says it came by transfer from the Evander Childs High School in the Bronx through the General Services Administration. The Smithsonian's audiovisual preservation catalogue gives the artist as born in New York in 1899 and dead in 1975, and files the print under Graphic Arts.
license: SAAM states: public domain (free of copyright restrictions)
collection: Smithsonian American Art Museum, Washington, D.C.

title: Cats
submovement: WPA Federal Art Project lithography (New York City, mid-1930s)
image_credit: © Chuzo Tamotzu estate / Smithsonian American Art Museum. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from ids.si.edu and is not stored on this site.
description: Eyes shut and body curled low in the foreground, a grey-and-white cat loafs in the lower centre of the sheet. Just behind its back a small kitten in black and white leans up and peers out toward the viewer. At upper left a tall dark vase holds a loose bunch of flowers drawn in quick dabs of crayon. The soft, grainy shading looks like lithographic crayon, and the whole composition is tucked into the upper two thirds of the sheet, leaving a wide pale margin below.
context: Amami Ōshima, an island in Kagoshima Prefecture, is where Chuzo Tamotzu was born in 1888. He taught himself to paint, lived in New York City, and settled in Santa Fe, New Mexico, in 1948. This lithograph reached the Smithsonian American Art Museum by transfer from the Evander Childs High School in the Bronx via the General Services Administration, and the museum links it to the Federal Art Project in New York City.
license: SAAM states: public domain (free of copyright restrictions)
collection: Smithsonian American Art Museum, Washington, D.C.

title: Cats
image_credit: Public domain per Smithsonian American Art Museum (Gift of the Harmon Foundation); image from ids.si.edu.
description: Quick pencil studies fill a half-sheet of cream paper. At upper left a cat sits hunched with its forepaws drawn in, brows knitted in a frown. Lower right, a second cat curls up with its head tucked into its chest, drawn in a few loose loops. A third animal is cut off by the top edge of the sheet, just a tail and a haunch, as if the artist ran out of paper before the cat ran out of poses. Under the first cat is a handwritten dedication and the signature 'C. Voll'.
context: Dried bread was Christoph Voll's first sculpting material: according to Voll himself, he made drawings and small sculptures from it while living in orphanages as a child. He grew up to be a German sculptor and graphic artist tied to Expressionism and the Dresdner Sezession, and died in Karlsruhe in 1939. SAAM dates the sheet only to about 1930 to 1938 and records it as a gift of the Harmon Foundation.
collection: Smithsonian American Art Museum, Washington, D.C.

title: Mr and Mrs Clark and Percy
title_eng: Mr and Mrs Clark and Percy
title_original: Mr and Mrs Clark and Percy
image_credit: © David Hockney / Tate. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from media.tate.org.uk and is not stored on this site.
description: Two fashionable newlyweds frame a tall open window in their Notting Hill bedroom, near life size. Celia Birtwell stands on the left in a dark dress with a hand on her hip; Ossie Clark lounges on a chrome-and-cane chair on the right, bare feet sunk in a shag rug, cigarette in hand. The cat is a small white shape on Clark's lap, just right of the picture's centre. Both humans look straight out at us. The cat does not: it stares through the window at the balcony and the trees beyond, the only figure in the room with something better to look at.
context: The title names a cat that is not even the one in the picture. According to published accounts of the painting, the white cat on Clark's knee was called Blanche, while Percy was another of the couple's cats, and Hockney simply thought Percy made a better title. The composition borrows from Van Eyck's Arnolfini double portrait with the roles flipped: the wife stands, the husband sits. Hockney worked on it from early 1970 to early 1971, and the Friends of the Tate presented it to the gallery in 1971.

title: Wild Cat (from Wild Animals)
submovement: British post-war figurative printmaking (Frink, Wild Animals lithographs, London 1970)
medium: Lithograph on paper, printed in colours
license: © Estate of Elisabeth Frink, all rights reserved
image_credit: © Estate of Elisabeth Frink. All rights reserved, DACS / Tate. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from media.tate.org.uk and is not stored on this site.
description: Caught mid-startle, a tawny cat fills the sheet with nothing else around it. Its back is arched stiffly, the legs are braced, and the tail stands straight up, its tip dabbed in dark brown. The head is turned sharply back over the shoulder, with one yellow-green eye wide open and a flash of white teeth and a pink tongue at the mouth. Loose black strokes mark the stripes along the flank, and the body is a single wash of ochre, left unsharpened at the edges. The pale paper does the work of a background.
context: Fight or flight: that is how the shop text at Tate reads the pose, a cat that "stands with tail erect and legs stiffened, perhaps engaging its fight-or-flight instincts." The lithograph belongs to Frink's 1970 Wild Animals series and reached Tate in 1975 as a gift from Curwen Studio, through the Institute of Contemporary Prints. Frink is better known as a sculptor of horses and men, whose style, the same shop says, generalised form and eliminated detail, and here the cat is likewise one tense shape. The sheet carries her signature at lower right.

title: Cat Catcher
submovement: Roger Ballen's Outland series (South African documentary-theatrical photography, 1990s)
image_credit: © Roger Ballen / Tate. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from media.tate.org.uk and is not stored on this site.
description: A young man in a grubby T-shirt grins at the lens with a tangle of chicken wire pulled down over his head like a ruined helmet. In his other arm, held up at the height of his face, hangs a ginger tabby, its body stretched out full length, forepaws clutching the air and eyes squeezed shut. The man's shadow and the cat's fall hard on a peeling, mottled wall behind them. Nothing else is in the frame. Everything the picture says comes from the pairing of that stiff, dangling animal and the wire cage on the man's head.
context: Paid by the kilogram: that, in Ballen's own telling in an interview with Vice, is how the man in this picture was rewarded for the cats he carried round in a bag. Ballen says he had known him for twenty years and sometimes drove him to the city, where he put the cats on a scale at the witch doctors' houses; at the back, Ballen says, the cats were killed and their ears, paws and fur used for medicine. The photograph, dated 1998, belongs to Ballen's Outland series, made in South Africa.

title: Lynx (from Wild Animals)
submovement: British post-war figurative printmaking (Frink, Wild Animals lithographs, London 1970)
license: © Estate of Elisabeth Frink, all rights reserved
image_credit: © Estate of Elisabeth Frink. All rights reserved, DACS / Tate. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from media.tate.org.uk and is not stored on this site.
description: Walking left across an empty sheet, a pale buff lynx is built from little more than a wash and a few dozen dashes. Short black flecks spot the haunches and the hind legs, longer strokes stripe the shoulder and neck, and a ringed tail ends in a dark tip. The ears carry their tufts, and one orange eye is the only spot of strong colour on the animal. The head is held low and level, the stride unhurried. As in the other prints of the set, there is no ground, no shadow and no landscape, so the animal simply walks through white paper.
context: A lynx is a long way from the horses and men Frink is best known for, yet it belongs to the same 1970 lithograph group, Wild Animals, which Curwen Studio presented to Tate through the Institute of Contemporary Prints in 1975. Frink's reputation rests on bronzes in which, as Tate's shop puts it, she "generalised the form and eliminated the detail." The lithograph does the same in ink: the lynx is a handful of marks, and the marks are enough. Tate gives the image as 520 × 655 mm.

title: Cheetah (from Four Heads of Wild Cats)
submovement: British figurative lithography (Organ, Four Heads of Wild Cats, 1974)
medium: Lithograph on paper, printed in colours
image_credit: © Bryan Organ / Tate. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from media.tate.org.uk and is not stored on this site.
description: Mouth slightly open, a cheetah looks left in profile with its head and spotted chest rising out of bare paper. Behind it sits a flat panel of sandy brown with an arched top edge, brushed with a few dark strokes of dry grass at the right. The face is built from pale buff and thin black lines, including the cheetah's dark tear mark running from eye to mouth. Spots of brown and black scatter down the neck and shoulder and then dissolve into the white sheet below, so the animal seems to be rising out of the paper.
context: A tiger, a lion, a lioness and this cheetah make up the four numbered prints Tate catalogues as Four Heads of Wild Cats, dated 1974, and Curwen Studio presented them through the Institute of Contemporary Prints in 1975. Their maker is far better known as a portrait painter: London's National Portrait Gallery holds sixteen of his portraits, six of them commissioned by its Trustees, and Wikipedia lists royal sitters from Princess Margaret to Prince Philip. The cheetah is the fourth and last of the set, the fastest cat of the four, drawn standing still.

title: Cat and Mouse
license: © The estate of James Lloyd, all rights reserved
image_credit: © The estate of James Lloyd / Tate. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from media.tate.org.uk and is not stored on this site.
description: A big, pinkish-grey cat lies flat along a thin green rail with its chin just over the edge, and its eyes, pale green and unblinking, are fixed on something below. Every hair of the fur and whisker has been drawn in separately against a dark, clipped hedge. Down in the lower right, small and grey, a mouse or rat sits on a post and has not noticed. The artist's signature, J. Lloyd, sits at lower left. The two animals have the whole picture to themselves, one watching from above and the other oblivious below.
context: "I gave it a pinky hue, I never like painting things pure white," Lloyd said of the cat, and of the animal below him: "I put the mouse or rat in entirely imaginary." Both remarks are credited to Tate's catalogue entry, first published in The Tate Gallery: Acquisitions 1968–9. Lloyd, born in Alsager in 1905, painted mostly animals and country landscapes, and Wikipedia calls him the first living self-taught artist to have a painting hung at the Tate. Eric Lister presented this gouache to the gallery in 1968.

title: Cat
submovement: British post-minimal sculptor's drawing and etching (Flanagan, London, 1970s)
license: © The estate of Barry Flanagan, all rights reserved
image_credit: © The estate of Barry Flanagan / Tate. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from media.tate.org.uk and is not stored on this site.
description: Four quick studies of cats share one small plate, each drawn in a single thin, wandering line with no shading. At far left the biggest, a curled-up cat seen from above, takes up most of the height, its ears and tail showing as tiny notches. A rounder, sitting cat fills the middle. Two small heads are crowded at the right, one pricked and one with whiskers streaming sideways. Below the sleeper, in the artist's own handwriting, one word labels the lot: "cat". The paper is left blank and speckled around the lines.
context: The single word "cat" written under the sleeping cat is the artist's own caption, and Tate's record dates the plate 1976 with the impression reprinted around 1983. It came to the museum in 1985, presented by Sue Flanagan, the artist's former wife. Flanagan is best known as a sculptor of leaping bronze hares, and the cat gets the same economy of line, plus a joke about the lettering: nothing in the picture needs the label.

title_eng: Papercut of a Cat Catching a Bird
title: Papercut of a Cat Catching a Bird
medium: Cut paper with small knife incisions
license: Rights holder not identified, all rights reserved
image_credit: © Maker unknown (rights holder not identified) / Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from framemark.vam.ac.uk and is not stored on this site.
description: Every hair on this small pink cat is a nick of the knife, and the nicks make it look like it is bristling. It crouches across the middle of the sheet with its tail swinging down at the right, face turned to a purple-winged bird that has landed at the upper left, right beside its head. Below them a fan of green leaves hangs with pink drop-shaped buds, and little round flowers sit on either side, all pasted on a dark brown mount. The whole sheet is about ten centimetres tall, so the fur is a matter of millimetres.
context: Paper cutting is one of China's oldest folk crafts, made for windows, doors, weddings and festivals, and UNESCO added it to its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2009. This sheet comes from Henan Province and is dated 1965; the V&A does not record who cut it, and holds it as accession FE.276-1992. The V&A's own description is quietly technical: the fur is suggested by small knife incisions, which means the cat is partly drawn by what was taken away. Wikipedia notes that red paper is the usual choice for luck and festivities, so a pink cat with a purple bird is a lively departure.

title_eng: Papercut of a Cat, Coloured with Inks
title: Papercut of a Cat, Coloured with Inks
submovement: Chinese folk papercut (jianzhi) with hand-coloured inks, Sanhe, 1980s
license: Rights holder not identified, all rights reserved
image_credit: © Maker unknown (rights holder not identified) / Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from framemark.vam.ac.uk and is not stored on this site.
description: Spikes of yellow fringe run round this cat from the crown of its head to the tip of its curled tail, as if it had been dipped in sunlight. The face is pink with green eyebrows and blue ears, the body orange, with a blue flower on the chest and a pink spiral on the haunch. A green collar of fur is cut in fine parallel lines. The cat lies sideways but turns its face straight out at the viewer, filling the centre of a dark blue mount.
context: Most Chinese paper cuts are called huā, "flower", according to Wikipedia, so this cat is technically a flower: the word names the pattern, not a plant. The V&A lists it as a paper cutout coloured with inks, made in Sanhe, China, in 1985, with no maker recorded (accession FE.130-1992). The outline and fringe are cut; the colour was added afterwards, which separates it from the single-colour red sheets most people picture. The V&A calls the cat "stylised", and the stylising shows most in the face, where the nose and mouth sit in a pink diamond.

title_eng: Papercut of a Mother Cat with a Kitten Inside
title: Papercut of a Mother Cat with a Kitten Inside
submovement: Shaanxi folk papercut (Luochuan), freehand scissor cutting, 1980s
medium: White paper coloured red on the upper surface, cut freehand with scissors
image_credit: © Lanpang Wang / Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from framemark.vam.ac.uk and is not stored on this site.
description: A red cat grins out of a dark blue mount, ears pricked, cheeks marked with short combed lines and a looped ribbon under its chin. Its round belly is cut open into a window, and inside the window a smaller cat curls up: the kitten the mother is carrying, as the V&A reads it. The cat sits three-quarter on to the viewer with its front legs together and its tail sweeping round behind it. The whole figure is a single red silhouette, with every stripe and curl made by what was cut away.
context: Scissors, not a knife, made this one. The V&A records it as cut freehand from white paper that is red only on the upper face, so the underside shows the paper's own white, and it was made by Lanpang Wang in Luochuan, Shaanxi, in 1985. "Freehand" means no pattern was followed: the shape came straight from the cutter's hands. Wikipedia notes that red is the usual colour because it is tied to luck and festivities, and that paper cuts are used at Chinese New Year, weddings and childbirth, which suits a cat carrying a kitten.

title_eng: Jaguar with Parrot on Tail (Cyrk poster)
title: Jaguar with Parrot on Tail (Cyrk poster)
submovement: Polish School of Posters, Cyrk (circus) series, Warsaw, 1960s–70s
medium: Colour lithograph, printing ink on paper
license: © Hubert Hilscher / estate, all rights reserved
image_credit: © Hubert Hilscher / estate / Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from framemark.vam.ac.uk and is not stored on this site.
description: Green, with brown rosettes ringed in yellow, a jaguar rears one forepaw and snarls up at a scarlet parrot with a turquoise beak. The parrot is perched on the end of the jaguar's own tail, which curls up out of the picture like a branch. The cat takes up the whole lower half of the sheet, mouth open on white teeth and claws out, and the word CYRK runs diagonally in the top left corner of a red-and-black frame. The ground is plain white, so every colour is a flat shape.
context: Poland's State Entertainment Agency (ZPR) began commissioning circus posters in the 1960s, and the V&A stresses that they were never ads for a particular show: they were poster art meant to 'conjure the spirit' of Polish circus. Hilscher was art director of the WAG publishing house from 1961 to 1970, and the V&A calls him one of the most colourful and amusing designers of the Polish School of Posters. This one, dated 1974, is held as S.3797-1995. Wikipedia lists the Cyrk series as a genre of the Polish School that took off in 1962.

title: Cyrk (striped cat poster)
submovement: Polish School of Posters, Cyrk (circus) series, Warsaw, 1970s
license: © Hubert Hilscher / estate, all rights reserved
image_credit: © Hubert Hilscher / estate / Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from framemark.vam.ac.uk and is not stored on this site.
description: Stripes of green, magenta, cyan and black wrap a seated cat from ears to paws, and its pink-and-red tongue hangs out of a green face. White cheeks with a spattered edge frame the mouth, long white whiskers fan out, and the eyes are green rings with red centres. It sits square in the middle of a flat red sheet, claws showing at the bottom, with CYRK chalked in white capitals across the top. The V&A calls it a 'colourfully striped cat holding its tongue out'.
context: A copy of this poster ended up on the cover of John Barnicoat's history of posters, a detail the V&A records from its Granville note. The printed credit line reads 'Poster No. 19, Printed in Poland, Copyright by DESA Foreign Trade Enterprise, Warszawa', which points to a foreign-trade audience as well as a Polish one. The V&A notes that the circus enjoyed a high status as an art form in communist Poland (1946 to 1989), and that Hilscher's posters stay popular for their vivid colours and charming humour. It was accepted in lieu of inheritance tax and allocated to the museum in 2007.

title_eng: Three Can-Can Cats: Cat Puppet (At the Moulin Rouge)
dimensions: Height 33 cm, length 41 cm (control rods about 60 cm)
title: Three Can-Can Cats: Cat Puppet (At the Moulin Rouge)
submovement: Czechoslovak State Puppet Theatre rod-and-feather puppet-making, Prague, 1970s
medium: Knitted and sewn wool with white feathers, rod controls of wood and metal
collection: Victoria and Albert Museum, London (Lanchester Collection)
license: © Marjanka Vrabcova / rights holder, all rights reserved
image_credit: © Marjanka Vrabcova / Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from framemark.vam.ac.uk and is not stored on this site.
description: White wool and white feathers make a cat in mid-leap: a knitted face with a pink nose and a green eye at the left, one arm stretched ahead, then a cloud of feather ruff and a feather tail trailing off to the right. Three thin metal rods drop from its body to wooden crossbars at the bottom, which is how a puppeteer held it. The V&A says it is one of the Can-Can cats in a group called At the Moulin Rouge.
context: Three metal rods and a pair of wooden crossbars are all that hold this cat up. The V&A says it was made by Marjanka Vrabcova of the State Puppet Theatre, Prague, for performances by Richard Gill in 1972, and that the group is in polystyrene, resin, metal and fabric. It reached the museum through the Lanchester Collection: the Lanchester Marionettes, founded in 1936 by Waldo and Muriel Lanchester in Malvern, ran what was said to be the only theatre in Britain used only for marionettes, and George Bernard Shaw's last play was written for them in 1949.

title: Fish Soup
submovement: Post-Soviet Russian illustrated lithography (Staraya Ladoga recipe series)
image_credit: © Tatyana Kozmina / Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from framemark.vam.ac.uk and is not stored on this site.
description: In the lower right corner, in a framed panel of its own, a ginger tabby with green eyes lies over the bones of the fish and gnaws them. The rest of the sheet is a recipe: an old man in a patterned jacket sits at a table in the centre, picking at a small fish, and around him are panels of a couple walking with fishing rods, figures fishing at a lake, a cloth of tiny fish and a bowl of soup. Cyrillic instructions run along every border.
context: The last step of the recipe is addressed to the cat. The V&A translates the closing line as 'give the scraps and heads to the nearest cat', and the print is one of a series that illustrates recipes, this one for ukha, a traditional fish soup. The museum adds that Kozmina lives with her husband in a small wooden house at Staraya Ladoga, on the Volkhov River near Lake Ladoga, and draws on village life. Wikipedia notes that the settlement dates back to the mid-8th century and is sometimes called the first capital of Russia, so this cat eats in old company.

title: Clockwork Tinplate Cat with Ball
submovement: Chinese lithographed tinplate clockwork toys for the home market, 1970s
license: Rights holder not identified, all rights reserved
image_credit: © Maker unknown (rights holder not identified) / Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from framemark.vam.ac.uk and is not stored on this site.
description: Crouched low over a polka-dotted ball, a yellow-and-brown striped tin cat looks down along its own paws. A red ribbon circles its neck, swirled stripes curl round its haunch, and a long thin wire tail trails out behind it. The ball sits between the front paws, green with yellow, pink, red and white spots. Every marking is printed flat on the metal, and the cat's face is a round brown eye and a small mouth, all from the lithograph.
context: A winding key sticks out of the cat's left flank, and the V&A notes that as it moves, the tail swings from side to side, though it adds that this may not be part of the mechanism. The V&A says it is one of a collection of toys picked up by the donor while studying at Peking University in 1978 and 1979, mostly made in China for its own market, and it was given by Clio Whittaker. Wikipedia explains that tin toys are tinplate printed by chromolithography, with spring-driven versions dating from 1850s Germany, so this cat belongs to a long line.

title: Cat and Three Kittens
submovement: Sosaku hanga (creative prints), postwar Tokyo, Ichimokukai circle
medium: Woodblock print, ink and colour on paper
license: © Sekino Jun'ichirō / estate, all rights reserved
image_credit: © Sekino Jun'ichirō / estate / Minneapolis Institute of Art. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from 1.api.artsmia.org and is not stored on this site.
description: A long-haired grey cat with yellow eyes takes up the upper left of a black sheet, her fur laid in flat planes of silver, grey and white. Three kittens crowd round her. One peers over her shoulder at the top right, a ginger-and-brown one with wide yellow eyes sits in the middle, and a third looks out from under her chest at the lower left. In the foreground her white tail sweeps across the bottom like a fan of feathers, and the print is signed in English, 'Jun Sekino'.
context: Aomori, a northern Japanese town, produced both the great printmaker Munakata Shikō and, a generation later, Sekino, who according to Wikipedia was inspired by Munakata from boyhood and often turned to him for advice. By 1960 he was a leading name in sosaku hanga, the 'creative print' movement in which the artist designs and carves the block personally, and he had begun his Tōkaidō series in 1959. Wikipedia credits him with over 400 prints, animals among them. Minneapolis records this sheet as a bequest of Frances H. Graham; the pencil title in the margin reads 'Three Kitten', singular, and the edition number is 29/100.

title_eng: Black Power (Retaliation to Crime: Revolutionary Violence)
title: Black Power (Retaliation to Crime: Revolutionary Violence)
submovement: Cuban revolutionary poster art, OSPAAAL Tricontinental series (Havana, 1960s–70s)
license: © Alfredo Rostgaard / estate, all rights reserved
image_credit: © Alfredo Rostgaard / estate / Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from framemark.vam.ac.uk and is not stored on this site.
description: A panther seen head-on is drawn in a few white lines on black, its jaws opened so wide that the mouth takes up most of the poster. Inside the dark throat, in heavy white capitals, are the words BLACK POWER. Two red ear tips poke up at the top, whisker lines fan from each cheek, and the fangs are long white curves. Below, in Spanish, French, English and Arabic: 'Retaliation to Crime: Revolutionary Violence', next to the OSPAAAL logo.
context: Four languages at the bottom tell you who this was for. OSPAAAL, the Havana organisation of solidarity with the peoples of Asia, Africa and Latin America, was founded after the 1966 Tricontinental Conference and published the magazine Tricontinental. Rostgaard was its artistic director from 1966 to 1975. The V&A holds some 200 OSPAAAL posters, over 50 of them in its Global Africa group, and records this design as widely reproduced, unlike his rare folded origami posters. The big cat here is a panther, the black form of a leopard or jaguar.

title: Big Cat
submovement: American self-taught art, Vinings, Georgia, ballpoint and felt-pen drawing, 1980s
medium: Ballpoint and felt tip pen on paper
collection: Smithsonian American Art Museum, Washington, D.C.
license: © Estate of Nellie Mae Rowe, all rights reserved
image_credit: Nellie Mae Rowe / Smithsonian American Art Museum. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from ids.si.edu and is not stored on this site.
description: A brown cat with a square head, two round dark eyes and a thin blue collar lies sideways across the sheet, its long body covered in overlapping scales of blue, green and brown that look more like a fish than fur. Whiskers are inked on the muzzle. Around it the paper is packed edge to edge: a woman in a blue coat and an orange cap at left, a yellow-faced ram and a blue lamb at top right, a pink sunburst of patterns behind the cat's back, small figures and flowers crowding the bottom. The artist's name is written on the right edge.
context: "Playhouse" was Rowe's name for the house she built with her second husband in 1939, and after he died in 1948 she turned fully to art. Wikipedia notes hybrid creatures in her work, such as a cow-woman or a winged dog, and quotes a scholar saying her multi-figure drawings of 1980 and 1981 leave almost no empty space. Big Cat fits: the scaled body is a creature of her own invention, and the cat is the largest thing in a crowd. She was diagnosed with multiple myeloma in November 1981 and died in October 1982. The Smithsonian bought this sheet in 2021.

title: Tiger Cat II
submovement: American studio woodcut, Ukrainian emigre printmaker, New York 1970s
license: © Estate of Jacques Hnizdovsky, all rights reserved
image_credit: © Estate of Jacques Hnizdovsky / Minneapolis Institute of Art. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from 1.api.artsmia.org and is not stored on this site.
description: Seen from the front, a striped cat crouches so low that its body becomes a round black-and-white oval, like a sea urchin with a face. The head sits at the bottom of the oval, with a small pale nose, long whiskers fanning out on both sides and two front paws tucked beneath the chin. Behind it a long tail rises straight up and curls over at the tip, patterned with leaf-shaped marks. Every stripe is cut as a clean wedge of black against white. The artist has signed and titled the sheet by hand along the bottom margin.
context: Number 242 of 250, signed and titled in pencil along the bottom: that is how the Minneapolis record describes this sheet. Its text says Hnizdovsky reached America in 1949, taught himself printmaking and, on a thin budget, drew plants and animals in New York's zoos and botanical gardens before cutting and printing his woodblocks in his home studio. Wikipedia adds that he printed on washi and that when the Bronx Zoo's orangutan Andy died, the zoo bought one of his woodcuts. The "tiger" in the title is only a tabby: the stripes do the work.

title: Cat in a Window
submovement: British designer tilework, sgraffito decoration on industrial ironstone blanks, 1970s
medium: Dust-pressed red earthenware with painted and sgraffito decoration in colour glazes
image_credit: © Christina Sheppard / Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from framemark.vam.ac.uk and is not stored on this site.
description: On a window-sill at the bottom right of the square, a ginger tabby sleeps curled into a tight loop with its chin on its paws, its tail wrapped under its belly. A pink flowerpot with red-flowered stalks stands on the sill at left. Behind the glazing bars, two green and olive hills rise to a yellow moon or sun, and spotted purple curtains frame the scene on both sides. The lines are scratched dark brown through the glaze. The designer's interlaced "CS" monogram sits in the lower right corner.
context: Scratching a drawing through white glaze to the bare clay below is called sgraffito, and Christina Sheppard described her own method to the V&A in detail: lines first, then red iron oxide sprayed on and brushed off, then colours painted in and a blue or yellow glaze sprayed over everything. Her designs were applied to ready-made blanks from Woolliscroft Ironstone in England. The V&A catalogues this as one of nine tiles she designed around 1970 and 1971, and says the range stayed in production until 1985. She gave the tile to the museum herself.

title: Cats beaker
submovement: British industrial tableware, Hornsea Pottery (East Yorkshire), screen-printed glaze-resist, designed 1969, made 1974
license: © John Clappison / Hornsea Pottery, all rights reserved
image_credit: © John Clappison / Hornsea Pottery / Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from framemark.vam.ac.uk and is not stored on this site.
description: A mustard-yellow cat stands square on to the viewer in the middle of a dark green mug, flat as a cut-out. It has two ringed eyes, a pointed nose, a small dark mouth and a medallion hanging from a collar. Round the side, at the left edge of the view, a second cat leans in towards two startled fish with open mouths. The decoration is screen-printed glaze-resist in brown and dark green over a white earthenware body, which gives it a slight relief, and the mug has a D-shaped handle, a small foot and a glossy glaze.
context: Hornsea Pottery began in 1949 as two brothers' plaster souvenirs for seaside tourists in the East Riding of Yorkshire and went into receivership in 2000. By 1986 the firm was in trouble, and, the V&A records, its chief staff designer John Clappison alone saw the need to save examples of its output, arranging 44 objects as a gift to the museum, kept until then in his garage, cellar and workplace. The record also notes a small piece of vocabulary: "mug" was not used before 1970, and earlier items like this were called beakers.

title: Cats
submovement: British theatrical poster design, Dewynters agency, West End musical, 1981
license: © The Really Useful Company Ltd / Dewynters, all rights reserved
image_credit: © The Really Useful Company Ltd / Dewynters Ltd / Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from framemark.vam.ac.uk and is not stored on this site.
description: Almost the whole sheet is black. Two slanted yellow eyes float in the top third, and if you look into the pupils you find tiny black silhouettes of dancers leaping inside each one. Nothing else of the cat is drawn, so the face is supplied by the viewer. At the bottom, the title CATS is brushed in white capitals, with small print below naming Andrew Lloyd Webber as composer, T. S. Eliot's "Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats" as the source and 30 April 1981 at the New London Theatre as the opening.
context: The poster changed the show's name. According to Wikipedia, producer Cameron Mackintosh hired the agency Dewynters, which after much back-and-forth proposed this pair of eyes; the team loved it but felt the working title, Practical Cats, did not suit the picture, so the musical was shortened to Cats. The V&A calls it one of the posters of the century, and notes that the show ran for 8,949 performances in London, was translated into more than 20 languages, and was the world's longest-running musical until Les Misérables passed it on 8 October 2006.

title: Old Cat
submovement: Contemporary Japanese copperplate etching, made in London at East London Printmakers, 2013
image_credit: © Toshihiko Ikeda / Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from framemark.vam.ac.uk and is not stored on this site.
description: A very small square of copper in the middle of a very large white sheet is all this cat gets, and it fills the space with a snarl. The head is shown in profile, mouth wide open on a row of small teeth, the fur drawn as dense dark grain that thins into pale patches around the cheek and neck, with a rough mottled ground behind. The expression is closer to a grudge than a threat. Below the plate, in pencil, the artist has signed it, numbered it and added the title in Japanese characters.
context: Dot by dot: Ikeda draws the tonal areas of his copper plates with a magnifying glass in one hand and a hand-made Swiss etching needle in the other, according to East London Printmakers, which is why the old cat's fur reads as dense grain. He made this plate for ELP Box '13, a portfolio published by the workshop, which gave a copy to the V&A. His Tokyo gallery records that he spent 2013 in London as an overseas trainee of Japan's Agency for Cultural Affairs, and that he was born in 1980.

title: Cheshire Cat
submovement: American psychedelic poster art, San Francisco (East Totem West), 1967
license: © Joseph McHugh / East Totem West, all rights reserved
image_credit: © Joseph McHugh / East Totem West / Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from framemark.vam.ac.uk and is not stored on this site.
description: A long-haired blue-grey cat reclines in the middle of the sheet with its front paws stretched out and a thick bushy tail drooping down on the right, looking straight out with pink-violet eyes. A glowing yellow-orange contour cuts it out from the background, which is a dense mat of squirming green, blue and magenta foliage on a red ground. Across the top, in wobbling dark blue letters that seem grown from the same vines, runs the line "We're all mad". At the bottom edge, small print gives the title Cheshire Cat.
context: WE'RE ALL MAD, printed across the top, borrows the Cheshire Cat's line to Alice in Wonderland, "we're all mad here". The V&A credits the poster to Joseph McHugh, whose signature is printed at the lower right of the image, and names East Totem West, with Orbit Graphic Arts, as publisher, in California in 1967, the year of San Francisco's Summer of Love. The museum bought this copy through its Julie and Robert Breckman Print Fund. The sheet is 88.9 × 58.6 cm, big enough to hang as a picture rather than a handbill.

title: Fat Cats
submovement: British newspaper editorial illustration, pen and ink, Sunday Telegraph, 1990s
image_credit: © Peter Till / Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from framemark.vam.ac.uk and is not stored on this site.
description: Sitting back in a swivel chair in a dark, empty office, a large striped tabby wears a pin-striped suit, waistcoat and tie, one hand on the armrest and the calm of a winner. A knot of smaller suited cats at the left lunges towards the chair, while a few at the far right scatter across the floor. A second empty chair stands in the background. Everything is built from fine cross-hatching against solid black, with the artist's name signed bottom left and layout notes in red pencil along the bottom.
context: Original artwork for an illustration in the Sunday Telegraph of 12 June 1994, heading an article that began "Amid the chaos, Europe's fat cats...", according to the V&A, and the printer's instructions are still on the sheet. "Fat cat" is itself an old joke: Wikipedia says the term was first used in 1920s America for rich political donors, credited to the journalist Frank Kent, and in Britain it came to mean executives whose pay others think excessive. The V&A's record says the artist gave the drawing himself.

title: Cat in Goldfish Bowl
submovement: British pictorial photography, Royal Photographic Society exhibition circle, 1960s
collection: Victoria and Albert Museum, London (Royal Photographic Society Collection)
image_credit: © Charles Wormald / Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from framemark.vam.ac.uk and is not stored on this site.
description: Furious about it, a striped tabby has somehow got itself into a glass goldfish bowl. Its head is twisted to the right with the mouth open in a snarl and one eye staring, its barred front legs pressed against the glass, while goldfish almost as big as the cat swim around the outside of the bowl, two in front and others at the upper right. That is the joke. The print is a soft grey, with the picture floating in a wide white mount. The V&A gives no account of how the scene was made, so how the cat came to be in the bowl stays a mystery.
context: Founded in 1853, the Royal Photographic Society built up a collection that moved from London to Bath in 1980, was sold to the Science Museum Group for its museum in Bradford in 2002 with help from the National Lottery Heritage Fund and Art Fund, and was transferred to the V&A in 2017. This print carries an RPS.395-2026 number, so it is one of the most recent arrivals. The V&A dates it only to the 1960s, attributes it to Charles Wormald and records a 23.5 × 30 cm image on a 48.5 × 41.8 cm mount.

title: Liggende sort kat
submovement: Danish late-modernist brush-and-ink drawing, Richard Mortensen (Den Frie Udstilling), 1980
medium: Brush and Indian ink on stiff Fabriano paper
collection: SMK – Statens Museum for Kunst, Copenhagen
license: © Richard Mortensen / VISDA, all rights reserved
image_credit: © Richard Mortensen / VISDA / SMK – Statens Museum for Kunst. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from iip.smk.dk and is not stored on this site.
description: One brushful of black ink makes a whole cat. It lies on its side across the sheet with the left front paw lifted up to its face, as if halfway through a wash, while the other front paw reaches forward on the ground. The ears are two sharp points and the eyes and teeth are just small gaps in the black, glinting white. Folds and thin patches in the ink give the body a faint grain, and the long tail trails off at the lower right. The artist has signed and dated the lower left corner "Mortensen 80".
context: Brush, Indian ink and a stiff sheet of Fabriano paper, 484 × 660 mm, are all SMK lists for this drawing, signed in pencil "Mortensen 80". Mortensen helped found the Danish group Linien in the 1930s, and the museum's biography says he made "automatic" ink drawings under the influence of psychoanalytic theory, some finished works in their own right and some raw material for paintings. After seventeen years in France he came home in 1964 as a professor at the Academy and retired in 1980, the year of this sheet.

title: Katten Mule
submovement: Danish late-modernist pen-and-ink drawing, Richard Mortensen (Den Frie Udstilling), 1975
medium: Pen and Indian ink on paper
collection: SMK – Statens Museum for Kunst, Copenhagen
license: © Richard Mortensen / VISDA, all rights reserved
image_credit: © Richard Mortensen / VISDA / SMK – Statens Museum for Kunst. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from iip.smk.dk and is not stored on this site.
description: Mule is drawn with one unhurried line and nothing else. A rounded, heavy shape that fills most of the page is the cat's back and haunches as it hunches over, with the line dipping in at the base to show the folded hind legs and ending in two small front paws at the bottom. At the right a short flick marks the tail. Not a single whisker or eye is shown, and none is missed. At the lower left the artist has written the date, 10 February 1975, and the cat's name, Mule, by hand in ink.
context: The Danish title Katten Mule and the inked note "10/II/75 MuLe." make this the portrait of one named animal on one particular day. SMK records it as pen and Indian ink, 294 × 210 mm, among a large group of Mortensen drawings with an accession date of 2000. Mortensen came home from Paris in 1964 to be a professor at the Academy, married in 1965 and settled at Ejby near Bramsnæsvig, and SMK notes that the monumental works of those years include his 9-metre painting on the My Lai massacre of 1971.

title: Bird and Stripy Cat
submovement: Danish figurative expressionism, Grønningen circle, large acrylic tondo, 1990
dimensions: 249 cm diameter, in a square frame
collection: SMK – Statens Museum for Kunst, Copenhagen
license: © Arne Haugen Sørensen / VISDA, all rights reserved
image_credit: © Arne Haugen Sørensen / VISDA / SMK – Statens Museum for Kunst. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from iip.smk.dk and is not stored on this site.
description: A huge striped cat, banded in grey, black and yellow, curls around the top and left of a round canvas set in a square gold frame. Its tail hooks up at the upper left and its head hangs down over a bird. The bird is blue and pink with a green eye, a long red-pink beak wide open in a scream, and one red wing raised like a hand. The cat's bold stripes cut across the bird's soft brushwork, and green dashes of water or grass run along the bottom.
context: A predator that pursues or attacks its prey in fairy-tale surroundings: that is how the SMK biography sums up the pictures Haugen Sørensen painted from the mid-1970s on, and here the predator is a cat. He settled in France in 1957 and, SMK says, worked in the early 1960s at the Clot et George print workshop alongside Asger Jorn, Matta and Antonio Saura. He moved back to Denmark in 1967 and to Spain in 1981. SMK dates this 249 cm acrylic tondo to 1990 and acquired it in 1991.

title: The Pets
title_original: The Pets (also catalogued as Girl and Pets)
submovement: American Genre Painting (Düsseldorf and Hague-trained domestic realism)
medium: Oil on academy board transferred to hardboard
collection: National Gallery of Art, Washington (Corcoran Collection)
image_credit: National Gallery of Art, Washington, Corcoran Collection (Gift of William Wilson Corcoran). Open Access image (CC0).
description: Hands folded, a girl in a pale dress perches on the edge of a rush-seated chair in a bare, sunlit room, watching a small menagerie. The animals are crowded into the bright corner on the right. A grey kitten sits on top of a wire cage, ears pricked, staring at a goldfish bowl on a glass stand just beside it. Behind them a green parrot waits on a tall perch. Plaster has fallen off the wall to show red beneath, and an empty saucer and a jug sit on the floorboards by her feet. The kitten is small and easy to miss, right of centre, upper half, next to the fishbowl.
context: Washington collector William Wilson Corcoran owned this panel by 1857, when it hung in the first annual exhibition of the Washington Art Association. He gave it to his own Corcoran Gallery in 1869, and it passed to the National Gallery of Art when the Corcoran collection was transferred in 2014. The Eastman Johnson catalogue raisonné files it under children with pets, a stock genre theme, and notes that pets were given to children to encourage responsibility and empathy. Johnson has staged a small drama of appetite: the kitten has eyes only for the fish, and the girl has eyes only for all of them.
feline_symbolism: Domestic predator held in check, watching the goldfish.

title: Le Maraudeur (from Bohémiens de Paris)
submovement: July Monarchy satirical lithography (Le Charivari, Daumier)
image_credit: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam. Public domain (CC0).
description: Tall, thin and top-hatted, a ragged man tiptoes along a cobbled back lane, one arm raised and a finger crooked as if to stroke something. His quarry is a tabby that watches him from a wooden ledge at the top left, head low, ears flat, wondering what the fuss is about. In the right foreground a dog lies flat on the paving. Beneath the picture the caption puts words in the man's mouth: he is the "general contractor of the gibelottes of Paris" (dinners at 32 sous), cooing "minet, minet, come, my rabbit". The cat is top left, on the ledge above the man.
context: A gibelotte is a rabbit stew, so the joke needs no translation: the cheap Paris eating-house, the hungry cook and the neighbourhood cat are all in the caption. The sheet comes from Bohémiens de Paris, a series Daumier drew for the satirical paper Le Charivari around 1841, and the Rijksmuseum catalogues it as a lithograph with letterpress text on the back, 359 by 252 mm. Its Dutch title is "Stroper probeert kat te vangen", a poacher tries to catch a cat. Daumier files the cat under "meat" and the man under "bohemian", a fine bit of social arithmetic.
feline_symbolism: Neighbourhood tabby as prospective stew meat.

title: The Fat Cat (Den tykke kat), drawing no. 6
submovement: Danish storybook illustration, pen-and-ink (Skovgaard circle, Copenhagen, 1910s)
image_credit: Niels Skovgaard, Den tykke kat (KKS6915), Statens Museum for Kunst, Copenhagen. Public domain.
description: Every short stroke of ink on this cat stands up like a bristle, and the stripes wrap around a belly so round that it almost drags on the ground. It sits side-on in the middle of the sheet with its head lowered and its nose pushed into the edge of a long, pale cloak lying on the grass. A shoe sticks out at one end of the cloak and a second at its lower edge, so whoever was inside has just become part of the meal. At right, a leafy little shrub; behind, two thin lines for hills. In pencil at top left someone has noted the title and "no. 6", and the date 25.7.11 is written bottom left.
context: "Den Tykke Kat / No.6" is pencilled at top left, and the date 25.7.11 sits at bottom left beside the artist's monogram, so this is one sheet of a numbered run made in July 1911; SMK acquired it in 1914. The story is the Danish tale of a cat that grows fatter with every creature it swallows, which is how an English picture-book edition from 1971 is described in library catalogues. Niels Skovgaard and his brother Joakim were both introduced to art by their father. Here a bloated cat is all comic menace, and the shoe is the only joke the picture needs.

title: Reclining Cat Flip
image_credit: Rik Wouters, Liggende poes Flip (RP-T-1916-8(R)), Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam, gift of R. Wouters. CC0.
description: Curled up with its head tucked down between its forelegs, the cat takes up most of the lower half of the sheet and is built from very few strokes: a dark saddle of ink across the back, quick hatching under the belly, a thick contour round the head. Nothing is spelled out, no floor, no cushion, only a heavy vertical line at left that stops the picture like a wall. Loose strokes at top right look like branches in a different drawing altogether. Pale traces of other lines show faintly through the paper around the sleeper.
context: Flip is the name the Rijksmuseum gives the animal, and it lists the sheet as a pen drawing in black dated 1915. Wouters, a Belgian sculptor and painter whose manner is compared with that of Matisse and Derain, died in Amsterdam on 11 July 1916, so the sheet dates from the last year or so of his life. A cat asleep is the perfect model for a draughtsman who worked fast: it holds still and settles into shapes that can be caught in a handful of lines. The result looks effortless, which it never is.

title: The Dog Max, the Tortoise Akbar and the Cat Poes
title_eng: The Dog Max, the Tortoise Akbar and the Cat Poes
title_original: Hond Max, schildpad Akbar en de kat Poes
submovement: Dutch Art Nouveau-influenced pen-and-brush graphic art (The Hague, 1910s)
medium: Pen and brush in black over pencil, corrections in white opaque paint
image_credit: Julie de Graag, Hond Max, schildpad Akbar en de kat Poes (RP-T-1927-88), Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam, gift of M.J. de Graag. CC0.
description: Three household animals are cut out of black like a miniature bookplate: a dog lying in profile with head raised, a tortoise walking at lower left, and, upper right, the cat, seated upright with her tail looped round her feet. The cat has a pale body, a dark mask and two big eyes that look straight out at us while the dog looks away. Each animal carries a hand-lettered name beside it, MAX, AKBAR and POES. A thin white line frames the black field; "VOOR ELSJE" runs across the top, with the year 1916 at upper left and the monogram A.J.D.G. at upper right.
context: At 77 × 123 mm the drawing is smaller than a postcard. The Rijksmuseum describes it as pen and brush in black over pencil, with corrections in white opaque paint, and notes the inscription "For Elsje" and the number 35 written on the front, which suggests one of a numbered run. "Poes" is simply Dutch for puss, so the cat has a name like a label. De Graag, born in Gorinchem in 1877, died in The Hague on 2 February 1924, only eight years after this sheet. Whoever Elsje was, she received a very small pet portrait gallery.

title: Walking Panther
submovement: Paris animalier bronze sculpture (Bugatti, cast by A. A. Hébrard)
image_credit: Rembrandt Bugatti, Walking Panther, 1903, Cleveland Museum of Art, gift of Mr. and Mrs. Noah L. Butkin (1977.132). CC0.
description: Head low, shoulders rolled forward and tail trailing behind in a long curve, the panther is caught in mid-stride with its weight on the near foreleg and the far hind paw just lifting. The surface is not smoothed: the bronze keeps ridges and pinched folds across the flank, so the skin seems to slide over the muscle. The animal walks along a thin, flat base that rests on a slab of green-veined marble. At right, the lowered head points the way, and the eyes are little more than pits in the face.
context: Panthers were among the first wild animals Bugatti modelled after meeting them at the Jardin des Plantes, the zoo in Paris, as Cleveland's label puts it. The record gives the signature R. Bugatti and the stamp of A. A. Hébrard, the founder who cast his work. Bugatti was 31 when he took his own life in Paris on 8 January 1916, after volunteering for paramedical work at a military hospital in Antwerp. A panther is no house cat, but the low, loose-shouldered walk is one any tabby on a garden wall would recognise.

title: Book of Hours, W.102: Tilbert the Cat Carries Reynard's Bier (fol. 77r)
title_eng: Book of Hours (Walters W.102), fol. 77r: cat carrying a bier
submovement: English Gothic Book of Hours Marginalia (Funeral of Reynard the Fox cycle)
medium: Ink and pigments on medium-weight parchment
dimensions: Not given on the Walters object page
image_credit: The Walters Art Museum, Baltimore (CC0). Image loads from the Walters website.
description: Along the foot of the page, a pale cat in a striped tunic walks upright with the front poles of a stretcher over its shoulders. A blue cloth hangs from the poles at the far left edge, and the rest of the bier runs off the page, so the cat is the only bearer you can see. Look at the bottom left, under the heavy Latin text and its big blue initial: the cat's tall ears and pointed muzzle stand out against bare parchment. It treads on a small tuft of green ground, and the whole scene takes up barely a thumb's width.
context: Reynard the Fox is dead, or pretending to be, and the margins of W.102 give him a funeral procession. The Walters says its Hours of Christ Crucified are graced with that funeral, and the museum's image captions, as repeated by bloggers, name the cat here as Tilbert, carrying the front of the fox's bier. The Walters catalogue also notes that the leaf's artist is the same hand found in a Bodleian Bible and a Cambridge psalter, so a book with serious devotional credentials hid this joke in its lower margins.

title: 25 Cats Name Sam and One Blue Pussy (Purple Sam)
medium: Offset lithograph with hand-coloring in Dr. Ph. Martin's aniline watercolor on Strathmore paper
license: © The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, all rights reserved
description: Striped in Warhol's wobbly, broken ink line, a pink-purple cat lies across the sheet with its tail curling under, printed by offset lithography and then washed by hand with transparent colour that wanders happily outside the outlines. Its eyes are narrowed and its whiskers splay like stray pen marks. No two copies are coloured quite alike, because friends did much of the painting. The pages are small, about 23 by 15 cm. Read the title lettering at top: it is in the looping hand of Warhol's mother, Julia Warhola, who left the 'd' off 'Named', and her son liked the mistake enough to keep it.
context: Mid-1950s New York is where Warhol made this book (usually dated 1954) as a privately printed promotion for himself as an illustrator. His friend Charles Lisanby supplied the title, which is also the only text, and said some drawings came from a book of cat photographs he owned. The edition was planned at 190 numbered copies; Warhol and friends coloured the lithographs by hand, and most copies went out as gifts to clients. Fun fact: copy no. 4, inscribed to the Bonwit Teller executive Geraldine Stutz, served as the model for the 1987 and 1988 facsimiles, boxed with Julia Warhola's own book Holy Cats.
title_eng: 25 Cats Name Sam and One Blue Pussy (Purple Sam)
title_original: 25 Cats Name Sam and One Blue Pussy
submovement: New York commercial illustration (pre-Pop Warhol artist's book)
image_credit: © The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from upload.wikimedia.org and is not stored on this site.
